It is typically determined based on historical actual sales data (such as sales from previous years) or set target values, serving as the original input value or reference benchmark for subsequent calculations (e.g., target labor costs).

Base period profit refers to the profit amount from the previous accounting period (typically the previous year or quarter) used as a comparative benchmark. It is a raw data point directly obtained from historical financial statements, employed to calculate financial metrics such as growth rates and operating leverage coefficients, in order to assess changes in current performance relative to the historical benchmark.

Base period commodity price refers to the original market price of goods or services during a specific historical period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison when calculating economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It is a fundamental observed value used directly in subsequent calculations, rather than a result derived from other financial indicators.

Base period quantity of goods refers to the sales or consumption quantity of a specific commodity during the period (base period) used as a comparative benchmark in statistical or financial analysis. It is a fundamental historical data point, typically derived directly from past sales records or statistical reports, and is used for comparison with data from subsequent periods (reporting period or current period) to measure changes.

term_en.name: Base Period Urban Household Total Income

chinese: 城镇居民家庭总收入（基期）
english: Base Period Urban Household Total Income

definition_en: Base Period Urban Household Total Income refers to the sum of all income received by members living together in an urban household during a specific reference period (base period) used as a benchmark in statistical surveys. It is directly calculated by aggregating four components: wage income, business income, property income, and transfer income, serving as the fundamental raw data for deriving indicators such as disposable income.

term_en.name: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure

english: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure

definition_en: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure refers to the total sum of direct, original costs incurred by a household during a specific reference period (the base period) for engaging in sideline production activities such as agriculture, handicrafts, and small-scale commerce, which are not the primary occupation. These expenditures represent essential foundational cash or resource consumption necessary for sideline production, typically not derivable from other financial metrics and must be recorded directly upon occurrence.

Base Period Total Household Income refers to the sum of all income received by all family members living together during a specific period (the base period) that serves as the benchmark for comparison in household income surveys. It is typically derived by directly aggregating wage income, business income, property income, and transfer income, and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating derived indicators such as base period disposable income.

Base period wage income refers to the aggregate original data of all wage income earned by individuals or groups during the period selected as the benchmark (base period) in statistical analysis or financial comparison. It typically includes time wages, piece-rate wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies, serving as the foundational input data for calculating derived indicators such as average wages and wage growth rates.

Base Period Total Shares Outstanding refers to the total number of all shares issued and outstanding by a company on a specific benchmark date selected for calculating or comparing financial metrics. This data is typically sourced directly from the company's share capital structure announcements or business registration information, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating indicators such as base period total market capitalization.

Base Period Total Expenditure refers to the aggregate sum of all costs and expenses actually incurred by an enterprise or project during a historical period designated as the benchmark for comparison (i.e., the base period). It is typically derived directly from the summarized data in historical financial statements (such as cost and expense budget reports) and serves as the foundational raw data for subsequent financial analysis and budget preparation.

term_en.name: Total Assets at the End of Base Period

english: Total Assets at Base Period End

definition_en: Total assets at the end of the base period refer to the total value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the conclusion of a specific reference period (the base period) used for comparative purposes. It is typically derived from the balance sheet at the end of the base period and serves as the foundational raw data for calculating dynamic indicators such as asset growth rate.

Base period operating liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities directly related to daily business operations held by an enterprise at the end of a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark in financial forecasting or analysis. It typically includes items such as accounts payable, advance receipts, employee compensation payable, and taxes payable, and serves as a fundamental data point on the balance sheet that can be directly obtained from the base period's financial statements.

Base period stock price refers to the market price of a stock on a specific benchmark date (base period) selected for calculating stock indices, conducting financial analysis, or valuation. It is a fundamental data point directly obtained from market transactions, typically serving as the starting point for comparing and calculating subsequent stock price movements or changes in market capitalization.

Base period revenue refers to the total operating revenue from a specific historical accounting period selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis. It is an original financial figure, typically taken directly from the income statement of that historical period, and is used to compare with the operating revenue of subsequent periods (such as the current period or planning period) to analyze growth or changes.

Base period bookkeeping subsidy refers to the amount initially recognized and recorded for government grants received during a specific accounting period (typically the starting period used as a comparative benchmark). It reflects the original book value or balance of the grant in the base period and serves as fundamental data for subsequent accounting treatment and financial analysis.

english: Net Property Income in Base Period

definition_en: Base period property net income refers to the net income earned by an individual or household from owned properties (such as deposits, stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.) during a specific reference period (the base period). It typically equals total property income minus related costs and expenses such as taxes, interest, and maintenance. It is an important component in calculating base period disposable income.

The Basic Deduction is a fixed deduction standard stipulated in China's Individual Income Tax Law. It is used to deduct a fixed amount from an individual's comprehensive income, such as wages and salaries, when calculating taxable income, in order to safeguard taxpayers' basic living needs. The current standard is RMB 5,000 per month, totaling RMB 60,000 annually.

Basic share capital refers to the total par value or stated value of ordinary shares actually issued by a company and for which shareholder contributions have been received. It constitutes the most fundamental part of a company's shareholders' equity and directly reflects the initial capital scale of the company.

The Value-Added Tax rate is the statutory percentage stipulated by national tax laws, used to calculate the amount of Value-Added Tax payable by taxpayers on the sale of goods, labor, services, intangible assets, or real estate. It serves as the fundamental raw data for VAT calculation and cannot be derived from other financial indicators.

term_en.name: Net Cash Received from Disposal of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units

chinese: 处置子公司收到的现金净额
处置营业单位现金净流入
english: Net Cash Received from Disposal of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units
Net Cash Inflow from Disposal of Subsidiaries

definition_en: Net cash received from disposal of subsidiaries and other business units is an item reported in the investing activities section of the statement of cash flows. It reflects the net cash inflow ultimately obtained from a specific transaction involving the sale or transfer of a subsidiary or other business unit (such as a branch or business line), calculated as the total cash actually received minus related expenses paid to complete the disposal (e.g., intermediary fees, taxes) and minus the cash and cash equivalents held by the disposed unit itself. If the calculation results in a negative amount (i.e., a net outflow), it is reported in other investing activities cash outflows on the statement of cash flows.

Disposal costs refer to the various expenses directly incurred and specifically attributable to the disposal of long-term assets such as fixed assets during the disposal process, including asset cleanup fees, transportation fees, dismantling fees, and related taxes. These costs constitute an important component of the total cost of asset disposal and are typically recorded based on actual payment vouchers rather than calculated through formulas.

english: Number of Compounding Periods per Year

definition_en: Compounding frequency refers to the number of times within a year that interest is calculated and added to the principal for subsequent interest accrual. It determines the frequency of compound growth and is a key parameter in compound interest calculations.

Foreign Exchange RMB Parity refers to the base exchange rate data directly quoted by banks based on factors such as market supply and demand, international exchange rates, and national policies. It indicates how much Renminbi can be exchanged for a unit of foreign currency (e.g., 1 US dollar or 100 units of foreign currency) and serves as the original reference price for foreign exchange transactions and settlements.

term_en.name: Change in Underlying Spot Exchange Rate of Foreign Exchange Options

definition_en: Refers to the numerical increase or decrease in the spot exchange rate (real-time trading price in the spot market) of a foreign currency against the domestic currency, which serves as the underlying asset of a foreign exchange option, over a period of time. This change is the fundamental data directly observed or obtained from the market and directly affects the value of the foreign exchange option, particularly its Delta.

english: Change in Foreign Exchange Option Premium

definition_en: Foreign exchange option premium variation refers to the upward or downward fluctuation of the market price (i.e., the option premium or premium) of a foreign exchange option contract over time. This variation results from the combined effects of various factors such as market supply and demand, underlying exchange rates, volatility, and time to expiration. It is directly observed market data rather than derived from formula calculations.

term_en.name: Purchased Raw Materials, Fuel, and Power Costs

chinese: 外购原材料燃料动力成本
english: Purchased Raw Materials, Fuel and Power Costs
Cost of Purchased Materials, Fuel and Power

definition_en: Purchased raw materials, fuel, and power costs refer to the expenses paid by an enterprise to external suppliers for acquiring raw materials, fuel (such as coal, petroleum), and power (such as electricity, steam) required for production and operational activities. These costs constitute fundamental original data in cost estimation and accounting, typically confirmed directly based on supporting documents such as procurement contracts and invoices.

Purchased service expenses refer to direct expenditures incurred by an enterprise for purchasing various services (such as consulting, technical, logistics, maintenance, etc.) from external suppliers to meet production, operational, or management needs. These expenses are typically recognized based on purchase invoices or contract amounts and constitute fundamental source data for enterprise costs or expenses.

Purchased goods cost refers to the direct costs incurred by an enterprise for acquiring raw materials, merchandise, components, and other goods used in production or sales, serving as fundamental source data for product or service costing.

Day count basis is a standardized convention in financial markets for calculating the number of days in an interest or investment return accrual period. It specifies how to determine the actual number of days in an accrual period (such as a month or a year) and serves as a fundamental parameter for determining interest amounts.

Consignment goods refer to merchandise delivered by an enterprise (the consignor) to another entity or individual (the consignee) for sale, while ownership of the goods remains with the consignor and constitutes part of the consignor's inventory.

Consigned processing materials refer to raw materials, semi-finished goods, or other materials owned by an enterprise that are entrusted to an external party for processing to produce inventory with new characteristics or uses. Their recorded cost primarily includes the actual cost of the materials issued, processing fees paid to the processor, round-trip transportation and miscellaneous expenses, and related taxes.

chinese: 子公司年初未分配利润
子公司未分配利润年初数

definition_en: Subsidiary's opening retained earnings refers to the amount of retained earnings directly taken from the subsidiary's individual balance sheet at the end of the previous period when preparing consolidated financial statements. It represents the portion of the subsidiary's accumulated net profit that has not been distributed to shareholders (including the parent company and minority shareholders) at the close of the prior accounting period, and serves as the starting point data for calculating consolidated retained earnings when preparing the current period's consolidated statements.

term_en.name: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Period

english: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Period

definition_en: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Period refers to the final operating result generated by a subsidiary through its independent business activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year), which is the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes from revenue. It is the final result on the subsidiary's income statement and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating consolidated indicators such as the parent company's net profit and net profit attributable to the parent company's shareholders.

Subsidiary's current period dividend distribution refers to the specific action in which a subsidiary, during the current accounting period, decides to distribute cash dividends or stock dividends to its shareholders (including the parent company and other minority shareholders) according to the profit distribution plan approved by its board of directors or shareholders' meeting. This is an occurred economic transaction in the profit distribution process, directly affecting the subsidiary's retained earnings and liabilities (such as dividends payable).

term_en.name: Subsidiary Current Period Income Tax Expense

chinese: 子公司当期所得税费用

definition_en: Subsidiary current period income tax expense refers to the amount of income tax calculated in accordance with tax laws, recognized in the subsidiary's current period income statement as an independent legal entity, and payable. It reflects the income tax liability arising from the subsidiary's current operating activities.

Deposit term refers to the length of time agreed between the depositor and a financial institution (such as a bank) during which the deposited funds remain fixed and unavailable for withdrawal. It serves as the fundamental time parameter for calculating deposit interest. It is typically expressed in days, months, or years, directly derived from the start and end dates specified in the deposit contract or a pre-agreed fixed number of days/years.

Beginning inventory value refers to the book value of all inventory (including raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods) held by a company and available for use or sale at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is directly equal to the ending inventory balance from the previous accounting period and serves as the base data for calculating inventory changes and costs during the current period.

english: Inventory at the End of Period

definition_en: Ending inventory value refers to the book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) when preparing the balance sheet, measured according to accounting standards (such as the lower of cost or net realizable value method) and ready for presentation. It reflects the asset value of inventory at the end of the period.

Finished goods output refers to the actual physical quantity of finished products that have completed all processing procedures, met predetermined quality standards, and undergone warehousing formalities during a specific accounting period. It is a fundamental data point obtained through direct inventory counting or production statistics, serving as a crucial basis for cost accounting (such as the equivalent units method) and inventory management.

Paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually received from shareholders, reflecting the funds that shareholders have actually contributed. It represents the paid-up portion of the company's registered capital and is a significant component of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.

The Paid-in Capital Eligible Portion refers to the capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise and already credited to the account. This portion of capital forms the foundation of the enterprise's owner's equity, reflects the actual capital contribution by shareholders, and serves as a crucial component in calculating regulatory capital such as Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1).

Increase in Paid-in Capital refers to the increment in the book value of the 'Paid-in Capital (or Share Capital)' account on a company's balance sheet during a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year). It reflects the actual increase in capital received by the company through means such as new investments from investors, or the conversion of capital reserves or surplus reserves into capital.

Beginning balance of paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by investors at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It serves as the starting point for accounting records, typically carried forward from the ending balance of the previous period or determined directly based on actual business transactions.

Actual Annual Cost of Funds refers to the total expenses actually paid by a company to its fund providers within a fiscal year for utilizing externally raised capital (such as loans, bonds, equity financing, etc.), primarily including interest, dividends, and similar payments. These expenses, typically obtainable directly from loan agreements, payment vouchers, or financial statements, serve as fundamental raw data for calculating metrics like the cost of capital and effective annual interest rate.

In the field of finance and accounting, 'Actual Time' typically refers to the raw, unadjusted time point or period used as a calculation basis. For example, in attendance management, it refers to employees' clock-in and clock-out times; in accounting treatment, it refers to a defined accounting period. It serves as the fundamental input data for calculating derived metrics such as work hours, attendance rates, and depreciation, and is not itself calculated from other financial indicators.

Actual production time refers to the direct labor hours or machine operating hours actually consumed during the production process to complete a specific quantity of products. It serves as fundamental raw data in cost accounting, used for allocating manufacturing overhead, calculating production efficiency, and conducting cost variance analysis.

Household sideline production expenditure refers to various direct costs incurred by households in the process of engaging in sideline production activities (such as household handicrafts, small-scale planting and breeding, online part-time work, etc.) to generate income. These expenditures constitute the fundamental raw data for calculating household net income and typically include expenses directly related to sideline activities, such as raw material procurement, tool and equipment depreciation, venue rental, utilities, etc.

Allowance rate measures the proportion of additional time allocated within standard working hours to account for factors such as employee physiological needs, fatigue recovery, and management requirements. It reflects the degree of compensation for non-productive but necessary time consumption when establishing standard working hours.

External claims refer to the rights held by an economic entity (such as a country, enterprise, or financial institution) against non-resident entities abroad, entitling it to future payments of currency or provision of goods/services. They represent a country's or unit's external financial assets and constitute a key component of the international investment position.

External processing fee revenue refers to the income generated by an enterprise from providing processing, assembly, repair, or other services to external entities under commission, for which processing fees are charged as agreed. In accounting, this revenue is typically recorded under 'Main Business Revenue' or 'Other Business Revenue' accounts based on the nature of the operations.

Corresponding capital deductions refer to the specific set of items that, according to regulatory requirements (such as the 'Capital Management Measures'), must be directly deducted from the total capital (e.g., Common Equity Tier 1 capital, Tier 1 capital, or Total capital) when calculating a commercial bank's capital adequacy ratio. These items typically include goodwill, other intangible assets, unconsolidated investments, etc., whose value is not recognized as eligible regulatory capital.

Corresponding Project Sales Revenue refers to the total revenue amount obtained by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services within a specific business project or product line. It is typically calculated directly by multiplying the sales volume of the project by the unit selling price, serving as fundamental financial data that reflects the market performance and business scale of the project.

chinese: 上年度与本年度销售收入

definition_en: Comparative annual sales revenue refers to the side-by-side presentation of a company's sales revenue data for two consecutive fiscal years (typically the previous year and the current year), providing a clear visual representation of the year-on-year changes in sales revenue. It serves as fundamental raw data in financial statements, used for subsequent calculations of absolute changes and percentage changes.

The minority interest ratio refers to the proportion of shares held by non-controlling shareholders (i.e., minority shareholders) to the total share capital of a company (typically a subsidiary consolidated in the parent company's financial statements). It is a fundamental metric derived directly from the company's ownership structure, reflecting the minority shareholders' ownership stake in the company.

Remaining useful life refers to the estimated remaining period during which a fixed asset is expected to continue providing economic benefits to the enterprise after the assessment date. It is a key parameter estimated based on the asset's total estimated useful life and the years already used, primarily employed in calculating fixed asset depreciation.

Construction in Progress is a cost accounting account used in construction enterprise accounting to record all contract costs and contract gross profits incurred from the commencement to the completion of a specific construction contract. Its ending balance reflects the accumulated costs and gross profits of projects that are either not yet completed or completed but not yet settled, and it constitutes a significant component of the 'Inventory' item on the balance sheet.

Construction materials refer to the value of various materials specifically reserved by an enterprise for fixed asset construction, installation, and other projects in progress, including materials for engineering, equipment not yet installed, and tools and instruments prepared for production.

Project settlement refers to the revenue recognized by a construction enterprise when settling the project payment with the client (owner) upon project completion or reaching specific milestones, as stipulated in the contract. It constitutes the primary source of operating revenue for construction enterprises and reflects the value of completed or finished projects.

english: Tax and Surcharges on Project Settlement

definition_en: Construction Settlement Taxes and Surcharges refer to the collective term for various taxes and fees that construction industry enterprises are required to pay and record in the current period's profit or loss according to relevant tax regulations when settling construction projects. These mainly include Business Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, and Education Surcharge, but exclude Value-Added Tax.

Salaries and benefits refer to the total compensation directly recorded and paid by an enterprise to its employees based on employment contracts, attendance, performance, etc. They constitute the fundamental raw data for payroll accounting and typically include base salary, bonuses, allowances, social insurance, housing provident fund, and various subsidies.

Wage income refers to the basic monetary compensation received by an individual for providing labor services through employment or engagement with a specific entity or organization. It typically includes wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increments, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other earnings related to employment or engagement, constituting a significant component of an individual's disposable income.

Wage and salary income amount refers to the total sum of all monetary income received by an individual due to employment or appointment, including wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other income related to employment or appointment. It serves as the original starting point data for calculating the taxable income for individual income tax.

Number of Common Shares Outstanding refers to the total quantity of common stock shares that a company has issued and are held by investors in the public market. It includes shares traded on the open market and those held by company insiders (such as executives and employees), but excludes treasury shares repurchased and held by the company itself. This figure serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as Earnings Per Share and Dividends Per Share.

Issued shares refer to the total number of shares that a company has issued and registered in the names of shareholders (including public investors, company insiders, etc.) since its establishment, through methods such as initial public offerings and additional share issuances. It reflects the company's total share capital scale and serves as fundamental data for analyzing the company's capital structure, market capitalization, and per-share metrics.

Capital repaid refers to the action and its corresponding accounting record where a company returns part or all of the received shareholder-invested capital (paid-in capital) to shareholders in accordance with legal procedures or shareholder agreements. This typically occurs during capital reduction, shareholder exit, or specific capital structure adjustments, directly resulting in a decrease in the company's paid-in capital account.

Completed contract work volume refers to the cumulative total of the actual completed engineering quantity or output value by an enterprise at a specific point in time, based on construction contracts or similar business contracts. It is fundamental operational data obtained through on-site direct measurement, statistics, or engineering progress reports, used to measure the progress of contract execution.

Number of Advancing Issues refers to the total count of listed company stocks whose closing price on a specific trading day (typically the current day) is higher than their closing price on the previous trading day. It is one of the fundamental trading data points reflecting overall market performance and investor sentiment.

chinese: 股票市场上市公司总数

definition_en: Total Number of Listed Companies, also known as the number of listed companies, refers to the total count of all companies listed on a specific stock market (e.g., Shanghai Stock Exchange, Shenzhen Stock Exchange). It is a fundamental statistical aggregate data point that reflects the scale and breadth of the market.

Market index historical return rate refers to the investment return rate calculated by analyzing the point changes of a specific market index (such as the Shanghai Composite Index or S&P 500 Index) over a past period (e.g., one year, five years, or ten years). It reflects the average performance of the overall market or specific sectors during historical periods and serves as fundamental data for evaluating market trends and conducting investment analysis.

Market index return refers to the investment return rate of the overall market or a specific sector over a corresponding period, calculated by comparing the price changes of a specific market index (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, CSI 300 Index, etc.) at two different points in time. It is a fundamental indicator for measuring overall market performance and is commonly used as a benchmark for evaluating the relative performance of individual stocks or investment portfolios.

Market index daily return refers to the percentage reflecting the overall price movement amplitude of a specific stock market (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, Shenzhen Component Index, etc.) within a single trading day. It is typically calculated by comparing the index's closing price on the current day with that of the previous trading day, serving as a fundamental indicator for measuring short-term market performance and volatility.

Market Index Opening Value refers to the original numerical value of a market index at the selected starting point when calculating market performance over a specific period (such as an accounting period or an investment cycle). It is typically directly published by stock exchanges or professional index compilers (e.g., China Securities Index Co., Ltd., Shenzhen Securities Information Co., Ltd.) and serves as the benchmark starting point for measuring market fluctuations during that period.

Market Index Closing Value refers to the raw point or price figure obtained directly from securities market trading data at the end of a specific reporting period (such as a trading day, month, or year), reflecting the overall price level of a specific stock portfolio. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating metrics such as market returns.

A market return series refers to a sequence of return data calculated from the price data of a market index (such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) at consecutive time points using specific methods (such as percentage return or logarithmic return), arranged in chronological order. It is one of the most fundamental time series data in financial modeling, risk analysis, and asset pricing.

english: Count of Market Yield Data Points

definition_en: Number of Market Return Observations refers to the total count of market return data points obtained through actual observation or data collection within a specific time period (such as a day, a month, or a year). It is a fundamental statistical measure that reflects the size of the data sample used for analyzing market returns.

Average liabilities refer to the average level of a company's total liabilities over a specific accounting period (typically a reporting period, such as one year). It is commonly calculated by adding the total liabilities at the beginning of the period to the total liabilities at the end of the period and dividing by two, which smooths out fluctuations in data at a single point in time. It serves as a fundamental metric for calculating other financial ratios, such as the average debt-to-assets ratio.

term_en.name: Number of Compounding Periods per Year

english: Number of Compounding Periods per Year

definition_en: Number of compounding periods per year refers to the frequency with which interest is compounded on a financial asset or liability within one year. It is a predetermined base parameter, such as 12 for monthly compounding or 4 for quarterly compounding, used to convert the nominal annual interest rate into the periodic interest rate or the effective annual interest rate.

Beginning inventory refers to the book value or cost amount of all inventory held by an enterprise at the start of the current accounting year (i.e., at the end of the previous accounting year). It is a fundamental data point on the balance sheet, reflecting the inventory balance determined through accounting records and physical counts at the end of the previous accounting period, and serves as the basis for calculating inventory changes and costs for the current period.

term_en.name: Paid-in Capital at Beginning of Year

english: Paid-in Capital at the Beginning of the Year

definition_en: Paid-in capital at the beginning of the year refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1st), in accordance with laws or the company's articles of association. It includes various forms of contributions such as cash, physical assets, intellectual property rights, and land use rights. It is a point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, reflecting the enterprise's capital base at the beginning of the year.

Beginning retained earnings refers to the cumulative balance of net profit carried forward from the previous accounting period at the start of the current fiscal year, which has not yet been distributed to shareholders or allocated for other specific purposes. It represents the portion of past operating results retained by the enterprise and is a significant component of owners' equity.

chinese: 年初留存收益（盈余公积部分）

definition_en: Beginning balance of surplus reserve refers to the cumulative balance of surplus reserve carried forward from the previous year's balance sheet at the start of each accounting year. It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the portion of retained earnings, earmarked for specific purposes, that the enterprise has accumulated through profit appropriations from prior years up to the beginning of the year. It is a fundamental financial datum and cannot be derived from the current period's profits.

term_en.name: Total Liabilities at Beginning of Year

english: Total Liabilities at the Beginning of the Year

definition_en: Total liabilities at the beginning of the year refers to the aggregate book value of all debts and obligations assumed by an enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1st). It is directly sourced from the balance sheet and serves as fundamental data reflecting the initial state of the enterprise's financial structure.

english: Carrying Value at the Beginning of the Year

definition_en: Beginning net book value refers to the book value of an asset on the first day of a fiscal year, which equals the historical cost of the asset minus the accumulated depreciation or amortization up to the end of the previous year. This figure is typically obtained directly from the balance sheet of the prior year.

term_en.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Year

english: Total Assets at the Beginning of the Year

definition_en: Total assets at the beginning of the year refer to the sum of the book values of all asset items presented on the balance sheet at the start of an accounting year (typically January 1st). It is a point-in-time figure directly taken from the opening balances in the company's books, reflecting the financial position and resource scale at the commencement of the fiscal year.

term_en.name: Capital Surplus at Beginning of Year

english: Capital Surplus at the Beginning of the Year

definition_en: Capital surplus at the beginning of the year refers to the balance of the 'capital surplus' account under the owner's equity section in the balance sheet at the start of each fiscal year (typically January 1). It reflects the cumulative surplus amount at the beginning of the year, formed by investors' contributions exceeding their share in the registered capital (such as share premium), as well as gains and losses directly recognized in owner's equity.

Annual interest refers to the amount of interest generated over a one-year period based on the principal of a loan or deposit and the agreed annual interest rate. It serves as fundamental data for calculating borrowing costs or investment returns.

The Annual Interest Rate (Simple Interest) is the base rate specified in a loan or investment contract, used to calculate interest under the simple interest method. It is applied directly to the principal amount, without considering the reinvestment of interest or compounding effects, serving as the original parameter for interest calculation.

Annual bad debt amount refers to the total amount of accounts receivable that a company ultimately confirms as losses within a fiscal year due to customers' inability to repay. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as the bad debt ratio.

Annual Cost of Goods Sold refers to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise within one year for selling goods or providing services, primarily including direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. It reflects the direct consumption of the enterprise's core business operations and is a key item on the income statement.

term_en.name: Total Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Year-End

chinese: 年末发行在外普通股总数
english: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Year-End

definition_en: Total number of common shares outstanding at year-end refers to the aggregate quantity of common stock actually issued and held by shareholders at the conclusion of each fiscal year (i.e., December 31 or the company's designated fiscal year-end date). This figure forms the foundation of a company's capital structure, is directly obtained from the company's shareholder register or capital stock records, and reflects the scale of equity at a specific point in time.

Total Assets at Year-End refers to the sum of the book values of all asset items listed on a company's balance sheet at the end of each fiscal year (typically December 31st). It directly reflects the total economic resources owned or controlled by the enterprise at a specific point in time and serves as fundamental raw data for assessing the company's scale, financial structure, and solvency.

english: Total Credit Sales for the Year

definition_en: Annual Total Credit Sales refers to the total sales revenue generated by a company within a fiscal year through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) for goods sold or services provided, representing the gross figure before any deductions for returns, allowances, or discounts.

Finished goods inventory refers to products that have completed the entire production process, passed inspection and warehousing, and are ready for sale as merchandise, as well as various purchased or outsourced processed goods that have been inspected, warehoused, and are intended for sale. It is an important component of enterprise assets and is presented under the 'Inventory' item on the balance sheet.

Inventory quantity refers to the physical count of goods, finished products, semi-finished products, etc., actually held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) and intended for sale or production processes. It is a fundamental data point obtained directly through physical counts or primary methods such as inbound/outbound records, serving as the core basis for calculating inventory value, assessing inventory status, and making inventory management decisions.

Production cost of inventory goods refers to the total of all expenses incurred by an enterprise during the production process for manufacturing finished products or goods available for sale. It primarily includes directly consumed raw materials (direct materials), compensation for workers directly involved in production (direct labor), and indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production (manufacturing overhead). These costs are accumulated and recorded as part of the carrying value of inventory when the finished products are completed and accepted into the warehouse.

Inventory quantity refers to the physical count of various goods, raw materials, work-in-progress, or finished products actually held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) that are available for sale or production consumption. It is a fundamental data point obtained directly through physical counts or primary methods such as stock movement records.

Cash on hand refers to the banknotes and coins held by an enterprise in its finance department, managed and handled by cashiers. It is the most liquid asset of an enterprise and a key component of monetary funds, distinct from bank deposits and other forms of cash equivalents.

Treasury stock refers to the number of shares that a company has repurchased from the open market or shareholders and has not yet canceled or reissued. These shares are held by the company itself, are no longer in circulation, and do not carry voting rights or dividend rights. It is a specific account under shareholders' equity on the balance sheet, reflecting the actual transaction results of the company's share repurchases.

Treasury stock shares refer to the number of a company's own shares that have been repurchased from the open market or shareholders and have not yet been canceled or reissued. It reflects the actual quantity of the company's own shares held and is a specific item on the balance sheet.

Increase in Bonds Payable (Issuance) refers to the increase in the book value of the 'Bonds Payable' account on the balance sheet resulting from the issuance of bonds (e.g., corporate bonds) by an enterprise during the current accounting period. It reflects the new long-term liabilities incurred by the enterprise due to financing activities.

Interest payable refers to the interest expense that has been incurred but not yet actually paid by an enterprise as of the balance sheet date due to financing activities such as borrowing, issuing bonds, or accepting deposits. It is a current liability of the enterprise, reflecting the interest obligation it bears as of a specific point in time.

Wages payable refers to the total amount of wages, including various salaries, bonuses, and allowances, that an enterprise owes to its employees based on wage rates, attendance, performance, and other fundamental data but has not yet actually paid. It constitutes a current liability of the enterprise.

Notes payable are liabilities arising from commercial bills of exchange issued or accepted by an enterprise for business activities such as purchasing materials, goods, or accepting services. They are presented as a current liability on the balance sheet, with their amount directly reflecting the face value of the notes and any accrued interest.

Accrued employee benefits refer to welfare expenses that an enterprise has accrued according to regulations or that have been incurred but not yet paid to employees, such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, and canteen subsidies. These are recorded as a liability on the balance sheet prior to payment.

Accrued Employee Benefits is a liability item on the corporate balance sheet, representing various welfare expenses that the enterprise has accrued for employees according to regulations but has not yet actually paid, such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, canteen and childcare facility expenditures, etc.

Employee Compensation Payable refers to the various forms of remuneration and other related expenses that an enterprise is obligated to pay to its employees in accordance with relevant regulations. It constitutes a current obligation of the enterprise to its employees and is classified as a current liability.

Dividends payable refers to the amount of dividends that a company has declared, based on a resolution by the board of directors or shareholders' meeting, but has not yet actually paid to shareholders. It is a current liability of the company and must be presented in the balance sheet.

Receivables for Subsidies is an asset account in a company's financial statements, specifically used to record various government subsidy amounts that the company is entitled to receive according to relevant national policies but has not yet actually received. It reflects the company's right to obtain subsidy income in the future.

Net increase in accounts receivable refers to the difference between the ending balance and the beginning balance of the accounts receivable account on a company's balance sheet during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It directly reflects the net change in the book value of accounts receivable during that period and serves as fundamental data for analyzing changes in a company's cash flow and working capital.

term_en.name: Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger Debit Balance

chinese: 应收账款明细账借方余额
应收客户款明细借方余额
客户欠款明细借方余额
english: Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger Debit Balance

definition_en: The accounts receivable subsidiary ledger debit balance refers to the amount in the debit balance direction of individual subsidiary ledger accounts established separately for each specific customer or debtor in the enterprise's accounting books. It directly records the original amount receivable from specific customers but not yet collected due to business operations such as sales of goods and provision of services, serving as the fundamental data for calculating the general ledger balance of accounts receivable when preparing financial statements.

The construction period is a fundamental phase in the project calculation period, referring to the entire time span from the initial capital investment for construction (such as construction work, equipment procurement and installation) until the project is completed and ready for operation or commissioning. It is typically determined directly based on project planning or contracts and serves as a critical time parameter for project financial evaluation and loan term calculation.

The amortization amount of organization costs refers to the specific amount, in accordance with accounting standards, that an enterprise recognizes as expenses either in full in the period when operations commence or over several periods after commencing operations, for costs incurred during the pre-operating period. The amount depends on the total actual organization costs incurred and the chosen amortization policy (e.g., one-time amortization or amortization over 4-5 years).

Starting Year refers to the base raw data used for calculating indicators such as length of service or number of historical periods. It typically denotes the year portion directly extracted from specific dates like an employee's hire date, system activation date, or project launch date. It is a starting point value, not a result derived from calculation.

Start Time refers to the designated initial moment point of an event, process, time period, or calculation. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a fundamental input value for calculating time intervals, costs, returns, or conducting time value analysis.

Starting Month refers to the original temporal benchmark point used for calculating other time-related metrics (such as length of service, number of service months, number of financial periods). It typically corresponds to the month of a specific date (e.g., hire date, project start date, contract effective date). It is a fundamental input datum, not a calculated result.

term_en.name: Terminal Point of Initial Cash Flow

definition_en: The terminal point of initial cash flow refers to the specific time point (e.g., the end of year 0 or year N) in project investment evaluation when the project's construction period ends and the operating period begins. It marks the transition point where the project shifts from the capital-investment construction phase to the cash-inflow generating operating phase, serving as the starting time benchmark for constructing the project's cash flow sequence.

The opening price refers to the transaction price of a security (such as a stock) at the first trade of a given trading day, serving as important fundamental data reflecting initial market supply and demand conditions.

term_en.name: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices

english: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices

definition_en: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices refers to the total accumulation of non-financial produced assets by resident units of a country or region during a specific accounting period (usually one year), measured at current market prices. It reflects the actual investment scale and capital accumulation level of the economy during the current period and is a fundamental aggregate indicator in national economic accounting.

Current market price refers to the latest, executable buying or selling price of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) in an open trading market. It is determined in real-time by market supply and demand and serves as fundamental data reflecting the immediate value of the asset.

Current date refers to the real-time date provided by a computer system, software environment, or specific application (such as Excel) that serves as a calculation benchmark. It is a fundamental data point commonly used in financial calculations as a temporal reference, for example, in calculating maturity periods or remaining terms.

The current period refers to the specific accounting period that serves as the primary focus and subject of description in financial reporting or analysis, such as the current month, quarter, or year. It provides a temporal benchmark for recording financial activities, performance, and conditions during that period, and is often compared with the 'prior period' or 'previous period' to assess trends of change.

Current period refers to the sequential parameter used to identify and measure a specific point in time or time interval in financial calculations (such as annuities, discounting, principal repayment, etc.). It typically serves as a known input variable and is the fundamental benchmark for time value calculations.

The current underlying asset price refers to the immediate transaction price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) observed or traded directly from an active market at a specific point in time, used for financial derivative pricing or valuation. It is unprocessed raw data and serves as the basis for calculating derived metrics such as price changes and yields.

Current market price per share refers to the latest transaction price per share formed through continuous bidding and real-time matching of trades between buyers and sellers in the secondary stock market. It is directly determined by the immediate market supply and demand relationship and serves as a fundamental observation data reflecting the value of a stock at a specific point in time.

Current Dividend Per Share refers to the amount of cash dividend per share actually declared and paid by a company to its common shareholders during a specific period (typically a fiscal year or a quarter). It is a fundamental figure calculated by dividing the total dividend payout by the total number of common shares outstanding, directly reflecting the cash return shareholders receive per share.

Current sales revenue refers to the total income generated by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during the current accounting period (e.g., this month, this quarter, or this year). It is a fundamental raw data item in financial statements, typically derived directly from business data such as sales volume multiplied by unit selling price, reflecting the scale of the enterprise's core business.

Current day stock price refers to the transaction price formed in real-time trading between buyers and sellers in the secondary market (such as a stock exchange) on a given trading day. It reflects the market's immediate valuation of the stock at a specific moment and serves as fundamental trading data.

term_en.name: Actual Work Volume for the Period

definition_en: Actual work volume for the period refers to the quantity or scale of work actually completed by an enterprise or department within the current accounting period, typically measured directly based on original business data such as production records, labor hour statistics, or output quantities.

Current period sales revenue refers to the total income obtained by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific accounting period (e.g., a month, a quarter, or a year). It is a fundamental raw data item in financial statements, typically calculated directly by multiplying sales volume by unit price, reflecting the scale and results of the enterprise's core business during the current period.

Intangible asset formation costs refer to the initial expenditures directly used to acquire or form intangible assets (such as land use rights, patents, proprietary technology, etc.) in project or enterprise construction investment estimates. These costs do not constitute fixed assets but are directly capitalized into the value of intangible assets.

The collection rate is a fixed percentage or tax rate stipulated by tax laws for calculating the tax payable of specific taxpayers (such as small-scale taxpayers). It is a fundamental policy parameter, not a composite indicator calculated from other financial metrics.

Prepaid expenses refer to payments made in advance by a company for which the economic benefits or services have not yet been received or fully received, and which need to be allocated to costs or expenses over a specific future period. Examples include prepaid rent and insurance premiums.

Decrease (or increase) in deferred expenses is an adjustment item used in the indirect method when preparing the cash flow statement to reconcile net profit to net cash flow from operating activities. It reflects the change in the balance of the 'Deferred Expenses' account on the balance sheet between the beginning and end of the period. If deferred expenses decrease at the end of the period compared to the beginning, it indicates that the actual cash paid (for forming deferred expenses) during the period is less than the amortization amount recognized as expenses in the period. Therefore, this non-cash expense needs to be 'added back' to net profit to restore the true operating cash flow. Conversely, if deferred expenses increase, this excess cash payment needs to be 'subtracted' from net profit.

Total population units is a fundamental concept in statistics, referring to the aggregate count of all individual units that constitute a statistical population. It describes the scale of the population and represents the most basic counting result.

term_en.name: Total Number of Common Shares Issued

definition_en: Total Number of Common Shares Issued refers to the aggregate quantity of all common stock shares that a company has issued to its shareholders. It constitutes fundamental data of the company's capital structure, reflecting the total number of shares corresponding to the capital raised through the issuance of common stock.

Total Shares Issued refers to the aggregate number of all common shares and preferred shares that a company has actually issued and are outstanding, based on its registered capital and share division. It is fundamental data of a company's capital structure and represents the total number of ownership shares in the company.

Total time refers to the aggregate duration obtained by summing multiple independent time periods or time point differences. In finance and project management, it typically serves as the foundational raw data for calculating work hours, evaluating project cycles, or analyzing time efficiency.

Total Number of Periods refers to the total number of time intervals over which an activity or contract lasts in finance, accounting, or project management. It is typically a directly given fundamental parameter, such as the total number of loan repayments, the total number of interest payment periods for a bond, or the total calculation cycles of a project.

Total Consumption Amount refers to the total monetary sum paid by individuals, households, enterprises, or specific groups for purchasing goods and services within a defined period (such as a day, month, or year). It serves as the fundamental raw data for measuring consumption levels.

Total shares outstanding refers to the total number of all shares issued by a company that are held by shareholders. It is a fundamental data point in a company's capital structure, typically determined directly by corporate actions such as registration, issuance of new shares, share repurchases, or stock splits.

Total number of shares outstanding refers to the aggregate quantity of all shares issued by a company that are held by shareholders, representing the company's entire equity base. It serves as fundamental data for calculating per-share metrics and evaluating the company's equity structure.

Total sales revenue refers to the aggregate sum of all income generated by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services within a specific period. It is typically calculated by multiplying sales volume by unit selling price and serves as a fundamental indicator for measuring business scale and market performance.

The sum of constituent stock prices refers to the total obtained by directly adding the real-time market prices of all constituent stocks included in a specific stock index (such as the SSE 50, CSI 300, etc.) at a given point in time. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating the value of a stock index.

A cost object refers to a specific entity or target identified in the cost accounting process for the purpose of accumulating and allocating costs, requiring separate measurement of its costs. It can be a tangible product (e.g., a machine), a service (e.g., consulting services), a project, a customer, a department, or an activity. The cost object serves as the fundamental carrier of cost information, with all related costs and expenses ultimately allocated to it to facilitate cost calculation, analysis, and control.

Contingent liability refers to a potential obligation arising from past transactions or events, the outcome of which depends on the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future events. It is not a currently confirmed debt, but may become an actual liability of the enterprise if specific future conditions occur (such as losing a lawsuit or being called upon to honor a guarantee).

Total product sales refers to the total revenue a company earns from selling all its products or merchandise during a specific period. It is typically derived directly from sales records, calculated by multiplying sales volume by the corresponding unit selling price, and serves as fundamental raw data reflecting the scale of a company's core business and its revenue level.

Contributed capital refers to the value of cash, physical assets, or other forms of assets actually invested by the owners (e.g., shareholders) to acquire company shares. It serves as the foundational funding source for a company's establishment and operations and is directly recorded in the equity section of the balance sheet.

Investment horizon refers to the length of time from the beginning to the end of an investment, typically measured in years. It is a key time input parameter for financial calculations such as computing future value, present value, or rate of return.

term_en.name: Fair Value Change of Investment Property

chinese: 投资性房地产公允价值变动损益
投资性房地产公允价值调整
投资性房地产价值变动
english: Fair Value Change of Investment Property
Change in Fair Value of Investment Real Estate

definition_en: Fair value change of investment property refers to the increase or decrease in the carrying amount of property held for rental or capital appreciation, resulting from its revaluation to market fair value at each accounting period end compared to the previous period end. This change arises directly from market assessment and is a fundamental data point in accounting.

chinese: 购建长期资产支付的现金

definition_en: Cash paid for investments refers to the total amount of cash actually disbursed by an enterprise during a specific accounting period for the purchase or acquisition of long-term equity investments, debt investments, and other long-term assets (such as fixed assets and intangible assets), including related transaction costs such as commissions and handling fees.

Investment income refers to the cash inflows or economic benefits obtained by an enterprise or individual through holding or selling various investment assets (such as bonds, stocks, funds, real estate, etc.), primarily including specific forms such as interest, dividends, distributions, and capital gains from asset sales.

Total investment income refers to the aggregate amount of all returns earned by an enterprise through external investment activities (such as holding or selling financial assets like stocks, bonds, and funds, as well as equity investments) within a specific accounting period. It typically includes dividends, interest income, realized gains or losses from the disposal of investment assets, and is a key item on the income statement reflecting the results of the enterprise's investment activities.

Investment period refers to the predetermined number of specific time intervals used for capital investment, cost incurrence, or revenue generation in project investment or financial analysis. It is typically a fundamental time parameter in project planning, contractual agreements, or financial models, serving as a known input condition for calculating financial metrics such as net present value and payback period.

Investment horizon refers to the length of time an investor plans or expects to hold a particular investment asset, serving as a fundamental parameter for investment decision-making and financial analysis.

Investment principal refers to the total amount of funds initially invested by an investor into a specific investment or loan, serving as the original base amount for calculating returns, interest, or profits.

chinese: 投资活动产生的现金流量

definition_en: Cash flow from investing activities is a crucial component of a company's cash flow statement. It reflects the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company's investing activities, such as the purchase or sale of long-term assets (e.g., property, plant, equipment, intangible assets) and equity or debt investments, during a specific accounting period.

Cash inflow from investing activities refers to the total cash actually received by an enterprise during the reporting period through the sale or disposal of long-term assets (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.) and other investing activities. This portion of cash inflow reflects the enterprise's ability to recover or liquidate investments and is a key component of the cash flow statement.

Cash outflow from investing activities refers to the total amount of cash actually paid out by an enterprise during a specific accounting period for activities such as acquiring or disposing of long-term assets (e.g., fixed assets, intangible assets), making external equity investments, and debt investments. This data is directly sourced from the enterprise's cash transaction records and is one of the fundamental data points for preparing the cash flow statement.

Cash flow from investing activities refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company during the reporting period due to investing activities, such as the acquisition or disposal of long-term assets (e.g., plants, equipment, intangible assets) and equity investments, debt investments, etc. It reflects the capital expenditures made for future operations and the recovery of investments.

Cash inflow from investing activities refers to the total cash received by an enterprise during a specific accounting period from transactions related to investing activities, such as the sale of long-term assets, recovery of principal from external investments, and receipt of investment returns. It is a key item directly presented in the enterprise's cash flow statement, reflecting the enterprise's ability to generate cash through investment activities.

Cash outflow from investing activities refers to the total amount of cash actually paid out by an enterprise during a specific accounting period for investing activities, such as acquiring or disposing of long-term assets (e.g., fixed assets, intangible assets) and making external equity investments or debt investments. It reflects the capital expenditures made by the enterprise for future development and income generation.

Investment management fees refer to the relevant fees paid by investors for entrusting professional institutions or individuals to manage their investment assets, typically including management fees, advisory fees, custody fees, etc., representing a direct cost expenditure in investment activities.

Portfolio beginning value refers to the total market value of all assets (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.) held within a portfolio at the start of a specific analysis or reporting period. It serves as the baseline data for measuring portfolio size, calculating period returns, or conducting performance analysis.

Investment End Date refers to the predetermined, formal termination date or time point of an investment activity or project. It serves as the fundamental time parameter required for calculating investment holding periods, evaluating investment returns, and other financial analyses.

Investment Start Date refers to the specific date on which an investor formally commits capital and begins to accrue investment returns or assume investment risks. It marks the commencement of the investment cycle and serves as the basis for subsequent calculations of holding periods, return on investment, and other metrics.

Depreciation and amortization are accounting methods used to systematically and rationally allocate the cost of long-term assets (such as equipment, plant, and intangible assets) over their estimated useful lives as expenses in each accounting period. Depreciation primarily applies to tangible fixed assets, while amortization primarily applies to intangible assets and long-term deferred expenses.

Depreciation period refers to the estimated number of years during which a fixed asset is expected to generate economic benefits for the enterprise, based on the asset's nature, usage patterns, technological obsolescence rate, or tax regulations. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating periodic depreciation expense.

Depreciation and amortization are accounting processes that systematically allocate the cost of long-term assets (such as equipment, buildings, and intangible assets) over their estimated useful lives. Depreciation applies to tangible assets, while amortization applies to intangible assets. The purpose is to match asset costs with the revenues generated during their usage periods, reflecting the consumption of asset value.

The reporting date refers to the specific cut-off date on which an enterprise prepares its financial statements (such as the balance sheet, income statement, etc.), marking the time point at which the financial position and operating results reflected in that statement are measured.

Reporting period price refers to the actual transaction price or quoted price of a specific commodity or service in the market during the reporting period (e.g., current month, current quarter) when compiling economic indices such as the Consumer Price Index. It is raw data collected directly from the market and serves as the basis for index calculation.

term_en.name: Nominal Value for the Reporting Period

english: Nominal Value for the Reporting Period

definition_en: Nominal value for the reporting period refers to the original or base data value within a specific reporting period, without any adjustments (such as removing price change factors). It typically serves as the starting point and reference benchmark for calculating other derived indicators (e.g., real growth rate, real interest rate).

Reporting Period Days refers to a predefined base time length, typically measured in days, used for financial calculations or analysis. It is a preset constant or a value directly determined based on the actual calendar, serving as a fundamental parameter for calculating periods, such as determining time weights when calculating weighted average shares outstanding.

Total days in the reporting period refers to a predetermined constant number of days used in financial calculations and analysis to standardize the time base, facilitate comparison and computation. It typically represents the length of a complete fiscal year or a specific analysis period, such as 365 days (calendar year) or 360 days (commercial year), and serves as a fundamental parameter in the calculation of many financial ratios (e.g., days turnover ratios).

term_en.name: Total Number of Months in the Reporting Period

definition_en: The total number of months in the reporting period refers to the aggregate count of complete calendar months contained within a specific financial reporting interval (such as a quarter, semi-annual period, or annual period). It serves as a fundamental time measurement parameter for subsequent financial processing, such as time-weighted calculations.

Reporting Period Total Duration refers to the specific length of time covered by a financial report, such as a quarter, half-year, or a full fiscal year. It serves as the fundamental time unit for financial data aggregation, time-weighted calculations, and financial ratio analysis.

The reporting date refers to the specific point in time on which a company prepares its financial statements (such as the balance sheet and income statement), marking the end of the accounting period covered by that financial report.

chinese: 资产负债表日公允价值
english: Fair Value on Balance Sheet Date

definition_en: Fair value at the reporting date refers to the immediate market value of an asset or liability determined by an enterprise based on active market quotations or valuation techniques on the cutoff date of financial statement preparation (such as year-end or quarter-end). It serves as the foundational data for subsequent fair value measurement and the calculation of gains or losses from changes in fair value.

Holding period refers to the number of calendar days or trading days from the date an investor purchases and confirms ownership of an asset (such as stocks or funds) to the date the asset is sold and ownership is relinquished.

Holding period (months) refers to the duration for which an investor or enterprise holds a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, or real estate) or maintains an investment, typically measured in months. It is a fundamental time metric calculated as the difference between the asset's purchase date and its sale date (or the current date).

Number of shares held refers to the original quantity of shares an investor directly owns in a listed company at a specific point in time (e.g., the record date), serving as fundamental data reflecting shareholder equity.

A sorted numerical sequence refers to a new data sequence obtained by rearranging a set of original numerical data according to ascending or descending order rules. It is not a composite indicator calculated through mathematical formulas, but rather a common data processing and presentation method for underlying data, with its results entirely dependent on the values of the original data.

Amortization expense refers to the cost of long-term assets such as intangible assets and long-term prepaid expenses that is systematically and rationally allocated to each accounting period's profit or loss over their estimated useful lives. It is the process of converting asset costs into expenses, reflecting the consumption of asset value.

term_en.name: Cash Paid for Other Investment Activities

chinese: 其他投资活动现金支出
支付的其他投资活动现金
投资活动其他现金流出
english: Other Cash Payments Related to Investing Activities
Cash Paid for Other Investing Activities

definition_en: This is a specific line item in the investing activities section of a company's cash flow statement, used to record cash payments that cannot be clearly classified into typical investing activities such as purchases of fixed assets, intangible assets, or equity investments. It is a base-level figure, typically reported directly based on actual business transactions rather than derived through calculation.

Expenses paid refer to the expenditures incurred by an enterprise in its daily operating activities for acquiring goods or receiving services, resulting in the actual payment of cash or cash equivalents. It is a significant original data item reflecting cash outflows in the statement of cash flows.

Payment type refers to the specific method or channel used to complete fund transfers or value exchanges in economic activities, such as cash, bank transfers, electronic payments, etc. It is a fundamental business attribute describing how transactions are settled.

term_en.name: Cash Received from Other Investment Activities

chinese: 投资活动其他现金流入
其他投资活动现金收入
english: Other Cash Received from Investing Activities
Cash Inflows from Other Investing Activities

definition_en: This is an item in the investing activities section of a company's cash flow statement, referring to other cash inflows related to investing activities received by the enterprise, apart from major investing activities such as recovering investments and obtaining investment returns. Examples include receiving cash dividends declared but not yet collected when purchasing stocks, or receiving bond interest that has reached the payment date but not yet collected when purchasing bonds.

term_en.name: Cash Received from Other Operating Activities

chinese: 收到的其他与经营活动有关的现金
english: Other Cash Received from Operating Activities

definition_en: This is an item under cash inflows from operating activities in the enterprise's cash flow statement, used to record all other cash receipts related to daily business operations, excluding cash received from sales of goods, rendering of services, and tax refunds. These receipts are typically not part of the enterprise's core business revenue, such as penalty income received, rental income from leasing packaging materials or equipment, deposits received, and scrap sales income.

term_en.name: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities

chinese: 筹资活动其他现金流入
其他筹资活动现金收入
english: Other Cash Received from Financing Activities
Cash Inflows from Other Financing Activities

definition_en: Other cash received related to financing activities is an item in the cash flow statement that reflects various other cash inflows related to financing activities received by an enterprise, apart from major items such as absorbing investments and obtaining borrowings, for example, receiving cash donations.

Closing volume refers to the total quantity of securities or contracts traded during the closing session of a financial market (typically the final minutes of a trading day or the closing auction period), such as stocks or futures. It is fundamental raw data reflecting the trading activity level during the market close.

Closing turnover refers to the total monetary value of all shares traded at the closing time of each trading day in the stock market, calculated based on transaction prices. It reflects market capital activity and trading scale during the closing phase, serving as an important indicator of market liquidity.

Numerical value is a general term referring to a specific number or data point. In the accounting and finance field, it typically denotes the fundamental data in financial statements, calculation models, or data analysis, serving as the basic input unit for financial analysis, indicator calculation, and decision support.

Count of values refers to the total number of all numerical data items or non-empty data items within a set of data, a specific range, or a dataset. It is a fundamental statistical measure used to gauge the size of a dataset or the quantity of valid data under specific conditions.

A numerical sequence refers to a column of consecutive or pattern-specific numbers generated by the ROW function, manual input, or simple formulas. It is primarily used for data sorting, row numbering, or as foundational parameters for other functions, representing basic raw data without complex financial calculations.
Number of observations refers to the total count of independent data items or observations contained in a dataset, which is the most fundamental descriptive metric in statistical analysis.

Data value refers to the specific numerical figure used to describe a particular attribute or variable in finance, statistics, or data analysis. It typically represents a raw or unprocessed fundamental number, serving as the basic unit for constructing datasets, conducting financial analysis, and calculating other composite metrics (such as variance, mean).

A data array is a fundamental unit in data processing, referring to a collection of raw values or data arranged in a specific order. It serves as the starting point for formula calculations, metric references, and data analysis, typically organized as an independent, indivisible basic data structure.

A data point refers to a single, fundamental, and indivisible unit of data obtained through observation, measurement, or recording in finance, statistics, or data analysis. It is the basic element that constitutes a dataset, enables summary calculations (such as sum or average), or forms the basis for constructing more complex metrics (such as variance).
