Number of data points refers to the total count of independent data items or observations contained within a dataset. It is typically obtained by applying a direct counting function (such as the COUNTA function in Excel) to a list or range of cells, reflecting the scale of the raw dataset and serving as a fundamental metric for subsequent statistical analysis.

Full Year Equivalent refers to a fundamental, indivisible unit of time measurement, typically expressed in complete years (e.g., 1 year, 2 years). It serves as the original time input parameter for calculations (such as depreciation, interest, and length of service) and is not a composite metric derived from complex formulas.

Full Months refers to the number of complete calendar months contained between two specific dates. It is a fundamental unit of time measurement, commonly used in financial calculations such as determining interest period lengths, calculating depreciation and amortization, or allocating expenses across periods.

New debt issuance refers to the total cash proceeds actually raised by a company from investors through the issuance of debt instruments such as bonds in the primary market. This represents a significant cash inflow in the company's financing activities and is directly recorded in the financing activities section of the cash flow statement.

term_en.name: Days Outstanding for Newly Issued Common Shares

english: Days Outstanding for Newly Issued Common Stock
Days Issued for New Common Shares

definition_en: Days Outstanding for Newly Issued Common Shares refers to the number of days that newly issued common shares during the current period have actually been in circulation, from the date of issuance to the end of the current financial reporting period (e.g., quarter-end or year-end). This number of days serves as a fundamental time data point for calculating the weighted average number of common shares outstanding.

term_en.name: Number of Newly Issued Common Shares

definition_en: Number of Newly Issued Common Shares refers to the quantity of common stock actually issued and newly added to the market or specific investors by a company within a specific period, through methods such as initial public offerings, seasoned equity offerings, rights issues, debt-to-equity swaps, or as consideration for mergers and acquisitions. It is the direct result of corporate financing and capital operations and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as earnings per share.

Number of Newly Issued Shares refers to the total quantity of shares newly issued and sold by a company to the market or specific investors through methods such as initial public offerings, seasoned equity offerings, or rights offerings, in order to raise capital or meet other needs. This figure is the raw data directly determined by the issuance activity itself and serves as the fundamental record for changes in the company's share capital.

chinese: 无形资产与长期待摊费用
无形资产及其他长期资产
非流动资产-无形资产及其他

definition_en: Intangible assets and other assets are a category of non-current assets presented on the balance sheet, primarily comprising assets without physical form but capable of generating economic benefits for the enterprise (such as patents, trademarks, land use rights, etc.), as well as long-term assets that do not meet the definition of other asset categories (such as long-term prepaid expenses). Their reported amounts are directly derived from accounting book records and constitute a significant component of the enterprise's total assets.

Non-interest-bearing long-term liabilities refer to long-term debts with a repayment period exceeding one year, as presented on the balance sheet, for which no interest payments are required during the debt's tenure according to relevant contracts or agreements. They are typically fundamental line items directly identifiable from financial statement accounts, such as the amount of long-term payables excluding the interest-bearing portion.

A risk-free rate series refers to a collection of yield data obtained from investing in assets considered to have almost no default risk (such as short-term government bonds) at a series of consecutive time points. It is commonly used as a fundamental input parameter in financial market analysis and asset pricing models (such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model).

Old interest rate refers to a predetermined interest rate value used for calculating interest or serving as a benchmark for subsequent rate adjustments during a specific historical period or the initial phase stipulated in a contract. It is a known input datum, not derived from other financial formulas.

Time horizon refers to the fundamental unit or concept used to measure the length or span of time, such as year, month, or day. In the field of finance and accounting, it typically serves as a given input parameter in analysis or calculations, used to describe the maturity period of bonds, the cycle of investment projects, the repayment period of loans, etc. It is a fundamental element for assessing the time value of money and risk-return trade-offs.

Time (Years) is the most fundamental unit of time in financial calculations, typically referring to the duration length for which a sum of money is invested, borrowed, or an asset is utilized. It is an essential raw input parameter for calculating financial metrics such as future value, present value, interest, depreciation, etc., and has no calculation formula itself, belonging to basic data.

term_en.name: Current Market Price of Common Stock

english: Current Market Price of Common Stock

definition_en: The current market price of common stock refers to the transaction price at which a company's common stock is bought and sold in real-time on public securities trading markets (such as stock exchanges). It is determined by market supply and demand, reflecting investors' immediate assessment of the company's future prospects and value. It is fundamental data obtained directly from the market and cannot be derived through formulas.

english: Total Number of Common Shares Outstanding

definition_en: Total number of common shares refers to the aggregate quantity of common stock issued and outstanding by a company. It is the most fundamental data in a company's capital structure, typically sourced directly from the company's share register or notes to the financial statements.

term_en.name: Market Price Per Share of Common Stock

definition_en: Market price per share of common stock refers to the transaction price per share formed by real-time trading between buyers and sellers on secondary markets such as stock exchanges for a listed company's common stock. It reflects the market's assessment of the company's value at a specific moment and serves as the direct basis for investors to buy and sell shares.

The number of common shares outstanding refers to the total quantity of common stock issued by a company and held by its shareholders. It is a fundamental datum of a company's capital structure, typically derived directly from the company's registered capital, total share capital and par value per share, or determined by the actual number of shares issued by the company. This figure serves as a crucial denominator for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and dividends per share.

Lowest Activity Level refers to the minimum level of business activity (such as production volume, sales volume, etc.) directly observed or selected from a company's historical operational data. It serves as a fundamental data point in cost behavior analysis (e.g., the High-Low Method), used as an original input value for calculating parameters such as variable cost per unit.

term_en.name: Total Cost at Lowest Activity Level

english: Total Cost at Lowest Activity Level

definition_en: Total cost at the lowest activity level refers to the actual total cost incurred when the activity level (such as production volume, sales volume, or labor hours) is at its minimum in the company's historical operational data. It serves as fundamental raw data for cost behavior analysis (e.g., the high-low method) and is used to separate fixed and variable components of costs.

Low-point activity level cost refers to the total cost corresponding to the lowest activity level selected from historical cost data in the high-low method. It is a raw observation value directly read from historical records, used for subsequent calculation of unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

Latest total shares outstanding refers to the sum of all shares issued by a company at a specific point in time (typically the most recent reporting period), serving as a fundamental quantitative metric measured in 'shares'.

The Final Consumption Price Index (commonly referring to the Consumer Price Index, CPI) measures the relative change over time in the price level of a representative basket of consumer goods and services. It reflects the price level changes of consumer goods and services generally purchased by households and serves as a key indicator for monitoring inflation levels.

The most recent dividend refers to the per-share cash dividend that a company has actually declared and paid to shareholders in its latest period (typically the previous payment cycle). It is a known historical fact and serves as the foundational starting point for future dividend forecasts and stock valuation calculations.

Highest activity level refers to the maximum value of the actual business volume (such as production output, sales volume, or operating revenue) achieved by an enterprise during a specific observation period (e.g., one year or an accounting period). In management accounting, it is one of the two key historical data points selected when applying the high-low method for cost behavior analysis to calculate the unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

term_en.name: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities

definition_en: The annual interest rate of marketable securities refers to the interest rate, calculated on an annual basis, that is either explicitly stipulated in the contract for securities such as bonds and notes or implied by their market price. It represents the ratio between the annual interest income obtainable from holding the security and the security's face value or investment principal, serving as a key known parameter for calculating interest income.

Service price refers to the direct fee amount charged by an enterprise or individual to a client for providing specific services, as stipulated in contracts or according to market conventions. It is typically determined based on service content, time, percentage, or fixed rates, and serves as the fundamental pricing data in service transactions.

Service revenue refers to the income recognized by an enterprise from payments received from customers, based on contractual agreements or service completion, during the process of providing labor or services (such as consulting, management, technical services, etc.). It is a significant component of an enterprise's operating revenue and is typically recognized directly upon the provision of services.

Service volume refers to the total sum of the original measurement units of services provided by an enterprise or institution to its customers within a specific period. It serves as fundamental data for measuring the scale of business operations. It is typically quantified in specific units such as number of times, duration, or person-times, rather than being a composite indicator derived from financial calculations.

Beginning price refers to the initial cost or market value of an asset, inventory, or security at the start of a specific accounting period or trading cycle. It serves as the starting point for financial records and calculations during that period, typically derived directly from bookkeeping entries rather than being calculated through formulas.

Beginning balance refers to the carryover amount in a specific accounting account (such as cash, bank deposits, inventory, accounts receivable, etc.) at the start of a particular accounting period (e.g., a month, quarter, or year). It is directly carried forward from the ending balance of the previous accounting period, reflecting the financial position as of the beginning of the current period, and serves as the starting point for the current period's accounting.

term_en.name: Total Borrowings at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total borrowings at the beginning of a period refers to the aggregate book balance of all borrowing accounts (such as short-term borrowings, long-term borrowings, etc.) at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the total principal amount of borrowings undertaken by the enterprise at the beginning of the period.

chinese: 期初净经营长期资产总额
期初净经营非流动资产

definition_en: Beginning Net Operating Long-term Assets refers to the net value of long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, land, etc.) used for core business operations at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or quarter), after deducting accumulated depreciation or amortization. It reflects the scale of net capital invested in long-term operations at the beginning of the period and is an important point-in-time data item on the balance sheet.

english: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
Opening Balance of Bad Debt Provision

definition_en: Beginning Allowance for Doubtful Accounts refers to the account balance of the 'Allowance for Doubtful Accounts' at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a contra-asset account on the balance sheet, reflecting the company's prior estimate and provision for the portion of beginning accounts receivable that may be uncollectible based on past experience. This balance is typically carried forward from the previous period-end and serves as the starting point for accounting calculations, rather than being derived from current-period computations.

Beginning balance of allowance accounts refers to the book balance carried forward from the previous accounting period for various allowance accounts (such as allowance for doubtful accounts, accumulated depreciation, inventory write-down allowance, etc.) at the start of an accounting period. It reflects the cumulative amount of provisions made by the enterprise for asset impairment or value depletion up to the beginning of the period.

Beginning inventory cost refers to the total book value of all goods, materials, or raw materials available for sale or use in a company's warehouse at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically the ending inventory cost carried forward from the previous accounting period and serves as the foundational data for calculating financial metrics such as the cost of goods sold and ending inventory cost for the current period.

Beginning paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders or investors to the enterprise, as recorded on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the capital base formed by actual owner contributions that the enterprise possesses at the beginning of that period, typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of paid-in capital from the previous period.

Beginning accounts payable balance refers to the total amount owed by a company to suppliers or creditors for goods purchased or services received in business operations that remains unpaid at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental item on the balance sheet, carried forward directly from the ending accounts payable balance of the previous period.

Beginning accounts receivable balance refers to the total book value of funds that a company is entitled to collect from customers for goods sold or services rendered but not yet received at the start of a financial reporting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental item on the balance sheet, directly carried over from the ending balance of the previous reporting period, serving as the starting point for calculating changes in accounts receivable and the ending balance for the current period.

Beginning Total Accounts Receivable refers to the aggregate book value of amounts owed to a company by customers for goods sold or services rendered in the ordinary course of business, which remain uncollected at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the baseline data for analyzing changes in accounts receivable during the current period and for calculating related financial metrics.

Total beginning owner's equity refers to the total amount of owner's equity at the start of the current accounting period. It is directly taken from the ending balance of the previous accounting period's (e.g., the prior year) financial statements and reflects the residual value of equity attributable to owners at the beginning of the period.

The initial investment amount refers to the total cash outflow required for an investment project at the beginning stage (typically at period 0 or the beginning of year 1). It is a fundamental data point that must be predetermined for project financial evaluation, such as calculating net present value and internal rate of return.

Opening balance refers to the initial book value of various assets, liabilities, or equity at the beginning of a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically carried forward directly from the closing balance of the previous period and serves as the starting point and foundational data for current-period accounting and financial statement preparation.

Beginning principal balance refers to the amount of principal that remains unpaid in an account at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is directly carried forward from the ending principal balance of the previous period and serves as the foundational starting point for calculating current-period interest, repayments, and other financial activities.

term_en.name: Total Current Liabilities at Beginning of Period

english: Total Current Liabilities at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total current liabilities at the beginning of the period refers to the aggregate balance of all debt items on the balance sheet that are due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle, as recorded at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). This figure is directly sourced from the company's accounting records or financial statements and serves as fundamental data reflecting the enterprise's short-term debt repayment pressure at the period's commencement.

term_en.name: Total Current Assets at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total current assets at the beginning of the period refers to the aggregate book value of all current asset items on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the total assets owned by the enterprise at the beginning of the period that are expected to be realized or consumed within a normal operating cycle (typically one year or an operating cycle longer than one year). This figure serves as fundamental data for analyzing the enterprise's short-term solvency and working capital position.

term_en.name: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period

chinese: 期初发行在外普通股股数
english: Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period

definition_en: The number of common shares outstanding at the beginning of a period refers to the total number of common shares actually issued and circulating in the market at the start of a financial reporting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It serves as the base data for calculating metrics like the weighted average number of common shares outstanding and is typically obtained directly from the company's balance sheet or the notes to the relevant financial reports.

english: Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of Period

definition_en: Beginning shares outstanding refers to the total number of common shares actually issued and circulating in the market at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year). It is a point-in-time figure reflecting the equity structure at the beginning of the period and serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as the weighted average shares outstanding.

term_en.name: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance

english: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance

definition_en: Beginning cash and cash equivalents balance refers to the total amount of cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise at the start of the current accounting period (i.e., at the end of the previous accounting period). It is directly taken from the ending balance of the 'Cash and Cash Equivalents' item on the previous period's balance sheet and serves as the starting point data for preparing the statement of cash flows.

Beginning Surplus Reserve refers to the balance in the surplus reserve account at the start of the current accounting period (e.g., the current year). It is directly carried over from the ending surplus reserve balance of the previous accounting period (e.g., the prior year). As a fundamental opening figure on the balance sheet, it is typically not calculated via a formula but serves as a given condition for computing changes in the current period's surplus reserve or the ending balance.

english: Accumulated Depreciation and Amortization at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Beginning accumulated depreciation/amortization refers to the total sum of depreciation and amortization expenses already recorded for all fixed assets and intangible assets of an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the cumulative reduction in asset value due to usage, wear and tear, or technological obsolescence from the acquisition date up to that beginning point, representing a historical cumulative book balance.

Beginning operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle, at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is a fundamental figure on the balance sheet, directly derived from the ending balance reported in the previous period's financial statements.

chinese: 经营性流动资产期初数
经营流动资产期初余额

definition_en: Beginning Operating Current Assets refers to the value of current assets used for daily business operations at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a project cycle). It typically serves as a known starting point for financial analysis or project evaluation and cannot be directly calculated from other financial metrics.

english: Opening Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents

definition_en: Beginning cash and cash equivalents refers to the balance of the cash and cash equivalents account on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the total amount of cash, bank deposits, and other cash equivalents held by the enterprise at the beginning of the period and is raw data obtained directly from the accounting records.

english: Beginning Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents

definition_en: Beginning balance of monetary funds refers to the book balance of the 'Monetary Funds' account in the balance sheet at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the total amount of cash, bank deposits, and other monetary funds held by the enterprise at the beginning of the period, representing the base data carried forward directly from the previous period's financial statements or accounting records.

Beginning asset value refers to the total book value of all asset accounts at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is directly derived from the ending balance of the previous accounting period or the opening accounting ledger records, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating current-period financial changes and financial ratios (such as holding period return).

term_en.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total assets at the beginning of a period refers to the aggregate value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It is typically carried forward directly from the total assets at the end of the preceding accounting period. As a fundamental point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, it is used for subsequent financial analysis and calculations (e.g., calculating average assets).

term_en.name: Beginning Net Book Value of Assets

english: Beginning Net Book Value of Assets

definition_en: Beginning net book value of assets refers to the total recorded net value of all assets in the accounting books at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It is directly carried forward from the previous period's ending balance and serves as the baseline original data for calculating current period depreciation, amortization, etc.

Beginning capital refers to the total capital or book value of owners' equity that a company possesses at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the starting point data for calculating current-period financial performance (such as economic profit, average cost of capital) and conducting financial analysis.

Beginning capital reserve refers to the book balance of the 'capital reserve' account on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the cumulative balance at the beginning of the period, including the portion of investor contributions exceeding their share in registered capital or share capital, as well as gains and losses directly recognized in owners' equity.

Beginning financial current assets refer to the liquid assets held by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter) that can be quickly converted into cash and are primarily used for financial activities, mainly including cash, bank deposits, trading financial assets, etc. It is a fundamental point-in-time data item on the balance sheet.

term_en.name: Total Financial Assets at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total financial assets at the beginning of the period refers to the aggregate carrying amount of all financial assets held by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It is typically derived directly from the carrying amount of financial assets at the end of the previous accounting period and serves as a fundamental data point on the balance sheet.

Beginning non-current liabilities refer to the total carrying value of liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year held by an enterprise at the start of the current accounting period (typically the beginning of the year or quarter). It is a fundamental historical data point on the balance sheet, reflecting the long-term liabilities balance at the end of the previous accounting period.

Periodic interest rate refers to the ratio between the interest amount and the principal within each interest calculation period (such as a year, a month, or a day). It is a fundamental parameter for calculating interest, typically predetermined by banks, markets, or contracts, and is used to determine the interest amount payable for each period.

The current period income tax rate refers to the statutory tax rate directly applicable when an enterprise calculates the income tax payable for a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year), based on national tax laws and regulations, the enterprise's own tax status (e.g., whether it is a high-tech enterprise), and the preferential tax policies it enjoys. It is a fundamental input parameter used to calculate the current period income tax expense, rather than being derived from other financial formulas.

Ending balance refers to the final account balance after recording all increases and decreases during a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It serves as the fundamental data for preparing financial statements and reflects the financial position of the account at the end of the period.

chinese: 期末负债总额（借款部分）

definition_en: Total borrowings at period end refers to the aggregate sum of all outstanding principal amounts of borrowings at the conclusion of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It is directly sourced from the company's accounting records or loan agreements, reflecting the scale of the company's borrowing liabilities at that point in time. This figure serves as fundamental data for analyzing the company's debt position and calculating related financial metrics.

term_en.name: Other Operating Current Assets at Period End

definition_en: Other operating current assets at period end refer to other current assets, excluding major items such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, and inventory, that are used in daily business operations and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, as presented in the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end).

term_en.name: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End

english: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End
Common Stock Outstanding at End of Period

definition_en: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End refers to the total quantity of common shares that have been actually issued by a company and have not been repurchased or cancelled by the company as of the cut-off date of an accounting period (such as quarter-end or year-end). It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the scale of the company's common share capital at a specific point in time.

Ending inventory cost refers to the total book value of all inventory items, including finished goods, work-in-progress, and raw materials, at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It represents the carrying cost of inventory on the balance sheet date and is a significant asset item on the balance sheet.

Ending accounts payable balance refers to the total amount owed to suppliers or creditors at the balance sheet date (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) for the purchase of materials, goods, or services received but not yet paid. It is directly recorded based on the actual closing balances in the general ledger or subsidiary ledgers, reflecting the company's short-term payment obligations at a specific point in time.

Ending accounts receivable balance refers to the net book value of receivables arising from the sale of goods or provision of services that have not yet been collected from customers at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the amount of claims against customers at the balance sheet date and serves as fundamental data for calculating other financial metrics (such as turnover ratios).

Ending balance refers to the final book balance of each accounting item in a company's financial statements at the close of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month). These figures are obtained directly from accounting records like the general ledger, reflecting the company's financial position at that point in time, and serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating various financial ratios and growth rates.

chinese: 期末现金及现金等价物
english: Cash and Cash Equivalents at Period End

definition_en: Ending cash and cash equivalents refers to the total amount of funds owned by an enterprise at the cut-off point of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) that can be immediately used for payment. It is directly reported on the balance sheet by summing the ending balances of the 'Cash on Hand', 'Bank Deposits', and 'Other Cash Equivalents' accounts from the accounting ledgers, reflecting the enterprise's immediate payment capability and liquidity.

Ending asset value refers to the total recorded book value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the closing point of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It is directly derived from the enterprise's accounting results or asset appraisal reports, serves as the core aggregate item on the balance sheet, and reflects the overall scale of the enterprise's resources at that point in time.

Total assets at period end refers to the aggregate value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise as reflected on its balance sheet at the conclusion of a specific accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, year-end). It is the most fundamental total item on the balance sheet, directly reflecting the financial scale and resource position of the enterprise at a specific point in time.

Ending capital refers to the book balance of owners' equity or invested capital at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the capital position of the enterprise at that specific moment, serving as the fundamental raw data for financial analysis and the calculation of other metrics (such as the weighted average cost of capital).

Ending capital reserve refers to the final book balance of the 'capital reserve' account under the owners' equity section on the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the public accumulation attributable to all shareholders, formed from non-operating factors since the company's establishment, such as shareholder contributions exceeding the registered capital, donations received, and revaluation surpluses of assets.

Financial assets at period end refer to the total carrying amount of various financial assets held by an enterprise at the cut-off point of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). These assets typically include trading financial assets, derivative financial assets, debt investments, other debt investments, etc. They are specific asset items on the balance sheet, directly sourced from the enterprise's accounting records.

Ending prepaid accounts refer to the total amount prepaid to suppliers for goods or services not yet received, as presented on the balance sheet date at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). This amount is calculated by analyzing the debit balances of detailed ledger accounts such as 'Prepaid Accounts' and 'Accounts Payable'.

The market price of an option, also known as the option premium or option price, refers to the real-time transaction price formed between buyers and sellers for an option contract in the open trading market. It is the actual amount paid or received by investors to obtain the rights (to buy or sell the underlying asset) conferred by the option contract. It is a fundamental data point observed directly from the market, not derived from formulaic calculation.

Futures price volatility refers to the phenomenon of upward or downward price movements of futures contracts over time in the futures market, influenced by various factors such as supply and demand, macroeconomic conditions, policy changes, and market sentiment. It represents the raw price movement data directly generated in market trading and serves as the basis for calculating derivative metrics such as volatility and profit/loss.

Periodic interest rate refers to the ratio of interest amount to principal within a specific interest calculation period (such as year, month, or day), usually expressed as a percentage. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating interest, present value, future value, and other financial metrics.

Period days refer to the number of days used to measure the length of a specific time interval in financial calculations. It typically serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating interest, discounting, turnover rates, etc. Its determination can be directly specified or agreed upon based on specific calendar conventions (e.g., a year calculated as 360 days, 365 days, or actual days).

Period revenue refers to the total income earned by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year). It is a fundamental primary account on the income statement.

Term refers to the length of a time period, typically expressed in units such as years, months, or days. In the field of finance and accounting, it is a fundamental time parameter required for calculating the time value of money, evaluating bonds, computing interest rates, and numerous other financial metrics.

Future Debt Amount refers to the estimated total value of debt that an enterprise or institution is expected to repay or assume within a specific future period (e.g., the next 3 months). It is typically derived from existing contracts, loan agreements, and forecasts of future financing needs, serving as crucial raw data for assessing an enterprise's future debt repayment pressure and financial risk.

term_en.name: Actual Costs and Expenses Incurred in the Current Year

english: Actual Cost Incurred in Current Year
Current Year Actual Costs and Expenses
Actual Costs and Expenses for the Year

definition_en: Actual costs and expenses incurred in the current year refer to the total sum of various costs and expenses directly recorded and aggregated by an enterprise within the current fiscal year based on source documents (such as invoices, material requisition slips, payrolls, etc.) generated from genuine business activities. It reflects the actual consumption of resources by the enterprise during the year, serves as fundamental data for preparing financial statements, and cannot be derived indirectly through other financial metrics.

term_en.name: Total Wages Payable for the Year

english: Total Wages Payable for the Year

definition_en: Total wages payable for the year refers to the total labor compensation that an enterprise is obligated to pay to all its employees during the current reporting year (typically a calendar year or fiscal year) under the accrual basis accounting principle. It reflects the wage cost that should be accrued by the enterprise for the year, regardless of whether the payment has been actually made in the current period. The data is usually compiled based on the cumulative annual credit turnover of the 'Employee Compensation Payable - Wages' account.

term_en.name: Total Welfare Benefits Payable for the Current Year

english: Total Accrued Employee Welfare Expenses for the Year

definition_en: Total welfare benefits payable for the current year refers to the cumulative amount of employee welfare expenses incurred by an enterprise during the current accounting year, recorded as costs or expenses based on actual occurrences. It reflects the actual expenditures or accrued amounts for various benefits provided to employees during the year (such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, canteen subsidies, etc.), serving as fundamental data in accounting.

Depreciation for the current year refers to the amount of asset value consumption calculated and recorded as a cost or expense in the current accounting period, based on the original value of fixed assets, estimated useful life, residual value rate, and selected depreciation method (such as the straight-line method, double-declining balance method, etc.). It reflects the value depletion of assets during the current year.

Current period price refers to the unit price at which a specific asset, commodity, or service is actually transacted in the market during the current financial reporting period. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as revenue and cost.

Current Period Debit Amount refers to the total sum of all transaction amounts recorded on the debit side (indicating an increase in assets or expenses, or a decrease in liabilities, owner's equity, or revenue) of a specific accounting account during a defined accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as one of the fundamental raw data points for determining the account's ending balance.

term_en.name: Total Foreign Demand in Current Period

definition_en: Total foreign demand in the current period refers to the aggregate demand for final goods and services produced by the domestic country (or economy) from the rest of the world and other countries/regions during a specific statistical period (such as a quarter or a year). It is a key macroeconomic indicator measuring the pulling effect of external markets on the domestic economy.

term_en.name: Decrease in Paid-in Capital for the Current Period

definition_en: Decrease in paid-in capital for the current period refers to the direct reduction in the amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders during the current accounting period. This typically occurs due to reasons such as excess capital, significant losses, adjustments to the capital structure, or shareholder withdrawals, and is implemented through methods like returning investment funds to shareholders after approval through statutory procedures. It represents the change in the paid-in capital account on the balance sheet for the current period, reflecting a direct reduction in shareholders' equity.

term_en.name: Increase in Paid-in Capital for the Current Period

english: Increase in Paid-in Capital for the Period
Current Period Addition to Contributed Capital

definition_en: Increase in Paid-in Capital for the Current Period refers to the actual increase in the amount of capital contributed by shareholders during the current accounting period, resulting from specific business activities such as new capital investments by investors, conversion of capital reserves or surplus reserves into paid-in capital. It represents the change in the paid-in capital account on the balance sheet, derived from actual transaction records rather than calculated through formulas.

Actual workload for the period refers to the total amount of work tasks actually completed or the effective working hours consumed by an enterprise or department within the current statistical or reporting period. It is typically used as fundamental raw data for subsequent cost accounting, performance evaluation, or resource planning.

term_en.name: Annual Credit Sales for the Current Period

english: Net Credit Sales for the Period

definition_en: Annual credit sales for the current period refer to the total sales of goods or services realized through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) within the current fiscal year, typically representing the net amount after deducting sales returns, allowances, and discounts. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as accounts receivable turnover and pre-credit-cost income.

Treasury stock - current period refers to a company's own issued shares that have been repurchased and held during the current accounting period through the open market or other means. After being reacquired by the company, these shares are no longer considered outstanding and are presented as a deduction within the shareholders' equity section of the balance sheet, reflecting the company's reacquisition of its own ownership.

term_en.name: Decrease in Accounts Payable for the Period

english: Decrease in Accounts Payable for the Period

definition_en: Decrease in Accounts Payable for the Period refers to the total reduction in the balance of the accounts payable account during a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). This reduction results from economic activities including repayment of supplier invoices, debt restructuring, debt forgiveness, or other transactions that lead to a decrease in accounts payable liabilities. It serves as fundamental raw data for analyzing a company's cash flow and short-term solvency.

Current period accounts receivable refers to the total amount of funds that a company is entitled to collect from customers but has not yet received within the current accounting period (such as the current month, quarter, or year), arising from operating activities like sales of goods or provision of services. It is a significant current asset item on the balance sheet.

term_en.name: Accounts Receivable Balance for the Current Period

definition_en: Accounts Receivable Balance for the Current Period refers to the original book value of customer credit sales that have not yet been collected, directly derived from the accounting records at the end of the current accounting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year). It reflects the company's right to collect payments from customers at the end of the reporting period.

Total number of shares outstanding refers to the aggregate quantity of all issued common shares and preferred shares of a company during the current reporting period (e.g., the current quarter or fiscal year). It constitutes fundamental data of the company's capital structure, reflects the scale of the company's capital, and serves as a crucial basis for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

Current Period Reported Value refers to the original amounts actually incurred for various accounting items (such as operating revenue and operating costs) during a specific financial reporting period (e.g., current month, current quarter, or current year). These data are obtained directly from the accounting ledgers and constitute the foundational data for financial statements, rather than being composite indicators derived through calculation.

Current period amount refers to the original, unadjusted base figure directly reported in financial statements for the reporting period (such as the current month, quarter, or year), which has not been calculated or adjusted by other financial metrics.

Current period data is a commonly used time label in financial and operational analysis, specifically referring to the original values directly obtained from accounting books or business records within a specific reporting period (such as the current month, quarter, or year). It is not derived through formula calculations but serves as the foundational input data for calculating derived metrics such as growth rates and proportions.

term_en.name: Current Period Current Liabilities Incurred Amount

chinese: 本期流动负债累计发生额
english: Flow of Current Liabilities for the Period

definition_en: Current Period Current Liabilities Incurred Amount refers to the total cumulative amount recorded in the debit or credit side of all current liability accounts (such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, employee compensation payable, etc.) in the accounting books during a specific accounting period (e.g., a month, a quarter, or a year). It reflects the total increase or decrease in current liabilities during that period and is raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

term_en.name: Current Period Current Liabilities Repayment Amount

chinese: 当期流动负债清偿金额
english: Current Period Liquidation of Current Liabilities
Repayment of Current Liabilities in the Period

definition_en: Current Period Current Liabilities Repayment Amount refers to the total amount of various current liabilities actually paid or settled by an enterprise during the current accounting period. It is an important original data item in the cash flow statement or funds flow statement, reflecting the actual repayment situation of the enterprise's short-term debts, and serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating ending current liabilities.

Current Period Unit Consumption Price refers to the average consumption price paid by an enterprise per unit of product or service within a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically calculated directly based on the total consumption expenditure incurred during the period and the total consumption quantity, serving as fundamental operational data reflecting the cost level.

term_en.name: Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period

english: Value of Finished Goods Produced in Current Period
Current Period Output Value of Finished Products

definition_en: Value of finished products produced in the current period refers to the total value of all industrial finished products (including semi-finished products) that have been completed during the current reporting period, require no further processing within that period, and have passed inspection, completed packaging, and been placed in inventory. It serves as a fundamental data point for calculating gross industrial output value.

term_en.name: Debit Turnover of Retained Earnings for the Current Period

chinese: 本期留存收益借方发生数
本期留存收益借方总额
当期留存收益借方发生额
english: Current Period Debit Amount of Retained Earnings
Debit Occurrence of Retained Earnings for the Period

definition_en: Debit turnover of retained earnings for the current period refers to the aggregate amount of all entries recorded on the debit side of the retained earnings account in the accounting books during the current accounting period. It directly reflects the total value of transactions or events that caused a decrease in retained earnings during the period and serves as one of the fundamental source data for preparing financial statements.

Current operating liabilities refer to the debts generated from a company's daily business operations during the current accounting period (such as the current year or quarter) that are expected to be repaid within one operating cycle (typically one year). They arise directly from the company's core business activities and constitute an important component of the balance sheet.

term_en.name: Increase in Operating Long-term Liabilities for the Current Period

chinese: 经营长期负债本期增加额
本期经营性长期负债增加
english: Increase in Operating Long-term Liabilities for the Period

definition_en: The increase in operating long-term liabilities for the current period refers to the amount by which the ending balance of a company's operating long-term liabilities (such as long-term payables, deferred income, and other non-current liabilities related to operating activities) exceeds its beginning balance during the current accounting period. This figure is typically derived directly from the difference between the beginning and ending balances of operating long-term liabilities on the balance sheet, reflecting changes in the company's long-term debt financing needs arising from its ongoing operations.

Current period statistical data refers to the fundamental raw data directly recorded, collected, or aggregated within a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as the direct input for calculating derived financial metrics like growth rates, year-over-year comparisons, and sequential comparisons, and is not itself derived from formulas.

Current period dividend distribution refers to the cash or stock dividends declared by a company's board of directors and actually paid to shareholders during the current accounting period. It reflects the portion of the company's profit distribution used to reward shareholders in the current period and is a significant actual amount recorded in the statement of profit distribution.

Current period share capital refers to the total par value of all shares outstanding (typically common shares) issued by the company during the current accounting period (e.g., the current year or quarter). It is a fundamental component of the company's owner's equity, directly reflecting the scale of capital contributed by shareholders. The data can be obtained directly from the company's balance sheet or share capital account.

term_en.name: Increase in Current Period Operating Revenue

definition_en: Increase in Current Period Operating Revenue refers to the difference between the total operating revenue of an enterprise in the current accounting period (current period) and the total operating revenue in the previous accounting period used as a comparative benchmark (base period). It directly reflects the absolute growth in the enterprise's core business revenue between two comparable periods.

term_en.name: Credit Turnover for the Current Period

definition_en: Credit turnover for the current period refers to the original aggregate total of all increases or decreases recorded on the credit side of a specific accounting account during a defined accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is derived directly from the item-by-item entries in accounting vouchers and serves as the fundamental data reflecting the total volume of credit-side activity for that account.

Total assets for the period refer to the aggregate value of all economic resources owned or controlled by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It is the most critical summary figure on the balance sheet, directly reflecting the scale of the enterprise.

Current period sales volume refers to the total quantity of products or goods actually sold to customers by an enterprise within the current accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating sales revenue and cost of sales, typically sourced directly from the enterprise's business systems or sales records.

Current period sales volume refers to the quantity of products or services actually sold to customers by an enterprise within the current accounting period (such as the current month, quarter, or year). It is one of the most fundamental raw data points in business operations, typically sourced directly from sales records, and serves as the basis for calculating other sales-related metrics (such as sales revenue and sales growth rate).

Current non-current liabilities refer to the portion of a company's long-term debt that is due for repayment within one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer) from the current balance sheet date. They typically consist of specific items such as the current portion of long-term borrowings, bonds payable due within one year, and long-term payables due within one year, reflecting the economic obligations the company must settle in the near term.

Quantity of Current Purchase refers to the physical quantity of goods or raw materials actually purchased and received (or put into storage) by an enterprise during a specific business occurrence. It is a fundamental business data point, typically sourced directly from original documents such as purchase orders and receiving reports, reflecting the scale of the actual purchase transaction completed in a single instance or within a specific period.

Book value of equity refers to the residual value attributable to the company's shareholders (owners) after subtracting total liabilities from total assets on the company's balance sheet. It represents the shareholders' equity stake in the company under accounting measurement and is commonly used as a basis for calculating other financial metrics.

Equity capital refers to the residual interest in the total assets of an enterprise after deducting all liabilities, which belongs to the owners (shareholders) and represents their ownership and investment in the enterprise.

Material price standard refers to the pre-determined, approved per-unit price for direct materials consumed in producing one unit of product under standard costing. It is typically determined based on comprehensive factors including market conditions, supplier contracts, and full cost elements such as freight, insurance, and inspection fees, serving as one of the foundational data points for calculating direct material standard cost.

Material original price refers to the price stated on the original invoice provided by the production unit or supplier when a company purchases materials. It serves as the fundamental data for material cost calculation and typically excludes subsequent additional expenses such as transportation and storage.

Actual material consumption refers to the quantity of materials actually requisitioned and consumed for product manufacturing during a specific production period. It is directly derived from original production records (such as material requisition forms and inventory count records) and serves as the fundamental data for calculating direct material costs and conducting cost variance analysis.

english: Standard Price per Unit of Material

definition_en: Material standard unit price refers to the predetermined base price per unit of material established for setting cost standards under a standard costing system. It typically includes all necessary expenditures such as purchase price, freight and miscellaneous charges, transportation losses, and procurement and storage costs, serving as fundamental input data for calculating composite indicators like direct material standard cost.

chinese: 单位产品材料消耗定额

definition_en: Standard material usage refers to the predetermined quantity of raw materials that should be consumed to produce one unit of product in a manufacturing process. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and cost control, used to calculate the standard cost of direct materials and as a benchmark for comparing actual material consumption to conduct cost variance analysis.

term_en.name: Standard Purchase Price per Unit of Material

definition_en: The Standard Purchase Price per Unit of Material is a predetermined base price standard established by an enterprise for implementing a standard cost system, used to account for the unit cost of materials. It is typically determined comprehensively based on market research, supplier quotations, historical purchasing data, and forecasts of future price trends, serving as a key input value for calculating the standard cost of direct materials.

Materials procurement refers to the actual expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies required for production and operation. These expenditures are typically recorded and recognized directly based on original documents such as invoices and freight bills, constituting a significant component of inventory cost.

Standard total wages refers to the aggregate sum of all labor remuneration paid to all employees within a specific period, directly calculated based on actual payments. It serves as the foundational data for payroll accounting, encompassing time wages, piece-rate wages, bonuses, allowances and subsidies, overtime pay, etc. The calculation is based on the actual amount disbursed, irrespective of the funding source or payment method.

The standard normal quantile refers to the specific value in a standard normal distribution (a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1) that corresponds to a given cumulative probability (or significance level). It indicates that the probability of a random variable being less than or equal to this value equals the given probability. In financial and statistical applications, it is typically obtained directly by consulting statistical tables or using statistical software functions (e.g., NORM.S.INV) and serves as a fundamental parameter.

The Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution Function is a fundamental mathematical and statistical function used to calculate the probability that a random variable in a standard normal distribution (with mean 0 and standard deviation 1) takes a value less than or equal to a specific point. It is the integral of the probability density function from negative infinity to that point, and is commonly used as a calculation tool or model input parameter in fields such as finance and risk management.

term_en.name: Value of Standard Normal Random Variable

definition_en: The value of a standard normal random variable refers to a specific numerical value of a random variable that follows a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. It is commonly used in probability and statistics as a fundamental input parameter for calculating the probability of specific events (such as default probability, Value at Risk).

The standard tax rate is the basic statutory percentage or scale directly stipulated in tax laws for calculating a taxpayer's tax payable. It does not depend on the calculation of other financial indicators and is one of the core data points in tax policy.

Sample size refers to the number of individuals or observational units contained in a sample in statistics and data analysis, typically denoted by the letter n. It is a fundamental parameter for sampling inference, hypothesis testing, and statistical analysis, and its magnitude directly affects the precision and reliability of research results.

Daily index return refers to the percentage change in the price of a stock market index (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, CSI 300, etc.) between two consecutive trading days, reflecting the overall market performance within a single day. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating composite metrics such as market excess return.

Annual interest income refers to the total interest return received by an individual or enterprise within a complete fiscal year from interest-bearing assets such as deposits, bonds, and loans, based on the contractually agreed interest rate and period.

term_en.name: Number of Compounding Periods Per Year

english: Number of Compounding Periods per Year

definition_en: The number of compounding periods per year refers to the frequency with which interest is calculated and added to the principal for subsequent interest calculations within a one-year period. For example, compounding twice a year means interest is calculated every six months and added to the principal.

term_en.name: Number of Compounding Periods Per Year

english: Number of Compounding Periods per Year

definition_en: The number of compounding periods per year refers to the frequency with which interest is calculated or compounded within one year. It is a predetermined contractual or agreed-upon parameter that defines the time unit for interest calculation (e.g., annually, semi-annually, quarterly, monthly, etc.) and serves as the basis for determining the periodic interest rate and the amount of interest per period.

Daily operating revenue refers to the total income generated by a company from selling goods or providing services during one day (typically a calendar day) of business operations. It serves as fundamental raw data reflecting the scale and effectiveness of daily business activities.

Periodic interest payment refers to the amount of interest that a debtor is required to pay to a creditor at the end of each interest accrual period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, or annually) as stipulated in a loan or bond agreement. It is calculated based on the principal, agreed interest rate, and interest accrual period, and constitutes a fundamental component of debt cash flow.

Cost per conversion refers to the fixed fee incurred each time a company converts marketable securities (such as bonds, stocks) into cash in financial management. It is a fixed cost parameter, independent of the number of conversions, primarily used to calculate total conversion costs.

Market price per share refers to the real-time transaction price of a listed company's stock formed through continuous bidding by buyers and sellers in secondary markets such as securities exchanges. It reflects the market investors' comprehensive assessment of the company's current value and future expectations, and is dynamically changing.

Cash dividend per share refers to the amount of cash dividend declared and actually distributed by a listed company to shareholders per share of stock, based on current earnings, cash flow, and distribution policy. It is a specific declared value or historical data that directly reflects the company's dividend policy.

Permanent difference refers to the discrepancy between pre-tax accounting profit (or total profit) and taxable income, arising from fundamental differences in the scope and criteria for recognizing revenues and expenses between accounting standards and tax laws, which cannot be reversed in future periods.

Registered capital is the total amount of capital subscribed by all shareholders or promoters at the time of a company's establishment, which is legally registered with the company registration authority. It is a fundamental figure stipulated in the company's articles of association, representing the maximum limit of shareholders' commitment to the company's liabilities and serving as the credit foundation for the company's business operations.

Beginning balance of current liabilities refers to the total book value of all debts that need to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle longer than one year at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is the opening figure of the current liabilities account on the balance sheet, typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous period's balance sheet, and serves as the fundamental baseline data for calculating changes in current liabilities during the current period.

Beginning balance of current assets refers to the total book value of all current asset items at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is directly taken from the ending balance of the previous accounting period's balance sheet and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as average current assets.

The ending balance of current assets refers to the total book value of all current asset items of an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). These assets include cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments, notes receivable, accounts receivable, inventory, etc., which are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. This figure is a point-in-time amount directly obtained from accounting ledgers or the balance sheet at period-end.

Shares outstanding typically refers to the total number of a company's issued common shares held by public investors, excluding treasury shares repurchased and held by the company itself. It is fundamental data for a company's capital structure and is usually obtained directly from the company's share register or notes to the financial statements.

Shares outstanding refers to the total number of common shares issued by a company and held by investors (including the public and insiders) at a specific point in time (such as the financial statement date), excluding treasury shares repurchased and held by the company. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating metrics such as market capitalization and earnings per share.

Shares outstanding refers to the total number of shares issued by a publicly listed company that are freely tradable on a stock exchange. It excludes shares that are subject to long-term lock-up or restricted from sale by company management, controlling shareholders, etc.

Number of shares outstanding refers to the total number of shares issued by a listed company that can be freely traded on a stock exchange. It excludes shares that are subject to long-term lock-ups or sales restrictions by company management, controlling shareholders, etc.

A floating rate refers to an interest rate in a borrowing or investment contract whose specific value is not fixed but is periodically adjusted according to changes in an agreed market benchmark rate (such as the Loan Prime Rate LPR or the London Interbank Offered Rate LIBOR). It is typically determined by adding or subtracting an agreed spread (floating points) from the benchmark rate.

The consumption tax rate is a statutory percentage or fixed amount standard stipulated by national tax laws for specific consumer goods or services, used to calculate the payable consumption tax. It is a fundamental policy parameter that cannot be derived from other financial indicators.

Consumption basket weight refers to the value derived from household consumption expenditure surveys when compiling the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It reflects the proportion or importance of various goods and services in total household consumption expenditure and determines the influence of different consumption items in CPI calculation.

Consumption amount typically refers to the total amount paid by individuals, households, or enterprises for purchasing goods and services within a specific period. It serves as the fundamental raw data for recording transactions, commonly found in sales documents, consumption records, or financial statements, and forms the basis for calculating related taxes (such as consumption tax) and analyzing consumption behavior.

english: Market Capitalization of Stock Connect-Hong Kong Stocks

definition_en: Southbound Stock Connect market capitalization refers to the total market value of all issued shares of Hong Kong-listed companies eligible for the Southbound Stock Connect program. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of the company's issued shares by the current market trading price of the stock, directly reflecting the overall market valuation size of the company.

Fuel cost refers to the actual expenses incurred by an enterprise or individual due to the use of fuel (such as gasoline, diesel). It is typically directly allocated based on original documents like refueling invoices, fuel consumption records, or mileage traveled, and constitutes a fundamental expense in cost accounting.

State transition probability refers to the likelihood of transitioning from a current state to various other states at the next moment during the development and change of a system or event. It is typically derived from historical data statistics and serves as the core foundational probability data in stochastic process models such as Markov chains.

chinese: 按现价计算的最终消费

definition_en: Final consumption at current prices refers to the total value of all goods and services purchased and used by households and government sectors to satisfy their own needs, measured at actual market prices during the accounting period (e.g., the current year) in national economic accounting. It is fundamental data obtained directly from sources such as household surveys and government consumption statistics, rather than being calculated from other financial indicators.

On-hand inventory refers to the quantity of materials or products actually stored in a company's warehouse at a specific point in time, which is readily available for production or sales. It is fundamental data obtained directly through physical counting or real-time recording in an inventory management system.

Current Period Consumption Quantity refers to the original quantity or value available for consumption in the current period (e.g., this year) within a consumption decision model. It is a given baseline figure, typically serving as an input variable for calculating present value or future consumption capacity, rather than a composite metric derived from other financial indicators.

Current market price refers to the actual transaction price of an asset or commodity at a specific point in time in an active, open market. It reflects the current market supply and demand relationship and is real-time data obtained directly from market observation, rather than derived from model calculations.

Spot price volatility refers to the phenomenon where the immediate transaction prices of commodities, securities, or financial assets in the spot market fluctuate upward and downward over time. This fluctuation results from the combined effects of various complex factors such as market supply and demand, macroeconomic conditions, policy adjustments, and unexpected events, and serves as fundamental market observation data.

Cash refers to monetary funds that a company can immediately use for payments, including cash on hand, bank deposits, and other monetary funds. On the balance sheet, it is typically combined with cash equivalents and presented as 'Cash and Cash Equivalents', representing the most liquid asset of an enterprise.

Cash and cash equivalents refer to assets held by an enterprise that are highly liquid, can be used for payment at any time, or can be rapidly converted into a known amount of cash. They primarily include cash on hand, bank deposits, other monetary funds, and short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value (such as short-term treasury bills, money market funds, etc.).

Total cash inflow refers to the aggregate sum of cash and cash equivalents actually received by an enterprise during a specific accounting period through all operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. It is a fundamental raw data item in the cash flow statement, directly reflecting the enterprise's ability to generate cash.

Cash equivalents refer to short-term investments held by an enterprise that have a very short maturity (typically within three months), high liquidity, are readily convertible to known amounts of cash, and are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. They are considered substitutes for cash and are presented together with cash in the statement of cash flows.

Cash dividend is a profit distribution method where a listed company directly pays a portion of its after-tax profits to shareholders in cash, serving as one of the primary forms of investment return for shareholders from the company.

Total cash dividends refer to the aggregate amount of cash dividends actually paid to all shareholders during a specific accounting period, as resolved by the board of directors or shareholders' meeting. It reflects the cash outflow from the company for profit distribution to shareholders.

Cash dividend refers to a method of distribution where a company pays a portion of its profits directly to shareholders in cash, representing a form of investment return for shareholders. The specific amount is typically determined by the company's board of directors based on profitability and dividend policy, and is directly reflected in the company's profit distribution plan.

Cash sales refer to the actual sales revenue received by an enterprise in the form of cash, bank deposits, or other immediate payment methods (such as electronic payments) when selling goods or providing services. It is the most fundamental raw data in sales operations, directly reflecting the revenue realized through cash sales models.

Production tax refers to the collective term for various taxes, surcharges, and fees levied by the government on production units for their production, sales, and business activities, as well as for the use of certain factors of production (such as land, labor, capital) in these activities. It is a primary data item directly generated from production and operating activities and serves as the basis for calculating net production tax.

Production subsidy refers to economic assistance or financial support provided directly by the government or relevant institutions to enterprises to support specific production activities or industries. It is typically used to reduce production costs, encourage the production of specific goods, or achieve specific socio-economic objectives.

Production volume refers to the quantity of products actually manufactured and completed by an enterprise or production unit within a specific period, which is available for sale or use. It is the most fundamental raw data in the production process, typically obtained directly through production records, statistical reports, etc., rather than being calculated from other financial or efficiency indicators.

Cost of capital amount refers to the periodic expenses that a company must pay for using externally raised or internal funds during production, operation, and investment processes, such as interest paid to creditors or dividends paid to shareholders. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating metrics like the cost of capital rate.

Surplus reserve refers to the accumulated funds that a company sets aside from its after-tax net profit at a certain proportion, retained internally for specific purposes, and constitutes an important component of owners' equity.

Direct labor cost refers to the total compensation paid by an enterprise directly to frontline production workers for manufacturing specific products or providing specific services. It typically includes wages, allowances, benefits, training expenses, etc., and is one of the core components constituting product manufacturing cost.

Direct labor cost refers to the labor costs directly incurred by an enterprise in producing specific products or providing specific services, which can be directly traced to specific cost objects (such as products, services, or projects). It typically includes wages, allowances, benefits, training expenses, etc., for direct production workers and is a key component of product production costs.

Total direct labor cost refers to the aggregate sum of all labor costs paid by an enterprise within a specific period for employees directly engaged in product manufacturing or providing specific services. It typically includes base wages, allowances, bonuses, benefits (such as social insurance and housing provident fund), and related training expenses, constituting a significant component of product cost.

Total direct manufacturing overhead refers to the sum of manufacturing costs that can be directly attributed to specific cost objects (such as products, batches, or production steps) during the production process. It is typically listed alongside direct materials and direct labor as an independent basic cost item for accumulation and recording in the cost calculation sheet.

Direct cost refers to production expenses that can be directly and conveniently attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, service, or project). The incurrence of these costs has a direct causal relationship with the specific product or service, typically including direct materials, direct labor, etc.

Direct material cost refers to the cost of materials that are directly incorporated into the product or are directly related to production and can be easily traced to specific cost objects during the production of goods or provision of services. It is typically calculated based on the actual quantity and unit price of materials issued, serving as fundamental raw data for cost accounting.
