Total direct material cost refers to the aggregate cost of all raw materials directly consumed and forming the physical substance of products during a specific accounting period (such as a month or a production cycle). It is typically calculated by directly summarizing source documents such as material requisition forms and purchase invoices, serving as fundamental data for product cost accounting.

A Relevant Price Index refers to a statistical indicator regularly published by official statistical agencies (such as the National Bureau of Statistics) to measure changes over time in the overall price level of specific goods, services, or industries. It is raw data directly collected from the market, reflecting trends of inflation or deflation, and is often used as an external reference in financial analysis and inventory measurement.

Relevant taxes and fees refer to the total of various taxes and surcharges that an enterprise is required to calculate based on tax bases such as operating revenue and sales, in accordance with national tax laws, and pay during its daily business operations. It primarily includes business tax, urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge, etc., and constitutes a fundamental data item forming part of the enterprise's costs and expenses.

Short-term investments refer to investments made by an enterprise to utilize temporarily idle funds, purchasing securities that can be readily converted into cash and are not intended to be held for more than one year (including one year), primarily including various marketable securities such as stocks and bonds.

term_en.name: Research and Development Expense Adjustment Item

definition_en: The Research and Development Expense Adjustment Item is a data entry in corporate financial statements, primarily used for adjustments when calculating metrics such as Economic Value Added (EVA). It is directly sourced from two parts of the financial statements: first, the 'Research and Development Expense' under the 'Administrative Expenses' line item on the income statement; second, the research and development expenditures capitalized as intangible assets during the period. This adjustment item is a fundamental raw data point and does not require calculation from other financial metrics.

Face value refers to the original amount or value explicitly stated on the face of a financial instrument (such as checks, drafts, promissory notes, bonds, stocks, etc.). It is the benchmark amount determined at the time of issuance and serves as the basis for calculating interest, discounting, or performing other financial processing. It is not derived from the calculation of other financial metrics.

The lease term refers to the total duration during which the lessee has the right to use the leased asset, as explicitly stipulated in the lease contract. It is the most fundamental time parameter in lease transactions, used for calculating financial metrics such as rent and lease payments.

The commencement date of the lease refers to the earlier of the date of the lease agreement signing and the date on which the parties to the lease commit to the principal terms of the lease. On this date, the lessee and lessor are required to classify the lease as either a finance lease or an operating lease based on the agreement terms and commence the relevant accounting recognition and measurement.

The lease end date refers to the specific date explicitly stipulated in the lease contract when the lease relationship terminates, the lessee is required to return the leased asset, or the lease right expires. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as the lease term and total lease payments.

chinese: 租赁资产公允市场价值
english: Fair Market Value of Leased Property

definition_en: Fair value of a leased asset refers to the market price that could be achieved in a fair transaction between knowledgeable, willing parties on the measurement date (such as the lease commencement date). It is typically determined based on the asset's normal selling price or professional appraisal value, and serves as critical data for lease accounting treatment (e.g., distinguishing between operating leases and finance leases) and rental calculations (e.g., break-even rent).

The lease commencement date is the date on which the lease contract formally takes effect or begins execution, typically referring to the earlier of the lease agreement signing date and the date on which the parties commit to the principal terms. It serves as the baseline date for determining the lease term, calculating lease payments, and performing related accounting treatments.

Rent payment frequency refers to the periodic time interval stipulated in a lease contract for the lessee to pay rent to the lessor, such as monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, or annually. It is a fundamental term of the lease contract and serves as a prerequisite input for calculating specific rent payment amounts and formulating repayment schedules.

Dilutive potential ordinary shares refer to potential ordinary shares that, if converted into ordinary shares during the current accounting period, would result in a decrease in the company's earnings per share. It is a qualitative concept representing a class of financial instruments with dilution potential, such as convertible corporate bonds, warrants, and share options.

Taxation is a form of fiscal revenue obtained by the state to meet public needs, whereby it compulsorily and gratuitously participates in the distribution of social products based on public power, in accordance with legally established standards and procedures. For enterprises, taxation constitutes a statutory obligation calculated and paid to the government according to tax laws, directly impacting their profits and cash flow.

term_en.name: Total Liabilities at End of First Quarter

english: Total Liabilities at the End of Q1

definition_en: Total liabilities at the end of the first quarter refer to the aggregate value of present obligations arising from past transactions or events, which are expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits from the enterprise, as reported at the financial reporting date of the first quarter (typically January 1 to March 31). It reflects all debts assumed by the enterprise at the end of the first quarter and is generally calculated by directly summing the ending balances of all liability accounts from the accounting ledgers.

First Period Cash Cost refers to various cost expenses that require actual cash payments during the first specific period (e.g., the first period) of a project or business operation. These costs arise directly from business activities, typically including immediate cash outlays for procuring raw materials, paying employee compensation, settling rent payments, etc., and constitute an important component of the expected cash outflows in the first period.

First Period Dividend typically refers to the first cash dividend a company is expected to declare or pay to shareholders within a specific evaluation period (e.g., the next fiscal year). It is a direct outcome of the company's profit distribution decision, constitutes fundamental financial data, and is commonly used in valuation analyses such as the Dividend Discount Model.

First Period Sales Revenue refers to the total revenue generated by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific reporting period (typically the first financial quarter or first period). Its calculation is generally based on the product of sales volume and unit selling price during that period, reflecting the initial results of business activities for that period.

Tertiary industry production subsidies refer to non-repayable payments made directly by the government to production units (such as enterprises or institutions) within the tertiary industry (service sector) to support or promote their production activities. It is one of the key original components in macroeconomic accounting for calculating net taxes on production and value added.

Secondary industry production tax refers to the total amount of various taxes paid to the government by the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) within a country or region during a specific period, arising from the use of production factors in production, sales, and operational activities. It is a fundamental production tax data item classified by industry in national economic accounting and serves as a crucial original component for calculating indicators such as net taxes on production.

Secondary Industry Production Subsidy refers to fiscal grant funds directly allocated by the government to relevant enterprises to support production activities in the secondary industry (primarily including manufacturing, construction, etc.). In accounting treatment, such subsidies are typically directly recorded in profit and loss accounts such as 'Subsidy Income' or 'Other Income', constituting fundamental raw data that does not require calculation through other financial metrics.

term_en.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter

english: Total Assets at the Beginning of Q2

definition_en: Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter refers to the total book value of assets on the first day of the second quarter (typically April 1), which is a direct line-item figure on the balance sheet, reflecting the overall asset scale of the enterprise at the start of the second quarter.

term_en.name: Total Liabilities at End of Second Quarter

english: Total Liabilities at the End of Q2

definition_en: Total liabilities at the end of the second quarter refer to the aggregate book value of all liabilities recognized and consolidated according to accounting books and standards at the conclusion of the second fiscal quarter (typically June 30). This figure reflects the total present obligations of the enterprise at a specific point in time that are expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits, and is generally directly reported under the 'Total Liabilities' line item on the balance sheet.

The vesting period refers to a predetermined, fixed duration in agreements such as insurance or share-based payments, starting from the grant date and lasting until the beneficiary (e.g., an employee or policyholder) becomes eligible to exercise the right (e.g., to exercise options or receive insurance benefits). During this period, the beneficiary must continue to provide services or meet other conditions for the right to ultimately vest.

Cash outflow from financing activities refers to the total amount of cash actually paid out by an enterprise during the reporting period due to financing activities (such as repayment of debt principal, payment of dividends or interest, repurchase of company shares, etc.). It is a fundamental item directly presented in the statement of cash flows, used to calculate the net cash flow generated from financing activities.

Financing costs refer to the various direct expenses incurred by an enterprise during the process of raising funds (such as issuing stocks or bonds, or obtaining loans), including handling fees, issuance fees, legal fees, audit fees, and appraisal fees. These costs are original expenditure items in accounting, typically recorded directly in the books, and serve as fundamental data for calculating the cost of capital.

Financing cost amount refers to the total sum of actual, directly recordable expenses incurred by an enterprise in the process of raising funds (such as borrowing, issuing bonds, or stocks) to obtain capital, including items like loan interest, bond issuance fees, and stock underwriting fees. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating metrics such as the cost of capital rate.

Amount of funds raised refers to the total amount of capital actually collected and received by a company within a specific period through equity financing (e.g., issuing shares), debt financing (e.g., issuing bonds, bank loans), or other financing channels. It is a fundamental metric reflecting the scale of corporate financing.

Administrative expenses refer to various costs incurred by the enterprise's administrative departments in organizing and managing the overall production and operational activities, such as management personnel compensation, office expenses, depreciation, travel expenses, etc. It is a period expense on the income statement and is directly charged to the current period's profit or loss.

term_en.name: Labor and Unemployment Insurance Premiums and Taxes in Administrative Expenses

chinese: 管理费用-税金及保险费
管理费中的社保与税金
行政费用中的劳动待业保险与税金
english: Labor and Unemployment Insurance and Taxes in Administrative Expenses
Administrative Expenses: Taxes and Social Insurance

definition_en: Labor and unemployment insurance premiums and taxes in administrative expenses are specific cost line items incurred by the enterprise's administrative departments for organizing and managing production and operational activities. Among these, 'Taxes' primarily refer to property tax, vehicle and vessel usage tax, land use tax, stamp duty, and other taxes recorded under administrative expenses; 'Labor and Unemployment Insurance Premiums' include the labor insurance and unemployment insurance premiums paid by the enterprise for its employees. These expenses are directly recorded in the accounting books based on their actual occurrence and serve as fundamental raw data for calculating indicators such as value added in the construction industry.

Taxes in administrative expenses refer to various tax expenditures incurred and recorded under the current profit and loss account 'Administrative Expenses' in accordance with tax laws during the daily organization and management of production and business operations, such as property tax, vehicle and vessel tax, land use tax, and stamp duty.

Cumulative actual contract costs incurred refer to the total sum of costs that an enterprise has actually expended and recorded in fulfilling its contractual obligations under a construction contract up to a specific date. These costs arise directly from actual expenditures, such as material costs, labor costs, and machinery usage fees, and serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics like the percentage of contract completion. According to accounting standards, their scope excludes material costs not yet utilized (e.g., materials not delivered to the site or not installed) and advance payments made to subcontractors for work not yet performed.

The pure interest rate refers to the fundamental rate of return that should be obtained from capital lending under ideal market conditions with no inflation and no risks (such as default risk, liquidity risk, etc.). It serves as the benchmark for asset pricing and interest rate structure analysis in financial markets, and is generally regarded as the interest rate on risk-free securities when expected inflation is zero.

Tax Adjustment Decrease Amount refers to the total sum of amounts that an enterprise needs to deduct from its total accounting profit when calculating taxable income, in accordance with tax regulations. These deductions typically involve tax-exempt, tax-reduced, or loss-offsetting preferential items permitted by tax law, such as government bond interest income, eligible dividends, and allowable carry-forward losses from prior years.

Operating long-term liabilities refer to debts arising from a company's daily business operations with a repayment period exceeding one year. They are typically presented directly under the long-term liabilities section of the balance sheet and represent financial obligations undertaken to support long-term business activities.

Cash outflow from operating activities refers to the total amount of cash actually paid by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal operations. It reflects the cash expended by the enterprise for purchasing goods, receiving services, paying employee compensation, settling taxes, and other operating activities.

term_en.name: Total Cash Outflow from Operating Activities

english: Total Cash Outflow from Operating Activities

definition_en: Total cash outflow from operating activities refers to the aggregate sum of all cash actually disbursed by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal functioning. This includes cash expenditures directly related to core business activities, such as purchasing raw materials, paying employee salaries, remitting various taxes and fees, and covering rent, utilities, and similar expenses.

term_en.name: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities

chinese: 经营活动现金流量净额
english: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities

definition_en: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities refers to the net amount of total cash inflows generated from a company's core business operations (such as sales of goods and provision of services) during a specific period, minus the total cash outflows paid to sustain these operating activities. It directly reflects the 'cash-generating' capacity of a company's core business and is a key indicator for assessing the quality of earnings and short-term solvency.

Cash inflow from operating activities refers to the total actual cash received by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as selling goods, providing services, and receiving tax refunds, during its daily production and operating activities. It is a key metric in the cash flow statement that reflects the core cash-generating capacity of the enterprise's main business.

Cash outflow from operating activities refers to the total amount of cash actually paid by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal operations. It primarily includes cash paid for goods and services received, cash paid to and on behalf of employees, cash paid for various taxes and fees, and other cash payments related to operating activities.

Beginning Operating Liabilities refers to the book value of the 'Operating Liabilities' account on a company's balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations (such as procurement, production, and sales) that is due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle at the beginning of the period, serving as fundamental data for calculating metrics like Net Operating Assets.

Beginning Operating Assets refers to the book value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter) that are used for daily business operations. It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous period's balance sheet and serves as a fundamental data point for calculating metrics such as Net Operating Assets.

Operating assets ending balance refers to the total book value of various assets used in daily production and business operations at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It typically includes assets directly involved in the operating cycle, such as inventory, accounts receivable, and fixed assets, and serves as fundamental data for assessing a company's operational scale and efficiency.

End Year refers to a specific point in time or period endpoint preset in financial calculations or analysis, serving as the cut-off date or benchmark date for calculating indicators such as service years, depreciation, and discounted cash flows. It is a fundamental input parameter that typically cannot be derived from other financial metrics.

Ending month refers to the month in which a specific financial period (such as an accounting period, project cycle, or calculation cycle) terminates. It is a fundamental temporal identifier used to determine the endpoint of the time range covered by a calculation or report.

Maintenance expense refers to the costs incurred by an enterprise to maintain or restore assets such as fixed assets, equipment, and vehicles to their normal operating condition. It typically includes expenditures on labor, materials, and spare parts. In management accounting, it is often treated as a mixed cost for cost behavior analysis to decompose into fixed and variable components.

Maintenance capital expenditure refers to the capital outlays or working capital investments that an enterprise must make during normal operations to sustain the continuous and stable functioning of existing production or service capacity. These investments are typically used for equipment maintenance, renewal, technological upgrades, or replenishing necessary working capital, ensuring the enterprise can consistently generate revenue and cash flow. It is not an ordinary operating expense but rather an essential investment project required to maintain long-term operational capability.

The Z-value for a confidence level is a critical point value on the standard normal distribution corresponding to a specific confidence level (e.g., 90%, 95%, 99%) in statistics. It represents the quantile point under the standard normal distribution curve where the central area equals that confidence level. For example, the Z-value for a 95% confidence level is approximately 1.96, meaning that 95% of the data in a standard normal distribution falls within the range of the mean ± 1.96 standard deviations. This value is typically obtained by consulting a standard normal distribution table or using statistical software, and is used for constructing confidence intervals or conducting hypothesis testing.

The Z-value corresponding to a confidence level refers to the critical value in a standard normal distribution that corresponds to a specific confidence level (e.g., 90%, 95%, 99%). It represents the distance from the mean to that point on the normal distribution curve, where the area (probability) covered equals half of the confidence level (for a two-tailed test). This value is typically obtained by consulting a standard normal distribution table or using statistical software and serves as a key foundational parameter for constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis testing.

Employee bonus and benefits refer to compensation expense items directly approved and disbursed by an enterprise to motivate and reward employees, based on company policies, performance agreements, etc. They constitute original costs and typically include various bonuses, allowances, and welfare expenses.

term_en.name: Number of Shares Held by Shareholders

definition_en: The number of shares held by shareholders refers to the quantity of shares directly owned and recorded by an individual shareholder or entity in a company. It is fundamental data reflecting the extent of a shareholder's ownership in the company, typically sourced from the shareholder register or securities transaction records.

Months of Shares in Circulation refers to the total duration, typically measured in months, during which a stock has been freely tradable from the date of its initial public offering or the lifting of trading restrictions to the current date. It is a time-based fundamental data point, not a financial metric derived from calculations using financial statement line items.

The share float period refers to the specific time frame or status during which shares issued by a company can be freely bought, sold, and transferred on public markets (such as stock exchanges) without restrictions. It serves as the fundamental condition for calculating metrics such as time-weighted average shares outstanding.

The stock split ratio refers to the proportional number of new shares into which one existing share is divided when a company conducts a stock split. For example, a 2-for-1 split has a ratio of 2. It is a parameter directly determined by the company's board of directors to adjust fundamental data such as the number of shares outstanding and the price per share.

Share repurchase reduces share capital refers to the financial action where a listed company uses its own funds to buy back a portion of its issued shares from the open market and subsequently cancels these shares, leading to a direct reduction in the company's registered capital (i.e., share capital). This is a method for companies to adjust their capital structure or return cash to shareholders.

Stock repurchase date refers to the specific date on which a listed company actually buys back its outstanding shares from the open market or specific channels. This is a point-in-time record of the actual execution of the repurchase transaction, classified as basic event data.

Stock market price refers to the transaction price of a stock formed through real-time trading between buyers and sellers on secondary markets such as stock exchanges. It reflects the market's immediate assessment of the company's value and is dynamically changing.

Stock current price, also known as the stock's spot price or market price, refers to the actual transaction price in the latest trade executed on a secondary market (such as a stock exchange), matched between buyers and sellers through real-time trading. It is directly determined by immediate market supply and demand, reflecting investors' real-time consensus on the company's value.

The stock split ratio is a predetermined plan resolved and announced by the company's board of directors, used to divide one share with a higher par value into multiple shares with a lower par value. It is a given fundamental parameter (e.g., 1:2), not derived through calculation, and is primarily used to adjust the company's number of shares outstanding.

term_en.name: Additional Share Capital from Stock Option Exercise

english: Additional Share Capital from Stock Option Exercise

definition_en: Additional share capital from stock option exercise refers to the specific number of shares newly issued by a company when employees or investors exercise their stock option contracts, resulting in an increase in the company's total share capital. This additional share capital constitutes a fundamental factual change in the company's equity structure, arising directly from the exercise of options rather than through financial calculations or adjustments.

Par value of stock is the legal amount explicitly stated on the face of a stock certificate when issued by a joint-stock company, denominated in 'yuan per share'. It is the legal face value stipulated in the company's articles of association or determined at issuance, serving as the basis for calculating share capital and does not represent the actual market value of the stock.

Self-manufactured semi-finished goods refer to intermediate products that are produced in-house, have undergone partial processing stages, but are not yet finalized as finished goods and require further processing. In accounting, they are classified as a type of inventory, and their cost typically includes raw materials consumed, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead.

Operating expenses refer to the total of various costs actually incurred by an enterprise in its daily business activities to maintain normal operations, such as employee compensation, logistics and transportation fees, marketing expenses, office space rent, and equipment maintenance costs. These expenses are typically recorded and accounted for based on actual occurrences and constitute one of the fundamental items in an enterprise's income statement.

Marketing expenses refer to the various direct costs incurred by an enterprise in the process of promoting and selling its products or services. These typically include advertising fees, promotional expenses, market research costs, sales personnel salaries, and travel expenses. These costs are directly allocated based on actual occurrences and are used to reflect the investment costs in the enterprise's marketing activities.

chinese: 融资活动产生的现金流量

definition_en: Cash flow from financing activities is a core component of the cash flow statement, directly recording the cash inflows and outflows generated by all activities related to raising capital and returning value to investors during a specific accounting period. These activities primarily include issuing stocks or bonds, borrowing from banks, repaying debt principal, paying dividends, or conducting share buybacks. It reflects how a company obtains funds through financing and how it distributes funds to capital providers, serving as a crucial basis for evaluating a company's financing strategy and the health of its financial structure.

Administrative expenses refer to various costs incurred by a company's board of directors, administrative departments, or costs that should be borne uniformly by the company in organizing and managing production and operational activities. It is a fundamental expense item on the income statement, directly recording the expenditures in the company's daily operational management.

chinese: 衍生金融工具公允价值

definition_en: The fair value of derivative instruments refers to the price that would be received to sell a derivative asset or paid to transfer a derivative liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. It is typically determined directly based on market quotations, valuation models, or third-party quotes, reflecting the true value of the derivative instrument under current market conditions.

term_en.name: Maximum Expected Profit of Abandoned Alternatives

chinese: 机会成本中的放弃收益
english: Maximum Expected Profit of Forgone Alternatives

definition_en: In decision analysis, when selecting one alternative from multiple options, the maximum expected profit of abandoned alternatives refers to the profit value of the alternative with the highest expected return among all unselected options. It represents the potential benefit that could have been gained from the best foregone alternative due to choosing the current option, serving as a key foundational data point for calculating opportunity cost.

Loading and unloading charges refer to the actual or payable expenses incurred by an enterprise during the transportation of goods for operations such as loading goods onto transport vehicles or unloading them from transport vehicles. It is an original cost in accounting, directly allocated to the cost of relevant assets (such as inventory) or recognized as a current period expense.

Total number of observations refers to the overall count of individuals, events, or records contained within a dataset in statistics or data analysis. It is the most fundamental counting metric, typically obtained by directly tallying the entries in the dataset, and is used to describe the sample size or the volume of data.

Number of observations refers to the total count of data points collected or used during data analysis or statistical calculations, i.e., the length of the data series or the total number of observations. It serves as a fundamental raw parameter for many financial and statistical calculations, such as computing standard deviation, mean, etc.

Planned production and sales volume refers to the quantitative targets set by an enterprise during the budgeting or planning stage for the expected production and sales of a specific product over a future period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annual). It serves as fundamental input data for formulating production and sales plans, production budgets, and sales budgets.

Planned Unit Selling Price refers to the pre-determined, expected market sales price set by an enterprise for each unit of product during operational planning. It is a fundamental planning parameter established based on a comprehensive analysis of market conditions, product costs, competitive landscape, and corporate strategic objectives (such as market share and profit targets), used for subsequent revenue forecasting, profit planning, and budget preparation.

Planned fixed costs refer to the pre-determined or estimated costs within a company's or project's financial budget or operating plan, where the total amount does not vary with changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume) over a specific period and within a certain range of activity.

Planned operating cost refers to the pre-estimated, expected operating costs that an enterprise anticipates incurring to achieve sales or service targets for a specific period, as outlined in its budget or business plan. It is typically derived directly from historical data, business volume forecasts, unit cost factors, etc., and serves as fundamental data for preparing profit budgets and calculating planned net profit.

Planned operating revenue refers to the expected income target directly set by an enterprise for a budget or forecast period, based on assumptions about business activities such as sales volume and unit selling price. It serves as the starting point data for preparing budget statements like the planned income statement and is not derived from calculations using other financial indicators.

Planned financial expenses refer to the total estimated financial expenses that are projected to occur during a specific future period (e.g., a fiscal year), based on historical data, financing plans, interest rate forecasts, and other factors, when a company prepares its budget or financial plan. It serves as a fundamental input in the budgeting process for forecasting and planning purposes, rather than representing actual accounting results.

Planned selling price per unit refers to the predetermined expected selling price set for each unit of product or service when formulating sales budgets or making pricing decisions. It is typically determined based on a comprehensive analysis of factors such as market research, cost analysis, competitive strategy, and profit targets, and serves as the foundational data for calculating planned sales revenue and sales volume.

Planned sales volume refers to the number of units of products or services that a company plans or expects to sell during a specific budget or forecast period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It serves as the fundamental raw data for developing sales budgets, revenue forecasts, and resource allocation.

Planned selling expenses refer to the total estimated and approved expenditures for various marketing and sales activities, pre-planned by an enterprise within the budget period to achieve its sales targets. It is a fundamental data item in the enterprise's budget statements, typically serving as the starting point for budget preparation or as a direct input item.

The Interest Accrual Start Date refers to the starting point of the interest calculation period, from which interest begins to accrue on the principal of deposits, loans, or investments. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating the number of interest-bearing days and the interest expense.

The number of interest periods refers to the length of time or the quantity of cycles, determined by the start date and end date stipulated in a contract or agreement, used for calculating interest. It is a fundamental parameter in interest calculation, typically expressed in days, months, or years.

Interest accrual period days refer to the actual number of days from the start date to the end date (inclusive of both days) used as the basis for calculating interest, serving as the fundamental time unit for determining the interest amount.

The Interest Accrual End Date refers to the termination date of the period for calculating interest, serving as a key parameter for determining the number of interest-bearing days. For instance, in financial instruments such as deposits, loans, or bonds, interest is calculated up to this date.

Calculation base refers to the original underlying amount used in finance and accounting to compute specific expenses, taxes, or accruals. It is typically the initial data directly drawn from business records or financial statements, such as total payroll, original asset value, or operating revenue, and serves as the foundation for subsequent rate or percentage calculations.

Subscribed capital refers to the total amount of capital that investors have committed to purchase shares from the company and pay the corresponding consideration. It forms the basis of the company's paid-in capital or share capital and is typically recorded directly in the accounting books.

Accounting subsidy treatment refers to the specific accounting process in accounting practice for recognizing, measuring, and recording various subsidy payments received by an enterprise (such as government grants, position subsidies, etc.). It involves allocating the subsidy amount to the correct accounting accounts (such as non-operating income, deferred income, administrative expenses, etc.) based on its nature and purpose, and completing the corresponding accounting entries.

Security B Single Period Return refers to the ratio of the return obtained from investing in Security B (including capital gains, dividends, etc.) to the initial investment cost over a specific period (such as a day, month, or year). It reflects the basic investment return performance of that security during the period. It is a raw market observation data point, typically used as a foundational input for calculating other risk or portfolio metrics.

term_en.name: Security B Average Rate of Return

definition_en: The Security B average rate of return typically refers to the average expected return or historical average return of all stocks in the market or a specific market (such as the entire stock market) over a period (e.g., one year). In financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), it is often used as a benchmark parameter for measuring overall market performance and calculating the required rate of return for individual securities or portfolios.

Securities market price refers to the final transaction price of securities reached through bidding or negotiation between buyers and sellers in an open trading market. It is a direct reflection of market supply and demand, representing real-time observed raw data rather than being calculated through financial formulas.

term_en.name: Total Cash Inflow for the Period

english: Total Cash Inflow for the Period

definition_en: Total cash inflow for the period refers to the aggregate sum of all cash received by an enterprise through operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is a direct summary item in the cash flow statement, reflecting the enterprise's ability to generate cash during that period.

The error function is a special function in mathematics and statistics, defined as erf(x) = (2/√π) ∫₀ˣ e^{-t²} dt. It describes the probability that a random variable in a standard normal distribution falls within a specific range around the mean, commonly used to calculate probability values for normal distributions. In finance, it primarily serves as a computational tool in models involving normal distribution assumptions (such as option pricing and risk management), but it is not itself a financial metric derived from financial indicators.

Pre-adjusted stock price refers to the market trading price of a stock before corporate actions such as ex-rights, ex-dividends, rights issues, or stock splits, typically the closing price on the last trading day prior to the event. It is the original, unadjusted price data used to calculate adjustment factors to maintain comparability in the price series.

Adjusted beginning inventory refers to the book value of inventory recognized at the start of a new fiscal year after audit adjustments, correction of accounting errors, or prior period adjustments. It reflects a revised and more accurate opening inventory figure, serving as the basis for calculating current period inventory changes and costs.

Adjusted stock price refers to the historical stock price adjusted for corporate actions such as ex-rights and ex-dividends, aiming to eliminate the impact of factors like dividends, bonus shares, and rights offerings on price continuity, thereby making stock prices at different points in time comparable and serving as fundamental data for long-term trend analysis.

Financial expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise in the process of raising and using funds, primarily including interest expenses, financial institution service charges, and exchange gains or losses.

Book cost refers to the original cost actually incurred when an asset or inventory is acquired or produced, as recorded in the accounting books, and serves as the fundamental data for subsequent accounting treatment and cost calculation.

Purchase price refers to the total amount actually paid or payable by the buyer to acquire a specific good or service in a procurement transaction. It is typically calculated directly by multiplying the unit price of the good by the quantity purchased, and serves as the fundamental raw data forming the basis of an asset's initial cost or expense.

Purchase price refers to the original transaction amount paid directly to the seller according to the contract for acquiring an asset (such as inventory, fixed assets) or service. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating procurement costs, cash outflows, and other financial metrics, and typically excludes subsequent expenses such as taxes, freight, and other charges.

Purchase unit price refers to the price paid for a single item or service in a procurement transaction. It serves as the fundamental data constituting the total procurement cost and is typically obtained directly from purchase contracts, orders, or invoices.

Purchase quantity refers to the specific number of units actually purchased or agreed upon in procurement or trading activities to acquire goods, services, or financial assets. It is the fundamental raw data constituting the transaction amount, typically obtained directly from business documents such as orders and invoices.

Cash received from purchase returns refers to the actual cash amount recovered by an enterprise from suppliers due to the return of previously purchased goods or materials. This cash inflow reflects the reverse cash flow of procurement activities and is a specific item of operating cash inflows when preparing the cash flow statement.

Purchase price refers to the original price directly paid by an enterprise to a supplier to acquire goods or services during procurement. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating purchase costs, input VAT, and other financial metrics, and typically excludes additional expenses such as transportation and customs duties.

Credit amount refers to the total sum of all economic transaction amounts recorded on the credit side (i.e., the right side) of a specific accounting account during a particular accounting period (such as a month or a quarter). It is directly derived from the entries in accounting vouchers and reflects the total increase or decrease in the account due to credit transactions during the period.

Loan principal refers to the original amount borrowed by the borrower from a lending institution (such as a bank), which is used to calculate interest and determine the repayment schedule. It is a core element in the loan agreement and serves as the foundation for all subsequent financial calculations.

The weight of Asset A refers to a predetermined proportion or coefficient assigned to a specific Asset A when calculating portfolio risk (e.g., standard deviation) or regulatory capital requirements (e.g., credit risk-weighted assets). It reflects the relative importance of that asset within the overall portfolio or risk exposure, typically set directly based on regulatory provisions, internal policies, or investment strategies, rather than derived from a formula.

In the context of banking regulation, the Asset B Weight specifically refers to the fixed risk weight percentage (e.g., 0%, 20%, 50%, etc.) assigned to different categories of on-balance-sheet assets (such as cash, corporate loans, residential mortgages, etc.) in the 'G4B-1 On-balance-sheet Credit Risk-Weighted Assets Calculation Table (Standardized Approach)'. This weight is directly prescribed by the regulatory authority (e.g., the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission) based on the risk characteristics of the asset. It is used to calculate credit risk-weighted assets and serves as fundamental data for regulatory capital requirements, rather than being derived from financial formulas.

Asset acquisition price refers to the consideration amount directly paid to the seller to obtain ownership of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, equipment, etc.) at the time of purchase. It is typically determined based on transaction contracts or documentation and serves as the fundamental original data for subsequent accounting treatment and financial analysis.

An asset price series refers to a data sequence formed by recording and arranging the market transaction prices of a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) at different consecutive time points (e.g., per minute, daily, weekly) in financial markets. It is the most fundamental raw observational data in financial analysis and serves as the basis for calculating derived metrics such as asset returns and volatility.

Asset impairment loss refers to the loss recognized in financial statements when the carrying value of an asset (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.) exceeds its recoverable amount. This reflects a decline in the asset's value and directly impacts the company's current-period profit.

Asset selling price refers to the actual transfer amount of an asset agreed upon by both buyers and sellers in a specific transaction, which is the actual transaction price determined upon completion of the transaction.

term_en.name: Original Value of Assets at Beginning of Period

english: Initial Asset Cost at Period Start
Opening Historical Cost of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Original value of assets at the beginning of the period refers to the original acquisition cost of fixed assets at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month), including the purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, installation expenses, and all other necessary expenditures incurred to bring the asset to its intended usable condition. It is a fundamental historical data point obtained directly from accounting ledgers or asset cards, serving as the starting point for subsequent depreciation calculations and the determination of net asset value.

term_en.name: Ending Balance of Monetary Capital in the Balance Sheet

english: Cash and Cash Equivalents at Period End

definition_en: Refers to the total amount of funds held by an enterprise on the balance sheet date (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, year-end) that can be used for immediate payment, including the aggregate ending balances of accounting items such as cash on hand, bank deposits, and other monetary funds.

chinese: 资本形成价格平减指数
资本形成总额平减指数
english: Price Index of Gross Capital Formation

definition_en: The Gross Capital Formation Price Index is an index used to measure changes in the price level of gross capital formation (such as fixed asset investment, inventory changes, etc.). Its primary function is to convert gross capital formation calculated at current market prices (nominal value) into constant-price gross capital formation, calculated at the prices of a fixed base period, by removing the effects of price changes through this index. This allows for a more accurate reflection of changes in the physical volume of capital formation.

Financing costs refer to the various direct expenses incurred by a company during the process of raising funds (such as issuing stocks, bonds, or obtaining loans), including handling fees, legal fees, appraisal fees, notarization fees, etc. These costs constitute the basic expenses of financing activities, typically determined directly based on actual amounts incurred or contractual agreements, and cannot be calculated through other financial indicators.

A sales discount is a price reduction offered by the seller in credit sales to encourage customers to pay early. It is typically expressed in specific credit terms, such as '2/10, n/30', meaning the customer can take a 2% discount if payment is made within 10 days; otherwise, the full amount is due within 30 days. For the buyer, the discount taken is usually recorded as a financing expense in financial expenses.

Sales allowance refers to a price reduction or discount granted by an enterprise to customers after selling goods or providing services on credit, due to reasons such as product quality issues, specification discrepancies, or early payment. It is a direct deduction item when calculating net credit sales revenue, reflecting the actual collectible amount from credit sales.

Sales returns on credit refer to the amount by which a company must reduce its original credit sales revenue when customers return goods due to reasons such as quality issues or specification discrepancies after the company has sold goods or provided services on credit terms. It is a direct deduction item when calculating net credit sales and originates from actual return documents or accounting records.
Start Date refers to an initial point in time set for time-related calculations or analyses, serving as the basis for calculating subsequent time periods, days, or derived metrics.

Total auxiliary production cost refers to the aggregate amount of all expenses incurred by a company's internal auxiliary production departments (such as power supply, water supply, machinery maintenance, transportation, etc.) within a specific period for providing products or services to basic production departments, administrative management departments, and others. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and is typically accumulated based on actual direct costs such as material costs, labor costs, and manufacturing overhead.

Transport volume refers to the quantity of transportation work completed by a transportation enterprise within a specific reporting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental operational metric for measuring the scale of production and operations. It is typically measured in physical units, such as freight turnover (ton-kilometers), passenger turnover (passenger-kilometers), or simple freight volume (tons) and passenger volume (passenger trips).

Transportation cost refers to the fee paid by an enterprise to carriers for moving goods or merchandise from one location to another. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded as a basic original expense and directly allocated to relevant cost or expense accounts based on supporting documents such as contracts and invoices.

Transport volume refers to the actual quantity of goods or passengers transported by transportation enterprises within a specific period, serving as a fundamental indicator for measuring the scale of transportation operations. It is typically expressed in units such as ton-kilometers (for freight) or passenger-kilometers (for passenger transport).

Total number of payment periods refers to the total number of installments required to repay both principal and interest over the entire loan or repayment schedule. It is typically determined directly by multiplying the loan term in years by the annual payment frequency (e.g., 12 months) and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating metrics such as the periodic payment amount.

Import value refers to the total price paid by an enterprise to acquire ownership of goods or services purchased from abroad, typically calculated on a Cost, Insurance, and Freight (CIF) basis. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as import duties, domestic selling prices, and import profits.

The applicable income tax rate refers to the statutory taxation percentage directly applied to the taxable income of an enterprise or individual as stipulated by national tax laws. It is a parameter predetermined by law, typically determined based on different income brackets (such as progressive tax rates) or taxpayer types (such as general taxpayers), rather than being calculated from other financial data.

Applicable tax rate refers to the percentage or fixed amount, as stipulated by tax laws, that is directly used to calculate the tax payable for specific taxpayers, taxable items, or income brackets. It is typically explicitly defined by law and is not derived from the calculation of other financial indicators.

Department business volume refers to the quantity or scale of business activities actually completed or processed by a department within a specific period. It serves as fundamental, raw data for measuring departmental operational activities, typically expressed in specific counting units such as the number of work orders processed, service instances provided, units of products produced, transactions completed, or work hours accounted for. This indicator directly reflects the operational activity level and output scale of a department, serving as an important basis for cost analysis, performance evaluation, and resource allocation.

Department Minimum Activity Level Cost refers to the historical total cost data corresponding to the lowest activity level of a specific department during a given period. It is a raw value directly extracted from historical records, used in cost behavior analysis methods such as the High-Low Method, serving as one of the fundamental inputs for calculating the variable cost per unit.

Department peak business volume refers to the highest level of business activity or output scale achieved by a specific department within an organization during a defined statistical period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It is typically derived directly from business records or statistical results, used to measure the department's historical best performance or serve as a benchmark for performance comparison.

Departmental selling price per unit refers to the base price negotiated with customers or directly set for each unit of product or service sold by a specific department within an enterprise. It serves as a direct input value for calculating financial metrics such as departmental sales revenue, and is typically determined based on market conditions, costs, or negotiations, rather than being derived from other financial formulas.

Department sales volume refers to the specific quantity of goods or services sold by a particular sales department within an enterprise over a defined period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually), representing fundamental operational data directly sourced from sales transaction records.

The rights issue price refers to the subscription price per share determined by a listed company when issuing new shares to existing shareholders during a rights offering for financing. This price is typically set directly by the company based on market conditions, its own valuation, and negotiations with underwriters, serving as a key basis for shareholders to decide whether to participate in the rights issue.

The rights issue ratio refers to the ratio between the number of new shares issued to existing shareholders and the company's original total share capital when a listed company conducts a rights issue for financing. It is directly determined by the company based on financing needs and shareholder structure, specifying how many new shares a shareholder can subscribe for per certain number of old shares held.

Intermediate consumption in mining refers to the total value of all non-fixed asset goods and services consumed during the mining production process to obtain final products. It primarily includes the costs of raw materials, fuels, power, and various external services (such as transportation, maintenance, and communication) consumed in production. It is a key input item deducted from gross output when calculating value added in the mining industry.

english: Wages and Salaries in Mining Industry

definition_en: Mining industry labor compensation refers to the total sum of all forms of remuneration paid to all personnel engaged in mining and related activities (including production workers, management personnel, technical personnel, etc.) in the cost accounting of mining enterprises. It is typically reflected as the aggregate of personnel wages and constitutes an important component of the value added in the mining industry.

term_en.name: Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Mining Industry

english: Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Mining Industry

definition_en: Depreciation of fixed assets in the mining industry refers to the process by which mining enterprises systematically allocate the cost of their fixed assets (such as mining equipment, mine facilities, transportation vehicles, etc.) with a useful life exceeding one accounting year over their estimated service life using determined methods (such as the straight-line method or units-of-production method). This reflects the gradual reduction in the asset's value due to usage, technological advancement, or natural wear and tear, and is a crucial component in calculating production costs and period expenses.

term_en.name: Total Output Value of Mining Industry

english: Gross Output Value of Mining Industry

definition_en: Total output value of the mining industry refers to the total monetary value of all final products (such as ores, coal, petroleum, etc.) and labor services produced by all mining enterprises within a specific reporting period (e.g., one year or one quarter). It is a fundamental aggregate indicator for measuring the overall scale and total output of the mining sector.

term_en.name: Net Production Taxes in Mining Industry

english: Net Production Tax of Mining Industry

definition_en: Net production taxes in the mining industry refer to the net amount of various production taxes paid by mining enterprises to the government during the production process, minus production subsidies received from the government. It is an important component in calculating the value added of the mining industry and reflects the net contribution of the mining sector to government finances during production activities.

The procurement and storage fee rate is a predetermined percentage rate set by an enterprise to compensate for various expenses incurred during material procurement, inspection, storage, and safekeeping (such as purchasing staff salaries, travel expenses, warehouse rent, and losses). It is typically determined directly based on historical data, industry practices, or contractual agreements and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating the specific amount of procurement and storage fees.

Interest on financial liabilities refers to the compensation that an enterprise must pay to creditors for borrowed funds (such as bank loans, bond issuances, etc.). It is a fundamental expense in the income statement, reflecting the cost of using debt capital.

Total financial assets refer to the aggregate carrying amount of all financial instruments held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (e.g., the balance sheet date), measured in accordance with accounting standards. It represents the total volume of assets existing in financial form for the enterprise and is a significant asset item on the balance sheet.

chinese: 金融资产公允价值变动
english: Fair Value Adjustment of Financial Assets

definition_en: Financial asset revaluation changes refer to the direct adjustments made to the carrying value of financial assets held by an enterprise and measured at fair value (such as trading financial assets, financial assets at fair value through other comprehensive income, etc.) during an accounting period due to fluctuations in their market fair value. These changes directly reflect market price movements and are typically recognized in current period profit or loss or other comprehensive income, rather than being derived through formula calculations.

Amount refers to the quantitative value expressed in monetary units, serving as fundamental data for describing the scale of economic activities, asset values, or transaction sizes. It is the most primitive and direct numerical unit in financial recording and calculation, typically used as an input value for computing profit margins, ratios, and other financial metrics.

Bank deposits refer to monetary funds held by enterprises or individuals in banks or other financial institutions, representing one of the most liquid components of corporate assets and constituting the primary component of monetary funds.

Bank deposit interest rate refers to the ratio at which financial institutions such as banks pay interest to depositors. It is typically set and announced by central banks or commercial banks based on market conditions and policies. It represents the proportion of interest that deposit principal can generate over a specific period (e.g., one year, one month, or one day) and serves as the basis for calculating deposit interest.

Total sales revenue refers to the total amount of income earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services within a specific period. It is typically calculated by multiplying sales volume by unit selling price and serves as a fundamental financial metric reflecting the scale of an enterprise's sales operations.

Sales discount refers to a price reduction directly granted by an enterprise on the marked price of goods or invoice amount to encourage customer purchases, accelerate payment collection, or maintain long-term cooperative relationships when selling goods or providing services. It is typically categorized into trade discounts and cash discounts, and serves as the basis for calculating actual sales revenue.

Sales discounts or allowances refer to price reductions granted directly to buyers from the original selling price due to reasons such as product quality issues, specification discrepancies, favorable payment terms, or promotional activities when a company sells goods or provides services. They are typically negotiated at or after the transaction occurs and directly reduce the revenue recognized in the current period.

Sales allowance refers to a price reduction granted by an enterprise to a buyer from the original selling price due to reasons such as product quality, quantity, or transaction terms after the sale of goods or provision of services.

Sales returns refer to the business where goods already sold are returned by the buyer due to reasons such as quality issues, specification discrepancies, or customer dissatisfaction. In accounting, sales returns directly reduce the current period's operating revenue and are a deduction to be considered when calculating a company's net operating revenue.

Long-term debt refers to obligations undertaken by an enterprise with a repayment period exceeding one year (or one operating cycle). It represents funds borrowed to raise long-term capital, typically used for long-term purposes such as fixed asset investments and project development, and constitutes a significant component of the enterprise's capital structure.

Long-term payables refer to various payable items with a repayment period exceeding one year or one operating cycle longer than a year, and constitute an independent liability account on the balance sheet. Their amounts are directly sourced from accounting records, such as actual unpaid amounts for installment purchases of assets or financing leases of fixed assets.

Long-term receivables refer to receivables with an expected collection period exceeding one year (or one operating cycle), typically associated with non-routine business activities such as finance leases, installment sales of goods, or provision of services. Their amounts are determined by discounting the future cash flows stipulated in the contracts.

Long-term prepaid expenses refer to costs that have been actually paid or incurred by an enterprise, but whose benefit period exceeds one year, requiring amortization over the current and subsequent multiple accounting periods. They are classified as a non-current asset of the enterprise, commonly seen in capitalized expenditures such as renovation expenses and fixed asset improvement costs.

Long-term prepaid expenses amortization refers to the accounting process by which a company systematically allocates various expenses that have been paid but have benefit periods exceeding one year into the costs or expenses of each period, according to the determined amortization period and method.

Long-term investments refer to equity or debt investments held by an enterprise that are not intended to be liquidated within one year or one operating cycle. Their book value is directly presented on the balance sheet and represents asset allocation undertaken to obtain long-term returns or achieve strategic objectives.

Increase in Long-term Liabilities refers to the increase in the book value of a company's long-term liabilities (or non-current liabilities) from the beginning to the end of an accounting period (e.g., one year). It directly reflects the amount of new debt with a repayment term exceeding one year that the company has incurred during the period through means such as long-term borrowing and bond issuance.

Indirect manufacturing overhead refers to various indirect expenses incurred by an enterprise during the production of goods or provision of services that cannot be directly attributed to specific products or cost objects. These expenses are necessary to support production activities but cannot be directly charged to individual product costs, requiring allocation through specific methods.

The add-on rate is a predetermined specific ratio used in lease transactions to calculate rental payments. It is typically applied directly as an input parameter to the cost or estimated cost of the leased asset to determine the periodic rental amount payable.

A random variable value refers to the outcome of a random experiment (such as investment returns, product qualification rates, or other uncertain events) expressed as a specific numerical result. It is the most fundamental data point in probability and statistics, used to describe and analyze uncertainty.

In the field of finance and accounting, 'Zero' typically refers to the specific numerical value zero or a zero-value state. It can indicate a cash balance of zero, the integer result after rounding down amounts, items counted as zero, or change given in cash transactions. It is a fundamental raw data point, not a financial metric derived from complex calculations.

Odd days refer to the actual number of days from the start date to the end date that are less than a full interest accrual period in financial operations such as interest calculation or discounting. They are commonly used in interest calculations for scenarios like demand deposits, loans, and bill discounting, serving as essential underlying data for determining the length of the interest period.

The demand function intercept is the constant term parameter 'a' in a linear demand function (e.g., Q = a - bP). It represents the theoretical market demand for a commodity when its price is zero. This parameter is typically determined by external market conditions or historical data and serves as the foundation for analyzing the relationship between price and quantity demanded.

The demand function slope is a parameter describing the rate or degree of inclination at which quantity demanded changes with variations in price (or other independent variables) within the demand function. In a linear demand function, it is represented as the slope of a straight line, typically negative, indicating an inverse relationship between quantity demanded and price—i.e., as price increases, quantity demanded decreases.

Non-controlling interest refers to the portion of equity in a subsidiary's consolidated financial statements that is not attributable to the parent company (i.e., the controlling shareholder). It represents the share of the subsidiary owned by other investors.

The increase in non-current assets refers to the difference in the ending balances of non-current asset accounts on a company's balance sheet between two consecutive accounting periods (e.g., the end of two fiscal years). It reflects the net increase in a company's long-term assets (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.) over a specific period.

Non-tradable shares refer to shares in a company's capital structure that, according to relevant laws, regulations, or the company's articles of association, cannot be publicly and freely traded on a stock exchange. These shares typically originate from company establishment, capital increases, or equity incentive programs, and their transfer is subject to specific conditions and procedures.

Non-recurring income adjustments refer to income items that need to be excluded from net profit when calculating metrics such as Economic Value Added (EVA). These items are not directly related to the company's core business operations, occur infrequently, or are of a special nature. They typically require identification and aggregation based on the specific substance of the business activities, such as gains from selling high-quality core business assets or reducing stakes in entities with substantive control, to ensure the financial data more accurately reflects the core profitability of the company's ongoing operations.

Face value principal is the original par amount set at the issuance of a debt security (such as a bond) or other financial instruments like stocks. It serves as the contractual base value for calculating interest, repaying principal, or determining issuance price, and is itself a known original datum rather than a calculated figure.

Prepayments refer to funds paid in advance by an enterprise to suppliers or other entities according to contractual agreements in the course of daily business operations, constituting a current asset of the enterprise. When preparing the balance sheet, its value is calculated by aggregating the ending debit balances of all subsidiary accounts under the two general ledger accounts: 'Prepaid Accounts' and 'Accounts Payable'.

Accrued expenses refer to liability items where a company, under the accrual basis accounting principle, estimates and records expenses that have been incurred but not yet actually paid into the current period's costs or expenses. This ensures that expenses are matched with related revenues in the correct accounting period, commonly seen in periodic payment items such as rent, interest, and insurance.

Advances from customers refer to payments received by an enterprise from customers in advance of the sale of goods or provision of services. This amount constitutes a liability for the enterprise at the time of receipt, as the corresponding goods or services have not been delivered and revenue has not been recognized. On the balance sheet, it is typically presented as an aggregate of the credit balances from the 'Advances from Customers' and 'Accounts Receivable' subsidiary ledgers.

Advance from customers refers to the funds received in advance from the buyer according to the contract before the enterprise sells goods or provides services. At the time of receipt, the enterprise has not yet fulfilled the corresponding performance obligations, thus constituting a liability to the customer and is classified as a current liability.

term_en.name: Net Increase in Advances from Customers

english: Net Increase in Advances from Customers

definition_en: Net increase in advances from customers refers to the difference between the ending balance and the beginning balance of the advances from customers account on the balance sheet over a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year). It reflects the net change in funds received in advance from customers during that period and serves as a fundamental raw data point for calculating cash flows from operating activities when preparing the statement of cash flows.

term_en.name: Debit Balance of Advance from Customers Subsidiary Ledger Account

chinese: 预收账款借方明细余额
预收账款明细借方余额
预收账款客户借方余额
english: Advance from Customers Subsidiary Ledger Debit Balance

definition_en: The debit balance of an advance from customers subsidiary ledger account refers to the debit balance calculated at period-end closing for a specific subsidiary ledger account, set up under the general ledger liability account 'Advance from Customers' for individual customers or projects in the accounting books. It indicates that the company received advance payments from specific customers, but subsequently, the value of goods or services actually provided exceeded the advance amount, causing that customer's subsidiary account to temporarily appear on the books as an asset receivable from the customer (similar to accounts receivable). It is fundamental accounting data that must be recorded and aggregated directly based on actual business vouchers.

Expected Other Comprehensive Income refers to the estimated gains or losses that an enterprise may generate in future accounting periods, based on forecasts or assumptions about future operating conditions, market environment, and other factors. These items are not directly included in current net profit but are directly recorded in owners' equity. It serves as a critical input variable in financial forecasting and valuation models.

Expected sales revenue refers to the forecasted total revenue that a company anticipates generating from selling products or providing services over a specific future period (such as a quarter or a year), based on historical data, market analysis, expert judgment, or specific forecasting models. It is a key foundational data point in financial budgeting and planning.

Forecast period refers to the specific years or time series set in a financial forecasting model for estimating future financial position, operating results, and cash flows. It is a fundamental time parameter used to determine the baseline point and time span of the forecast.

The forecast period refers to the specific time frame set for detailed forecasting and estimation of future financial data in financial forecasting, business valuation, or earnings prediction models. It is a fundamental time parameter used to define the span from the base forecast date to the beginning of the subsequent period.

term_en.name: Revenue in the Final Period of the Forecast Horizon

english: Forecasted Revenue for the Final Period
Revenue in the Last Forecast Period

definition_en: Revenue in the final period of the forecast horizon refers to the estimated total income that a company is projected to generate from its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods or provision of services, in the last period (e.g., the final year or quarter) of a specified forecast timeframe (e.g., the next 3 or 5 years) within a financial forecasting model. It serves as a fundamental input for financial projections and is typically used as the starting point for cash flow forecasts in the subsequent period (e.g., the terminal or perpetuity period).

Total Budgeted Hours refers to the pre-estimated total number of labor hours required to complete the production plan or work tasks for a specific period (such as a budget cycle) during the budgeting process. It serves as fundamental input data for developing financial budgets such as labor cost budgets and manufacturing overhead allocation rates.

chinese: 生产工人工资预算总额
english: Budgeted Total Wages for Production Workers

definition_en: Budgeted Total Production Worker Wages refers to the total wages estimated or determined during the enterprise budgeting process, based on the production plan, projected number of workers, working hours, and wage standards, for paying workers directly involved in product production. It serves as the fundamental raw data for preparing the manufacturing overhead budget and product cost budget.

Budgeted sales volume refers to the planned quantity of products or services to be sold in a specific future period, directly determined during the enterprise budgeting process based on market forecasts, historical sales data, and operational targets set by management. It serves as the starting point and fundamental input data for preparing the sales budget, production budget, and other components of the comprehensive budget.

Estimated production and sales volume refers to the projection of the quantity of products a company plans to produce and sell during a specific future period, based on market research, historical data, sales forecasts, or target profit back-calculation methods during the financial forecasting and budgeting process. It serves as fundamental input data for calculating various financial metrics such as estimated production output, projected sales revenue, and target profit.

Estimated useful life refers to the length of time an asset (such as a fixed asset) is expected to provide economic benefits or services to an enterprise. It is professionally estimated by management based on factors such as the asset's physical characteristics, technological obsolescence rate, intensity of use, maintenance condition, and market changes, and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating asset depreciation or amortization.

Estimated Other Expenses refer to the projected amount for various relatively minor or miscellaneous expenditures expected to occur, apart from major cost items (such as materials, labor, interest, etc.), during the preparation of financial budgets or financial forecasts. It typically serves as a fundamental input in the budgeting process.

The Estimated Net Salvage Value Rate is a predetermined percentage used by enterprises to calculate the depreciation of fixed assets. It represents the proportion of the estimated net salvage value (the amount after deducting disposal costs from disposal proceeds) of a fixed asset at the end of its estimated useful life to the asset's original cost. This ratio is a policy parameter estimated by the enterprise based on asset characteristics, tax regulations, or industry practices.

Estimated unit product price refers to the anticipated selling price set for a single product by an enterprise during budget preparation, financial forecasting, or product pricing. It is typically determined based on a comprehensive analysis of market supply and demand, product cost structure, target profit margin, competitive environment, and other factors, serving as a key foundational data point for calculating financial metrics such as expected sales revenue and profit.

term_en.name: Estimated Total Financial Assets at Period End

definition_en: Estimated Total Financial Assets at Period End refers to the projected total value of all financial assets held by an enterprise at a specific future accounting period end (e.g., year-end, quarter-end), based on business plans, investment arrangements, or historical data. It serves as a fundamental input assumption in financial forecasting models.

Estimated disposal costs refer to the anticipated expenses related to the future disposal or retirement of a fixed asset (such as machinery, equipment, or plant). These costs typically include expenses for dismantling, transportation, site cleanup, waste disposal, and similar activities.
