It is typically not derived through complex financial formulas but serves as a key input in cost estimation templates, such as benchmark working days, one-way kilometer distance, etc., or constitutes components of the final freight rate (e.g., base origin-destination price, base operating price).

english: Cost of Basket in Base Period

definition_en: Base period basket cost refers to the total expenditure required to purchase a fixed, representative set of goods and services (i.e., the 'basket') in a selected reference period (the base period) when calculating price indices such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This cost serves as the starting point and benchmark for subsequent calculations of price changes and inflation rates.

Base period sales refers to the actual sales revenue of a specific period (typically the previous period or a historical period) selected as the comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as the foundational historical data for calculating sales growth rates, conducting sales percentage method forecasting, and other financial analyses.

Base period sales refer to the sales revenue data from a specific historical period used as a benchmark or reference point in financial analysis or comparison. It is typically the raw data directly obtained from past financial statements, used to calculate metrics such as growth rates and indices, in order to measure changes in current or future sales relative to that benchmark.

Prime cost refers to the costs incurred in the production or provision of services that can be directly and clearly attributed to specific products or services, primarily including direct materials and direct labor—original expenditures that can be directly traced to the product. It represents the most fundamental cost data in accounting records and serves as the starting point for subsequent cost calculation and analysis.

The incremental borrowing rate refers to the interest rate negotiated and determined by an enterprise with financial institutions such as banks for obtaining additional (incremental) borrowing, based on its own credit status, loan term, collateral conditions, and other factors, on top of existing borrowings. It reflects the marginal cost of the enterprise obtaining new financing, serves as raw data from external markets or contractual agreements, and is commonly used in the discount calculation of lease liabilities under the new leasing standards.

Foreign currency liabilities refer to debts that an enterprise undertakes, which are denominated and repayable in foreign currencies (such as US dollars, euros, etc.). It is a specific item on the enterprise's balance sheet, directly reflecting the amount of debt settled in foreign currency arising from business operations or financing activities.

Foreign currency assets refer to various assets held by an enterprise that are denominated or settled in currencies other than the functional currency, such as foreign currency bank deposits, foreign currency accounts receivable, and financial assets denominated in foreign currencies. Their amounts are directly derived from records at the time of foreign currency transactions or are translated into the functional currency amount using the spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date.

Actual cost of multimodal transport refers to the total sum of all direct and indirect expenses actually incurred by an enterprise in organizing multimodal transport operations to complete the entire transportation of goods from origin to destination. These expenses typically include freight charges for different transport segments, cargo handling and transshipment fees, insurance premiums, warehousing costs, and related management and coordination expenses, which are directly collected from actual business documents or reasonably allocated.

Subsidiary net profit refers to the final operating result generated by a company (subsidiary) from its business activities during a specific accounting period, which is the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes from revenue. It is the core data on the subsidiary's individual income statement and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating consolidated indicators such as net profit attributable to the parent company when preparing consolidated financial statements.

Inventory cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire inventory and bring it to a condition ready for sale or use, primarily including purchase costs, production costs, and related expenses such as processing, transportation, and storage. It serves as the basis for measuring the inventory item on the balance sheet.

Market value of inventory refers to the estimated value that can be obtained through sale or use in the normal course of business for inventory held by an enterprise on the balance sheet date. In accounting practice, it is typically measured using the lower of cost or net realizable value principle to reflect potential inventory impairment. It is not derived from formula calculations but is determined as raw data based on accounting records or professional valuation.

Tuition refers to the basic fee charged by schools or educational institutions to students to compensate for the provision of educational services (such as teaching, facility usage, etc.). It is typically determined directly based on the program of study, academic year, credits, or specific policies, and constitutes a core component of a student's educational expenses.

Installation cost refers to the various necessary expenditures that must be incurred before a fixed asset (such as machinery and equipment) can be put into normal operation and reach its intended usable state. These expenditures form part of the total purchase price of the asset and typically include expenses for constructing foundations, assembling equipment, conducting commissioning tests, and hiring professional services.

Standard hours for completed products refer to the predetermined standard labor time allocated for producing one qualified product in manufacturing cost accounting. It is a standard time consumption benchmark established by enterprises based on production processes, equipment conditions, and historical experience, primarily used for cost calculation and efficiency evaluation.

A Certificate of Deposit (CD) is a deposit certificate issued by a bank or financial institution, where a customer deposits a sum of money for a fixed term (e.g., several months or years), and the bank promises to repay the principal and pay interest at an agreed-upon rate upon maturity. It is a low-risk, fixed-income savings or wealth management instrument.

Interest Received Percentage refers to the proportion of interest actually collected by an enterprise or financial institution relative to the total interest income accrued under the accrual basis of accounting. It reflects the cash collection efficiency of interest income and asset quality.

Actual working hours refer to the time actually spent by workers on product production or the actual operation of machinery during the production process. It serves as the fundamental raw data for cost accounting and expense allocation. This data is typically collected directly through methods such as attendance records, production work tickets, or equipment operation logs, rather than being calculated from other financial indicators.

Actual working hours refer to the total hours directly calculated from original attendance records, including employee actual attendance, support received, overtime, etc. It serves as foundational data for cost accounting (such as manufacturing overhead allocation) and is not derived from other financial metrics.

Actual output refers to the quantity of products or services actually completed and recorded through the production or harvesting process by an enterprise within a specific accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It is a fundamental production data point, typically entered directly based on production cost ledgers, production records, or product cost summaries, rather than being calculated from other financial indicators.

Actual labor cost refers to the total sum of labor expenditures actually incurred and recorded during a specific accounting period for the completion of products or services. It typically includes the base wages, bonuses, benefits, taxes, and other related expenses for personnel directly involved in production or service provision, and constitutes a significant component of the actual cost of products.

Actual variable manufacturing overhead refers to the total amount of indirect costs actually incurred during the production process within a specific accounting period, which vary proportionally with product output or activity volume. It is obtained directly through actual statistics or accounting and represents the original incurred amount data in cost accounting.

chinese: 实际固定制造费用总额

definition_en: Actual fixed manufacturing overhead refers to the total amount of fixed indirect costs actually incurred and recorded in the accounting books during a specific accounting period to support production and manufacturing activities. These costs are independent of production or activity volume within a certain range, such as factory rent, managerial salaries, and equipment depreciation, and serve as the fundamental raw data for cost accounting and variance analysis.

Actual hours worked refers to the total duration an employee actually devotes to work during a specific period (such as a day, week, or month). It is typically captured directly by attendance systems, timesheets, or project management systems and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating compensation, analyzing labor costs, and evaluating production efficiency.

Minority interest ratio refers to the proportion of a subsidiary's shares held by shareholders other than the parent company (controlling shareholder) in the consolidated financial statements. For example, if the parent company holds 80% of a subsidiary's shares, the minority shareholders hold the remaining 20%, making the ratio 20%.

Wages refer to the labor compensation directly paid by an employer to an employee based on the employment contract, considering factors such as attendance records and performance results. It serves as the fundamental raw data for payroll accounting and is typically recorded as an expense account in accounting treatment.

Incurred expenses refer to costs or expenditures that have been actually consumed or assumed by an enterprise during a specific accounting period due to business operations or other events, and have been recorded and recognized in the books according to accounting standards. They reflect the actual outflow of enterprise resources or the increase in liabilities, and constitute fundamental data for the income statement.

Bonus shares issued refer to additional shares distributed free of charge to existing shareholders in proportion to their current holdings, by converting earned profits (such as retained earnings or surplus reserves) into share capital. This is a non-cash form of dividend distribution; after issuance, the company's total share capital increases while total shareholders' equity remains unchanged.

Issued shares refer to the total number of shares that a company has actually sold to investors (including the public and company insiders) and for which it has received corresponding capital, in accordance with its articles of association and issuance plan. They form the foundation of a company's capital structure and represent the actual ownership stakes in the company held by investors.

Total Processed Tax Returns refers to the aggregate number of all types of tax returns that have been reviewed, filed, or finalized by a tax authority (such as the IRS) within a specific period. It reflects the actual workload completed by the tax authority and serves as a fundamental metric for measuring its processing efficiency and service capacity.

Submitted interest rate estimate refers to the proposed expected interest rate level that financial institutions (such as banks) submit to the market or regulatory authorities when issuing bonds, setting loan interest rates, or designing financial products, based on factors such as current market conditions, credit risk, and funding costs. It serves as a preliminary proposal in the pricing process, providing a reference for the final determination of the actual interest rate.

Market price, typically referring to the price per share, is the real-time transaction price at which a stock is bought and sold on public securities exchanges. It is determined by market supply and demand, reflecting investors' immediate assessment of the company's current and future value, and is one of the most fundamental and direct trading data in capital markets.

Market price refers to the immediate price at which an asset or financial instrument is voluntarily traded between buyers and sellers in an open market based on supply and demand. It is a concrete manifestation of fair market value, fluctuates in real-time, and differs from the historical cost value recorded on a company's books.

A market participant refers to a buyer or seller in the principal market (or most advantageous market) for the relevant asset or liability, who is independent, knowledgeable, willing, and able to transact. They are hypothetical ideal counterparties assumed when determining the fair value of an asset or liability.

Market entry costs refer to the various direct expenditures incurred by a company in the initial phase to successfully introduce and penetrate a new product, new service, or new business into the target market. These expenditures are primarily used to overcome market barriers, establish initial brand awareness and sales channels, laying the foundation for subsequent sustainable operations.

Beginning-of-year investment refers to the funds or asset value invested at the start of each fiscal year (typically January 1st), used to support annual operations or obtain long-term returns. It serves as the original baseline data for calculating performance metrics such as return on investment.

Annual interest expense refers to the total interest costs actually paid or accrued by a company within one year due to the use of external borrowings (such as bank loans, bond issuances, etc.), and is a significant cost item on the income statement.

Day count basis is a fundamental standard in finance and accounting used to convert actual interest-bearing days into an annualized proportion when calculating time-related financial metrics such as interest and yield. It specifies how many days are considered in a year for calculation purposes, and different standards directly affect the interest amount.

Annual coupon payment refers to the actual cash interest amount paid by the bond issuer to bondholders each year according to the terms agreed upon at the time of bond issuance. It is a fundamental payment obligation in the bond contract, directly reflecting the fixed interest income obtainable annually from holding the bond.

The annual discount rate is the benchmark ratio used to discount expected returns or cash flows from the next year or a finite period to their present value. It reflects the time value of money, risk level, and opportunity cost, and is a key parameter for evaluating the value of investment projects, bonds, and other financial assets.

In the field of finance and accounting, 'Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits' specifically refers to the 'Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits Method', an accelerated depreciation calculation method. It calculates the annual depreciation expense by multiplying the total depreciable amount of a fixed asset by a fraction that decreases each year. The denominator of this fraction is the sum of the years of the asset's estimated useful life, and the numerator is the remaining useful life of the asset.

Start date refers to the beginning point of a time period or the initial time point of a calculation process, typically used as known input data for calculating period length, length of service, depreciation, etc. It is a fundamental raw data point itself, not a composite indicator derived through formulas.

Attribution ratio is a fundamental concept describing ownership, equity, or profit distribution relationships, used to define the share or percentage of specific interests (such as net profit, assets, cash flow, etc.) ultimately attributable to which entity (e.g., parent company shareholders, minority shareholders, etc.). It is not a financial ratio calculated by formula per se, but rather the core concept for understanding the meaning of 'attribution' in composite indicators such as 'attributable net profit'.

Current actual output quantity refers to the specific number of products or services actually completed and recorded within a specific time period (such as a shift, a day, or a month) through production or operational activities. It is fundamental data obtained directly from the production process, used to measure production results and calculate other efficiency or cost metrics.

The Current Price Index refers to the original statistical data directly compiled and published by statistical agencies for a specific reporting period (such as a month, quarter, or year), used to measure changes in the price level of a representative basket of goods and services relative to a base period. It reflects the overall price level during that period and serves as fundamental data for observing macroeconomic phenomena such as inflation.

term_en.name: Actual Activity Output for the Period

english: Actual Activity Output for the Period

definition_en: Actual Activity Output for the Period refers to the actual quantity or volume of activities consumed by an enterprise during the current accounting period to complete products or services under Activity-Based Costing. It serves as fundamental raw data, typically measured in specific units such as machine hours, production batches, inspection counts, or order processing quantities, and is used to allocate activity costs to specific cost objects (e.g., products or services).

term_en.name: Actual Activity Costs Incurred in the Current Period

english: Actual Activity-Based Cost for the Period
Actual Activity Cost Incurred in Current Period
Actual Cost of Activities for the Period

definition_en: Actual activity costs incurred in the current period refer to the total sum of resource costs, under Activity-Based Costing, that are actually consumed and allocated to various activity cost pools for performing specific activities (such as order processing, equipment setup, quality inspection, etc.) during the current accounting period. These costs originate directly from actual resource consumption, such as labor wages, power expenses, equipment depreciation, etc., and serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating activity cost allocation rates.

Current project price refers to the market price or fair value of an asset, product, or service at the current accounting period or transaction date, reflecting present market conditions as distinct from historical cost.

Total Transaction Count refers to the aggregate number of all financial transactions (such as buying, selling, transfers, settlements, etc.) conducted by an enterprise or institution within a specific period (e.g., one year or one quarter). It is a fundamental counting metric used to gauge business activity levels.

Total tax liability refers to the aggregate sum of all taxes payable to tax authorities by an enterprise as of the balance sheet date, determined in accordance with tax regulations and accounting standards, constituting a significant component of the enterprise's liabilities.

Constituent stock price refers to the real-time trading price of individual stocks selected for inclusion in a specific stock index (such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) in the securities market. It serves as the raw underlying data for calculating the stock index and reflects the value of each stock that constitutes the index.

Constituent stock market capitalization refers to the total market value of all individual stocks that constitute a specific stock index (such as the CSI 300 or S&P 500). It is typically calculated by summing the product of each constituent stock's share price and its total shares outstanding (or free-float shares). It reflects the overall size of the market segment represented by the index.

english: Number of Shares Outstanding for Free Float

definition_en: Constituent shares outstanding refers to the number of shares of the companies included in a stock index (such as the CSI 300 or S&P 500) that are freely tradable on the public market. It excludes shares that are long-term locked up and not freely tradable, such as those held by company insiders, governments, or strategic investors (e.g., restricted shares). This figure is fundamental for calculating index weights and reflecting the true trading scale of the market.

Constituent stock price refers to the real-time trading price of each individual stock that constitutes a stock index (such as the CSI 300 Index or the S&P 500 Index) in the securities market. It reflects the market's immediate assessment of the value of these listed companies and serves as the fundamental data for calculating and constructing stock indices.

The income tax rate refers to the statutory percentage or policy ratio stipulated by tax laws, used as the basis for calculating the income tax payable by enterprises or individuals. It is typically determined directly based on the type of enterprise, the nature of income, or the tax policies of the country/region, and serves as fundamental data for tax calculation.

The income tax rate is a fixed or statutory percentage ratio stipulated by national tax laws or relevant policies, used to calculate the amount of income tax payable by enterprises or individuals. It is a fundamental policy parameter that cannot be derived from other financial indicators but is directly applied to taxable income to determine the tax liability.

The strike price is the predetermined fixed price specified in an options contract at which the buyer and seller must transact the underlying asset on or before a specific future date (expiration date). It is a key element in determining whether an option has exercise value.

Underwriting fee is the compensation charged by investment banks or securities firms for providing underwriting services to companies issuing securities (such as stocks or bonds). This fee represents a core cost paid by the issuer to obtain the underwriter's professional services in areas such as securities pricing, sales, and distribution.

Initial investment refers to the total amount of cash outflow required as a one-time or initial input at the beginning of a project when making an investment project decision. It serves as the fundamental known data for calculating financial metrics such as the project's net present value.

The discount period refers to a preferential time frame set by the seller to encourage early payment from the buyer. Payment within this period allows the buyer to enjoy a specified percentage discount on the invoice amount (e.g., common terms like '2/10, n/30' indicate a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days).

The quote currency is the second currency in a currency pair in foreign exchange trading, indicating the amount of that currency required to purchase one unit of the base currency. For example, in the exchange rate EUR/USD = 1.10, USD is the quote currency, meaning 1.10 US dollars are needed to purchase one euro.

Holding quantity refers to the specific number of shares, fund units, or other financial assets that an investor actually holds in their securities account at a specific point in time, such as holding 1,000 shares of a company's stock. This data is directly sourced from the transaction system's trade records or position records and serves as fundamental raw data reflecting the size of an investor's position.

Number of Shares Held refers to the actual quantity of a company's shares owned by an investor (such as an individual, institution, or corporation) in their account or under their name at a specific point in time. This is fundamental data reflecting the magnitude of an investor's ownership.

Index shares (typically referring to ETFs) are investment funds listed and traded on stock exchanges, which can be bought and sold at any time like stocks. Their primary objective is to replicate and track the performance of a specific market index (such as the CSI 300 Index or the S&P 500 Index). By purchasing one index share, an investor essentially holds a portfolio of the basket of securities included in that index.

Loss amount refers to the original, directly observable or measurable numerical value of economic losses actually incurred during a specific event or period. It serves as fundamental data in risk management, insurance claims settlement, and financial analysis, used for subsequent calculation of derived metrics such as loss ratios and expected losses.

Expenditure amount refers to the total sum of cash or cash equivalents actually paid or committed to be paid by an enterprise or individual within a certain period for economic activities such as purchasing goods, receiving services, or repaying debts.

Revenue refers to the total inflow of economic benefits obtained by an enterprise through its ordinary business activities, such as selling goods, providing services, or transferring the right to use assets. It is the starting point of corporate profit and reflects the scale of operations and the ability to acquire resources.

In financial contexts, revenue amount typically refers to the total inflow of economic benefits generated by an enterprise during a specific accounting period from its ordinary operating activities, such as selling goods, providing services, or transferring the right to use assets. It is a fundamental, uncalculated data point in financial statements.

Government expenditure refers to the total amount of funds spent by the government of a country or region within a specific period (usually a fiscal year) to perform its functions, provide public goods and services, make investments, and implement transfer payments, among other activities. It is a significant component of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and reflects the scale and direction of government activities.

Government subsidies refer to economic resources obtained by enterprises from the government without compensation, typically used to offset related costs incurred or to support specific activities. In accounting treatment, depending on whether they are related to assets or ordinary activities, they may be recorded in accounts such as deferred income, other income, or non-operating income.

In the field of finance and accounting, 'Quantity' typically refers to the basic physical or operational unit of measurement for products or services. It is one of the most fundamental raw input data points for economic analysis and financial calculations, such as sales quantity, production quantity, or inventory quantity. It is an independent measurement value that cannot be derived from other financial metrics, but is often combined with other variables (e.g., unit price) to calculate derived metrics such as total amount, cost, etc.

New sales revenue refers to the revenue generated for the first time by an enterprise within a specific period through the sale of products or services to new customers, or through the sale of new products/services. It excludes repeat purchases or renewal income from existing customers and is a key metric for measuring a company's market expansion capability and growth potential.

Average Daily Demand refers to the average daily quantity required for a specific inventory item (such as raw materials or finished goods), calculated or forecasted based on historical sales data or production consumption data. It serves as fundamental operational data for inventory planning and control (e.g., calculating Economic Order Quantity and safety stock).

term_en.name: Proportion of Old Customers Taking Cash Discount

chinese: 原有客户现金折扣使用率
历史客户折扣享受比例
原有现金折扣客户比率
english: Historical Customer Cash Discount Take-up Rate
Proportion of Existing Customers Taking Cash Discount
Historical Percentage of Customers Taking Cash Discount

definition_en: The proportion of old customers taking cash discount refers to the ratio of the number (or amount) of existing customers who chose to pay within the discount period to enjoy the cash discount to the total number of credit sales customers (or total credit sales amount), prior to the implementation of a new cash discount policy or adjustment of credit terms by the enterprise. This data serves as the baseline historical data for assessing the impact of changes in cash discount policies (such as calculating the increase in cash discount costs).

Old sales level refers to the baseline value of sales revenue achieved by an enterprise during a specific past period (e.g., the previous fiscal year or quarter). It is a historical data point primarily used for comparison and analysis with current or future sales performance.

In the field of finance and accounting, time refers to the dimension over which the value of money changes, with its core being the time value of money, meaning that a unit of currency today is worth more than the same unit in the future. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating discounting, valuation, risk management, and numerous other financial metrics.

Common stock market price refers to the real-time trading price of a company's common shares formed by buyers and sellers based on supply and demand relationships in secondary markets such as stock exchanges. It directly reflects the market's valuation of the company and fluctuates with various factors including company performance, industry conditions, macroeconomic environment, and market sentiment.

Common stock market price refers to the real-time transaction price of a company's common stock formed through continuous bidding by buyers and sellers in the secondary market (i.e., stock exchanges). This price is directly determined by market supply and demand, representing the actual trading price at which investors buy and sell shares, rather than being calculated through financial models.

term_en.name: Total Number of Common Shares Outstanding

english: Total Number of Common Shares Outstanding

definition_en: Total number of common shares outstanding refers to the aggregate quantity of all common shares issued and held by shareholders of a company. It is the most fundamental data in a company's capital structure, typically sourced directly from the company's share capital registry records, stock issuance documents, or the share capital account on the balance sheet, rather than being calculated from other financial metrics.

english: Flotation Cost Ratio for Common Stock

definition_en: The Common Stock Flotation Cost Rate refers to the percentage of the total amount raised (gross proceeds from issuance) accounted for by the total of various related expenses (such as underwriting fees, legal fees, audit fees, promotional expenses, etc.) incurred by a company during the process of raising capital through issuing common stock. It is a fundamental ratio calculated based on actual contracts and expenses, used to measure the direct cost efficiency of issuing common stock.

Maximum Delivery Time refers to the latest permissible point or deadline for completing the delivery of products or services, as stipulated by suppliers, manufacturers, or contract terms in supply chain, production, or trade agreements. It typically serves as fundamental business data for production scheduling, logistics planning, or performance evaluation (e.g., calculating delivery achievement rates) and is not derived through formulaic calculation.

Final execution price refers to the actual transaction price agreed upon and paid by both parties in financial transactions, commodity trading, or contract fulfillment. It is typically the market price at the time of transaction completion, the settlement price stipulated in the contract, or the actual price determined through negotiation, serving as the fundamental data for subsequent financial analysis and calculations (such as execution shortfall).

term_en.name: Actual Wages of Work-in-Process at Beginning of Month

chinese: 月初在制品实际人工费
期初在产品实际人工费用
english: Beginning Work in Process Direct Labor
Beginning Work in Process Actual Labor Cost

definition_en: Actual wages of work-in-process at the beginning of the month refer to the total actual wage costs incurred for all unfinished work-in-process at the start of each month (i.e., the opening balance) in cost accounting. These costs are directly collected from source documents such as attendance records and payrolls, or allocated to work-in-process based on certain standards (e.g., labor hours). They serve as foundational data for subsequent cost allocation, such as calculating wage allocation rates.

term_en.name: Actual Material Cost of Work in Process at Beginning of Month

chinese: 期初在制品实际材料成本
月初在制品实际材料成本
english: Beginning Work in Process Actual Material Cost
Actual Material Cost of Opening WIP

definition_en: Actual Material Cost of Work in Process at Beginning of Month refers to the cost value of direct materials actually consumed by all products that are in the production process but not yet completed (i.e., work in process) at the start of each accounting period (typically monthly). This data is usually obtained directly through physical inventory counts or cost records, and serves as the foundational starting point for accumulating and allocating production costs for the current month, as well as for cost allocation between completed products and work in process.

term_en.name: Beginning Work in Process Inventory Cost

definition_en: Beginning Work in Process Inventory Cost refers to the total accumulated production costs of all products that are not yet completed and remain in the production process (i.e., work in process) at the start of an accounting period (typically a month). It usually includes direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead, and serves as a crucial opening figure for calculating the total cost of goods completed during the current period.

term_en.name: Daily Interest Rate on Marketable Securities

definition_en: The daily interest rate on marketable securities refers to the ratio of the daily interest generated by fixed-income securities such as bonds and notes to their face value or invested principal. It is typically derived by converting the annual interest rate based on a 360-day or 365-day year and is used to precisely calculate the interest income from short-term security holdings.

An orderly transaction refers to a transaction that has been publicly available in the market for a period prior to the measurement date, where both parties are knowledgeable, acting voluntarily and not under compulsion, and the transaction is conducted under fair conditions. It is a fundamental prerequisite that must be met when determining the fair value of an asset or liability.

chinese: 有限合伙人承诺出资总额
有限合伙人认缴出资总额

definition_en: Limited Partner Total Committed Capital refers to the total amount of capital that all limited partners collectively commit to contribute to the limited partnership as stipulated in the limited partnership agreement. This represents the maximum capital contribution obligation that each limited partner is required to fulfill in the future according to the agreement, and serves as the core foundational data for the fund's fundraising size.

chinese: 期初固定资产账面价值
固定资产期初账面价值

definition_en: Beginning fixed assets refer to the carrying value of tangible assets (such as plants, machinery, vehicles) owned by an enterprise at the start of each accounting period (e.g., a month or a year), which are used for production and operation and have an expected useful life exceeding one year. This figure is carried forward directly from the data at the end of the previous accounting period.

Beginning balance refers to the specific quantity or amount of an asset, liability, or equity item held by an enterprise or organization at the start of an accounting or statistical period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It typically represents the ending balance from the previous period and serves as the starting point for new period accounting and comparison.

Beginning total assets refers to the total value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending total assets of the previous accounting period. As a fundamental point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, it serves as the starting point for analyzing changes in assets during the current period and for calculating related financial metrics.

Beginning retained earnings refers to the cumulative net profit or net loss carried forward from the previous fiscal year (or accounting period) at the start of a new accounting year, which has not yet been distributed to shareholders. It represents part of the enterprise's accumulated operating results over the years and directly constitutes shareholders' equity.

chinese: 期初未分配利润与盈余公积合计

definition_en: Beginning retained earnings refers to the balance of retained earnings carried forward from the previous accounting period at the start of the current accounting period. It represents the portion of accumulated net profits from past operations that has not been distributed to shareholders, serving as a key item on the balance sheet. Typically carried forward directly from the prior period's ending balance, it forms the basis for calculating changes in retained earnings during the current period.

Ending price refers to the market price or book value of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) at the end of a specific accounting period or investment horizon (e.g., at the close of a trading day, month, quarter, or year). It is a raw data point obtained directly from market transaction data or accounting records, typically serving as a fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as returns.

Option price is the premium paid by the option buyer to the option seller to acquire the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying asset at a specified price on or before a specific future date. This premium consists of two components: intrinsic value, which is the favorable difference between the current price of the underlying asset and the strike price; and time value, which represents the additional value attributable to the potential for market fluctuations during the remaining life of the contract.

Outstanding balance refers to the total amount in an account that has not been paid or settled at a specific point in time (e.g., statement date or reporting date). It typically includes unpaid principal, accrued interest, and other related charges, serving as fundamental data reflecting the current debt level.

Outstanding invoices refer to sales invoices issued to customers for which payment has not yet been received, or purchase invoices received from suppliers for which payment has not yet been completed. They represent a state of receivables or payables where the transaction has been confirmed but funds have not yet been settled.

term_en.name: Production Costs Incurred in the Current Month

english: Production Costs Incurred in Current Month

definition_en: Production costs incurred in the current month refer to the total of all expenses actually incurred by an enterprise within the current accounting month for producing goods or providing services. It is directly aggregated from source documents such as material requisition forms, payroll sheets, and depreciation calculation tables, and serves as the foundational data for subsequent allocation in cost accounting.

term_en.name: Expenses Incurred in the Current Month

definition_en: Expenses incurred in the current month refer to various costs and expenditures that are actually incurred and attributable to the current accounting month due to production, operational activities, or other business operations, in accordance with the accrual basis principle. It represents the transaction amount in profit and loss accounts for the current period and serves as fundamental data for calculating current period profit.

term_en.name: Actual Wages Incurred in the Current Month

chinese: 当月应付职工薪酬实发额
english: Actual Wages Incurred in the Current Month
Actual Wages Incurred in Current Month

definition_en: Actual wages incurred in the current month refer to the total wages actually borne by the enterprise for employees and recorded as costs or expenses during the current month (accounting period). This includes base salaries, allowances, bonuses, and the social security contributions paid by the enterprise for employees. It is typically accounted for under the accrual basis principle, regardless of whether payment has been made.

term_en.name: Actual Material Cost Incurred in Current Month

english: Actual Material Cost Incurred in Current Month

definition_en: Actual material cost incurred in the current month refers to the cost of various raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies actually consumed or input by an enterprise for production or operational activities during the current accounting month. Its amount is the total actual expenditure directly aggregated and measured based on original documents such as purchase invoices, warehouse receipts, freight documents, and sorting/processing fees, serving as the fundamental raw data for cost accounting.

Current period dividend refers to the amount of profit distribution formally declared and actually paid to shareholders by a company within a specific accounting period (such as the current quarter or fiscal year), based on resolutions of the board of directors or shareholders' meeting. It reflects the company's cash return to shareholders during that period, directly embodies the company's profit distribution decisions, and is typically sourced from official company announcements or the cash flow statement.

Current period sales refer to the total revenue earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services during the current accounting period (such as a month, a quarter, or a year). This figure is recognized based on the accrual basis of accounting, meaning that revenue is recognized in the period when the ownership of goods is transferred to the customer or services are rendered, regardless of whether cash has been received.

Principal amount refers to the original sum of money initially invested or borrowed in financial calculations (such as calculating interest, future value, or present value). It serves as the basis for computing financial metrics like interest and future value, typically functioning as a known input variable rather than a calculated result.

The principal amount refers to the original sum of money initially invested or loaned in a financial transaction or borrowing, excluding any interest, earnings, or additional fees. It serves as the basis for calculating interest and evaluating returns.

Equity, also known as shareholders' equity or owners' equity, is a core item on the balance sheet. It represents the residual claim on the company's assets that ultimately belongs to the company's owners (shareholders) after all liabilities have been repaid. Simply put, it is the portion remaining after subtracting total liabilities from total assets, reflecting the investment value of shareholders in the company and accumulated retained earnings.

chinese: 单位产品材料消耗标准

definition_en: Material standard consumption quantity refers to the predetermined quantity standard of a specific material allowed for consumption in producing one unit of qualified product under conditions of reasonable material usage. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and material management.

Standard price is a pre-determined unit price benchmark used for cost accounting and control within the standard costing system. It is typically established based on market conditions, long-term contract prices, or historical data, and serves as the fundamental input for calculating standard costs and conducting cost variance analysis (e.g., material price variance).

chinese: 单位标准变动制造费用
变动制造费用标准成本
标准变动制造费用分配率
变动制造费用标准分配率

definition_en: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead is the predetermined standard cost per unit of product for indirect production expenses that vary with production volume, such as indirect materials and power costs. It serves as a crucial internal benchmark for cost control and performance evaluation.

Standard quantity refers to the predetermined benchmark value for the consumption of resources such as materials and labor hours required to produce one unit of product or complete a service under the standard costing method. It is a planning or budgeting figure used for cost control and variance analysis.

Probability is a numerical measure of the likelihood of a random event occurring, with a value between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates the event is impossible, while 1 indicates the event is certain. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a known weight or base data for calculating metrics such as expected rate of return.

Coupon frequency refers to the number of times a fixed-income product, such as a bond, pays interest to investors within one year, for example, once per year (annual), twice (semi-annual), or four times (quarterly). It is directly stipulated by the bond's issuance terms and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating bond cash flows and effective yield.

Annual interest amount refers to the total interest generated over a one-year period based on the principal amount borrowed and the agreed annual interest rate. It is the most fundamental data in interest calculation, typically derived directly through the simple multiplication of 'principal × annual interest rate', and serves as a basic input value for more complex financial calculations (such as interest coverage ratio).

Annual interest expense refers to the total amount of interest that a company is required to pay or accrue to creditors within a complete fiscal year, based on the principal, interest rate, and term stipulated in borrowing agreements (such as bank loans, bonds, etc.). It is typically reported directly as a financial expense on the income statement.

Daily consumption/usage refers to the average daily quantity of raw materials, products, labor, or other resources consumed or required in the production, operation, or management processes of an enterprise. It is a fundamental business metric, typically derived directly from daily business records, statistics, or forecasts, and serves as a crucial input parameter for inventory management, cost control, and budget preparation.

Daily Delivery Volume refers to the total quantity or total number of shipments that a company actually delivers to customers or designated locations within a single day through its logistics or distribution system. It is typically sourced directly from primary business records such as daily delivery reports and logistics documents, and serves as fundamental data reflecting the intensity of daily operational activities.

Periodic interest refers to the amount of interest generated in each specific period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, annually) within a financial transaction (such as a loan, bond, or installment payment), based on the agreed principal, interest rate, and interest calculation period. It serves as fundamental data for calculating more complex financial metrics (such as bond present value and installment repayment amounts).

Trade size refers to the quantity or monetary amount of assets involved in a single transaction in financial markets, such as the number of shares purchased in a stock trade or the currency units exchanged in a foreign exchange transaction. It serves as fundamental data for analyzing market microstructure and trading behavior.

term_en.name: Transaction Cost per Sale of Marketable Securities to Replenish Cash

definition_en: In financial management, this refers to the fixed costs incurred by a company each time it sells its holdings of marketable securities (such as bonds, stocks, etc.) to convert them into cash. These costs typically include broker commissions, handling fees, taxes, and are a key input parameter for calculating the optimal cash balance under the inventory model.

term_en.name: Fixed Conversion Cost per Securities Transaction

chinese: 有价证券转换固定费用
english: Fixed Transaction Cost for Securities Conversion

definition_en: Fixed conversion cost per securities transaction refers to the fixed fee that a company must pay each time it sells securities and converts them into cash in cash management (such as the inventory model). This cost is independent of the conversion amount and typically includes transaction costs such as handling fees and commissions.

Ordering cost per order refers to the total of various expenses incurred by an enterprise from placing an order to receiving goods into inventory for a single procurement of raw materials or merchandise. These expenses typically include salaries of purchasing personnel, travel expenses, order document processing fees, communication costs, and indirect costs such as transportation arrangements. It is directly proportional to the number of orders placed but is not directly related to the quantity ordered each time.

Variable cost per order refers to the total of various expenses directly related to and varying with each order placement, such as travel expenses, postage, telephone and telegraph charges, and order processing fees. These costs increase with the number of orders placed and serve as key foundational data for calculating economic order quantity and other inventory management models.

Order quantity refers to the planned or actual quantity of a specific raw material, commodity, or supply that a company purchases or orders in a single procurement or ordering activity. It is a fundamental operational data point in inventory management and procurement decision-making, used for subsequent calculations of ordering costs, holding costs, and other financial metrics.

Share repurchase price refers to the actual price paid by a listed company for each share of its outstanding stock repurchased in a share buyback transaction. It is typically based on market price or a specific price set by the company and serves as the core raw data in share repurchase transactions.

Market price per share refers to the real-time transaction price at which a specific stock is bought and sold on secondary markets such as stock exchanges. It reflects the market's consensus on the current value of the stock, serves as fundamental market data that cannot be directly calculated from financial statements, and is a key input for calculating valuation metrics such as the price-to-earnings ratio and price-to-book ratio.

Par value per share refers to the legal price per share set in the company's articles of association when a joint-stock company issues shares, usually denominated in yuan/share. It represents the amount of legal capital corresponding to each share and serves as the basis for share issuance and accounting. In China's A-share market, the par value per share for the vast majority of stocks is fixed at 1 RMB, with exceptions for individual companies (such as Zijin Mining).

Active market is a fundamental concept in accounting standards, specifically referring to a market in which assets or liabilities are traded with sufficient volume and frequency to continuously and reliably provide pricing information, thereby serving as a basis for fair value measurement.

Outstanding common shares refer to the total number of common stock shares issued by a company and actually held by investors in the public market. It excludes shares repurchased and held as treasury stock by the company, serving as fundamental data for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

Number of Common Shares Outstanding refers to the total quantity of common shares issued by a listed company that are freely traded on the open market. It excludes treasury shares held by the company or restricted shares, and serves as fundamental data for calculating key financial metrics such as market capitalization and earnings per share.

Testing expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise to inspect and verify the performance, safety, and compliance of products, technologies, systems, or services with established standards.

In the field of finance and accounting, drift primarily refers to the phenomenon where the predictive or decision-making accuracy of financial forecasting models, risk measurement models, or investment strategies, constructed based on historical data, gradually declines over time and with changes in the market environment.

The base period price of goods refers to the price of goods in a specific period (known as the base period) selected as a benchmark in statistical or financial analysis to eliminate the effects of price changes. This price remains constant during subsequent analysis periods and is used to calculate real value changes, thereby more accurately reflecting changes in quantity or real value.

Spot price refers to the transaction price for the immediate delivery and settlement of an underlying asset (such as stocks, commodities, foreign exchange, etc.) at the current moment in financial or commodity markets. It is directly determined by the immediate market supply and demand and represents raw market data reflecting the current value of the asset.

Cash and cash equivalents refer to highly liquid assets held by an enterprise at the balance sheet date. They include cash on hand, demand deposits and other monetary funds readily available for payment, as well as short-term investments (typically with maturities of three months or less) that are highly liquid, readily convertible to known amounts of cash, and subject to insignificant risk of changes in value, such as short-term treasury bills and commercial paper.
A cash dividend is a return on investment paid directly to shareholders in cash, distributed from a listed company's after-tax profits in proportion to the shares held by each shareholder.

Cash assets refer to assets held by an enterprise or individual that can be used immediately for payment or debt settlement, primarily including cash on hand, bank deposits, other monetary funds, and short-term investments that can be quickly converted into cash with minimal risk of value fluctuation (such as cash equivalents). They are among the most liquid asset items on the balance sheet.

Total production worker wages refer to the aggregate sum of labor compensation, including wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies, paid by an enterprise to all frontline production workers directly involved in product manufacturing or service provision during a specific accounting period. It typically serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and is directly aggregated from payroll records or detailed accounts of employee compensation payable.

Production capacity is a predetermined or estimated baseline capacity figure used in management accounting for cost control and variance analysis, typically representing the maximum production capability under ideal or budgeted conditions. It serves as a fundamental parameter, primarily used to calculate metrics such as fixed manufacturing overhead capacity variance.

Living expenses refer to the total of various basic expenditures incurred by individuals or households to maintain daily life, typically including specific consumption items such as rent, food and beverage, transportation, utilities, communication, and daily necessities. In a financial context, it is an expenditure item composed of multiple original consumption categories, rather than a composite indicator calculated through formulas.

The target inflation rate is the level of inflation that a central bank or government monetary authority aims to maintain over a future period. It is a forward-looking policy objective used to guide public expectations and direct monetary policy operations, rather than a result calculated from historical data.

Direct labor refers to all compensation costs, including wages, allowances, and benefits, for workers directly engaged in product manufacturing or service provision during the production process. It is a key component of product cost and can be directly traced to specific products or services.

Direct materials refer to the costs of various raw materials, primary materials, purchased semi-finished goods, and auxiliary materials that are directly used in the production of goods and provision of services, form the physical substance of the product, and are consumed in the process.

Direct costs refer to expenditures that can be directly and unequivocally attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, project, or service). These costs are directly related to the production or provision process of the cost object and can be included in its cost without requiring complex allocation procedures.

Research and development expenses refer to the total amount of expenditures directly related to internal research and development activities incurred by an enterprise. In accounting, these expenses are typically recognized directly in the current period's profit or loss, serving as a fundamental line item on the income statement that reflects the enterprise's investment level in technological innovation and product development.

Coupon payment refers to the interest paid by a bond issuer to bondholders according to the interest rate and payment cycle agreed upon at the time of bond issuance. This is a contractual obligation that the bond issuer must fulfill, representing a cash outflow, and is directly recorded as original transaction data in accounting.

Face value refers to the original value or denomination explicitly stated on the instrument for financial instruments such as bonds, notes, and stocks. It is the base amount set at issuance, representing the nominal value of the instrument or the principal amount to be repaid at maturity.

In accounting, 'Employee Benefits' typically refers to the accrued employee welfare expenses, which are various forms of compensation and treatment provided by an enterprise to its employees beyond salaries, bonuses, and allowances. They are usually accrued at a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll or expensed based on actual occurrences, charged to relevant cost accounts, and used to cover employees' medical expenses, hardship allowances, collective welfare facility expenditures, etc.

Lease expense refers to the periodic payments made by a business or individual to the lessor for the right to use an asset (such as equipment, property, etc.) as stipulated in the lease agreement. It represents a direct, fundamental cash outflow under the lease contract and typically cannot be derived from other financial statement line items.

chinese: 租赁负债初始计量金额

definition_en: Leased asset cost refers to the present value, discounted at a specific interest rate to the commencement date of the lease, of all future payments (such as lease payments, bargain purchase option price, etc.) that the lessee is required to make to obtain the right to use an asset over the lease term. It represents the initial amount at which the lessee recognizes both the asset and the liability under a finance lease.

english: Initial Direct Cost of Leased Asset

definition_en: Leased asset acquisition cost refers to the total direct costs paid by the lessor to acquire the leased asset (e.g., equipment) in a leasing transaction. It typically includes the purchase price of the equipment, transportation fees, insurance premiums, tariffs, and other necessary expenditures incurred to bring the asset to its intended usable condition. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating lease payments and conducting lease financial analysis.

Rent refers to the payment made by a lessee to a lessor in accordance with a lease agreement to obtain the right to use an asset (such as property, equipment, etc.) for a specified period. It constitutes the fundamental payment amount in a lease transaction and is typically presented as a direct expense or revenue item in financial statements.

Rental income refers to the total inflow of economic benefits obtained by an enterprise or individual from leasing the right to use fixed assets (such as buildings, equipment, land, etc.), packaging materials, or other assets, and is a fundamental revenue item in accounting.

Pre-tax rent refers to the original rental payment amount in finance leases or operating leases before deducting any related taxes and fees (such as value-added tax, income tax, etc.). It serves as a fundamental input value for calculating financial metrics like the net present value of leases and after-tax cash flows.

Tax rate is the statutory ratio or fixed value stipulated by tax law, serving as the fundamental parameter for calculating a taxpayer's tax payable. It is typically expressed as the proportion between the tax payable and the taxable base amount (such as income, sales revenue, etc.).

Immediate exercise value refers to the profit that an option holder can directly obtain if they choose to exercise the option immediately at the current moment. For a call option, it equals the current market price of the underlying asset minus the strike price (if the result is negative, the value is zero); for a put option, it equals the strike price minus the current market price of the underlying asset (again, negative values are counted as zero). This value reflects the intrinsic value of the option at the current point in time and is an important basis for determining whether to exercise immediately.

The weight of security j refers to the proportion of the total portfolio value allocated to security j (such as a specific stock or bond) when constructing an investment portfolio. It reflects the relative importance and investment share of that security within the portfolio.

Cash outflow in year k refers to the total amount of cash actually paid by an enterprise during a specific fiscal year (year k) due to operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. It constitutes the fundamental raw data for the cash flow statement and reflects the enterprise's actual cash expenditures during that year.

term_en.name: Standard Deviation of the k-th Security

definition_en: The standard deviation of the k-th security is a fundamental statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of that security's own rate of return. It is calculated based on the security's historical return data. A larger value indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, signifying higher risk. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating more complex risk metrics such as portfolio risk and covariance.

Operating long-term liabilities refer to non-financial debts generated from a company's daily business operations with a repayment period exceeding one year. They primarily arise from operating activities rather than financing activities and typically do not require collateral or interest payments.

End Date refers to the specific point in time when an event, activity, project, contract, or financial instrument (such as bonds, options) terminates or matures. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a fundamental input parameter for calculating periods, days, or interest.

Outcome probability refers to the likelihood of a specific financial result or market event occurring in the future within financial and accounting activities, typically expressed as a percentage or a value between 0 and 1. It is a fundamental data point estimated based on historical data, statistical models, or expert judgment.

In the field of finance and accounting, maintenance primarily refers to the ongoing management, upkeep, and investment required to ensure the continuous normal operation and stable value of financial systems, data, assets, customer relationships, and compliance status. It is typically reflected as actual incurred maintenance expenses or costs, serving as a fundamental raw data point in financial accounting.

The Wiener process is an important continuous-time stochastic process in mathematical finance and probability theory, used as a mathematical model to describe the irregular motion (i.e., Brownian motion) of particles subjected to numerous tiny random collisions in a fluid. In finance, it is commonly used as the foundation for modeling the stochastic fluctuations of asset prices.

Confidence level is a predetermined parameter in statistics used to measure the probability or reliability that an estimate (such as a sample statistic) falls within a certain interval of the true value of a population parameter. It is a subjectively set standard, not a calculated result, commonly used in constructing confidence intervals and assessing risk.

Joint cost refers to the cost incurred jointly in the production process for manufacturing multiple products or serving multiple departments, which needs to be allocated among these products or departments. It typically occurs before the split-off point of joint products and serves as the basis for cost accumulation and allocation.

The Federal Funds Rate is the weighted average of overnight lending rates at which U.S. banks lend excess reserves to each other. It is determined by market transactions, guided and targeted by the Federal Reserve through open market operations, and serves as the core benchmark interest rate for U.S. monetary policy.

Stock price refers to the trading price of a listed company's shares on a stock exchange. It reflects the consensus and expectations formed by market participants regarding the company's value, based on various factors such as current performance, future development prospects, industry conditions, and the macroeconomic environment. Stock price is directly determined by the supply and demand relationship in the market and is dynamically changing.
Stock price change refers to the upward or downward movement in the price of a stock traded in the market over a period of time, typically expressed in specific points or percentage terms.

term_en.name: Stock Price on Dividend Distribution Right Transfer Date

chinese: 股利分配权转移日股价
english: Stock Price on Dividend Distribution Right Transfer Date

definition_en: The stock price on the dividend distribution right transfer date refers to the opening reference price or market trading price of a stock on the first trading day following the record date (i.e., the ex-dividend date) when a listed company distributes dividends. On this day, the stock's trading price is adjusted for the ex-dividend effect to reflect changes in the company's value after the dividend distribution. This price is fundamental data obtained directly from real-time stock market trading and cannot be calculated using other financial indicator formulas.

Dividend refers to the cash or stock-based return distributed by a listed company to its shareholders based on its profitability and profit distribution policy. It originates from the company's after-tax profits, is an amount directly declared and paid following a board resolution, and constitutes fundamental financial data.

Equity capital issuance refers to the act of a company increasing its share capital by selling new shares (such as common stock or preferred stock) to investors in order to raise funds. This is a primary method of equity financing for companies and constitutes a specific financing activity.

Total shares outstanding refers to the total number of all common shares issued by a company and held by shareholders, including shares held by the public and shares held by company insiders (such as management), but excluding treasury shares repurchased and held by the company itself.

Stock investment refers to an investment activity where enterprises or individuals purchase shares issued by listed companies to become shareholders, with the expectation of obtaining dividend income or capital appreciation. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded under accounts such as trading financial assets, available-for-sale financial assets, or long-term equity investments. Its initial value is measured at cost, with subsequent adjustments potentially made based on fair value or the equity method.

Stock current price refers to the latest transaction price of a particular stock at a specific moment in the securities trading market, agreed upon by buyers and sellers. It is determined by real-time market supply and demand, reflects investors' consensus on the stock's current value, and serves as fundamental data for trading and valuation.

Equity assets refer to the total market value of stocks held by investors or enterprises calculated at current market prices. It is a fundamental figure derived directly by multiplying the market price by the number of shares held, reflecting the book value of stock investments.

An independent variable refers to a variable that is actively selected, set, or observed by the researcher in a statistical model, mathematical formula, or experiment. Its variation is used to explain or predict changes in another variable (the dependent variable). In financial analysis, it typically consists of fundamental data directly obtained from business activities or markets, such as operating revenue, interest rates, etc.

Euler's number (e) is a fundamental mathematical constant that serves as the base of the natural logarithm function, with an approximate value of 2.71828. It is an infinite, non-repeating decimal and a transcendental number. In finance, it frequently appears as a fixed parameter in formulas such as those for continuous compounding.

Free float shares refer to the number of outstanding shares of a listed company that are actually available for free trading in the market. Typically determined by exchanges or index providers based on the shareholding structure, it excludes shares held by specific shareholders (such as state-owned shareholders, strategic investors, company founders, etc.) whose holdings exceed a certain threshold (e.g., 5%). It serves as the fundamental data for calculating free float market capitalization.

Operating expenses refer to various indirect costs incurred by an enterprise in its daily business activities for selling goods, providing services, and maintaining overall company operations. These expenses are not included in product costs but are directly recognized in the profit or loss statement in the period they occur, primarily including selling expenses and administrative expenses.

A subsidy refers to funds or benefits directly provided by the government or relevant institutions to support specific industries, enterprises, projects, or individuals, typically without requiring repayment. In accounting treatment, it is often recognized as non-operating income or recorded under specific grant items, serving as a fundamental data point in financial statements.

Observation refers to the raw data or variable values obtained through direct measurement, recording, or collection in statistical analysis, financial analysis, or scientific research. It is not a composite indicator derived from formulas, but rather the fundamental input information for analysis, modeling, and calculation.

Number of observations refers to the total count of independent samples, transaction records, time series points, or other observational units collected and used in financial and accounting data analysis or research. It serves as the foundation for any statistical analysis and directly impacts the reliability and accuracy of the results.

Accrual period refers to the specific time interval used as the basis for calculating interest, typically determined by a start date and an end date, serving as the fundamental time parameter for computing financial metrics such as accrued interest.

Order type refers to the specific form and conditions of trading instructions that investors send to brokers when buying or selling securities or derivatives. It stipulates how a trade is to be executed, including key parameters such as price, timing, and quantity.

Ordering fixed cost refers to a fixed fee that a company must pay each time it places an order, regardless of the quantity ordered. This cost is independent of the specific order quantity and is incurred whenever an order is placed, such as salaries of procurement personnel, administrative expenses for order processing, communication fees, and fixed logistics starting prices.

Equipment refers to tangible assets held by an enterprise for the production of goods, provision of services, rental, or management purposes, with a useful life exceeding one accounting year. It is a significant component of fixed assets on the balance sheet. Its value is recorded at historical cost (original value) and subsequently amortized through methods such as depreciation.

Design expenses refer to the direct expenditures incurred by an enterprise to obtain external or internal design services (such as product design, engineering design, survey and design, etc.) during product development, engineering construction, and other processes. In accounting treatment, they are typically treated as an original cost or expense and directly included in the cost of the relevant asset or in the current period's profit and loss.

In Activity-Based Costing, this refers to the actual quantity of activities consumed in producing or providing a specific product or service. These are fundamental operational data points, such as the number of orders processed, times of material handling, machine running hours, or duration of customer service. They are typically sourced directly from production records, business systems, or statistical reports and serve as the primary raw data for calculating activity costs.

english: Actual Hours Worked for the Product

definition_en: Actual hours for the product refer to the effective working time actually spent in the production process of a specific product, typically measured in hours. It includes direct product processing, necessary auxiliary operations, and reasonable rest intervals, serving as fundamental data for measuring production efficiency and calculating product costs.

term_en.name: Consumption of the Workshop, Product, or Department

definition_en: Consumption of the workshop, product, or department refers to the actual quantity of resources consumed by a specific cost object (such as a production workshop, a product, or a functional department) within a given period. These resources include raw materials, labor hours, electricity, water, etc., and are typically measured in physical units (e.g., kilograms, hours, kilowatt-hours). It constitutes the most fundamental and direct raw data for cost accounting and expense allocation.

chinese: 美国财务会计准则委员会

definition_en: The Financial Accounting Standards Board is an independent private-sector organization in the United States responsible for establishing and issuing standards for financial accounting and reporting. The rules it develops form the core of U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, aiming to ensure the uniformity, transparency, and comparability of corporate financial information to protect the interests of investors and capital markets.

Fiscal assistance refers to funds or asset support provided by the government or other external entities to enterprises or individuals that does not require direct repayment. It is typically used to encourage specific economic activities, offset costs, or provide relief. In accounting treatment, it is generally recognized as non-operating income or deferred revenue.

Book value refers to the remaining value of an asset or liability recorded in a company's financial statements. For assets, it is typically the original acquisition cost minus accumulated depreciation, amortization, and any impairment provisions; for liabilities, it is the outstanding principal portion. This figure is based on historical cost and accounting rules and does not necessarily equal the current market value.

Monetary payment amount refers to the total cash actually paid or receivable/payable in monetary form (including cash, electronic transfers, mobile payments, etc.) in economic transactions, which directly reflects the actual fund flow situation in the transaction.

Value of goods imports refers to the total original transaction value of all goods purchased from abroad and brought into a country or enterprise during a specific period. It is typically based on customs statistics or the contract price declared by enterprises, determined according to international trade terms (such as CIF or FOB), and serves as fundamental data for calculating the trade balance, customs duties, and conducting macroeconomic analysis.

Purchase price refers to the total consideration paid by an enterprise to acquire an asset (such as goods, equipment, stocks, etc.), including the purchase cost, taxes, transportation, installation, and all other necessary expenses. It serves as the basis for recording asset value, calculating costs, and evaluating investments.

term_en.name: Estimated Uncollectible Amount of Loans and Leases

english: Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses
Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses (ALLL)

definition_en: The estimated uncollectible amount of loans and leases is the total principal and interest of loan and lease assets that a bank or financial institution subjectively estimates may not be recoverable in the future, based on credit risk models, historical default data, current economic conditions, and assessments of borrowers' future repayment capacity. It serves as the foundational data for provisioning loan loss reserves.

Assets refer to resources arising from past transactions or events, owned or controlled by an enterprise, which are expected to generate economic benefits for the enterprise. On the balance sheet, total assets equal the sum of current assets and non-current assets.

Cost of asset refers to all necessary and reasonable expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire an asset and bring it to its intended usable or salable condition. These expenditures typically include the purchase price of the asset, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, installation and commissioning costs, and other direct costs attributable to the asset. It serves as the original base value for subsequent depreciation, amortization, or impairment testing of the asset.

Capital improvement expenditure refers to a one-time, significant capital investment made by an enterprise to enhance the performance of existing fixed assets, extend their useful life, or increase their future economic benefits.
