Examples include technological upgrades to plant equipment, expansion of buildings, or replacement of key components. Such expenditures are capitalized as part of the fixed asset cost and amortized through depreciation over their beneficial periods.

The useful life of an asset refers to the period over which an enterprise expects to use a fixed asset, or the number of production or similar units of output it expects to obtain from the asset's use. It is a fundamental estimated parameter for calculating fixed asset depreciation, typically determined through professional judgment based on experience, technical characteristics, operating environment, and other factors, or by reference to industry standards.

Asset management fee refers to the compensation paid by asset owners (such as fund investors) to professional managers (such as fund management companies) for the investment operation and management of assets. This fee is typically accrued periodically as a certain percentage of the assets under management, serving as one of the primary revenue sources for the manager and is recorded as an expense in the income statement.

term_en.name: Market Value of Asset Class i

english: Market Value of Asset Class i
Fair Value of Asset Class i
Current Market Price of Asset i

definition_en: The market value of asset class i refers to the prevailing transaction price agreed upon by willing buyers and sellers in an open, active, and orderly market on the valuation date, for the i-th category of assets after dividing the portfolio's assets into different classes based on specific criteria (such as stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.). It serves as the core foundational data for asset allocation, financial reporting, and risk management.

Asset acquisition cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire an asset and bring it to its intended usable condition, typically including purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, installation and commissioning fees, and other direct expenses. It forms the basis for the initial recorded value of the asset.

term_en.name: Premium of Lower Strike Price Call Option

chinese: 低行权价看涨期权价格
低执行价看涨期权权利金
english: Premium of Lower Strike Price Call Option

definition_en: The premium of a lower strike price call option refers to the fee that an investor pays to the option seller in order to obtain the right to purchase an asset (such as a stock) at a predetermined price (the strike price) that is below the current market price at a future date. Because this purchase price is more favorable than the market price, such an option has intrinsic value (known as an in-the-money option), and therefore its premium is typically higher.

term_en.name: Premium of Call Option with Higher Strike Price

chinese: 高行权价看涨期权价格
高执行价看涨期权权利金
english: Premium of Higher Strike Price Call Option
Call Option Premium with Higher Exercise Price

definition_en: The premium of a call option with a higher strike price refers to the trading price of a call option contract in the options market where the strike price is above the current market price of the underlying asset. This price is directly formed by market transactions, reflecting the fee paid by the buyer to the seller for obtaining the right to purchase the asset at a specific higher price in the future. Its specific value is influenced by various factors such as market supply and demand, underlying asset price, strike price, volatility, and time to expiration, and must be obtained directly from real-time market quotes or historical trading data.

term_en.name: Total Output of Auxiliary Production Products or Services

definition_en: Total output of auxiliary production products or services refers to the aggregate physical quantity of products produced or the total volume of service activities provided by an enterprise's auxiliary production departments (such as power supply, water supply, machinery maintenance, transportation, etc.) during a specific accounting period (e.g., a month or a quarter). It is a fundamental operational statistic directly derived from the production or service process and serves as the primary basis for calculating and allocating auxiliary production costs.

Total auxiliary production costs refer to the aggregate of all production expenses incurred by an enterprise's auxiliary production workshops (such as power supply, water supply, machinery maintenance, etc.) within a specific period for providing products or services. In accounting, these costs are accumulated on the debit side of the 'Auxiliary Production Cost' account and serve as the basis for calculating the unit cost of auxiliary production products or services.

Transportation cost refers to the direct expenses incurred by an enterprise in the process of moving goods, raw materials, or personnel from one location to another. These costs are fundamental to business operations and arise directly from actual transportation activities, such as driver compensation, vehicle fuel expenses, toll fees, and vehicle maintenance and repair costs. In accounting, it is typically recorded and aggregated as a separate expense account.

Transportation distance refers to the actual path length traveled by goods or services from the point of origin to the destination, typically measured in kilometers or miles. It is a fundamental raw data point in logistics and transportation activities, directly sourced from business operations or measurements, and serves as a critical input value for calculating composite indicators such as freight charges, logistics costs, and carbon emissions.

Departmental assets refer to the operational assets that an enterprise divides and aggregates according to different responsibility centers (such as business units, branches, or specific project teams) for internal management and performance evaluation. These assets typically include fixed assets, inventory, receivables, etc., that can be directly attributed or reasonably allocated to the department, and are used to measure the benefits generated by the resources occupied by that department.

In the field of finance and accounting, procurement primarily refers to the total price actually paid or payable by an enterprise to acquire materials such as raw materials and goods for production or sales, as well as directly related expenses such as transportation, handling, insurance, and taxes. It forms the basis of the initial cost of inventory and directly impacts subsequent cost of sales and profit.

Face value of a financial instrument refers to the nominal value explicitly stated on the instrument (such as bonds or stocks) at issuance. It serves as the basis for calculating interest, repaying principal, and accounting entries, is typically fixed, and differs from the fluctuating market value.

Financial liabilities refer to present obligations of an enterprise arising from past transactions or events, which are expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits from the enterprise, and the settlement of which requires the payment of cash or other financial assets. They primarily include bank borrowings, bonds payable, notes payable, etc., and constitute an important method for enterprises to raise funds.

Financial assets refer to various financial instruments held by enterprises or individuals that represent future benefits or rights to dispose of assets and can be traded in financial markets. In accounting, they are reflected as assets on the enterprise's balance sheet, primarily including cash, bank deposits, accounts receivable, bonds, stocks, fund shares, derivative financial instruments, etc. Their value is typically measured based on fair value or amortized cost.

Railway transportation costs refer to various related expenses incurred by an enterprise for utilizing railway transportation services, primarily including railway freight charges, construction funds, electrification surcharges, loading and unloading fees, and warehousing fees. These constitute a significant component of the enterprise's logistics costs.

Total Amount Payable to Depositors is a core liability on a bank's balance sheet, referring to the aggregate sum of all deposits absorbed by the bank from various clients, including individuals and enterprises, representing the total debt the bank owes and must repay to its depositors.

A banker's acceptance is a commercial bill issued by an enterprise, reviewed and accepted by a bank, which promises to pay a specified amount to the payee or holder unconditionally on a designated date. It is essentially a short-term payment instrument backed by a bank's credit guarantee, serving both payment and settlement functions as well as short-term financing.
Sales volume refers to the quantity of products or services actually sold by an enterprise within a specific period, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating sales revenue.

Selling expenses refer to various direct costs incurred by an enterprise during the process of selling goods and providing services, such as advertising and promotion expenses, sales personnel compensation, travel expenses, business entertainment expenses, transportation costs, exhibition fees, etc. These expenses are directly related to the enterprise's marketing and sales activities, aiming to promote product sales and expand market share.

Sales revenue refers to the total sum of all payments and additional charges (excluding value-added tax) collected from buyers through the sale of goods or provision of services within a specific period. It is a core financial metric for measuring the scale of a company's sales activities.

Long-term assets refer to assets that an enterprise plans to hold for more than one year or one complete operating cycle, which are expected to generate long-term economic benefits for the enterprise. They primarily include plant and equipment, land use rights, patents, long-term equity investments, etc.

The hurdle rate is a minimum rate of return standard set by investors or companies when making investment decisions. An investment project is considered worthwhile only when its expected rate of return exceeds this benchmark. It is commonly used to evaluate project feasibility, fund performance fee structures, and risk management.

Indirect tax refers to a tax whose burden can be shifted to the final consumer. It is typically collected by businesses during production, distribution, or consumption stages but ultimately transferred to consumers through the price chain. Common indirect taxes include Value-Added Tax (VAT), Consumption Tax, and Customs Duties.

A limit price is a specific price pre-set by a trader when placing an order; the trade will only be executed when the market price reaches or is better than this pre-set price. It is one of the most fundamental order types in financial trading, primarily used to control transaction costs or lock in profits.

term_en.name: Price at the End of the Restriction Period

english: Price at the End of Lock-up Period

definition_en: Price at the end of the restriction period refers to the market price of a stock at the specific point in time (typically the lock-up expiration date) when the share lock-up period concludes and the relevant shares become freely tradable on the market. This price is a direct market-derived or contractually agreed-upon base figure used for assessing share value or calculating related financial derivatives, rather than a composite value computed through other financial formulas.

english: Maximum Price within a Restricted Period

definition_en: The highest price during a restricted period refers to the highest trading price achieved by a financial asset on the public market within a pre-agreed time frame (e.g., a stock's lock-up period or restricted sale period). It is a specific numerical value directly obtained from historical market data and is commonly used as a key reference benchmark in various financial agreements.

In the field of finance and accounting, a divisor is a benchmark value used to standardize or adjust financial data. In stock index calculation, it serves as an adjustment coefficient that converts the total market capitalization or price of constituent stocks into index points, ensuring the continuity and comparability of the index when constituent stocks undergo changes (such as stock splits or dividends). In financial ratio analysis, the divisor (e.g., number of shares outstanding) is used to convert aggregate indicators into per-unit indicators for cross-sectional comparison.

Total Employer Contributions refers to the sum of all welfare payments made by an enterprise for its employees, including statutory pension insurance, medical insurance, etc. (the five social insurances and one housing fund), as well as voluntarily provided benefits such as enterprise annuities and supplementary medical insurance.

Non-current liabilities refer to debts that a company is required to repay after more than one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer). They represent long-term funding sources raised by the enterprise to support long-term development, such as purchasing equipment or expanding facilities.

Non-current assets refer to assets that an enterprise expects to hold for more than one year or one normal operating cycle, and are not intended or cannot be converted into cash, sold, or consumed in the short term. These assets typically require substantial capital investment, have slow turnover rates, and relatively poor liquidity, forming the foundation for long-term operations and investments of the enterprise.

Advisory fee is the compensation paid by an enterprise for services such as consultation, advice, and planning provided by external professionals or institutions. In accounting treatment, it is typically directly recorded under accounts such as administrative expenses and constitutes a fundamental cost in the enterprise's operational process.

The predetermined discount rate is a ratio set in advance based on factors such as market interest rates, the company's cost of capital, and project-specific risks, before conducting financial valuation or investment decisions. It is used to discount future cash flows to their present value and serves as a key input parameter for calculating metrics like net present value, rather than being derived from a fixed formula.

Budget appropriation refers to the original funds allocated by the government or superior units to budget units for specific purposes according to the approved budget. It serves as the fundamental funding source for budget units' accounting and operational activities, typically allocated directly rather than calculated through formulas.

Estimated activity output refers to the projected quantity or level of various activity measures (such as machine hours, labor hours, production batches, etc.) for a future specific period (e.g., a quarter or a year), based on business planning like sales forecasts and production plans during the budgeting process. It serves as fundamental input data for calculating cost management metrics such as budgeted activity cost allocation rates.

chinese: 资产拆除移除预估成本

definition_en: Estimated dismantling and removal costs refer to the anticipated future cash outflows related to dismantling, cleanup, and transportation that an enterprise expects to incur when disposing of or abandoning a specific asset (such as property, plant, and equipment) in accordance with contractual agreements, legal requirements, or internal management policies. These costs are estimated based on engineering assessments, market quotations, or historical experience and serve as fundamental data for financial forecasting and initial asset measurement.

Projected sales revenue refers to the forecasted total revenue expected to be generated from the sale of products or provision of services over a specific future period (such as a quarter or a year), based on methods including historical sales data, market trend analysis, and expert judgment. It serves as a critical foundational data point for corporate financial budgeting and operational decision-making.

term_en.name: Prior Year Stock Price per Share

english: Previous Year's Stock Price per Share
Prior Year Closing Price per Share

definition_en: Prior year stock price per share refers to the market price of a listed company's stock at the end of the previous complete fiscal year, typically based on the closing price on the last trading day of that year. It reflects the market's assessment of the company's value at a specific point in time and serves as fundamental data for calculating metrics such as stock returns and growth rates.

term_en.name: Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders for the Prior Period

chinese: 前期普通股股东净利润
上期归属普通股净利润
前期归属于普通股股东的净利润
上期普通股股东净利润
english: Net Income Attributable to Common Shareholders of Previous Period
Prior Period Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders

definition_en: Net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders for the prior period refers to the portion of net profit in the income statement for the previous reporting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) that ultimately belongs to the company's ordinary shareholders. It serves as the base data for calculating metrics such as basic earnings per share and is directly sourced from the financial statements of the prior period.

Previous Period Consumption Amount typically refers to the total consumption expenditure from the last comparable period (e.g., the same period in the previous fiscal year) used for comparison with the current period's consumption amount in financial statements (such as the Cash Flow Statement). It is directly sourced from historical ledgers or statements and serves as the foundational data for reflecting consumption changes.

term_en.name: Net Cash Flow from Previous Period

english: Net Cash Flow of Previous Period

definition_en: Net Cash Flow from Previous Period refers to the net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents reported on the cash flow statement at the end of the prior accounting period (e.g., previous quarter or fiscal year). It is a historical figure directly taken from the prior period's cash flow statement, reflecting the combined effect of operating, investing, and financing activities on the company's cash position in that period.

english: Operating Current Liabilities of Previous Period

definition_en: Prior period operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within a normal operating cycle (typically within one year), as of the closing date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). They generally include short-term liability items directly related to core business operations, such as accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable.

chinese: 上一会计期间销售收入

definition_en: Previous period sales revenue refers to the total income earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services during the preceding accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). It is typically sourced directly from financial statements such as the income statement and serves as fundamental historical data for budgeting and financial analysis.

Prior period sales refers to the total revenue amount generated by a company from selling goods or providing services during a specific period preceding the current period (e.g., the previous fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is a fundamental historical financial data point, typically obtained directly from the company's accounting records or financial statements, and is used for comparative analysis with current period data.

Next period dividend refers to the expected per-share cash dividend amount that a company is anticipated to pay to its common shareholders over a specific future period (typically the next fiscal year or quarter). It is a forecasted or assumed value based on the company's dividend policy, historical payment patterns, or management guidance, and is commonly used as the starting point for calculations in stock valuation models such as the Dividend Discount Model.

chinese: 辅助生产车间原始费用
交互分配前发生费用额

definition_en: Pre-reciprocal allocation costs refer to the total expenses directly accumulated by each auxiliary production department (such as power supply and maintenance workshops) before mutual service provision when using the reciprocal allocation method to distribute auxiliary production costs. These costs typically originate directly from raw cost data such as materials and labor, and serve as the foundational data for subsequent reciprocal allocation.

Preferred stock equity is a separate line item within the shareholders' equity section of a company's balance sheet, representing the claim of preferred shareholders on the company's net assets (i.e., the residual portion after total liabilities are subtracted from total assets). This figure is typically sourced directly from the company's financial statements as a fundamental financial datum, not derived from calculations involving other metrics.

The Preferred Stock Amount is an account presented in the shareholders' equity section of the balance sheet, representing the total amount of outstanding preferred stock calculated at par value or issue price. It is a fundamental, raw data item directly sourced from the company's capital records, not a composite metric derived from other financial indicators.

The Credit Conversion Factor (CCF) is a coefficient used by financial institutions such as banks in risk management to convert the potential risk exposure of off-balance-sheet items (e.g., loan commitments, letters of credit) into an equivalent on-balance-sheet asset risk exposure according to a predetermined ratio. It is a key regulatory and internal model parameter used to calculate total risk-weighted assets.

Debt maturity refers to the length of time from the inception of a debt to its scheduled repayment date, as stipulated in the debt contract or by legal provisions. It directly determines the duration of the debt and is one of its fundamental attributes.

Debt principal refers to the original contractual amount initially borrowed by the borrower or bond issuer from the creditor. It serves as the basis for calculating interest and structuring repayment schedules, and is typically obtained directly from loan agreements or bond issuance documents.

Debt amount typically refers to the aggregate book value of all liabilities assumed by an enterprise at a specific point in time (e.g., the balance sheet date), representing the portion of total assets financed by creditors. It is a fundamental figure on the balance sheet and serves as a core component for calculating various financial ratios (such as the debt ratio and cash-to-total-debt ratio).

chinese: 以摊余成本计量的金融资产

definition_en: Debt investment refers to bonds or other debt instruments purchased and held to maturity by an enterprise to earn interest income. In accounting, it is typically classified as a financial asset measured at amortized cost. Its initial measurement is at fair value plus transaction costs, with subsequent measurement using the amortized cost method, where the carrying amount changes with the amortization of interest adjustments.

english: Non-operating Income and Expenses (in a broad sense)

definition_en: Other business income and expenses refer to the revenue generated and corresponding cost expenditures from business activities other than the main operations of an enterprise. It is directly derived from accounting records and serves as a fundamental line item on the income statement, used to account for the operating results of non-core business activities such as material sales and asset leasing.

chinese: 指定为以公允价值计量且其变动计入其他综合收益的金融资产
english: Financial Assets at Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI)
Financial Assets at Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI) - Debt Instruments

definition_en: Other debt investments are a type of financial asset held by an enterprise, typically referring to investments in debt instruments such as bonds that are held with the objective of both collecting contractual cash flows and selling the financial asset. In accounting treatment, they are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. Their carrying amount is directly formed through initial recognition and subsequent measurement (such as fair value changes and amortization of interest adjustments).

chinese: 非交易性权益工具投资

definition_en: Other alternative investment assets, in accounting, typically refer to non-trading equity instrument investments held by an enterprise that are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. They belong to a category of alternative investments, distinct from traditional assets such as stocks, bonds, and cash, and represent a specific asset account on the balance sheet.

Other Income is a line item on the income statement, classified as a profit and loss account under accounting standards. It primarily accounts for various gains that are not directly related to the enterprise's ordinary operating activities but result in an increase in owners' equity, excluding operating revenue and investment income. It serves as one of the fundamental data items for calculating operating profit.

chinese: 指定为FVOCI的权益工具投资
非交易性权益工具投资
以公允价值计量且变动计入其他综合收益的权益投资

definition_en: Other equity instrument investments refer to non-trading equity instrument investments that an enterprise actively designates as measured at fair value with changes in fair value recognized in other comprehensive income, in accordance with accounting standards. They are a type of financial asset whose value fluctuates directly with market fair value, and the holding purpose is typically for long-term strategic holding rather than short-term trading gains.

chinese: 其他非流动资产金融资产
非流动金融资产其他项
其他非流动资产-金融资产

definition_en: Other non-current financial assets are items in the balance sheet used to aggregate financial assets that are not separately presented in the financial statements and have a holding period exceeding one year. They typically include infrequent or immaterial long-term financial assets that are not practical to present separately.

Other Non-cash Adjustments is an aggregate adjustment item in the supplementary information of the cash flow statement, used to reflect all other non-cash adjustment items not separately listed during the process of reconciling net profit to cash flows from operating activities, apart from the explicitly enumerated items (such as asset impairment provisions, depreciation of fixed assets, etc.). It serves as a catch-all item to ensure the completeness of the reconciliation process.

Total Allocation Base refers to the aggregate volume of fundamental business activities used as the basis for allocating indirect costs (such as manufacturing overhead and administrative expenses) to various cost objects (e.g., products, services, departments) in cost accounting. It typically consists of raw data directly obtainable from production or operational activities, such as total production labor hours, total machine operating hours, or total output volume, and serves as the key denominator for calculating the cost allocation rate.

term_en.name: Cash Paid for Dividends, Profit Distribution and Interest Payments

english: Cash Paid for Dividends and Interest
Cash Paid for Dividends, Profits and Interest

definition_en: This is an item in the enterprise's cash flow statement, specifically recording the cash actually paid by the company during a certain period for dividends to shareholders, profit distribution to other investment units, as well as cash payments for interest on borrowings and bonds. Regardless of which expense account these interest payments are accounted for in accounting (such as financial expenses, construction in progress, etc.), their cash payments are aggregated and reflected in this item.

Initial dividend typically refers to the cash dividend per share paid by a company during a specific period (usually the first period), either when it first distributes dividends to shareholders or as the starting point for calculations in specific financial models (such as the Dividend Discount Model). It is a base data point, usually obtained directly from the company's dividend announcements, historical dividend records, or financial statements, rather than being derived from formulas.

The previous closing price refers to the final transaction price of a stock or security at the end of the last formal trading day. It is the consensus price reached by market trading activities at the close of that day and serves as a crucial benchmark for calculating the day's price change, opening reference price, and other metrics.

Fair value of remaining investment refers to the objectively and impartially assessed value of the retained portion of equity after a partial disposal of a long-term equity investment, determined based on current market conditions. It is not derived from a formula but is an original data point obtained from market information or valuation models, used for subsequent accounting measurement.
category_en: Business Combinations and Consolidated Financial Statements

definition_en: Compensation of employees refers to the total remuneration that employees should receive for their participation in production activities. This includes wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies paid in monetary form, as well as benefits provided in kind, and social insurance contributions and housing provident fund contributions paid by the employer on their behalf.

Historical stock price refers to the actual transaction price records of a stock on specific past trading days or periods within a securities exchange. It reflects the historical market trading activity of the stock and serves as fundamental data for technical analysis, backtesting research, and investment performance evaluation.

Original stock price refers to the initial stock price used as the starting point for calculation in stock market trading, which is unadjusted or not derived from further calculations. It serves as the fundamental raw data for market transactions and is typically used to compute derivative metrics such as stock price change percentages.

Number of Comparable Companies refers to the total count of listed or unlisted companies that can be selected from the market for comparison with the subject company during business valuation, based on qualitative or quantitative criteria such as industry, company size, products or services, market position, and financial performance. It is a fundamental statistical result when conducting valuation using the market approach (e.g., Comparable Company Analysis).

Credit Period Days refer to the maximum number of days allowed by a company's credit policy for customers to pay for goods or services after purchase. It is a fundamental duration parameter set based on the company's operational strategy and customer relationships, used to manage accounts receivable and cash flow.

Current price of individual commodities refers to the actual transaction price or listed price of a single commodity or service in a specific market at a specific point in time (e.g., a trading day, month-end). It is the most fundamental and original data unit that constitutes more complex price indices, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Periodic expansion investment cost refers to the actual cash outflows for capital expenditures incurred during specific periods (e.g., annually, quarterly) of a project's construction or investment implementation when a company undertakes expansionary investments (such as building new production lines, expanding capacity, opening new stores, etc.). These costs form the original base data for the total project investment, typically including direct expenditures for equipment procurement, engineering construction, installation, and commissioning. They must be recorded period by period according to the investment plan or actual circumstances and cannot be derived from other financial indicators.

Number of periods refers to the predetermined total number of time segments used in financial calculations for computing future cash flows, interest, or other financial metrics, based on time cycles (e.g., years, quarters, months) or contractual terms (e.g., loan tenure, investment horizon). It is a fundamental input parameter, not derived from other financial data.

Individual Asset Investment Cost refers to the total consideration or transaction price actually paid to acquire a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, equipment, real estate, etc.). It constitutes the fundamental raw data for the total cost of an investment portfolio, typically not derived from calculations using other financial metrics but sourced directly from transaction records.

Total capital contributed by partners refers to the aggregate sum of capital actually invested into a partnership (such as a general partnership, limited partnership, or private fund) by all partners in accordance with the partnership agreement. It is directly sourced from accounting records or the partnership agreement, representing the simple summation of the actual capital contributions made by each partner, and reflects the actual capital base received by the enterprise for operations and liability assumption.

Notional principal is a specified base amount in a financial derivatives contract (such as an interest rate swap or currency swap) used to calculate the cash flows to be exchanged between the contracting parties. It does not involve actual borrowing or transfer of funds itself, but serves solely as a reference benchmark for calculating interest payments or returns.

Fixed transportation cost refers to the portion of costs in transportation operations that does not vary with changes in transportation volume (such as ton-kilometers or freight volume). These costs are typically associated with maintaining transportation capacity and must be paid regardless of whether transportation services are performed, including expenses such as vehicle depreciation, loan interest, salaries of permanent staff, insurance premiums, and fixed administrative fees.

Base period constituent stock prices refer to the closing market prices of each individual stock that constitutes an index on the selected reference date (i.e., the base period) when calculating a stock index. These prices serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating the initial value of the index or for subsequent comparisons.

Base period dividend refers to the actual amount of dividends paid to shareholders by a company during a specific historical period (typically the starting point or benchmark period used for calculations). It is a historical figure, not a forecast derived from formulas, and is often used as a foundational input for calculating future expected dividends or the cost of capital.

The Base Period Index Value refers to a fixed initial numerical value, such as 100 points or 1000 points, artificially assigned to a selected reference date (base period) when compiling various indices like stock indices and price indices. It serves as the absolute reference starting point for calculating and comparing all subsequent period indices. It is a directly set original datum and cannot be derived from other financial indicators or formulas.

Base period sales revenue refers to the total sales revenue from a specific historical period (such as the previous fiscal year or a specific quarter) selected by a company as a benchmark for comparison. It is typically obtained directly from the financial statements or business records of that period and serves as fundamental data for calculating sales growth rates, conducting financial forecasting, and preparing budgets.

term_en.name: Other Owners' Equity Items of Subsidiaries

definition_en: Other owners' equity items of subsidiaries refer to the equity interests in the net assets of subsidiaries attributable to investors other than the parent company (i.e., non-controlling interests) as presented in consolidated financial statements. They represent the portion of the subsidiary's owners' equity that does not belong to the parent company.

Total assets of a subsidiary refer to the aggregate value of all resources owned or controlled by the subsidiary as of the balance sheet date that are expected to generate economic benefits. It represents the sum of the book values of all asset items (such as current assets, fixed assets, intangible assets, etc.) and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics like return on assets.

Finished goods quantity refers to the physical quantity of products that have completed all production processes, met predetermined quality standards, and are ready for warehousing or direct sale within a specific accounting period. It is a fundamental data point in the production process, typically sourced from workshop production records or warehouse receiving slips, and serves as a crucial basis for product cost calculation (such as allocating production costs using the equivalent units of production method).

Issue Date refers to the specific date on which securities such as stocks or bonds are formally issued or sold to investors. It is a fundamental point-in-time data point, typically sourced directly from issuance announcements or relevant legal documents, and serves as a crucial input value for subsequent financial calculations such as weighted average number of shares.

The number of annuity payment periods refers to the total count of payments made during a series of equal, equally spaced cash flows (i.e., an annuity). It is a fundamental parameter required for calculating the present value or future value of an annuity, typically predetermined by external conditions such as contracts or retirement plans.

Bonds payable represent a liability arising from the issuance of marketable securities by an enterprise to raise long-term funds, with an obligation to repay principal and interest within a specified period. On the balance sheet, it is presented as a non-current liability (or the portion due within one year is reclassified as a current liability), and its amount directly reflects the actual transaction records of the bond's face value, interest adjustments (such as premium or discount), etc.

term_en.name: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders

chinese: 归属于普通股股东的净利润
english: Net Income Attributable to Common Shareholders

definition_en: Net profit attributable to common shareholders refers to the portion of a company's net profit realized during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) that ultimately belongs to common shareholders after deducting dividends payable to preferred shareholders. It is a fundamental item on the income statement, directly reflecting the operating results attributable to common shareholders for that period.

term_en.name: Current Year Federal Tax Rate Schedule

definition_en: The Current Year Federal Tax Rate Schedule is an official document issued by the government (e.g., the U.S. Internal Revenue Service) that details the progressive tax rates applicable to different income brackets and their corresponding income thresholds. It serves as the foundational reference data for calculating federal income tax liabilities for individuals or businesses and is not derived from other financial metrics.

Current price refers to the actual transaction price of goods, services, or assets in the market during the current accounting period or reporting period. It is typically derived directly from market quotations, sales records, or transaction contracts, and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and output VAT.

term_en.name: Number of Common Shares Repurchased in the Current Period

english: Number of Common Shares Repurchased in the Current Period
Shares of Common Stock Repurchased in the Current Period

definition_en: Number of Common Shares Repurchased in the Current Period refers to the total quantity of a company's issued common shares actually bought back from the open market during a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year), using methods like internal funds. This figure serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating metrics such as the weighted average number of common shares outstanding.

term_en.name: Number of Newly Issued Common Shares in the Current Period

english: Number of Newly Issued Common Shares in the Period
New Common Shares Issued During the Period
Newly Issued Common Shares in Current Period

definition_en: The number of newly issued common shares in the current period refers to the quantity of common shares actually issued and included in the company's total share capital during the current accounting period, through methods such as initial public offerings, additional share issuances, rights offerings, debt-to-equity swaps, and consideration paid for business combinations. This data serves as fundamental raw data for calculating metrics like earnings per share and is directly sourced from the company's share issuance records.

Total population count refers to the total number of all individuals or observations within a complete data set (population). It is a fundamental counting metric derived directly from the data itself, not calculated through computation.

Total Report Count refers to the cumulative number or aggregate quantity of all reports (such as financial reports, audit reports, analytical reports, etc.) generated, submitted, or tallied within a specific period or scope. It is a fundamental statistical metric used to measure the output scale of reporting activities or the volume of a data collection.

Total shares outstanding refers to the aggregate number of all shares issued by a company, representing the company's capital scale. It is a fundamental figure on the balance sheet, typically calculated by directly summing the quantities of various issued share types (such as common shares, restricted shares, etc.).

Total Number of Surveyed Enterprises refers to the aggregate count of all enterprises or units included within the scope of a specific statistical survey and directly enumerated. It is one of the most fundamental raw data points in statistical surveys, used to describe the scale of the study population.

Real estate investment refers to the act of individuals or institutions allocating funds into immovable assets such as land, residential properties, commercial buildings, and industrial plants, with the objective of obtaining future returns (e.g., rental income, capital appreciation) or for self-use. In accounting, it is typically recognized as the actual cash paid or capital expenditure incurred when acquiring these assets.

Investment property refers to real estate held by an enterprise to earn rental income, capital appreciation, or both, such as leased land use rights and leased buildings, and is a long-term asset of the enterprise.

Investment amount refers to the total cash directly invested by an investor in the initial stage of a project or asset to obtain future returns, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating derived metrics such as return on investment and total investment.

Reported Improvement Count refers to the total raw sum of various improvement events or improvement proposals recorded and reported within an enterprise or organization during a specific period. This data is directly sourced from frontline records, such as improvement suggestions submitted by employees or process optimization event reports, and represents foundational data not calculated by any formula.

term_en.name: Number of Enterprises Reporting No Change

chinese: 报告期状态不变企业数
经营状况未变企业数量
english: Number of Enterprises Reporting No Change

definition_en: Number of Enterprises Reporting No Change refers to the raw count of corporate legal entities whose core operating conditions (such as operating revenue, asset scale, number of employees, etc.) show no significant change compared to the previous period during a specific statistical survey or reporting period. This data is a direct result of statistical surveys and cannot be calculated from other financial indicators.

term_en.name: Constituent Stock Prices in the Reporting Period

definition_en: Constituent stock prices in the reporting period refer to the actual trading prices of each individual stock that constitutes a specific stock index in the securities market during a designated reporting period (such as a trading day, a week, or a month). These prices are raw data directly generated by market transactions and serve as fundamental inputs for calculating index values, analyzing index performance, and constructing other financial indicators.

The reporting period refers to the specific time frame covered by a financial report, used to define the start and end dates for the statistics and calculations of various financial data in the statements. It is typically predetermined by accounting standards or company policies, such as monthly, quarterly, or annual periods.

Reporting Period Item Amount refers to the original recorded value or base amount of a specific item (such as operating revenue, cash inflow from operating activities, etc.) in the financial statements during the specific period covered by the financial report (e.g., a quarter or a fiscal year). It reflects the actual occurrence amount or ending balance of that item during the reporting period and serves as the fundamental data for financial analysis and indicator calculation.

Position quantity refers to the specific number or units of a particular financial asset (such as stocks, bonds, fund shares, futures contracts, etc.) held in an investor's trading account or investment portfolio at a specific point in time. It serves as fundamental data for calculating profit and loss, risk assessment, and asset allocation.

term_en.name: Total Cash Return During Holding Period

english: Total Cash Income During Holding Period

definition_en: Total cash return during holding period refers to the sum of all cash-form returns actually received by an investor throughout the entire period of holding a specific asset (such as stocks or bonds), including, for example, stock dividends and bond interest. These returns are cash directly flowing into the investor's account, which can be directly traced from transaction records or financial statements without requiring complex calculations.

term_en.name: Cash Paid for Other Financing Activities

chinese: 支付的其他与筹资活动有关的现金
筹资活动其他现金支付
其他筹资活动现金流出
支付的其他筹资活动现金
english: Cash Paid for Other Financing Activities

definition_en: This is an item in the financing activities section of a company's cash flow statement, used to record actual cash payments related to financing activities other than major items such as debt repayment, dividend or profit distribution, and interest payments. These payments typically cannot be calculated by formula and must be directly entered based on actual accounting records.

Cash paid for interest refers to the total cash outflow from a company during a specific accounting period for interest payments made to creditors due to debt financing activities such as borrowing or issuing bonds. It is a component of cash outflows from operating activities in the cash flow statement and is directly derived from the company's cash transaction records.

Number of Payments refers to the total agreed-upon number of payment installments in financial arrangements such as installment plans, loans, or annuities. It is a fundamental parameter, typically stipulated by contract, used to calculate financial metrics such as the periodic payment amount and total interest.

term_en.name: Expected Return of the Best Alternative Investment Foregone

english: Expected Return of the Best Foregone Alternative
Expected Return of the Best Alternative

definition_en: The expected return of the best alternative investment foregone refers to the return rate of the option, among all other feasible investment alternatives, that is expected to yield the highest return but is abandoned when making a specific investment decision. It is a key reference value for measuring opportunity cost, typically requiring estimation based on market conditions or subjective judgment rather than being directly calculated from a company's internal financial data.

term_en.name: Market Return Rate of Government Bonds

definition_en: The market return rate of government bonds refers to the yield to maturity or the yield implied by the trading price of government bonds (such as treasury bonds) with a specific maturity, directly observed from the financial market. It is a raw market data point, typically used as a fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as corporate debt cost.

Data sorting is a fundamental operation in data processing, referring to the process of rearranging records in a dataset according to specific rules (ascending or descending) of one or more key fields (such as numerical value, alphabetical order, date sequence, etc.). It is an important data organization step prior to data analysis, statistics, and visualization.

Number of data points refers to the total count of independent raw observations or records contained within a dataset or statistical sample. It serves as the fundamental input data for subsequent statistical analysis, such as calculating the mean and standard deviation.

Old debt typically refers to the total amount of liabilities that already existed and remained unpaid by an enterprise at a specific point in time (such as the beginning of an accounting period). It is a fundamental financial datum that reflects the cumulative debt burden accumulated from the enterprise's past financing or operational activities.

Beginning value refers to the recorded balance of an accounting account (such as an asset, liability, or equity account) at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a month, quarter, or year). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the starting point for current financial recording and calculations.

Beginning Net Asset Value refers to the book value of the total equity owned by the enterprise's owners (shareholders) at the start of an accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is directly derived from the balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the base data for calculating financial metrics such as average net assets.

term_en.name: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period

english: Beginning Number of Common Shares Outstanding
Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period
Number of Common Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of the Period

definition_en: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period refers to the total quantity of common shares that have been issued by a company and have not been repurchased or retired by the company at the start of a financial reporting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It serves as the base data for calculating metrics like the weighted average number of common shares outstanding.

Beginning inventory value refers to the book value of all inventory (including raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, etc.) available for use or sale in a company's warehouse at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending inventory value of the previous period and serves as the basis for calculating inventory changes and costs during the current period.

Beginning actual cost refers to the accumulated actual cost of work-in-process (or the production cost account) carried forward from the previous accounting period at the start of a new accounting period. It serves as the starting point data for cost calculation and allocation in the current period, typically derived from the cost accounting results of the prior period, representing the accumulation of historical expenses.

Initial investment value refers to the total capital invested to acquire an asset or equity interest at the commencement of an investment project or business valuation. It typically serves as a fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as net present value and internal rate of return. Estimation methods include using the asset's book value, replacement value, or realizable value.

chinese: 期初所有者权益（普通股）

definition_en: Beginning Common Shareholders' Equity refers to the total amount of owners' equity attributable to common shareholders at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the net asset value at that specific point in time, comprising capital contributed by common shareholders and accumulated retained earnings not yet distributed to shareholders.

Beginning value per share refers to the value corresponding to each common share at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It typically denotes the stock's market price on the first day of the period or the book value per share calculated from the company's financial statements, serving as fundamental data for measuring the stock's value level at the period's commencement.

Beginning current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that a company is obligated to repay within one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer) at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). This figure is typically derived directly from the balance sheet data at the end of the previous accounting period.

Beginning current assets refer to the total value of all current assets owned by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). These assets are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle longer than a year. It is a critical point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, directly derived from the account balances in the accounting books or financial statements.

Opening price refers to the first transaction price of a stock in the securities market at the beginning of a specific time period (such as a trading day, week, month, or fiscal year). It serves as fundamental raw market data and is typically used as a benchmark for calculating indicators such as percentage price changes.

term_en.name: Total Liabilities at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Total liabilities at the beginning of a period refer to the aggregate value of present obligations that an entity is expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits, as recorded at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). This figure is directly taken from the total liabilities at the end of the previous period as reported in financial statements (e.g., the balance sheet) and serves as the baseline data for financial analysis in the current period.

chinese: 普通股股东权益期末数

definition_en: Ending Common Shareholders' Equity refers to the total amount of owners' equity attributable to common shareholders at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It reflects the residual claim value enjoyed by common shareholders in the company's net assets at the reporting date, after deducting preferred stock equity.

english: Long-term Operating Liabilities at Period End

definition_en: Ending operating long-term liabilities refer to the total amount of debt directly related to daily business operations with a repayment term exceeding one year, as presented on the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., year-end or quarter-end). They typically consist of the operating-related portions of items such as long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables, and serve as fundamental data for calculating metrics like net operating assets.

Closing stock price refers to the closing price of a stock on the last trading day of a specific reporting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month) in the securities market. It is fundamental data directly obtained from market transactions, reflecting the market's valuation of the stock at that point in time.

Option expiration time refers to the pre-determined final date or point in time specified in an option contract when the contract rights become void. It is a fundamental and fixed parameter of an option contract, determining the final deadline by which the option holder may exercise their rights.

Total Days in Period refers to the complete number of calendar days between two specific dates, derived directly from date calculations. In the accounting and finance field, it is commonly used to calculate derived metrics such as daily averages and turnover rates, serving as a fundamental input parameter for many financial analyses.

term_en.name: Current Year Stock Price Per Share

definition_en: Current year stock price per share refers to the trading price of a listed company's stock on the securities market during the current fiscal year, typically represented by the closing price on the last trading day of the year or the annual average price. It is a fundamental data point reflecting the company's market value, determined by market supply and demand rather than directly calculated from financial statements.

Current Period Consumption Amount refers to the total monetary sum actually paid by an individual or household for purchasing goods and services within a specific time period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as the fundamental raw data reflecting the consumption level during that period.

term_en.name: Total Dividend Payments for the Period

english: Total Dividend Paid in Current Period

definition_en: Total dividend payments for the period refer to the aggregate amount of cash dividends actually paid by the company to its shareholders during the current accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It reflects the scale of funds outflow used by the company to reward shareholders during that period and is typically presented in the financing activities section of the cash flow statement.

Standard quantity refers to the predetermined basic technical parameters, such as the amount of materials or labor hours that should be consumed under normal efficiency conditions, for producing one unit of product or providing a service under a standard cost system. It is a core input value for calculating standard costs such as direct materials and direct labor.

english: Price Movement of the Underlying Asset

definition_en: Underlying asset price change refers to the fluctuation in the market price of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis or reference for a financial derivative contract (e.g., options, futures) over a period of time. This change is a direct result of market trading and constitutes a critical external input data required for financial analysis and derivative pricing.

english: Market Price of the Underlying Asset

definition_en: Underlying asset market price refers to the immediate transaction price agreed upon for a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) in an open, active trading market where buyers and sellers engage in voluntary and fair transactions. It is raw price data directly observed and obtained from the market, serving as fundamental input information for asset valuation, financial derivative pricing, and investment decision-making.

Underlying asset current price refers to the real-time trading price or observable market quotation of an asset (such as stocks, commodities, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis for derivative contracts (e.g., options, futures) in financial markets at a specific point in time. It is the fundamental data for financial product pricing and trading decisions.

Underlying asset current price refers to the real-time market trading price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) corresponding to a financial derivative contract (e.g., options, futures). It is fundamental market data for determining derivative value, typically obtained directly from exchanges or quotation systems rather than calculated through formulas.

A sample observation refers to an individual raw data point obtained through direct measurement, recording, or investigation from a sample drawn from a population in statistical or financial analysis. It serves as the fundamental input data for subsequent statistical analysis (such as calculating mean and variance) and cannot itself be derived from other metrics.

The periodic deposit amount refers to the fixed amount deposited or withdrawn each period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annually) in a deposit, savings, or annuity plan. It is a fundamental original data point stipulated in business contracts or financial plans, typically used as a known input value for calculating the future value of deposits or interest.

Exchange gain refers to the book profit generated by an enterprise due to exchange rate fluctuations when translating or settling foreign currency monetary items (such as foreign currency deposits, accounts receivable, accounts payable, etc.) or foreign currency transactions at the new exchange rate at the end of the period. Simply put, it is the increase in value of foreign currency held by the enterprise resulting from exchange rate changes.

Consumption expenditure refers to the total value of goods and services purchased by individuals or households within a given period to meet their living needs. It is an important indicator for measuring the standard of living and consumption capacity of residents in a country or region, and also constitutes a significant component in calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

Number of Tax Returns refers to the total count of various tax declaration forms submitted by a tax entity (such as an enterprise or individual) to the tax authority within a specific tax period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annually). It is a fundamental quantitative metric reflecting tax compliance and tax workload.

Short-term borrowings refer to various loans obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions with a repayment period of one year or less. They are a significant source of short-term financing for enterprises and are directly recorded as liability items on the balance sheet.

term_en.name: Probability of Occurrence of Scenario i in Year t

chinese: 第t年特定情况i的可能性
english: Probability of Scenario i in Year t
Occurrence Probability of Case i in Year t
Occurrence Probability of Event i in Year t

definition_en: In financial forecasting or risk assessment models, this refers to the likelihood of a specific scenario i (e.g., favorable, average, or poor market conditions) actually occurring in future year t. This probability is typically set directly based on historical statistical data, expert judgment, or model assumptions, and serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating derived metrics such as expected values.

term_en.name: Compensation of Employees in the Tertiary Industry

english: Compensation of Employees in Tertiary Industry

definition_en: Compensation of employees in the tertiary industry refers to the total monetary and in-kind remuneration received by all workers engaged in production activities within the tertiary industry (service sector) during a given period for the labor they provide. It is a core component when calculating the value added of the tertiary industry using the income approach, typically sourced directly from statistical surveys or enterprise accounting data.

term_en.name: Total Assets at End of Third Quarter

english: Total Assets at the End of the Third Quarter

definition_en: Total Assets at End of Third Quarter refers to the aggregate book value of all economic resources owned or controlled by an enterprise at the specific point in time marking the conclusion of the third fiscal quarter (typically September 30). It is a critical point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, directly reflecting the scale of the enterprise's assets at quarter-end.

term_en.name: Compensation of Employees in the Secondary Industry

chinese: 工业及建筑业劳动者报酬
english: Remuneration of Employees in Secondary Industry

definition_en: Compensation of employees in the secondary industry refers to the total sum of monetary and in-kind remuneration received by all workers engaged in production activities within the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) during a given period, in return for their labor. It typically includes wages, salaries, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, as well as welfare expenses such as social insurance and housing provident fund contributions paid by employers on behalf of employees. It constitutes a major component of the value added of the secondary industry.

Total output of the secondary industry refers to the total value of goods and services produced by all resident units in the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) of a country or region during a specific period (usually one year). It serves as fundamental raw data in national economic accounting, typically obtained through direct aggregation of statistical surveys. For instance, the industrial sector often employs the 'factory method', while the agricultural sector (which may involve related processing activities within the secondary industry) commonly uses the 'product method' for accounting.

term_en.name: Total Cash Outflows from Operating Activities

english: Total Cash Outflows from Operating Activities

definition_en: Total cash outflows from operating activities refers to the aggregate sum of all cash actually disbursed by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal functioning. It is a fundamental data point in the cash flow statement, derived directly from accounting records, and reflects the enterprise's cash expenditures in routine business activities such as procurement, salary payments, and tax payments.

Total Number of Shareholders refers to the aggregate count of natural persons or legal entities (institutions) registered on a company's shareholder register who hold shares in that company. This data is fundamental raw information, typically obtained directly from the company's periodic reports (such as quarterly reports, semi-annual reports, and annual reports), and cannot be derived through calculation from other financial metrics.

Stock issuance refers to the act by a joint-stock limited company of selling company shares (stocks) to investors in accordance with legal procedures to raise capital. This is the primary method for a company to conduct equity financing. Through issuing shares, a company can increase its share capital and obtain funds for operational development.

Stock repurchase refers to the action of a listed company using its own cash or other means to buy back a certain number of its own shares that have been issued and are outstanding in the open market. The repurchased shares are typically cancelled or held as treasury stock, thereby reducing the number of shares outstanding.

Non-operating expenses refer to various expenditures incurred by an enterprise outside its daily operating activities that are not directly related to its main business, such as fines, compensation payments, losses on asset disposals, and donation expenses. These expenses typically do not occur frequently and do not constitute the cost of the enterprise's core operations.

Non-operating income refers to various revenues or gains incurred by an enterprise outside its daily business operations, which are not directly related to its main business activities. It is not generated from selling products or providing routine services, but rather from incidental or special events.

Operating transportation expense refers to the costs incurred by an enterprise in its daily business activities related to the transportation of goods for the sale of products or provision of services. It is a significant component of transportation costs and is typically recorded directly as a specific expense item in accounting.

Derivative instrument effective notional principal refers to the explicitly agreed value of the underlying asset or reference amount specified in a derivative financial instrument contract (such as futures, options, swaps, etc.). It serves as the initial benchmark for calculating contract payments, measuring potential risk exposure, or performing accounting measurements, and is obtained directly from the contract terms rather than through calculation.

term_en.name: Total Admitted Value of On-balance-sheet Assets

definition_en: Total Admitted Value of On-balance-sheet Assets refers to the net admitted value of assets obtained by aggregating all on-balance-sheet assets of an insurance company after risk adjustment and admission processing according to solvency regulatory rules under the insurance regulatory framework. It reflects the actual asset value recognized by the regulatory authority that can be used to cover the insurer's liabilities and risks, serving as a crucial foundational data point for calculating regulatory metrics such as the solvency adequacy ratio.

Notional principal of off-balance-sheet items refers to the original amount specified in contracts or agreements for off-balance-sheet activities (such as loan commitments, standby letters of credit, financial derivatives, etc.) conducted by commercial banks and other financial institutions. It serves as the initial base value for calculating risk exposure and risk-weighted assets of off-balance-sheet items, and does not itself represent the final accounting book value or risk exposure.

An observation refers to an individual data point or sample value obtained through actual measurement, determination, or observation. It is unprocessed raw data that cannot be derived from other financial metrics. Observations serve as fundamental inputs for statistical analysis and the calculation of composite indicators such as standard deviation and population mean.

Observation Period Days refer to the fundamental time span, typically measured in days, set for collecting and analyzing data in financial analysis or data modeling. It is either directly given as an original parameter or derived by counting a continuous data series, serving as the foundational time framework for subsequent calculations (such as calculating cash flow volatility).

Calculation period days refer to the standard number of days set for a specific calculation period (e.g., month, quarter, year) in financial analysis or calculations, or the actual number of days calculated based on specific start and end dates. It is a fundamental time parameter used to convert periodic financial data (such as sales, costs) into daily averages, or to serve as the denominator in turnover ratio calculations.

Subscribed capital refers to the total amount of capital that shareholders or promoters of a company commit to contribute to the company according to legal documents such as the company's articles of association and investment agreements, i.e., the company's legal registered capital. It represents the amount of the shareholders' obligation to contribute capital to the company and serves as the foundational capital commitment for the company's establishment and operation.

The Security Market Line (SML) Y-axis intercept refers to the value at which the SML intersects the vertical axis (representing the required rate of return) when the asset's systematic risk (beta coefficient) is zero. This value is theoretically and practically defined as the risk-free rate (Rf), representing the certain return an investor can obtain without bearing any systematic risk.

Cost object allocation base refers to the original measurement unit or underlying data used in cost accounting to allocate common costs or indirect expenses to various cost objects (such as products, services, departments). It is a simple, directly obtainable or measurable indicator, such as product weight, labor hours, machine hours, raw material consumption, or output volume, serving as the starting point for calculating the allocation rate and the final allocated amount.

Explicit Forecast Period Years refer to the number of years in which an analyst makes detailed year-by-year projections of a company's future financial condition (such as revenue, profit, cash flow, etc.) within a business valuation or financial forecasting model. It is a subjective time parameter set by the analyst based on factors such as industry characteristics, the company's development stage, and the purpose of the forecast, typically around 5 years, after which it enters a subsequent period (perpetuity period) with an assumed stable growth rate.

Trough price typically refers to the lowest point or bottom price level reached by a commodity or asset price fluctuation within a specific time period. In contexts such as agricultural product cost-benefit analysis, it may refer to fundamental raw price data, such as purchase price or unit price, serving as a critical starting point for cost-benefit calculations and market analysis.

Original asset value refers to the initial cost or value of an asset recognized and recorded on the books according to accounting standards at the time of its initial acquisition or construction. It reflects all necessary expenditures incurred before the asset is put into use and serves as the basis for subsequent accounting treatments such as depreciation, amortization, and impairment.

english: Cash and Cash Equivalents after Restructuring

definition_en: Post-restructuring cash and cash equivalents refer to the amount of cash and cash equivalents presented in a company's financial statements after completing a restructuring (such as debt restructuring, business reorganization, or mergers and acquisitions). It reflects the actual holdings of cash on hand, bank deposits, other monetary funds, and short-term investments meeting the definition of cash equivalents (short-term, highly liquid, readily convertible to known amounts of cash, and subject to insignificant risk of value changes) that are available for immediate payment following a specific restructuring event.

Total financial liabilities refer to the aggregate book value of all financial liabilities that an entity is obligated to settle by delivering cash or other financial assets at a specific point in time (e.g., the balance sheet date). It typically includes short-term borrowings, long-term borrowings, bonds payable, etc., and serves as a fundamental financial metric reflecting the scale of an enterprise's financing-related debt.

Long-term borrowings refer to various loans obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions with a repayment term exceeding one year (excluding one year). It constitutes a significant non-current liability for the enterprise, primarily used to fund long-term asset investments and business expansion.

term_en.name: Outstanding Amount of Long-term Debt Securities

chinese: 长期债务证券在外流通数
长期债务证券发行在外的数量
长期债务证券流通份额

definition_en: Outstanding amount of long-term debt securities refers to the total number of units or certificates of long-term debt securities (such as long-term bonds) that have been issued by an issuer (e.g., government, corporation) and are currently being traded among investors in the financial market, not yet matured or redeemed. It is a fundamental statistical value directly obtained from market records or issuer data, reflecting the supply scale of the security in the secondary market.

Long-term equity investment refers to equity investments held by an enterprise to exercise control, joint control, or significant influence over the investee, with the objective of obtaining long-term returns. It is an independent asset whose value is recognized and measured based on actual transaction costs and subsequent accounting policies (such as the equity method).

Long-term liabilities refer to debts that a company is obligated to repay over a period exceeding one year or one operating cycle. They are a significant item on the balance sheet, primarily including long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables, reflecting the company's financial obligations requiring long-term repayment.

Prepaid expenses refer to payments made in advance by a company to obtain future services or goods, where the corresponding economic benefits have not yet been consumed or realized, and are therefore recorded as an asset at the time of payment.

Forecast base value refers to the financial data or business metric value at a specific point in time (typically the base period or current period) that serves as the starting point in a financial or business forecasting model. It forms the input foundation and initial reference for the entire forecasting process, such as revenue, assets, user count, etc., in the base period. It is usually determined based on historical actual data or currently known data, rather than being derived through formula calculations.

Forecast period years refer to the length of time used for detailed year-by-year projections in financial forecasting or business valuation models. It is a preset input parameter, typically determined based on industry practice or specific valuation requirements, during which key financial metrics (such as revenue, costs, cash flow, etc.) are projected annually. After the forecast period ends, the business is usually assumed to enter a stable growth phase (terminal period).

The forecast period refers to the length of the future time segment, set by analysts or appraisers for detailed financial projections in business valuation or financial forecasting models. It is typically determined subjectively based on factors such as the business lifecycle, industry characteristics, and strategic planning, serving as the fundamental time parameter for constructing the forecasting model.

Estimated useful life refers to the total estimated length of time that a fixed asset is expected to be usable, from the date it is put into service until it is projected to be scrapped or disposed of. It is a key fundamental parameter for calculating fixed asset depreciation, typically estimated and determined by management or professionals based on factors such as the nature of the asset, intensity of use, pace of technological obsolescence, and maintenance condition.

Estimated Future Selling Price refers to the projected market transaction price that an asset (such as inventory, fixed assets, or financial assets) is expected to achieve when sold at a specific future point in time. It is a predictive estimate based on factors such as market trends, asset condition, and industry outlook, serving as a crucial foundation for investment decisions, asset valuation, and cash flow forecasting.

The 360-degree assessment score is a comprehensive performance evaluation result.
