It involves selecting a group of publicly traded companies in the same industry that are similar to the target company in terms of key drivers (such as growth, risk, and profitability), calculating the arithmetic average of specific market multiples (such as P/E ratio, P/B ratio, P/S ratio) for these comparable companies, and then using this average as a multiplier to estimate the market value of the target company.

term_en.name: Comparable Company Underlying Asset Price Volatility

chinese: 可比公司资产价格波动率

definition_en: Comparable company underlying asset price volatility is a parameter used for risk adjustment when evaluating financial instruments such as expansion options. It measures the uncertainty of future price movements by selecting comparable companies similar to the target company or underlying asset in terms of business, scale, and growth, and analyzing the volatility of historical price data of their related assets (e.g., stocks). This volatility is typically expressed as a percentage and is one of the key input variables for calculating option value or performing risk adjustments.

Available assets refer to the portion of assets that an enterprise or individual can freely dispose of, use for payments, investments, or to meet financial needs at a specific point in time or over a period. It typically denotes the part of total assets, after deducting liabilities or specific restricted assets, that can be quickly liquidated or directly utilized, reflecting financial flexibility and payment capacity.

Expected rate of return refers to an estimate or judgment made by investors regarding the average return that an investment may achieve in the future, based on historical data, market analysis, or predictive models. It reflects the anticipated level of investment return after considering various possible outcomes and their probabilities of occurrence.

chinese: 可行性研究报告编制费

definition_en: Feasibility Study Fee refers to the cost paid to professional institutions or individuals for preparing a feasibility study report to evaluate the technical, economic, financial, and environmental viability of a project before its initiation. It is part of other construction costs and is used to determine whether the project is worth investing in and how to optimize its implementation.

Total number of vested shares refers to the aggregate quantity of options or shares that grantees are entitled to purchase at a predetermined price, or the corresponding equity instruments they are entitled to receive, within a specified future period, after fulfilling all preset vesting conditions (such as service period, performance targets, etc.) under an equity incentive plan.

Number of Convertible Preferred Shares refers to the total quantity of preferred shares issued by a company that can be converted into common shares under specified conditions according to predetermined conversion ratios or conversion prices.

The conversion price of a convertible bond refers to the price per share that a bondholder must pay when exercising the conversion right to convert one convertible bond into common shares of the issuing company. It is typically set by the issuing company at the time of bond issuance and is a key parameter determining the conversion ratio.

Convertible bond face value refers to the base amount set at bond issuance and printed on the bond certificate. It serves as the benchmark value for calculating bond interest, principal repayment at maturity, and determining the conversion ratio (Conversion Ratio = Bond Face Value / Conversion Price).

term_en.name: Total Face Value of Convertible Bonds

english: Total Face Value of Convertible Bonds
Aggregate Par Value of Convertible Bonds

definition_en: Total face value of convertible bonds refers to the aggregate par value of all convertible bonds issued by a company, as set at the time of issuance. It serves as fundamental data for calculating conversion ratios, assessing potential equity dilution effects, and conducting related financial analysis.

chinese: 可辨认资产公允市场价值

definition_en: Fair value of identifiable assets refers to the amount at which identifiable assets (such as fixed assets, inventory, accounts receivable, identifiable intangible assets, etc.) would be exchanged between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's length transaction at a specific point in time, such as during a merger, acquisition, or asset valuation. It excludes the value of unidentifiable assets such as goodwill.

Unit count is a measurement unit, typically used to quantify the specific number of equipment, machinery, vehicles, or particular products. In financial and operational management, it is commonly employed to measure the physical scale of production, sales, or inventory.

Unit Contribution Margin by Product refers to the amount remaining when the selling price per unit of a specific product is subtracted by the corresponding variable cost per unit. This amount is used to cover the company's fixed costs and ultimately forms profit, serving as a key indicator for measuring the profitability of individual products.

term_en.name: Weight of Individual Assets in a Portfolio

definition_en: The weight of individual assets in a portfolio refers to the proportion or percentage of the market value of each asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) relative to the total value of the entire portfolio. It measures the degree to which that asset influences the overall performance and risk of the portfolio, serving as key foundational data for asset allocation and risk management.

In statistics and data analysis, 'variable values' refer to the specific numerical values corresponding to each individual or observation unit within a particular sample or population for a given variable. For example, when studying the return on assets of a group of companies, the specific ROA figure for each company represents one value of that variable.

Workload of individual subtasks refers to the quantitative assessment of resources, time, or effort consumed by each smaller, more specific sub-task after decomposing an overall task or project. It constitutes the fundamental unit of the total workload.

term_en.name: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity by Production Stage

chinese: 月末各工序在产品数量
english: Work-in-Process Quantity by Process at Month-End

definition_en: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity by Production Stage refers to the physical quantity of products or semi-finished goods that remain at each specific production stage at the end of each month (accounting period) in a multi-step production process, which have not completed all processing stages and cannot be transferred to finished goods inventory. It serves as critical data in cost accounting for calculating equivalent units of work-in-process and allocating production costs.

Other comprehensive income by scenario refers to the gains and losses that, according to accounting standards, are directly recorded in changes of owners' equity but not recognized in the current period's income statement, excluding net profit generated from ordinary business activities during a specific accounting period. It primarily reflects unrealized or temporary gains and losses, which do not affect current period net profit but impact total comprehensive income.

Scenario probability refers to the estimated likelihood of occurrence for each specific scenario in financial decision-making or risk assessment, based on historical data, expert judgment, or model predictions regarding different possible future operating conditions, market environments, or event outcomes. It is typically expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1 or as a percentage.

Probability of each scenario refers to the assignment of a numerical value to each possible future occurrence (or state) of an event in decision analysis, investment evaluation, or risk management, quantifying the likelihood of that scenario occurring. The sum of the probabilities of all possible scenarios equals 1.

Scenario probabilities refer to the numerical likelihood values assigned to different possible future business conditions, market environments, or event outcomes (i.e., various 'scenarios') in financial decision-making or risk assessment. These probabilities are typically derived from historical data, expert judgment, or model predictions and are used to calculate metrics such as expected returns and risk (e.g., variance).

chinese: 不同情境下的现金流量

definition_en: Scenario-based cash flows refer to the future cash flows calculated based on different assumption conditions (such as optimistic, pessimistic, and base-case scenarios) in financial forecasting or analysis. They are used to assess a company's funding position and risks under various possible circumstances.

Indicator values refer to specific quantitative data used in the accounting and finance fields to measure and evaluate various aspects of an enterprise, including its financial condition, operating results, solvency, profitability, and market performance. These values are typically derived from specific calculation formulas and serve as the foundation for financial analysis, investment decision-making, and performance management.

In the field of finance and accounting, 'individual values' typically refer to a series of independent, specific numbers or data points involved in calculation, analysis, or modeling processes. For example, when calculating a weighted average, 'individual values' are each original data item that forms the basis of the average calculation.

Net cash flow by period refers to the difference between the total inflow and total outflow of cash and cash equivalents during a specific accounting period (such as a year or a quarter). It reflects the net increase or decrease in cash ultimately generated by the enterprise through operating, investing, and financing activities during that period, serving as a core indicator for assessing the enterprise's liquidity, earnings quality, and financial health.

Historical prices by period refer to the time-series data of recorded transaction prices for a financial asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) at different past time points (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly). This data serves as the foundation for technical analysis, return calculation, risk assessment, and financial modeling.

Periodic historical return refers to the rate of return generated by an investment over specific past time periods (such as daily, monthly, or annually), used to measure the investment's performance across different historical periods.

Treasury bond yields by maturity refer to the annualized return rates investors can obtain by holding bonds with different remaining maturities (e.g., 1-year, 5-year, 10-year, etc.) to maturity when traded in the market. They reflect the market's assessment of the time value of money and risk premiums over different time horizons, serving as fundamental data for constructing the treasury yield curve and acting as crucial benchmark rates in financial markets.

Periodic investment amount refers to the capital invested at different time points (such as different years, quarters, or months) throughout the life cycle of a project or investment. It reflects the temporal distribution of investment cash outflows and serves as essential data for calculating financial metrics such as Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return.

Periodic rate of return refers to the ratio of the income (including capital gains and cash inflows such as interest and dividends) earned by an investor from a specific investment during a particular investment period (e.g., one month, one quarter, or one year) to the initial investment cost, used to measure the investment performance during that period.

Periodic amortization expense refers to the amount of cost allocated to each accounting period for long-term assets (such as intangible assets and long-term prepaid expenses) or financial assets (such as bond investments), spread over their estimated useful lives or benefit periods according to a specific method.

Periodic rent refers to the fixed or variable amount that the lessee is required to pay to the lessor during each agreed payment period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually) within the lease term under a finance lease or operating lease agreement.

Periodic stock returns refer to the total return an investor obtains from investing in a specific stock over a particular holding period, typically consisting of two components: dividend (or interest) income received during the period and capital gains (or losses) resulting from changes in the stock price.

Period demand refers to the quantity of products, materials, or funds required within each independent time segment, obtained by dividing the total future demand over a specified period into specific time cycles (such as years, quarters, or months) in financial, production, or inventory management.

Periodic expected cash flows refer to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows that an enterprise is projected to generate in specific future periods (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually). Based on current information and reasonable assumptions, it represents a forecast of the future cash-generating capacity of an asset, project, or enterprise, serving as critical foundational data for investment appraisal, asset valuation, and financial planning.

Expected dividends per period refer to the estimated value of dividends per share that a company is likely to pay to its shareholders in future periods (e.g., quarterly, annually), based on factors such as the company's historical performance, earnings forecasts, and dividend policy. It is a crucial input variable for stock valuation (e.g., Dividend Discount Model) and investment decision-making.

english: Amount of Tax Payable for Each Tax

definition_en: Tax payable by tax type refers to the amount of tax that an enterprise or individual is required to pay to the tax authority within a specified tax period, calculated separately for different tax categories (such as Value-Added Tax, Corporate Income Tax, Consumption Tax, etc.) in accordance with national tax laws and regulations.

Individual Employee Working Hours refers to the total time each employee within an enterprise actually spends on work or providing labor services during a specific period (such as day, week, month, quarter, or year), in accordance with the labor contract or company regulations. It is typically measured in hours and serves as fundamental data for calculating compensation, assessing labor efficiency, accounting for total labor costs, and conducting human resource planning.

term_en.name: Number of Shares Held per Security

definition_en: Number of Shares Held per Security refers to the specific quantity of a particular security or a class of securities (such as stocks) held by an investor or portfolio at a specific point in time. It serves as fundamental data for calculating portfolio value, conducting asset allocation, and managing risk.

english: Expected Terminal Value of a Security

definition_en: Expected terminal value per security refers to the forecast or estimation of the per-share value of each individual security (e.g., a stock) within a portfolio at a specific investment horizon (e.g., the end of an accounting period or investment cycle). It is typically calculated based on expectations of future prices, dividends, and other factors, and serves as a fundamental component for calculating the total expected terminal value of the entire portfolio.

term_en.name: Expected Terminal Value Per Share of Each Security

chinese: 证券期末预期每股价值

definition_en: Expected terminal value per share of each security refers to the forecasted estimate of the price or value per share of each individual security at the end of the investment horizon (e.g., at the conclusion of an investment period) in portfolio analysis. It is used to calculate the overall expected terminal value of the portfolio and serves as crucial foundational data for evaluating investment returns and making investment decisions.

term_en.name: Expected Rate of Return on Individual Securities

definition_en: The expected rate of return on individual securities refers to the average expected rate of return calculated through a weighted average based on the various potential future returns (such as dividends, interest, capital gains, etc.) and their respective probabilities of occurrence when an investor invests in a particular security. It reflects the investor's average expectation of the security's future returns and serves as a crucial foundation for investment decision-making and asset pricing.

Asset weight in portfolio refers to the proportion of each asset's value (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) to the total value of the constructed investment portfolio. It reflects the importance and influence of that asset on the overall portfolio and serves as key foundational data for asset allocation and risk management.

term_en.name: Market Value Weights of Individual Assets

definition_en: Market value weights of individual assets refer to the weights determined by the proportion of each asset's total market value (e.g., total market capitalization of a stock) to the total value of the entire market portfolio when calculating the market portfolio return. They reflect the relative importance of each asset within the overall market.

english: Expected Rate of Return on Individual Assets

definition_en: The expected return of an individual asset refers to the estimated or predicted average future return level of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) based on various possible future economic scenarios and their probabilities of occurrence. It serves as the foundation for investment decision-making and portfolio construction.

english: Expected Rate of Return on Assets

definition_en: Expected return of individual assets refers to the estimated average rate of return that an investor or analyst projects for a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) in the future under uncertain conditions, based on historical data, market conditions, and probability distributions. It serves as a crucial foundation for investment decision-making and risk assessment.

Various other expense items refer to the aggregate of miscellaneous, secondary, or difficult-to-classify expense outlays in an enterprise's total costs and expenses, excluding major cost items (such as direct materials, direct labor, depreciation, amortization, interest expense, etc.). These items are typically consolidated as 'Total Other Expenses' in business operating costs, income statements, or specific expense calculations (e.g., super-deduction).

Specific overhead costs refer to the aggregate of various expense items incurred by an enterprise in its production and operating activities that are not directly associated with the production of specific products or provision of services but are necessary for maintaining overall organizational operations. These costs typically cannot be directly attributed to a particular product or service and must be allocated to different cost objects using certain allocation bases (such as labor hours, machine hours, direct costs, etc.).

The fair value of identifiable assets refers to the amount at which assets could be exchanged, or liabilities settled, between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's length transaction. These assets are capable of existing independently, can be separately identified and measured, and exclude non-identifiable assets such as goodwill.

chinese: 单项可辨认资产账面价值

definition_en: The book value of identifiable assets refers to the value of each asset recorded on a company's financial statements at a specific point in time, such as during a merger, acquisition, or asset valuation, that can be separately identified and measured. This value is typically the net amount after deducting accumulated depreciation, amortization, and any impairment provisions from the original cost of the asset.

term_en.name: Investment Expenses Attributable to Other Assets

chinese: 其他资产相关投资成本
english: Investment Costs Capitalized to Other Assets
Costs of Investments Attributable to Other Assets

definition_en: Investment expenses attributable to other assets refer to various expenditures incurred by an enterprise during specific investment activities that should not be directly recognized in current profit or loss. Instead, they should be treated as part of the investment cost and ultimately included in the carrying amount of the relevant other assets (such as investments in other equity instruments, investments in other debt instruments, etc.). These expenses typically include directly related costs such as transaction fees and handling charges. Their accounting treatment differs from that of financial assets at fair value through profit or loss (where transaction costs are recognized in investment income).

Total deductions refer to the sum of various expenses, costs, losses, and other specific items that are permitted to be subtracted from an individual's or enterprise's gross income according to tax laws and relevant regulations when calculating taxable income. The purpose is to reasonably deduct necessary expenditures before taxation to determine the final taxable profit or income.

Standard surcharges refer to additional fees levied beyond the base charges, in accordance with industry practices, contractual stipulations, or specific criteria. These fees typically have clearly defined billing standards or rates and are used to cover specific services, costs, or risks, commonly seen in fields such as transportation, finance, and international trade.

term_en.name: Total Amount of Taxable Income Adjustment Items

english: Amount of Taxable Income Adjustments Increase

definition_en: Total Amount of Taxable Income Adjustment Items refers to the aggregate amount of specific items that require an increase in taxable income when calculating corporate income tax payable, based on tax regulations that adjust accounting profit for tax purposes. These items typically include adjustments related to revenue, deductions, assets, and special transactions, with the summarized result reported in the 'Adjustment Increase Amount' column of the tax return.

term_en.name: Estimated Net Cash Flows from Planned Disposal of Financial Assets

chinese: 计划处置金融资产净现金流
预计处置金融资产现金净流量
金融资产处置预计净现金流
english: Estimated Net Cash Flow from Planned Disposal of Financial Assets
Projected Net Cash Flow from Financial Asset Disposals

definition_en: Estimated net cash flows from planned disposal of financial assets refer to the net amount expected to be generated from the sale, transfer, or other disposal of held financial assets (such as stocks, bonds, fund shares, etc.) during specific future periods, according to the enterprise's operational or investment plans. This amount is calculated by offsetting the anticipated cash inflows against related disposal costs (such as transaction fees, taxes, etc.). It serves as a crucial indicator for forecasting future cash flow conditions and assessing the financial impact of asset disposal plans.

Current prices of various resources refer to the prevailing market prices required to acquire or replace the various resources (such as raw materials, equipment, labor, etc.) needed for enterprise production and operations at a specific point in time. It serves as an important basis for assessing asset replacement costs.

Current Resource Consumption refers to the total value of various economic resources actually consumed by an enterprise within a specific accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual) to maintain its daily business operations (such as production, sales, and management). It reflects the actual usage of resources such as labor, materials, and capital by the enterprise during the current operating cycle, serving as essential foundational data for measuring operational efficiency and cost control.

Sundry surcharges refer to additional fees levied beyond principal charges (such as freight or payment for goods) based on specific conditions, regulations, or services. These fees are typically applied to cover extra expenses arising from fuel costs, port operations, exchange rate fluctuations, specific services, etc.

Total surcharges refer to the sum of all additional fees levied according to regulations or agreements, beyond the base fee, in specific business operations or transactions. These surcharges may include fuel surcharges, education surcharges, local education surcharges, etc., commonly found in transportation, international trade, financial services, and tax calculation.

term_en.name: Market Value Weights of Individual Risky Assets

english: Market Value Weights of Risky Assets

definition_en: Market value weights of individual risky assets refer to the proportion of each risky asset's market value relative to the total market value of the entire investment portfolio composed of multiple risky assets. It reflects the relative importance of each asset within the portfolio and serves as a key input parameter for calculating the portfolio's overall risk and return (such as the expected return of the market portfolio).

english: Expected Rate of Return on Risky Assets

definition_en: The expected return on risky assets refers to the average rate of return an investor anticipates earning from investing in a risky asset, given the assumption of specific risks (such as market risk, company-specific risk, etc.). It is a core metric for evaluating and comparing the attractiveness of different risky investment projects, typically estimated based on historical data, probability distributions, or asset pricing models (such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model, CAPM).

Consolidated net profit refers to the net profit attributable to the owners of the entire group, calculated after eliminating internal transactions and unrealized profits and losses, when a parent company and all its subsidiaries are treated as a single economic entity in the preparation of consolidated financial statements.

Consolidated financial statements refer to financial statements prepared by a parent company that treat the parent and all its subsidiaries as a single economic entity, comprehensively reflecting the overall financial position, operating results, and cash flows of the group.

chinese: 合格投资者基础投资额

definition_en: Qualified Investor Base Quota refers to a fundamental investment quota standard or calculation starting point established for qualified investors in accordance with relevant regulations, used to determine the investment scale they may participate in for specific financial products (such as asset management plans). This quota is typically linked to factors such as the investor's asset size, type, or historical performance.

Reasonable profit refers to the profit level at which an enterprise can cover all its costs (including explicit and implicit costs, such as the opportunity cost of capital) and achieve a normal return on capital under specific market conditions and operational circumstances. It is generally regarded as the minimum profit threshold for an enterprise to maintain long-term survival and sustainable development, and serves as an important reference benchmark for evaluating corporate performance and making business decisions such as rent and pricing.

Contract multiplier refers to a fixed amount, predetermined by the exchange, used to convert the price of the underlying asset (such as index points) into the total contract value in financial derivatives trading such as futures or options. It determines the change in contract value corresponding to each unit price movement.

Year-over-Year Growth Rate is a key financial and economic indicator used to measure the growth magnitude of a specific economic metric (such as sales revenue or profit) in a given period (e.g., current month or quarter) compared to the same period in the previous year. It is primarily employed to eliminate the effects of seasonal fluctuations and reflect the true development pace of the indicator across years.

Nominal growth rate is a method of measuring the growth of economic or financial indicators, calculated directly using the nominal values (without adjusting for price changes) of the current period compared to the previous period, reflecting the apparent growth change of the indicator.

Nominal income refers to the total income of an individual or enterprise over a specific period, calculated in current monetary units (without inflation adjustment). It reflects the absolute monetary amount of income but does not account for the impact of price level changes on purchasing power.

english: Rate of Change in Nominal Income

definition_en: Nominal income growth rate refers to the rate of increase or change in the total income of an individual or enterprise over a specific period, measured at current monetary value without adjusting for inflation.

Nominal yield refers to the ratio of the coupon interest income of an investment (such as a bond) to its face value (or principal), without considering the impact of factors such as inflation, taxes, or market price fluctuations on real purchasing power. It reflects the nominal return level of the investment.

The nominal risk-free rate refers to the idealized interest rate that can be obtained by investing in an asset with no default risk or reinvestment risk (such as short-term government bonds), without considering inflation factors. It is a theoretical benchmark rate that is not adjusted for changes in the purchasing power of money.

english: Nominal Value of Goods and Services

definition_en: Nominal goods and services value refers to the total value of all final goods and services calculated at current market prices within a given period, without removing the effects of price changes (inflation or deflation).

term_en.name: Nominal Total Exports of Goods and Services

english: Nominal Total Exports of Goods and Services

definition_en: Nominal total exports of goods and services refer to the aggregate market value of all goods and services sold abroad by a country or region within a specific period (typically one year), calculated at current prices without adjusting for price changes (inflation or deflation). It is a key macroeconomic indicator for measuring the scale of a country's external economy and trade activities.

term_en.name: Nominal Total Imports of Goods and Services

english: Nominal Total Imports of Goods and Services

definition_en: Nominal total imports of goods and services refer to the total value of all goods and services purchased from foreign countries by a nation or region during a specific period (typically a year or a quarter), calculated at current market prices. It reflects the total scale of imports without considering price changes (i.e., inflation or deflation) and serves as a key indicator for measuring a country's external economic linkages and demand.
In grouped statistical data, specifically refers to the frequency of the group immediately following the current group, i.e., the number of occurrences of data within that group.

term_en.name: Operating Current Liabilities in the Year Prior to the Continuing Period

chinese: 预测期前一年经营性流动负债
永续期前一年经营性流动负债
稳定期前一年经营性流动负债
english: Operating Current Liabilities in the Year Before the Terminal Period

definition_en: Operating current liabilities in the year prior to the continuing period refers to the amount of operating current liabilities in the year immediately before entering the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in business valuation or financial forecasting. It is primarily used to calculate the increase in operating working capital for the first year of the continuing period and serves as a key input variable for forecasting a company's future free cash flow.

term_en.name: Operating Current Assets in the Year Preceding the Continuing Period

chinese: 预测期前一年经营性流动资产
永续期前一年经营性流动资产
稳定期前一年经营性流动资产
english: Operating Current Assets of the Year Before the Terminal Period

definition_en: Operating current assets in the year preceding the continuing period refer to the total amount of operating current assets in the year immediately before a company enters its stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in business valuation or financial forecasting. It typically includes operating assets such as accounts receivable, prepaid expenses, inventory, and cash that can be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. This figure serves as the basis for calculating the increase in operating working capital in the first year of the continuing period.

term_en.name: Operating Working Capital in the Year Preceding the Continuing Period

chinese: 预测期前一年经营营运资本
永续期前一年经营营运资本
稳定期前一年经营营运资本
english: Operating Working Capital in the Year Before the Continuing Period

definition_en: Operating Working Capital in the Year Preceding the Continuing Period refers to the base value used in business valuation to calculate the increase in operating working capital for the first year of the continuing period (also known as the terminal period or stable growth period). It represents the amount of net current assets required to maintain daily business operations in the year immediately before the company enters the stable growth phase, typically estimated based on the financial data of the final year of the forecast period.

Terminal Growth Rate refers to the constant, long-term growth rate used in business valuation (such as the Discounted Cash Flow model) to forecast the perpetual growth of a company's free cash flow or related financial metrics (e.g., net income, net operating assets) after it enters a stable development phase. It is typically a low and sustainable rate used to calculate the terminal value beyond the explicit forecast period.

term_en.name: Incremental Working Capital in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 后续期首年营运资本增加额
稳定期第一年营运资本变动
永续期第一年营运资本增量
english: Incremental Working Capital in the First Year of the Terminal Period
First-Year Terminal Period Working Capital Change

definition_en: Incremental working capital in the first year of the terminal period refers to the additional working capital requirement in the first year of the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period) after the forecast period ends in business valuation, compared to the previous year (typically the last year of the forecast period). It equals the working capital at the end of the first year of the terminal period minus the working capital at the end of the last year of the forecast period, where working capital is typically defined as current assets minus current liabilities. This metric is used to calculate the free cash flow for the first year of the terminal period.

chinese: 永续期首年息税前利润
english: EBIT of First Year in Terminal Period

definition_en: Year 1 EBIT of the continuing period refers to a company's earnings before interest and taxes in the first year after the forecast period ends, when the company enters a stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in business valuation. It reflects the company's core operating profitability under a long-term steady state and serves as the key starting point for calculating the continuing period's free cash flow to the firm and net operating profit after tax.

term_en.name: EBIT in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 稳定期第一年息税前利润
english: EBIT of First Year in Terminal Period

definition_en: EBIT in the first year of the terminal period refers to, in business valuation, the operating profit generated from business activities in the first year after the forecast period ends and the company enters a stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period), before deducting interest expenses and income taxes. It serves as the key starting point for calculating the free cash flow in the terminal period.

term_en.name: Depreciation and Amortization in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 永续期首年折旧与摊销
稳定期第一年折旧摊销
english: Depreciation and Amortization in the First Year of the Terminal Period
First-Year D&A of the Continuing Period

definition_en: In financial forecasting or business valuation, this specifically refers to the total amount of depreciation and amortization expenses expected to be charged for fixed assets and intangible assets in the first year after a company enters the stable growth stage (i.e., the terminal or perpetuity period).

term_en.name: Net Operating Assets at the Beginning of the First Year of the Continuing Period

chinese: 永续期首年初净经营资产
稳定增长期起点净经营资产
english: Net Operating Assets at the Beginning of the First Year of the Continuing Period
Initial NOA of the Terminal Period

definition_en: Net Operating Assets at the beginning of the first year of the continuing period refers to the value of net operating assets at the start of the first year of the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or perpetual period), which coincides with the end of the final year of the forecast period, in business valuation. It serves as a critical baseline for calculating the free cash flow of the continuing period and discounting the terminal value.

term_en.name: Net Operating Assets at the End of the First Year of the Continuing Period

chinese: 后续期首年末净经营资产
永续期第一年末净经营资产
稳定期第一年末净经营资产
english: Net Operating Assets at the End of First Year in Continuing Period
Ending NOA of First Year in Terminal Period

definition_en: Net Operating Assets at the end of the first year of the continuing period refers to the value of net operating assets at the end of the first year when the forecast period ends and the company enters the stable growth stage (i.e., the continuing or perpetual period) in business valuation. It is a key foundational data point for calculating the continuing period cash flows and company value.

term_en.name: After-Tax Net Profit in the First Year of the Terminal Period

english: After-Tax Net Profit in the First Year of the Terminal Period
First-Year Terminal Period Net Income After Tax

definition_en: After-tax net profit in the first year of the terminal period refers to the net profit attributable to shareholders after all taxes have been paid in the first year when a company enters the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period) after the forecast period ends, within the context of business valuation. It is one of the key input parameters for calculating the company's free cash flow and terminal value in the terminal period.

term_en.name: After-Tax Interest Expense in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 后续期首年税后利息费用
稳定期第一年税后利息费用
永续期第一年税后利息费用
english: After-tax Interest Expense in the First Year of the Terminal Period
Terminal Period Year 1 After-tax Interest Expense

definition_en: After-tax interest expense in the first year of the terminal period refers to the net amount of interest expense a company must pay due to debt financing, after deducting the impact of income taxes, in the first year of entering the stable growth stage (i.e., the terminal period, perpetuity period, or continuing value period) in business valuation or financial forecasting. It reflects the actual cost of debt capital under the company's long-term stable operating condition.

term_en.name: First Year Operating Current Liabilities in the Continuing Period

chinese: 经营期第一年流动负债
投产首年经营性流动负债
english: Operating Current Liabilities in the First Year of the Following Period
First-Year Operating Current Liabilities of the Subsequent Phase

definition_en: First Year Operating Current Liabilities in the Continuing Period refer to the debts arising from daily business operations (such as purchasing raw materials, receiving services, etc.) in the first year after a project or operation enters a stable phase (i.e., the starting year of the continuing period), which are expected to be repaid within one year. It is one of the key underlying data for calculating changes in operating working capital.

term_en.name: Operating Current Assets in the First Year of the Subsequent Period

chinese: 经营期第一年流动资产
投产第一年经营性流动资产
后续期首年经营性流动资产
english: Operating Current Assets in the First Year of the Subsequent Period

definition_en: Operating current assets in the first year of the subsequent period refer to the total assets necessary to maintain normal production and operating activities at the beginning of the first year when entering the stable operation phase (i.e., the subsequent period) of an investment project or business operating cycle, which are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or within one operating cycle exceeding one year. This typically includes cash, accounts receivable, inventory, etc.

term_en.name: Operating Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period

chinese: 后续期首年经营营运资本
永续期第一年经营营运资本
稳定期第一年营运资本
english: First Year Operating Working Capital in Continuing Period
Continuing Period Year 1 Operating Working Capital

definition_en: Operating working capital in the first year of the continuing period refers to the net current assets required to support daily business operations in the first year after entering the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in enterprise valuation or project cash flow forecasting. It typically equals the operating current assets minus operating current liabilities for that year, reflecting the level of working capital employed by the enterprise at the beginning of the stable growth phase.

term_en.name: First-Year Maintenance Capital Expenditure in the Terminal Period

chinese: 稳定期第一年资本性支出
后续期首年维持性投资
english: First Year of Terminal Period Maintenance Capital Expenditure
Sustaining Capex in First Year of Perpetuity Period

definition_en: In financial forecasting, when a company enters the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period), this refers to the cash outlay required in the first year for the acquisition, replacement, or upgrading of long-term operating assets (such as plants and equipment) to maintain the existing scale and capacity of operations. This expenditure is not for expansion but to sustain the company's current profitability and asset base.

term_en.name: Change in Working Capital in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 永续期第一年营运资本变动
稳定期首年营运资本变动
后续期首年营运资本需求变动
english: Change in Working Capital for the First Year of the Terminal Period
First Year Terminal Period Working Capital Change

definition_en: In financial forecasting or business valuation, this refers to the change in working capital requirement in the first year of the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period) compared to the previous year (typically the final year of the high-growth phase). Working capital generally refers to current assets minus current liabilities, and its change reflects the additional short-term funds that need to be invested or released to support sales growth or changes in the operating model.

term_en.name: Increase in Working Capital in the First Year of the Terminal Period

chinese: 后续期首年营运资金增加额
稳定期第一年营运资本变动
永续期第一年营运资本增量
english: First Year of Stable/Continuing Period Working Capital Increase
Change in Working Capital for First Year of Terminal Period
Incremental Working Capital in First Year of Perpetuity

definition_en: In corporate financial forecasting or valuation models, this specifically refers to the increase in working capital required by a company to support its ongoing operations in the first year after transitioning from a high-growth phase into a stable-growth phase (i.e., the terminal period or perpetuity period), relative to the previous year. It reflects the additional investment required in net operating working capital (operating current assets minus operating current liabilities) to maintain expected revenue or business scale after the company enters a steady state.

term_en.name: First Year Capital Expenditure in the Continuing Period

chinese: 永续期第一年资本性投资
english: Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Terminal Period
First-Year CapEx in the Perpetuity Phase
Initial CapEx of the Continuing Period

definition_en: First Year Capital Expenditure in the Continuing Period refers to the cash paid by a company in the first year of entering the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or perpetual period) in business valuation (such as the Discounted Free Cash Flow model) for investments in assets with a benefit period exceeding one year, aimed at maintaining or expanding long-term operational capacity. It is primarily used for acquiring or updating long-term assets such as fixed assets and intangible assets, and serves as a crucial deduction item when calculating the free cash flow for the first year of the continuing period.

Posterior probability refers to the updated and revised probability of a hypothesis or event occurring after obtaining new evidence or data. It is a core concept in Bayesian statistics, calculated by combining prior probability with new observational information.

The floor function is a mathematical operation that rounds a real number (which may be a decimal) down to the greatest integer less than or equal to it. For example, the floor of 5.4 is 5, and the floor of -3.7 is -4.

Dividends distributed to shareholders refer to the portion of profits that a joint-stock company allocates to its shareholders in the form of cash or stock from its retained earnings or current profits, representing a return on investment for shareholders due to their ownership of company shares.

Net dividends paid to shareholders refer to the total cash dividends actually distributed by a company to its shareholders over a specific period (such as a fiscal year), typically including cash dividends paid to both common and preferred shareholders. This represents a significant component of the company's cash outflows and reflects the company's profit distribution to its shareholders.

The ton-trip fee is an additional charge levied based on cargo weight when calculating freight for full-load road cargo transportation. It primarily compensates for loading, unloading, and handling costs incurred at origin and destination during short-haul transportation, constituting a component of road freight rates.

Tax-inclusive purchase price refers to the total price paid by an enterprise to suppliers for purchasing goods or services, which includes value-added tax and other turnover taxes. It serves as the basis for calculating tax-exclusive costs, input VAT, and final profits.

Tax-inclusive purchase cost refers to the total cost of purchasing materials or goods by an enterprise, which includes relevant taxes and fees (such as value-added tax). It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating actual procurement expenditures and conducting cost accounting.

term_en.name: Allowance for Bad Debts Balance at Prior Year-End

english: Allowance for Loan Losses at Prior Year-End
Beginning Balance of Loan Loss Provision

definition_en: Allowance for Bad Debts Balance at Prior Year-End refers to the book balance of the provision set aside by banks or financial institutions at the end of the previous fiscal year to cover potential losses from loans. It serves as one of the base figures for calculating the current year's required allowance for bad debts.

In the field of finance and accounting, a cycle typically refers to the time span required for a company to complete one full capital cycle or a series of financial activities. It measures the total time needed for the entire process from investing funds to purchase inventory, through production and sales, to the final collection of cash.

Daily demand within a cycle refers to the average daily quantity of a specific item, raw material, or funds that needs to be consumed or utilized during a defined time period (such as a year, a production cycle, or an order cycle). It serves as a crucial foundational metric for inventory management, production planning, and capital requirement forecasting.

Selling price refers to the monetary amount charged by an enterprise or individual to purchasers when selling goods or providing services. It is the monetary representation of the value of goods or services, typically determined based on factors such as cost, expected profit, and market supply and demand.

The trade discount rate is the percentage reduction from the original selling price granted by a seller to a buyer to establish or maintain a long-term cooperative relationship. It is a type of discount rate used to calculate the magnitude of a trade discount.
Original price of goods refers to the initial selling price before any discounts, promotions, or price adjustments, typically serving as the base price for calculating discounts, profits, or costs.
Selling price refers to the price charged by an enterprise when selling goods to end consumers or downstream buyers, representing the market transaction value of the goods.

Cost of Goods refers to the total of all direct costs incurred by an enterprise for producing or purchasing goods intended for sale, typically including raw materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. It serves as the basis for calculating gross profit and net profit.
The own price of a good refers to the monetary amount a consumer must pay to purchase one unit of the good, serving as a direct factor influencing consumer purchasing decisions and market demand.

Purchase price of goods refers to the total price paid by an enterprise to suppliers to obtain ownership of goods, constituting the core cost incurred during the procurement phase. In retail or trading enterprises, it typically denotes the actual acquisition cost per unit of goods after deducting factors such as wastage and discounts.

Merchant transaction limit setting refers to the maximum payment amount restriction established by a merchant or payment service provider for a single transaction or cumulative transactions within a specific period, aimed at controlling transaction risk, managing cash flow, or complying with specific regulations.

The Merchant Risk Coefficient is a comprehensive metric used by financial institutions or payment platforms to quantify the potential risk level of partner merchants. It is typically calculated based on multi-dimensional data including the merchant's operational stability, transaction behavior, compliance records, and credit status, and is used to assist in formulating risk management strategies, such as setting transaction monitoring thresholds, adjusting settlement cycles, or determining partnership eligibility.

Goodwill refers to the portion of the purchase price in a business acquisition that exceeds the fair value share of the identifiable net assets of the acquired entity. It represents the potential economic value of the acquired business to generate excess future profits, stemming from intangible resources that cannot be separately identified, such as brand reputation, customer relationships, and superior management teams.

The regression coefficient is a core parameter in regression analysis, used to quantify the direction and magnitude of the effect of one or more independent variables (explanatory variables) on the dependent variable (explained variable). In a simple linear regression model, it appears as the slope of the line, indicating the average change in the dependent variable for each unit change in the independent variable.

Recovered amount typically refers to the funds recovered through cash inflows or other means during the operation of an investment project or asset. It can refer to the recovery amount within a specific period (e.g., one year) or the cumulative total recovered over the entire project cycle, serving as a key indicator for measuring investment recovery and cash flow status.

The repurchase date refers to the specific date on which a listed company or corporation, in accordance with its share repurchase plan, actually executes and completes the purchase of its own issued common shares in the open market or through a specific agreement.

The repurchase term refers to the entire period in a repurchase transaction, from the time the fund provider (reverse repo party) pays funds to purchase securities, until the fund borrower (repo party) repurchases those securities at an agreed price and pays interest. It is typically expressed in days, months, or years and is a key parameter for calculating repurchase interest and returns.

Number of shares repurchased refers to the total quantity of a company's outstanding shares bought back from the open market or specific transactions using internal funds or other means within a specified period.

Market value of repurchase assets refers to the market price of the assets (such as securities, stocks, etc.) serving as the transaction subject in a repurchase agreement at a specific point in time. It serves as the basis for calculating the repurchase price and is typically used to determine the initial value or reference value of the repurchase transaction.

Factor score refers to the value calculated through linear combination of original variables in statistical models such as factor analysis, representing a sample's score or level on a certain latent factor (common factor). It reflects the relative position or intensity of the sample on the comprehensive characteristics represented by that factor.

Factor return refers to the portion of an asset's excess return that is explained or contributed by specific risk factors (such as value, size, momentum, etc.) in a factor investment model. It measures the additional return earned by a portfolio exposed to a particular factor relative to a benchmark (such as the risk-free rate or the market portfolio).

Fixed price refers to a price predetermined in a contract or agreement that remains unchanged throughout the contract period. It is not adjusted for market fluctuations, cost changes, or variations in production volume, providing both parties with a clear and stable cost or revenue expectation.

The fixed manufacturing overhead budget refers to the total amount of manufacturing overhead costs, planned and approved in advance for the budget period to maintain normal production capacity, which does not vary with changes in business volume (such as output or labor hours). It serves as the foundation for cost control and variance analysis.

Fixed costs refer to expenses whose total amount does not change with variations in business volume (such as production or sales) within a certain period and a specific range of activity. Examples include rent, equipment depreciation, and management salaries. These costs remain essentially constant regardless of whether production occurs or the level of production.

The constant dividend growth rate is a financial concept referring to the assumption, in dividend growth models (such as the Gordon Growth Model), that a company's dividends will grow at a constant rate (g) indefinitely into the future. It is a key parameter for calculating a stock's intrinsic value or the cost of equity capital.

Fixed Dividend Payout Ratio refers to a dividend policy adopted by a company, whereby the company commits to distributing a fixed percentage of its net profit as dividends to shareholders each year. This percentage is the dividend payout ratio, which directly links dividend payments to the company's profitability level—higher profits result in higher dividends, and lower profits result in lower dividends.

Fixed costs refer to costs or expenses whose total amount does not vary with changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume) within a certain period and a certain range of business activity. Examples include rent, administrative salaries, and depreciation of fixed assets. These expenses are typically incurred regardless of whether the enterprise produces or how much it produces.

The useful life of a fixed asset refers to the period over which an enterprise expects the asset to generate economic benefits, serving as a crucial basis for calculating fixed asset depreciation. It is typically determined by considering factors such as the asset's technical characteristics, operating environment, maintenance condition, and industry practices.

english: Net Book Value of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Net fixed assets refer to the remaining book value of a company's fixed assets after deducting accumulated depreciation and impairment provisions, reflecting the current actual value and the degree of wear and tear of the fixed assets.

term_en.name: Net Salvage Value of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Net salvage value of fixed assets refers to the net amount of the estimated residual value recoverable by the enterprise at the end of the asset's estimated useful life, minus the estimated disposal costs. It represents the estimated net realizable value of the asset upon retirement.

Impairment provision for fixed assets refers to a contra account established by an enterprise in accordance with accounting standards to reflect the reduction in asset value when the recoverable amount of its fixed assets (such as buildings, machinery, and equipment) falls below the carrying amount due to factors such as sustained market price declines, technological obsolescence, damage, or changes in economic conditions.

Original cost of fixed assets refers to the total monetary expenditure incurred by an enterprise in acquiring, constructing, installing, renovating, expanding, or technically upgrading a fixed asset to bring it to its intended usable condition. It typically includes the purchase price, packaging fees, transportation and handling charges, installation and commissioning costs, and related construction expenses.

The Fixed Asset Formation Rate is a financial metric that measures the growth or renewal scale of fixed assets within a specific period (typically an accounting period), reflecting the speed and efficiency of a company's capital investment and asset expansion.

Fixed asset investment refers to the total monetary amount spent by enterprises, governments, or institutions on constructing and acquiring fixed assets within a specific period (usually one year). It is a key indicator for measuring capital investment and economic growth potential in a country or region.

term_en.name: Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets

english: Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Loss on disposal of fixed assets refers to the difference between the carrying amount of a fixed asset (original cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment provisions) and the net proceeds from its disposal (residual value income minus relevant taxes and disposal expenses) when the asset is retired due to reaching the end of its useful life, technological obsolescence, or damage. When the carrying amount exceeds the net disposal proceeds, the resulting net loss is recorded as non-operating expenses.

term_en.name: Fixed Assets Transferred from Construction in Current Period

chinese: 本期购建固定资产转入额
english: Current Period Transfer-in of Fixed Assets Acquired or Constructed
Fixed Assets Acquired or Constructed in Current Period

definition_en: Fixed Assets Transferred from Construction in Current Period refers to the total value of assets that are newly added through purchase, self-construction, or installation, reach their intended usable state within the current accounting period, and are formally transferred from accounts such as 'Construction in Progress' to the 'Fixed Assets' account for accounting purposes. It reflects the scale of fixed assets actually put into use by the enterprise during the period.

chinese: 固定资产账面余额减折旧与减值
english: Net Book Value of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Carrying value of fixed assets refers to the value of fixed assets reported on the balance sheet, reflecting the remaining book amount after deducting accumulated depreciation and asset impairment provisions, representing the current book value of the asset for the enterprise.

term_en.name: Net Book Value of Fixed Assets

english: Net Book Value of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Net book value of fixed assets refers to the remaining value after subtracting the accumulated depreciation accrued up to the current accounting period from the original acquisition cost (original value) of the fixed assets. It reflects the current book value of fixed assets after deducting value impairment.

term_en.name: Estimated Net Residual Value of Fixed Assets

english: Estimated Residual Value of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Estimated net residual value of fixed assets refers to the final remaining amount that a company expects to obtain from disposing of an asset, after deducting estimated disposal costs (such as cleaning fees, transportation fees, etc.), assuming the fixed asset has reached its estimated useful life and is in a scrapped state. It is one of the important bases for calculating fixed asset depreciation.

Gross Fixed Capital Formation refers to the total value of fixed assets acquired by resident units of a country or region within a given period (usually one year) through purchases, self-construction, etc., minus the value of fixed assets disposed of (e.g., sold, scrapped) during the same period. These fixed assets typically have a service life of more than one year and exclude natural assets such as land. It is a key indicator for measuring the scale of investment in fixed assets in a country or region and is an essential component in calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) using the expenditure approach.

The Treasury Bond Market Average Yield refers to the average yield of all or a representative group of treasury bonds (e.g., bonds with different maturities) in the market over a specific period (such as a day, week, month, or year). It reflects the overall return level of the treasury bond market during that period and serves as a key indicator for gauging market interest rate trends and investors' average return requirements for treasury bonds.

Domestic expenses refer to the aggregate of all costs incurred within a country related to goods or services during domestic operations or import-export trade. In international trade, it specifically denotes expenses occurring between the production site in the exporting country and the port of shipment (or between the port of discharge in the importing country and the final destination), constituting a significant component of the final commodity price.

International freight refers to the transportation costs incurred in import and export trade for shipping goods from the exporting country to the designated location in the importing country. In international trade terms, it is typically a key component constituting the final price of goods (e.g., CIF price).

National Disposable Income refers to the total income available to all resident units (including households, enterprises, and the government) of a country or region within a given period (usually one year) after primary and secondary distribution, which can ultimately be used for final consumption and savings. It reflects the total amount of economic resources that the nation can freely allocate for consumption and accumulation.

Land Use Tax is a type of property tax levied by the state on entities and individuals using land within the scope of cities, county towns, designated towns, and industrial and mining districts, based on the actual area of land occupied.

Compensation for construction-in-progress personnel refers to the labor remuneration paid by an enterprise to employees directly involved in construction-in-progress projects (such as the construction, renovation, expansion, or technical transformation of fixed assets), including wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies. In accounting treatment, this portion of compensation is not recognized as a current period expense but is capitalized as part of the construction-in-progress cost.

term_en.name: Beginning Balance of Construction in Progress

definition_en: Beginning balance of construction in progress refers to the cumulative book value of all actual expenditures incurred for capital construction projects, installation projects, technical renovation projects, etc., that are not yet completed or have not reached their intended usable state at the beginning of a specific accounting period (usually a fiscal year). It reflects the investment progress and incomplete status of these long-term assets at the beginning of the period.

Construction in Progress Ending Balance refers to the carrying value of actual expenditures on projects that are not yet completed or, although completed, have not undergone final completion settlement as of the balance sheet date (typically year-end or quarter-end). It reflects the actual invested cost of unfinished projects at period-end and is generally reported as the net amount of the ending debit balance in the 'Construction in Progress' account minus the ending credit balance in the 'Provision for Impairment of Construction in Progress' account.

term_en.name: Income Tax Actually Paid in that Country (Region)

definition_en: Refers to the amount of income tax actually paid by the taxpayer (enterprise or individual) to the local tax authority in accordance with the laws of the source country or region of the income derived outside China. This portion of tax can generally be credited against the tax payable within China to avoid double taxation.

On-order inventory refers to the quantity of goods for which a company has placed orders with suppliers but which have not yet been delivered to the company's warehouse and are currently in transit or in the delivery process.

The Local Education Surcharge is a local government fund levied in accordance with national regulations to increase local education funding and promote the development of local education. Its revenue is primarily used to supplement local education expenditures.

english: Rate of Local Education Fee Surcharge

definition_en: The Local Education Surcharge Rate refers to the percentage applied by local governments to collect local education surcharges from entities and individuals who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax, based on a certain proportion of the actual VAT and Consumption Tax paid, for the purpose of raising education funds. The current nationwide uniform rate is 2%.

chinese: 地方教育费附加征收率
english: Rate of Local Education Fee Surcharge

definition_en: The Local Education Surcharge Rate refers to the percentage applied by local governments when levying a surcharge on entities and individuals who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax, based on a certain proportion of the actual amount of VAT and Consumption Tax paid, in order to increase funding for education.

chinese: 地方教育费附加征收率

definition_en: The Local Education Surcharge Rate refers to the percentage applied to the actual amount of Value-Added Tax (VAT), Consumption Tax, and other taxes paid by taxpayers when calculating the local education surcharge. It is a fund collection standard established by local governments to raise funds for education.

term_en.name: Site Preparation and Temporary Facilities Cost

chinese: 场地平整及临时设施费
english: Site Preparation and Temporary Facilities Cost
Temporary Facilities and Site Preparation Expenses

definition_en: Site preparation and temporary facilities cost refers to the expenses incurred before the commencement of a construction project, including site leveling, removal and clearance of obstacles to make the construction site ready for work, as well as the costs associated with the construction, maintenance, demolition, and restoration of temporary buildings, structures, and other temporary facilities required to meet construction needs.
The mean, also known as the arithmetic average, is the sum of all values in a dataset divided by the number of data points, serving as a primary indicator of central tendency in statistics.

The Mean-Variance Model is the core model of modern portfolio theory, proposed by Harry Markowitz. This model quantifies a portfolio's expected return (mean) and risk (variance or standard deviation), helping investors seek the highest expected return for a given level of risk, or the lowest risk for a given expected return, thereby determining the optimal asset allocation proportions.

Allowance for Doubtful Accounts is a loss reserve provisionally set aside by a company to cover potential future uncollectible receivables, such as accounts receivable. It is a contra-asset account used to reduce the carrying value of receivables to reflect their estimated recoverable amount. The provision is recognized in current period profit or loss, and when an actual bad debt occurs, this reserve is used to write off the corresponding accounts receivable.

term_en.name: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

english: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
Opening Balance of Bad Debt Provision

definition_en: Beginning balance of allowance for doubtful accounts refers to the book value of the reserve provisionally set aside at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month) to cover potential non-collection risks of accounts receivable and similar items. It reflects the carryover balance of this reserve account from the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the basis for calculating changes in the current period's allowance and the ending balance.

english: Rise in Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

definition_en: Increase in bad debt loss refers to the growth in the amount of bad debt provisions recognized or actual bad debt losses incurred by an enterprise due to uncollectible accounts receivable during a specific accounting period (e.g., compared to the previous period). This typically reflects an increase in the enterprise's credit risk, a decline in customers' debt repayment capacity, or a deterioration in the quality of accounts receivable resulting from changes in sales policies.

chinese: 应收账款坏账计提比例

definition_en: The bad debt provision rate is a predetermined percentage set by an enterprise in accordance with accounting standards and its own operational risks, used to estimate the portion of assets such as accounts receivable that may be uncollectible, and to accordingly provide for bad debts. This rate is typically determined based on factors such as historical experience, customer credit status, and industry practices.

The Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax (UMCT) is a surtax levied by the state on entities and individuals engaged in industrial and commercial operations who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax. The revenue is specifically earmarked for the maintenance and construction of urban public utilities and facilities.

term_en.name: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable

english: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable

definition_en: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Payable refers to the amount of Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax that should be paid by entities and individuals engaged in industrial and commercial operations who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax. It is calculated based on the actual amount of VAT and Consumption Tax (and potentially the exempted or credited VAT amount) paid during a specific period, multiplied by the applicable prescribed tax rate.

term_en.name: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate

chinese: 城市维护建设税适用税率
english: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate

definition_en: The Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax rate refers to the statutory percentage applied when calculating the tax payable for Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, which varies according to the administrative division of the taxpayer's location (e.g., urban area, county town, designated town, etc.). This rate is one of the key parameters for calculating the Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, and its tax base is the actual amount of Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer.

Benchmark value refers to a specific numerical value or standard used as a basis for comparison, evaluation, or calculation in financial, investment, or project analysis. It can be a predetermined rate of return (e.g., benchmark yield), price (e.g., benchmark price in bidding), market index, etc., used to measure the performance of other assets, projects, or indicators.

chinese: 参考国家股票市场波动性

definition_en: Benchmark country equity market volatility typically refers to the overall price fluctuation level of a mature, developed stock market selected as a reference standard (e.g., the United States), commonly measured by the historical return standard deviation of its stock index (e.g., S&P 500). It serves as a key input parameter when calculating the equity risk premium for other countries (especially emerging markets), used to measure market systemic risk.

Benchmark market capitalization typically refers to the total market capitalization of a listed company used as a calculation or comparison benchmark in specific scenarios (such as IPO pricing or cross-market valuation comparisons). Its core calculation method is the same as that of ordinary market capitalization, i.e., the company's total shares outstanding multiplied by a specific benchmark price (e.g., the A-share price), but it emphasizes its use as a reference standard.

The benchmark market risk premium refers to the excess return over the risk-free rate that investors require for bearing market systematic risk (i.e., risk that cannot be eliminated through diversification). It typically serves as a basis for measuring the overall market risk level and calculating risk premiums for other assets (such as specific countries or industries).

A benchmark indicator refers to a reference standard or baseline value used for comparison, measurement, or evaluation of other data, results, or performance in financial, performance, or analytical processes. It can be a budget target, industry average, historical data, or a set standard value, used to assess the quality of actual performance or the degree of deviation.

Benchmark stock price refers to a specific stock price used as the basis for calculation, comparison, or adjustment in financial transactions or financial instrument pricing. For example, in convertible bonds, it is often used as a key reference for determining the conversion price.

Baseline sales level refers to a referential, fundamental sales volume or standard used as a basis for comparison, evaluation, or setting new targets. It is typically employed to measure sales performance, calculate achievement rates, or serve as a starting point for performance assessment.

chinese: 基期国内生产总值平减指数

definition_en: The Base Year GDP Deflator is an index used to measure the price level of a specific benchmark year (base year), typically set at 100 or 1. It is a key tool for calculating real GDP. By dividing nominal GDP by this index, the effects of price changes are eliminated, thereby reflecting the real quantitative changes in economic output.

chinese: 基期国内生产总值指数

definition_en: The Base Period GDP Index is a statistical indicator used to measure and compare the total volume of economic activity across different periods. It uses the GDP level of a specific year (the base period) as a benchmark (typically set at 100). By calculating the ratio of GDP in other periods relative to the base period level, it reflects the actual economic growth or contraction, eliminating the impact of price changes.

term_en.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Base Period Prices

chinese: 不变价固定资本形成总额
基期固定资本形成总额
可比价固定资本形成总额
english: Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices of Base Period
Constant Price Gross Fixed Capital Formation

definition_en: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Base Period Prices refers to the total value of new fixed assets (such as machinery and equipment, buildings, intellectual property products, etc.) added by a country or region during a specific period (e.g., one year), measured and calculated using the price level of a specific base period. It eliminates the impact of price changes to accurately reflect the real physical volume change in capital formation and serves as a crucial indicator for long-term economic analysis and comparison.

term_en.name: Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base

chinese: 个人养老保险缴费基数
养老保险个人缴费基数
english: Pension Insurance Contribution Base for Individuals

definition_en: The Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base refers to the wage-based income amount used as the calculation benchmark for determining an individual's required pension insurance premium contributions. It is typically based on the insured individual's average monthly wage from the previous year, assessed within the upper and lower limits for the contribution base stipulated by local policies, and serves as the fundamental data for calculating the individual's actual monthly contribution amount (contribution base multiplied by the individual contribution rate).

term_en.name: Base Period Individual Medical Insurance Contribution Base

chinese: 个人医保缴费计算基数
english: Medical Insurance Contribution Base for Individuals

definition_en: The base period individual medical insurance contribution base refers to the amount of wage income used as the calculation benchmark for determining the individual's payable medical insurance premiums. It is typically determined based on the individual's average monthly wage during the base period (e.g., the previous year), subject to upper and lower limits defined by the local average social wage.

term_en.name: Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base

chinese: 个人失业保险缴费基数
失业保险个人缴费基数
english: Base Period Individual UI Contribution Base

definition_en: The Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base refers to the calculation basis used to determine the amount of individual unemployment insurance premiums payable during a specific period (the base period) that serves as the calculation benchmark. It is typically based on the individual's wage income during the base period and is subject to the upper and lower limits of the contribution base stipulated by local policies.

term_en.name: Base Period Production and Sales Volume

english: Base Period Production and Sales Volume

definition_en: Base period production and sales volume refers to the quantity of products produced or sold by an enterprise during the selected benchmark period (base period) in financial or economic analysis. It serves as the fundamental reference value for calculating indicators such as change rates and growth rates.

The base period price index is the price index of a selected period used as a benchmark for measuring changes in price levels. Its value is typically set at 100 or 1 to calculate the magnitude of price changes in subsequent reporting periods relative to this base period, serving as the foundation for computing indicators such as the inflation rate.

Base period net profit refers to the net profit achieved in a specific accounting period (usually the previous fiscal year or reporting period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis. It serves as the denominator reference value when calculating growth rates, trend analysis, and other dynamic indicators.
