Base period unit price refers to the average or standard unit price of a specific good or service during the base period, which serves as the benchmark for comparison when calculating dynamic indicators such as price growth rates. It is the foundational value for measuring price changes.

Base period variable costs refer to the total costs in a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for cost analysis or budgeting, which change in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume). It serves as the foundational data for calculating indicators such as the base period contribution margin.

chinese: 基期名义国内生产总值

definition_en: Base year nominal GDP refers to the nominal gross domestic product of a specific year (i.e., the base year) selected as the price benchmark when calculating real GDP. It reflects the total market value of all final goods and services produced by a country or region in that base year, measured at the price level of the base year. In the base year, since the price benchmark is itself, the nominal GDP of the base year is numerically equal to the real GDP of that base year.

english: Income Tax Expense for Base Period

definition_en: Base period income tax expense refers to the income tax expense that an enterprise should calculate and recognize for a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark, based on its operating profit. It is a deduction item when calculating base period net operating income, reflecting the income tax burden the enterprise should bear during the base period.

Base period revenue refers to the revenue amount of a specific period (typically a past accounting period) selected as the benchmark or reference point for financial analysis, forecasting, or comparison. It serves as the foundational data for calculating growth rates, preparing budgets, or conducting trend analysis.

Base Period Dividend Per Share refers to the amount of cash dividend paid per common share by a company during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It serves as important fundamental data for calculating indicators such as expected dividend growth rate.

Base period level refers to the numerical value of a specific period selected as the reference standard in statistical analysis or financial comparison. It serves as the foundation and starting point for calculating dynamic indicators such as growth rates and growth amounts, and is used to measure changes in subsequent periods (current periods). For example, when comparing a company's profits in 2024 with those in 2023, the 2023 profit data is the base period level.

Base period current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that a company is obligated to repay within a normal operating cycle (typically one year or one operating cycle longer than a year) at the end of the period used as a comparative benchmark (usually the previous period or a specific period) in financial analysis.

Base period current assets refer to the total assets owned by a company at the end of a specified period (typically the starting period or the previous period) that are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, serving as a comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as the foundational data for calculating metrics such as changes in working capital.

chinese: 参考期消费者物价指数

definition_en: The Base Period Consumer Price Index is the price level at a reference point in time set for calculating the Consumer Price Index (CPI), typically assigned an index value of 100. The CPI for subsequent periods measures the degree of inflation or deflation by comparing it to this base period price level.

The base period price level refers to the average price level of a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison when calculating price indices or measuring inflation. It serves as the starting point and reference standard for measuring the magnitude of price changes in subsequent reporting periods.

chinese: 工业品出厂价格指数基期

definition_en: The Base Period Producer Price Index serves as a benchmark point for measuring changes in the Producer Price Index (PPI). It typically designates a specific period (e.g., a particular year) as the base period, setting the producer price level of that period to 100 or 1. This is used to calculate and compare the magnitude of changes in producer prices in subsequent periods relative to the base period. It is one of the fundamental datasets for analyzing inflation trends.

chinese: 基期主营业务税金及附加
english: Taxes and Surcharges in Base Period

definition_en: Base Period Taxes and Surcharges refer to the total sum of various taxes and fees incurred by an enterprise due to its operating activities, which are recognized in the profit or loss of the current period, during a specific benchmark period (base period) used for comparative purposes in financial analysis. It typically includes consumption tax, urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge, resource tax, property tax, urban land use tax, vehicle and vessel tax, stamp duty, etc.

term_en.name: Base Period Operating Assets to Sales Percentage

english: Base Period Operating Assets Sales Percentage

definition_en: The Base Period Operating Assets to Sales Percentage refers to the ratio of total operating assets to total sales revenue in a specific base period (typically the previous year or period) used as the calculation benchmark in the percentage of sales method for financial forecasting. It reflects how much operating assets are required to generate one unit of sales revenue in the base period and serves as a key parameter for forecasting future operating asset requirements.

Base period operating costs refer to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise during a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark for daily business operations such as selling goods and providing services. They typically include main business costs and other business costs. This serves as a crucial reference benchmark for financial analysis, budget preparation, and trend comparison.

english: Base Period Selling, General and Administrative Expenses (SG&A)

definition_en: Base period operating expenses refer to the various expenses incurred by an enterprise to maintain daily business operations during a specific period selected as the benchmark for comparison (i.e., the base period) in financial forecasting, budgeting, or trend analysis. These expenses typically include selling expenses, administrative expenses, etc., and exclude cost of sales, taxes, and surcharges.

Base period working capital refers to the working capital amount in the starting period (typically the previous period or a specific period) used as a comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It equals current assets minus current liabilities for that benchmark period, reflecting the enterprise's short-term financial health and the level of operating funds employed at the benchmark point in time.

term_en.name: Base Period Price of Goods and Services

definition_en: The base period price of goods and services refers to the average price level of a representative basket of goods and services in a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison when calculating price indices (such as the Goods and Services Price Deflator). It serves as the reference point for measuring price changes in subsequent periods.

Total assets in the base period refer to the aggregate value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the end of a specific period designated as the benchmark for comparison. It serves as the reference basis for calculating subsequent changes in assets or related financial indicators, such as projected total assets.

chinese: 基期流动资金平均占用额
english: Average Fund Occupancy in Base Period

definition_en: Base Period Average Fund Occupancy refers to the average level of fund (typically working capital) utilization by an enterprise during a specific reference period (base period). It reflects the average scale of fund usage during the base period and serves as essential baseline data for calculating fund utilization efficiency, turnover rates, and other related metrics.

Base period transfer expenditure refers to the expenditure during a specific period used as a comparative benchmark (base period) in which the government or an institution unilaterally and gratuitously transfers funds or resources to other governments, institutions, enterprises, or individuals. Such expenditures do not directly exchange for goods or services and are primarily used for purposes such as social security, fiscal subsidies, debt interest payments, and donations.

Base period transfer income refers to the various regular income transfers received gratuitously by households or units from the state, social organizations, other units, or other households during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It is an important component in calculating net transfer income for the base period.

Base Period Amount refers to the indicator value of a specific historical period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark in statistical analysis or financial analysis. It serves as the fundamental reference value for calculating dynamic analysis indicators such as growth rates and changes.

Base period financial assets refer to the total amount or book value of financial assets held during a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis or indicator calculation. It is typically used to compute dynamic indicators such as growth rates and change rates, in order to assess changes in the scale or value of financial assets in subsequent periods.

Base period sales volume refers to the quantity of products or services sold during a specific period (such as the previous fiscal year, previous quarter, or a particular historical period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as a crucial reference data point for calculating sales growth rates, conducting trend analysis, and performing financial projections.

chinese: 基期非经常性损益净利润

definition_en: Base period non-operating net profit refers to the net profit generated by a company from non-recurring, non-core business activities during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It typically represents profit after deducting gains and losses not directly related to daily operations (such as gains from asset disposals, government grants, investment gains and losses, etc.), used to more accurately reflect the profitability of the company's core business.

The Basic Pension Insurance Premium refers to the contribution mandated by the national pension insurance system, jointly paid by employers and employees, to fund the basic pension insurance fund. The employer's contribution portion enters the social pooling account, primarily used to pay basic pensions; the employee's individual contribution portion enters the personal account, accumulating for individual retirement benefits.

Basic Medical Insurance Premium refers to the contributions jointly paid by employers and employees according to national regulations, used to establish the basic medical insurance fund. The individual contribution portion is typically calculated based on the employee's own wage at the locally prescribed rate and is deductible when calculating the taxable income for Individual Income Tax.

The Basic Safety Factor is a fundamental metric that measures the safety margin of a system, structure, or process under normal or expected conditions. It reflects the basic proportional relationship between the system's capacity to withstand loads or risks and its design or allowable limits, serving as the starting point for more complex safety assessments.

The base rate refers to the fee ratio or unit price used as the calculation basis or reference standard in specific economic activities or services. It typically excludes any surcharges, discounts, or adjustments under special circumstances, serving as the core benchmark for cost calculation.

Basic freight refers to the core transportation cost calculated by the carrier based on fundamental billing units such as transportation distance, cargo weight, or volume, without considering any additional charges (e.g., bunker adjustment factor, port congestion surcharge). It constitutes the foundational component of the total freight cost.

The Basic Freight Rate refers to the benchmark freight price charged by the carrier (such as a shipping company or freight conference) per unit of cargo (e.g., per ton or per cubic meter) according to its established tariff schedule. It serves as the fundamental unit price for calculating total ocean freight costs.

Basic contingency reserve refers to a pre-allocated sum of money in the investment estimate or budget estimate of an engineering project, intended to cover unforeseen expenditures that may arise during project implementation and are difficult to predict during budget preparation. It is primarily used to address additional costs resulting from design changes, potential increases in construction expenses, natural disasters, and other unforeseeable factors.

The Basic Contingency Rate is a percentage coefficient used to calculate the basic contingency reserve. The basic contingency reserve, also known as the unforeseen expenses reserve, is a pre-allocated fund in project investment estimates or budgetary estimates to cover potential expenditures during project implementation that are difficult to foresee during budget preparation (such as design changes, general natural disaster handling, concealed work acceptance, etc.). This rate is typically determined based on factors such as project characteristics, complexity, and risk level.

Basic net profit refers to the final residual profit obtained by an enterprise from its operating activities within a specific accounting period, after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes. It is a key indicator for measuring the core operating efficiency and profitability of an enterprise.

Basic credit line refers to a fundamental credit loan or overdraft limit preliminarily approved by a financial institution (e.g., a bank) based on an initial credit assessment of a client (individual or corporate), taking into account factors such as their basic financial condition, repayment capacity, and credit history. It serves as the foundation and starting point for subsequent adjustments or the granting of a final credit limit.

The base rate of return typically refers to the rate of return used as a benchmark or minimum acceptable standard in investment decision-making. It represents the minimum level of return required by investors or a company for an investment, used to evaluate the feasibility of investment projects. In capital budgeting, if a project's expected rate of return is lower than the base rate of return, the project may be rejected.

english: Spot Price of the Underlying Asset

definition_en: Underlying asset current price refers to the immediate market trading price of the asset serving as the contract subject for financial derivatives (such as options, futures) at a specific point in time.

A fund share is a certificate issued by the fund sponsor to investors, representing the holder's rights to income distribution, entitlement to residual assets after liquidation, and other related rights in proportion to their shareholding, as well as corresponding obligations. Its value is typically represented by the net asset value per share, which is the net asset value of the fund divided by the total number of fund shares.

Net Asset Value (NAV) refers to the asset value corresponding to each fund share, calculated by subtracting the fund's total liabilities from its total assets and then dividing by the total number of fund shares. This figure reflects the actual value of the fund at a specific point in time and serves as the basis for the subscription and redemption prices of open-end funds.

Fund net income refers to the total actual profit earned by investors during the holding period of a fund, derived from changes in the net asset value per share and dividends (if any), typically after deducting related transaction costs (such as subscription fees, redemption fees) and management fees. It reflects the real return ultimately obtained by investors from the fund investment.

Daily Earnings Per 10,000 Units refers to the actual earnings amount generated on a given day for every 10,000 units of fund shares, typically calculated for money market funds and other funds with daily earnings accrual. It is an important indicator for measuring a fund's short-term profitability, usually expressed in Renminbi (yuan).

Total Fund Value refers to the aggregate market value of all assets held by a fund at a specific point in time (typically the valuation date), including its holdings of stocks, bonds, bank deposits, and other marketable securities, and serves as the basis for calculating the fund's net asset value.

Net Asset Value (NAV) of a fund refers to the value of the fund's total assets minus its total liabilities, reflecting the actual value of the fund at a specific point in time. It is typically expressed as the NAV per unit, representing the net asset value corresponding to each fund share.

english: Value-Added Activity Standard Hours per Unit

definition_en: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Hours refer to the predetermined, theoretically required standard time allocated for the value-added portion of an activity to complete one unit of product or service in activity-based cost management. It serves as a benchmark for measuring the efficiency of value-added activities and is used for cost calculation, budgeting, and performance evaluation.

chinese: 增值作业标准单位成本
单位增值作业标准成本
增值作业标准成本单价
english: Standard Cost per Unit of Value-Added Activity

definition_en: Value-Added Activity Unit Standard Cost refers to the predetermined standard cost per unit of activity output (e.g., per labor hour, per machine hour) that should be consumed to complete a value-added activity in Activity-Based Costing. It typically consists of standard unit variable cost and standard unit fixed cost, and is used for cost control and performance evaluation.

term_en.name: Total Standard Hours for Value-Added Activities

english: Standard Total Hours for Value-Added Activities

definition_en: Total Standard Hours for Value-Added Activities refers to the pre-determined total labor or machine hour standard required under ideal or efficient conditions to complete a certain quantity of value-added activity outputs (products or services) in activity-based cost management. It is typically used as a benchmark for cost control and efficiency evaluation.

term_en.name: Total Standard Cost of Value-Added Activities

chinese: 增值作业标准成本总额
english: Standard Total Cost of Value-Added Activities
Total Standard Cost of Value-Added Work

definition_en: Total Standard Cost of Value-Added Activities refers to the estimated total cost incurred to complete all value-added activities (i.e., activities that directly add value to a product or service) under ideal or efficient production conditions. It is typically calculated based on standard activity output quantities and standard unit costs (including both variable and fixed components), serving as a key benchmark for measuring activity efficiency, implementing cost control, and preparing value-added and non-value-added cost reports.

Value-Added Tax (VAT) is a turnover tax levied on the incremental value of goods or services at each stage of production, circulation, and consumption. Its core calculation method is output tax minus input tax.

Value-Added Tax input tax refers to the VAT amount paid or borne by taxpayers when purchasing goods, labor services, services, intangible assets, or real estate. This portion of tax can be credited against output tax when calculating the VAT payable for the current period.

Output VAT amount refers to the value-added tax calculated based on the current period's sales revenue and the prescribed VAT rate, which is charged to the buyer by a general taxpayer when selling goods, providing taxable services, or engaging in deemed sales activities. It is a key component in calculating the enterprise's current period VAT payable.

Value added refers to the portion of an economic entity's (such as an enterprise or department) output value that exceeds the value of intermediate inputs consumed (such as raw materials and services) over a specific period through production or business activities. It measures the new value created by the entity and serves as the basis for calculating value-added tax, assessing enterprise contribution, and conducting economic analysis.

Increased operating revenue refers to the growth in total operating revenue of an enterprise over a specific period (e.g., compared to the previous period), reflecting the expansion of business scale or growth in business activities.

english: Total Registered Capital After Capital Injection

definition_en: Total capital after capital increase refers to the total amount of a company's registered capital after it has been increased through methods such as introducing new shareholders or existing shareholders making additional investments. It reflects the total capital subscribed by the company's shareholders in the articles of association after the capital increase transaction is completed.

Growth potential refers to the possibility and capability of a company, industry, or economy to achieve scale expansion, revenue growth, or value appreciation over a future period. It is typically based on a comprehensive assessment of factors such as market space, technological development, management capability, financial condition, and competitive advantages.

term_en.name: Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets

english: Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Loss on disposal of fixed assets refers to the loss incurred by an enterprise when selling, transferring, or scrapping fixed assets, resulting from the disposal proceeds being lower than the asset's carrying amount (i.e., the net value after deducting accumulated depreciation and impairment provisions from the original cost). It reflects the negative impact of asset disposal activities on the enterprise and is typically recorded as a non-operating item in the income statement.

Disposal cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred in the process of disposing of an asset (such as fixed assets, inventory, etc.) to complete the disposal action. These expenditures typically include the asset's net book value, related taxes and fees (such as value-added tax, income tax), labor handling fees, transportation costs, cleanup fees, and other expenses directly related to the disposal.

Gain on disposal of assets refers to the net profit portion obtained when a company disposes of long-term assets such as fixed assets or intangible assets through sale, transfer, etc., where the disposal proceeds exceed the carrying amount of the asset and related disposal expenses.

Spare parts and components cost refers to the procurement cost incurred for replacing and repairing equipment, parts, materials, and components, which is calculated and reserved based on a certain percentage of equipment cost or installation engineering cost to maintain the normal operation of production equipment.

The number of compounding periods refers to the frequency with which interest is calculated and added to the principal for subsequent interest calculations in the compounding process. It is typically measured in years, such as annual compounding, quarterly compounding, or monthly compounding, and directly affects the future value of an investment or loan.

Replacement cost refers to the total cost required to repurchase or reconstruct a brand new asset that is identical to the original asset in terms of function, specifications, performance, and condition under current market conditions. It serves as the basis for the replacement cost method in asset valuation and is used to measure the current value of an asset.

Purchased semi-finished goods cost refers to the expenses incurred by an enterprise for acquiring partially processed but not yet finalized products from external suppliers for further processing or assembly. These costs typically constitute part of the direct material cost of the product.

term_en.name: Purchased Raw Materials, Fuel and Power Costs

chinese: 外购原材料及动力成本
english: Purchased Raw Materials, Fuel and Power Costs
Cost of Purchased Materials, Fuel and Power

definition_en: Purchased raw materials, fuel and power costs refer to the expenses incurred by an enterprise for externally purchased and consumed raw materials, fuel (such as coal, petroleum), and power (such as electricity, steam) during the production and operation process to manufacture products or provide services. It constitutes a significant component of the enterprise's total cost and expenses.

term_en.name: Externally Provided Labor and Service Fees

definition_en: Externally provided labor and service fees refer to the expenses paid by an enterprise for outsourcing or hiring external personnel or institutions to provide labor or professional services in order to carry out its business operations. These fees typically require compliant invoices and are accounted for under relevant cost or expense accounts.

The Major Repair Fund is a special source of funds that enterprises pre-withdraw and accumulate from production costs according to state-prescribed withdrawal rates, specifically designated for covering large-scale, periodic repair expenses of fixed assets (such as machinery, equipment, buildings, and structures).

Days Payable Outstanding (DPO), commonly referred to as 'Days' in finance and accounting, is an indicator measuring the average number of days a company takes to pay its suppliers. It falls under the category of operating efficiency analysis. A shorter DPO typically indicates faster payment to suppliers, while a longer DPO suggests the company is utilizing supplier financing for a longer period.

Unemployment insurance is a social insurance system mandated by national legislation, funded through collective social contributions, which provides material assistance to workers who have temporarily lost their livelihood due to unemployment, ensuring their basic living standards and promoting their re-employment.

chinese: 个人失业保险缴费比例

definition_en: The unemployment insurance individual contribution rate refers to the percentage of an employee's monthly wage that must be contributed to unemployment insurance. According to current regulations, this rate is typically 1% of the employee's monthly wage and is withheld by the employer from the employee's salary.

chinese: 失业保险个人缴纳金额

definition_en: The Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Amount refers to the unemployment insurance premium calculated and paid by individual workers participating in the urban employee unemployment insurance scheme, based on a specified percentage of their monthly wages as stipulated by national regulations. It constitutes a component of individual social security expenditures and is used to provide basic living security and employment assistance during periods of unemployment.

chinese: 失业保险缴费工资基数

definition_en: The unemployment insurance contribution base refers to the wage income benchmark used to calculate the amount of unemployment insurance premiums payable by employers and individuals. Typically, the employer's contribution base is the total wages of the unit in the previous year, while the individual's contribution base is the individual's total wages in the previous year. Specific upper and lower limits are determined by local governments based on factors such as the average social wage.

The unemployment insurance contribution rate refers to the percentage rate determined by national regulations, under which employers and individual employees respectively contribute unemployment insurance premiums based on a specified percentage of the employer's total payroll or the employee's individual wage. Typically, employers contribute 2% of their total employee payroll, while individual employees contribute 1% of their own wages, though specific rates may be adjusted according to local policies.

Unemployment insurance premium refers to the fee paid by employers and individual employees according to state regulations, calculated as a certain percentage of the employee's wage income, used to establish the unemployment insurance fund. It is one of the prerequisites for employees to claim unemployment insurance benefits after becoming unemployed.
Deed tax is a property tax levied on the new property right holder when ownership of real estate such as land or buildings is transferred (e.g., through sale, gift, or exchange).

chinese: 跨国子公司当地货币投资
english: Investment Denominated in Host Country Currency

definition_en: Refers to an investment made by a parent company in its foreign subsidiary using the currency of the country or region where the subsidiary is located (i.e., the local currency). This investment method involves cross-border capital flows and exchange rate risks. When preparing consolidated financial statements, related monetary items require specific accounting treatment and the elimination of exchange differences.

chinese: 子公司所有者权益总额

definition_en: Total equity of a subsidiary refers to the aggregate residual interest in the assets of the subsidiary, as an independent legal entity, after deducting its liabilities, which is collectively owned by the subsidiary's owners (including the controlling parent company and other minority shareholders). In consolidated financial statements, it serves as the foundational component for calculating the equity attributable to owners of the parent and minority interests.

Total equity of a subsidiary refers to the aggregate residual interest, at a specific point in time, that belongs to the owners of the subsidiary (typically its parent company and other shareholders) after deducting total liabilities from total assets. In consolidated financial statements, it is used to calculate consolidation items such as non-controlling interests.

Subsidiary earnings refer to the final financial results generated by a subsidiary, which is owned or controlled by a parent company, through its operating activities during a specific accounting period, typically represented as net profit. It is a core indicator for measuring the independent operating performance of a subsidiary and serves as the basis for calculating consolidated group financial statements and net profit attributable to the parent company.

Subinterval count refers to the total number of data points whose values fall within a specific numerical range in a given dataset. For example, when analyzing a set of product prices, the number of products priced between 100 and 200 yuan is the subinterval count for that price range.

A subinterval node refers to the key points or boundary points used to partition a large time interval or numerical interval (such as a return calculation period) into several smaller subintervals. For example, when calculating fund returns, the entire calculation period can be divided into multiple subintervals based on the timing of cash flows, where the start and end points of each subinterval are the subinterval nodes.

Term (Years) refers to the length of time from the deposit (or investment) date to the maturity (or withdrawal) date, typically calculated and expressed in years. It is one of the key factors determining the interest amount in interest calculations.

Total reserve requirement refers to the aggregate sum of deposit funds that all financial institutions in a country must hold at the central bank, in accordance with central bank regulations, to meet customer withdrawal demands and fund clearing needs. It typically comprises both the statutory reserve requirement and the excess reserve requirement.

chinese: 存货可变现净值计量基础

definition_en: Estimated selling price of inventory refers to the expected sales price that an enterprise can obtain from the external sale of its held inventory on the balance sheet date. It is a key input value for calculating the net realizable value of inventory, typically determined based on contract prices or general market selling prices.
category_en: Lower of Cost or Market Method

definition_en: Inventory balance refers to the total book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (e.g., the end of an accounting period) that is intended for sale or use in the production process. It reflects the scale of the enterprise's inventory assets at that point in time.

Unit cost of inventory refers to the average cost value corresponding to each unit of inventory held by an enterprise (such as one piece, one kilogram, or one carton), used to measure the cost level of stock goods or materials.

term_en.name: Increase in Imputed Interest on Inventory Capital

chinese: 存货资金占用利息增加
库存占用资金利息增量
english: Increase in Imputed Interest on Inventory Capital
Growth of Carrying Cost Interest on Inventory

definition_en: Increase in imputed interest on inventory capital refers to the growth in the calculated interest cost for the funds tied up in holding inventory, resulting from either a rise in the average inventory balance or an increase in the cost of capital (interest rate). Although this cost does not represent an actual cash outflow, it is accounted for as an opportunity cost in financial analysis to evaluate the efficiency of inventory management and its true economic cost.

Beginning inventory balance refers to the book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (i.e., the beginning of the year or the end of the previous fiscal year). It serves as the base data for calculating financial metrics such as average inventory balance and inventory turnover ratio.

Inventory year-end balance refers to the total book value of all inventory items presented on a company's balance sheet at the end of a specific fiscal year (typically December 31st). It reflects the amount of inventory held by the company on the annual cutoff date, including raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, and other stock intended for sale or production processes.

Beginning inventory balance refers to the total book value of all types of inventory (such as raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, etc.) held by an enterprise and available for use or sale at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or month). It typically equals the ending inventory balance of the preceding accounting period.

Ending inventory balance refers to the total book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It reflects the value of inventory items, including raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods, that have not been sold or used by the enterprise at the reporting date.

Reversal of inventory write-down loss refers to the accounting process where, upon the sale, consumption, or disposal of inventory, the previously recognized inventory write-down provision (i.e., inventory write-down loss) is removed from the asset impairment provision account, with a corresponding reduction in the carrying value of inventory or recognition in current period profit or loss. This reflects the final realization of the inventory write-down loss.

Installation engineering investment refers to the actual expenditures incurred for completing the installation of various equipment and apparatus in fixed asset investment. This portion of investment must be realized through construction activities, primarily including the assembly and installation of production, power, lifting, transportation, transmission, medical, and experimental equipment; the installation of workbenches, ladders, railings, and other structures connected to equipment; insulation, anti-corrosion, insulation, and painting work for installed equipment; as well as single-unit trial runs and system linkage no-load trial runs conducted to assess installation quality.

Installation engineering cost refers to the total production expenses paid by the construction unit to the construction and installation engineering contractor. It constitutes a significant component of the construction investment within the total investment of a construction project. It covers the direct costs, indirect costs, profit, and taxes incurred for completing installation work such as equipment, piping, electrical, and instrumentation.

Percentage of completion is an accounting method primarily used for long-term construction contracts or long-term service contracts, which recognizes current period revenue and expenses based on the progress of contract completion. It reflects the proportion of the project completed at a specific point in time relative to the total project.

Budget at Completion refers to the total budgeted or approved cost planned for the entire project or engineering work before its commencement. It represents the estimated total cost upon completion of the full project scope and serves as the baseline for measuring project cost performance.

Dutiable value refers to the price of goods used by customs as the basis for calculating taxes such as customs duties, value-added tax, and consumption tax during importation. For imported goods, the dutiable value is typically the Cost, Insurance, and Freight (CIF) price, which is based on the transaction price examined and approved by customs.

Fixed labor cost refers to the labor expenses required to complete specific project quantities, calculated according to predetermined quota standards (such as consumption quotas) in project budgeting or cost accounting. It is typically derived by multiplying labor consumption (e.g., number of workdays) by the fixed labor unit price (budget price), and constitutes an important component of project cost.

Specific consumption tax is a method of calculating consumption tax based on the sales quantity of taxable consumer goods (such as weight, volume, number of units, etc.) and a predetermined fixed unit tax amount, rather than on the price or sales revenue of the goods. This method is typically applicable to specific commodities such as beer, yellow wine, and refined oil products.

Fixed amount tax rate refers to a form of tax rate stipulated by tax law, where a fixed tax amount is directly levied per unit of taxable object, and does not change with the increase or decrease in the amount of the taxable object. For example, in stamp duty, certain documents are taxed per piece with a fixed amount of 5 yuan per piece, which is a type of fixed amount tax rate.

Physical depreciation refers to the loss in value of an asset caused by a decline in its utility, performance, or appearance due to physical wear and tear, natural aging, accidental damage, or similar factors. It is a type of value impairment considered in asset valuation, particularly under the replacement cost method, when calculating the current value of an asset.

Actual operating time refers to the time actually consumed to complete a specific task or operation, determined through actual observation, measurement, or recording. In the field of finance and accounting, it is commonly used for cost accounting, labor hour management, and efficiency analysis, serving as essential baseline data for calculating setup time, evaluating production efficiency, and formulating budgets.

Actual cost at actual output refers to the total sum of all costs actually incurred and recorded during a specific period for producing the actual quantity of output. It reflects the value of resources consumed in the real production process and serves as a crucial basis for cost control and performance evaluation.

chinese: 实际生产量下的标准成本

definition_en: Standard cost at actual output refers to the total cost calculated based on the actual quantity of products completed during a specific period, using predetermined standard consumption per unit (e.g., materials, labor hours) and standard prices (e.g., material price per unit, wage rate). It serves as one of the benchmarks for measuring variances between actual costs and standard costs (such as price variances and efficiency variances).

Actual Activity Driver Quantity refers to the actual number of drivers consumed or utilized by various activities during a specific accounting period to produce actual output of products or services in Activity-Based Costing. It serves as the fundamental basis for allocating costs from activity cost pools to specific cost objects (such as products or services).

Actual Activity Cost refers to the total cost actually incurred and recorded for completing specific activities or operations within a given accounting period under Activity-Based Costing. It is typically used to calculate the actual activity cost allocation rate for more accurate cost assignment to products or services.

Actual Activity Level refers to the specific quantity of labor hours, resources consumed, or output produced to complete a specific activity or production operation within a given period. It serves as fundamental data for measuring activity execution efficiency, cost accounting, and budgetary control.

Actual usage refers to the quantity of materials, labor hours, or other resources actually consumed to complete specified tasks or outputs within a given production, operation, or analysis period. It reflects the true level of resource consumption and serves as the basis for calculating efficiency metrics such as wastage rates and scrap rates.

Actual Total Export Value refers to the total monetary value of all goods and services that enterprises in a country or region have actually completed exporting and have left the country's ports or borders during a specific reporting period. It reflects genuine export performance and typically includes general trade exports, processing fees for processing with supplied materials, and compensation trade exports.

The real interest rate refers to the true rate of return on interest earned by investors or depositors after adjusting for inflation. It reflects the real time value of money after accounting for changes in purchasing power.

chinese: 购进货物实际负担的增值税

definition_en: Actual incurred input VAT refers to the value-added tax amount actually paid or borne by an enterprise during a specific period due to the purchase of goods, receipt of taxable services, or services. It reflects the actual VAT cost incurred by the enterprise during that period, which can be used to offset output VAT.

Actual achievement refers to the specific numerical value or result ultimately attained for a given indicator, task, or objective within a specified period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It serves as key data for measuring plan execution and performance.

Actual physical output refers to the quantity of products actually produced or completed by a production unit (such as an enterprise, project, or industry) within a specific period, measured in natural physical units (e.g., tons, cubic meters, units, square meters). It reflects the actual scale of production achievements and serves as important foundational data for calculating gross output value and evaluating plan fulfillment.

Actual service life refers to the actual length of time an asset has been in use from the date it was put into service until the valuation date. It reflects the actual wear and tear of the asset and is a key parameter for calculating physical deterioration and obsolescence in asset valuation.

Actual Cost Driver Rate refers to the unit cost allocation rate per driver calculated in Activity-Based Costing based on the actual incurred activity costs and the actual consumed quantity of activity drivers. It reflects the proportional relationship between the actual cost of performing an activity and the actual volume of activity drivers that cause that cost during a specific period, and is used to allocate actual activity costs more accurately to products or services.

Actual indicators refer to the financial or operational performance values calculated by an enterprise based on actual business data after a specific accounting period or operating cycle. They reflect the true operating results and financial condition of the enterprise during that period and serve as the foundational data for budget comparison, performance evaluation, and factor analysis.

Actual usage refers to the real quantity of raw materials, supplies, or resources consumed to achieve a certain output or turnover within a specific production or operating period. In accounting and production management, it is typically compared with standard usage or budgeted usage to analyze cost variances and efficiency.

Actual consumption volume refers to the total quantity or total value of resources such as raw materials, energy, and labor actually consumed by an enterprise for producing goods or providing services during a specific accounting period or production cycle. It serves as fundamental data for calculating wastage rates, cost analysis, and efficiency evaluation.

Actual exercise quantity refers to the specific number of underlying assets that holders of financial derivatives such as stock options or warrants actually choose to purchase or sell by exercising their rights. It reflects the volume scale at which options or warrants are converted from potential rights into actual transactions.

chinese: 不变价货物与服务价值

definition_en: Real goods and services value refers to the production or transaction value of goods and services measured at the prices of a specific base period, after removing the effects of price changes. It reflects the real quantitative changes in economic activity and serves as the basis for calculating price deflators (such as the GDP deflator).

Actual purchase volume refers to the quantity of goods or services that consumers or enterprises ultimately complete transactions and make payments for, after considering factors such as discounts, promotions, and returns. It reflects genuine consumption or procurement behavior, rather than planned or nominal purchase intentions.

Actual Total Import Value refers to the total value of goods actually imported by enterprises in a country or region during a specific period, as recorded by customs statistics. It is typically calculated based on the declared amount on customs declaration forms and serves as a key economic indicator for measuring the scale of a country's import trade.

Actual sales amount refers to the final amount actually received from customers after the sale of goods or provision of services. It is typically the net amount after deducting factors such as discounts, allowances, or returns granted to customers from the total sales price.

Actual sales revenue refers to the net amount received by an enterprise after deducting price concessions such as sales discounts and allowances from the total price and extra-charges (excluding output VAT) collected from buyers following the sale of goods or provision of services. It reflects the enterprise's true sales performance.

The Customer Credit Score Coefficient refers to the weight or impact factor assigned to each evaluation indicator used by financial institutions to calculate the final credit score or credit rating when assessing a customer's creditworthiness. It is typically based on the customer's financial data (such as debt repayment capacity and profitability) and non-financial information, quantifying the customer's credit risk through a specific scoring model, and serves as a key basis for credit decisions such as determining credit limits.

Disposable income refers to the total income available to an individual or household over a specific period (typically one year) for final consumption and savings. It is the net amount after deducting personal income tax, personal social security contributions (such as pension insurance, medical insurance, etc.), and other mandatory transfer payments from total income, reflecting the actual financial resources available for discretionary use by the customer.

Total Monthly Customer Repayment Amount refers to the aggregate sum of all loan or installment payments that a customer is required to repay within a specified period (typically one month). It reflects the customer's fixed monthly debt expenditure level and serves as a crucial indicator for assessing their repayment capacity and credit risk.

Customer Monthly Income refers to the total revenue generated for a company by a single customer within a calendar month. In subscription or service-based businesses, it often refers to the customer's Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR), serving as crucial foundational data for assessing customer value and conducting financial forecasting.

term_en.name: Average Customer Utilization Over the Past Six Months

chinese: 近六个月平均使用额度
english: Average Credit Utilization Over the Past Six Months

definition_en: Average Customer Utilization Over the Past Six Months refers to a metric used in personal credit reporting or bank credit management to measure a customer's average usage of their credit facilities, such as credit cards or loans, over the past six months (180 days). It reflects the average level of credit resource occupation by the customer over a period and is one of the key indicators for assessing customer credit behavior and repayment capacity.

Refers to various returns obtained by a company through external equity investments (e.g., purchasing stocks) or debt investments (e.g., purchasing bonds), primarily including profits distributed from investee companies (such as dividends and bonuses) and interest income earned from holding bonds.

Scenario occurrence probability refers to the quantitative estimation of the likelihood that a specific future scenario (such as market conditions or operational status) will actually occur in financial forecasting, risk assessment, or decision analysis. It serves as a key input parameter for calculating financial metrics such as expected cash flows.

Corresponding weight refers to the numerical value assigned to each data item when calculating a weighted average to reflect its relative importance or influence. The larger the weight, the greater the contribution of that data item to the average calculation.

Expected frequency, also known as theoretical frequency, refers to the number of data points anticipated to be observed in a specific category or interval under a given theoretical distribution or when the null hypothesis is true, as used in statistical hypothesis testing (e.g., chi-square test). It serves as the basis for comparison with the actually observed frequency.

Log price refers to the value obtained by taking the natural logarithm (usually base e) of the price of a commodity or financial asset. In financial analysis, using log prices simplifies calculations, particularly when computing continuously compounded returns or price change percentages. The log return (i.e., the difference in log prices) approximates the percentage change in price and exhibits superior statistical properties, such as approximate normal distribution.

Log old price refers to the value obtained by taking the natural logarithm or common logarithm of the price of an asset or commodity at a specific historical point in time (i.e., the old price). In financial analysis, logarithmic prices are often used to calculate price change percentages or returns under continuous compounding, eliminating the influence of price levels and simplifying calculations.

term_en.name: Sales Revenue of the Comparative Year

definition_en: Sales revenue of the comparative year refers to the total revenue generated by a company from the sale of goods or provision of services in a specific year selected as a reference benchmark (typically the previous year or a historical year) for financial analysis or performance comparison.

english: Minority Interest in Profit or Loss

definition_en: Minority interest refers to the portion of net profit or net loss attributable to non-controlling shareholders (i.e., shareholders holding less than 50% of shares) of subsidiaries in a company's consolidated financial statements. It reflects the operating results of subsidiaries within the consolidation scope that are not attributable to the parent company and is presented as a deduction from net profit in the income statement.

Remaining useful life refers to the estimated number of years an asset can continue to be used from the valuation date, based on its physical deterioration (such as wear and tear) and foreseeable forms of obsolescence (such as technological obsolescence). It serves as a critical basis for calculating asset depreciation or amortization.

Household consumption expenditure refers to the total expenditure by residents of a country or region on goods and services to meet daily living needs over a specific period (usually one year). It reflects residents' consumption levels and living conditions, serving as a key indicator for measuring domestic demand and economic development.

Industrial intermediate input refers to the externally purchased raw materials, fuels, power, and other physical products that are consumed once during the reporting period by industrial enterprises for industrial production activities, as well as various service fees paid externally. The value of these inputs is entirely transferred to the value of products produced in the current period and serves as a key deduction item in calculating industrial value added.

term_en.name: Lost Time Due to Work Injury

definition_en: Lost time due to work injury refers to the total time employees are unable to work normally as a result of occupational accidents, typically measured in hours. It is a key indicator for assessing the severity of occupational accidents and the level of corporate safety management.

Work Injury Insurance is a social insurance system designed to provide workers or their dependents with medical treatment, financial compensation, and vocational rehabilitation assistance from the state and society in the event of accidental injury, occupational disease, temporary or permanent loss of working capacity, or even death arising from work or work-related causes.

Work Loss Value refers to the monetary measurement of economic losses caused by the inability to work normally due to casualties in enterprise occupational injury and fatality accidents. It is typically calculated based on data such as the total lost workdays resulting from the accident, the enterprise's pre-tax profits of the previous year, and the total number of employees, and is used to assess the indirect impact of the accident on the enterprise's production and operations.

Work efficiency refers to the ratio between work output completed within a specific period and the resources invested (such as time, manpower, and material resources), used to measure the effectiveness and economy of work processes.

The workload coefficient is an adjustment parameter used to quantify factors such as task complexity, technical difficulty, and risk level. In project management, cost estimation, and financial accounting, it typically serves as a multiplier, combined with baseline data such as labor input and project duration, to more accurately calculate or assess total workload, resource requirements, or project costs.

Tooling cost refers to the expenses incurred by an enterprise for the purchase, use, and maintenance of various tools and implements during production, operations, or project construction. Depending on the value and useful life of the tools, these costs may be capitalized as fixed assets, recorded as low-value consumables, or expensed as current period administrative costs.

Time standard refers to the standard time required to complete a specific process or work unit, serving as an important basis for production planning, cost accounting, and determining staffing and equipment requirements.

Project duration refers to the total time length required to complete an engineering project or specific work task, typically calculated from the project commencement date to the date when the project is fully completed and passes acceptance inspection. It is a core metric for measuring progress and efficiency in project management.

Engineering insurance premium refers to the fee paid to insurance companies during the construction process to transfer various risks that the project may face (such as natural disasters, accidents, third-party liability, etc.). It is a component of other construction costs.

Other construction costs refer to the various expenses that must be incurred during construction investment, in addition to engineering costs such as construction engineering fees, installation engineering fees, and equipment purchase costs, to ensure the smooth construction and delivery of the project.

Project settlement cost refers to the total cost calculated and recognized by a construction enterprise upon completion of a specific project or reaching a contractually agreed settlement milestone, based on the actual expenditures directly related to the project. It is a key component in calculating project settlement profit.

Project settlement revenue refers to the price income obtained by a construction enterprise from the client unit for settlement of completed or finished construction projects according to contract agreements. It is a core component for recognizing the operating revenue of a construction enterprise.

Total wages refer to the aggregate sum of labor compensation directly paid by an enterprise or organization to all its employees within a specific period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It typically includes basic wages, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, overtime pay, etc., and serves as a key indicator for measuring an enterprise's labor costs.

Wages and welfare expenses refer to various welfare expenditures provided by an enterprise to its employees beyond direct compensation such as wages, bonuses, and allowances. They are typically accrued at a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll and are used to cover employee medical expenses, living hardship subsidies, expenditures for collective welfare facilities (such as canteens and bathrooms) and related personnel salaries, aiming to improve employees' living and working conditions.

Wages and salaries income refers to all forms of labor remuneration received by an individual due to holding an office or being employed by a specific unit or organization. This typically includes basic wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, various allowances, subsidies, and all other income related to the office held or employment. It is one of the taxable items stipulated under China's Individual Income Tax Law, and the tax payable is usually calculated based on monthly income.

Total Taxes Paid refers to the aggregate sum of all taxes that a taxpayer has actually remitted to the tax authorities during a specific tax period. It reflects the taxpayer's fulfilled tax obligations and serves as a crucial basis for calculating the actual tax payable or the amount of tax refundable.

In the repayment process of debts such as loans or bonds, the portion of each periodic payment that is used to reduce the original principal amount (i.e., the initial debt amount). It does not include the interest portion.

The present value of principal repaid refers to the total value, discounted to a specific point in time (typically the current date or an evaluation reference date) at a certain discount rate (such as the loan interest rate or market rate), of the principal amounts that have already been repaid in financial activities like loans or bonds. It reflects the current value of the principal portion the borrower has actually repaid, taking into account the time value of money.

Cumulative principal repaid refers to the total sum of all principal amounts repaid from the beginning of the repayment period to the current point in time for financial instruments such as loans or bonds. It reflects the portion of the original borrowed principal that the borrower has already repaid and is a key component in calculating the remaining outstanding principal balance.

Distributed Preferred Return refers to the portion of preferred return that has been actually paid out to preferred shareholders or senior-level investors at specified times (such as upon project exit or profit distribution) according to the agreement, within structures like private equity, venture capital, or partnership funds. This return is typically calculated based on the agreed rate of return (e.g., an annualized interest rate) and the invested principal, and is paid out prior to the participation of general partners or common shareholders in the distribution.

term_en.name: Total Face Value of Issued Debt

english: Total Face Value of Issued Debt
Total Par Value of Debt Issued

definition_en: Total face value of issued debt refers to the aggregate principal amount (i.e., face value) stated on all debt instruments, such as bonds and notes, issued by a company to raise funds from investors. It represents the total principal amount of debt that the company is obligated to repay and serves as a key foundational data point for calculating metrics such as the company's total market value.

Number of Issued Common Shares refers to the total quantity of common stock shares that a company has issued and are held by investors (including public shareholders, company insiders, etc.). It excludes treasury shares that the company has repurchased but not yet retired. This figure serves as the basis for calculating key financial metrics such as the company's total market capitalization.
Recovered quantity refers to the total number of items, resources, or funds actually retrieved through recovery activities within a specific time period or project.

Work completed refers to the total volume or value of work that has been actually finished for a project or task at a specific point in time. It is commonly used to measure project progress and serves as a key component in calculating the project completion percentage.

term_en.name: Present Value of Repaid Loan Principal

definition_en: The present value of repaid loan principal refers to the total value, discounted to the loan origination date or a specific valuation date at a certain discount rate (typically the loan interest rate), of all principal portions already repaid by the borrower during the loan term. It reflects the time value of the loan principal that the borrower has actually repaid.

Amortized periods refer to the total number of accounting periods (such as months, quarters, or years) that have elapsed and been fully amortized from the commencement date of amortization for an asset (e.g., fixed assets, intangible assets) or a long-term deferred expense up to the current calculation point. It reflects the duration over which the asset cost or expense has been allocated to the income statement.

Value-Added Tax Paid refers to the amount of value-added tax calculated based on taxable activities during a specific tax filing period, which has been actually declared to and paid to the tax authorities. It reflects the actual cash outflow for value-added tax borne by the enterprise in the current period.

Approved credit line refers to the maximum loan or credit limit formally granted to a borrower by a financial institution (such as a bank) after review. Within this limit, the borrower may draw funds in multiple installments or as a lump sum according to agreed conditions and purposes.

Elapsed time refers to the actual length of time that has passed or been consumed from a specific starting point (such as project commencement, asset activation, contract effectiveness, etc.) to the current moment.

Market capitalization weight refers to the proportion of a company's (or asset's) market value relative to the total market value of its market or portfolio. It is commonly used to calculate the average return of market indices or investment portfolios. Companies with larger market capitalizations typically have higher weights and exert greater influence on the overall indicator.

The Price-to-Book Ratio Multiple is a valuation metric that measures a stock's market value relative to its book value (net assets), reflecting the price multiple investors are willing to pay for each unit of the company's net assets per share.

The Market Benchmark Liquidity Ratio is a reference standard or target value used to measure and compare the short-term solvency of an enterprise or the overall market. It is typically established based on industry averages, historical data, or specific market conditions to assess whether a specific entity's liquidity position meets or exceeds the prevailing market level.

Market Average Return on Investment refers to the average return level of all investment targets or portfolios in the entire market or a representative market index (such as the CSI 300 Index) over a specific period. It is commonly used as a benchmark for measuring investment performance or calculating the opportunity cost of investment.

Total market sales refers to the aggregate revenue amount generated by all participants (such as companies, product lines, or industries) within a specific market through the sale of goods or provision of services over a defined period.

The Market Sentiment Coefficient is an indicator used to quantify the psychological state of investors or the market as a whole (such as optimism, pessimism, excitement, or fear). It is calculated by analyzing multiple data sources including survey data, social media sentiment, financial news sentiment, or market trading behavior, and is commonly used to predict market trends and assess asset price volatility.

term_en.name: Expected Downside Return of the Market Portfolio

chinese: 市场组合预期下行收益
下行市场组合预期回报
english: Expected Downside Return of Market Portfolio

definition_en: The expected downside return of the market portfolio refers to the estimated average future return of the overall market portfolio (such as a market index comprising all risky assets) during periods of poor market performance or decline. It focuses on measuring the expected return under downside risk scenarios and serves as a key input parameter for calculating metrics such as the downside market risk premium.

A market index is a statistical indicator used to measure and reflect the overall price level movements of a specific stock market or a segment of its stocks. It is typically constructed from the prices of a representative group of stocks using specific calculation methods (such as weighted averaging) and serves as a crucial benchmark for investors to observe market trends and evaluate investment performance.

term_en.name: Number of Market Return Data Points

english: Number of Market Return Data Points

definition_en: Number of Market Return Data Points refers to the total count of historical market return observations used in calculating statistical metrics such as the standard deviation of stock market returns. It represents the sample size, directly affecting the calculation accuracy and reliability of risk measures like standard deviation.

Expected market return refers to investors' expectation of the average rate of return for the overall market (typically represented by a broad market index such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) over a future period. It is a key parameter in financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), used to measure the overall market risk premium level.

Market return standard deviation is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of the overall market return, typically represented by the return of a market index such as the CSI 300 Index. It reflects the average extent to which market returns deviate from their mean value. A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility and higher risk in market returns.

Variance of market returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or dispersion of returns for the entire market, typically represented by a market index. It measures market risk by calculating the weighted average of the squared deviations of possible market returns from their expected value (mean return).

The market risk-free rate of return refers to the theoretical rate of return an investor can obtain from an investment with no default risk. It is generally regarded as the minimum expected return benchmark for all other risky investments, consisting of the pure time value of money and inflation compensation. In practice, short-term government bond yields or bank deposit rates are often used as its approximations.

term_en.name: Possible Returns of Market Portfolio under Various Scenarios

chinese: 市场组合预期收益率情景
english: Possible Returns of Market Portfolio under Various Scenarios

definition_en: Possible returns of the market portfolio under various scenarios refer to the potential returns that may be achieved by the market portfolio, which consists of all risky assets in the market, under different economic or market conditions (such as boom, normal, recession, etc.). It reflects the performance of the market portfolio under different future scenarios and serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating market portfolio risk (e.g., standard deviation) and asset pricing (e.g., the CAPM model).

term_en.name: Historical Returns of Market Portfolio by Period

english: Historical Returns of the Market Portfolio

definition_en: Historical returns of the market portfolio by period refer to the sequence of returns achieved by a portfolio representing the overall market (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, CSI 300 Index, etc.) over specific past periods (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly, or annually). It reflects the performance of the market across different historical stages and serves as fundamental data for calculating market risk (such as standard deviation) and assessing the risk of other assets (such as beta coefficient).

The market portfolio average return rate refers to the expected return calculated as the weighted average of all risky assets in the market based on their market values. It represents the average return level of the entire market (or a representative market index, such as the CSI 300 Index) and serves as a key benchmark for measuring overall market performance and calculating asset risk premiums (such as the market risk premium in the Capital Asset Pricing Model, CAPM).

Total market portfolio value refers to the aggregate value of all investable assets (typically all issued stocks) in a specific market, calculated at their market prices. It represents the overall scale of the market and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as market weights and market portfolio returns.

In financial theories such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), the expected return of the market portfolio refers to the predicted average return that investors anticipate from a portfolio comprising all risky assets in the market (i.e., the market portfolio) over a future period. It serves as a crucial benchmark for measuring the overall return level of the market.

term_en.name: Beta Coefficient of the Market Portfolio

definition_en: The beta coefficient of the market portfolio is an indicator that measures the systematic risk of the market portfolio (typically referring to a portfolio representing the entire market, such as a broad market index) relative to itself. By definition and calculation formula, the correlation coefficient between the market portfolio and itself is 1, therefore its beta coefficient is always equal to 1. It serves as the benchmark in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) for measuring the systematic risk of other individual assets or investment portfolios.

term_en.name: Expected Return of the Market Portfolio

definition_en: The expected return of the market portfolio refers to the expected rate of return calculated as the market-value-weighted average of all risky assets in the market. It represents the average expected return level of the entire market as a whole and serves as a key benchmark parameter in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

term_en.name: Expected Return of the Market Portfolio

definition_en: The expected return of the market portfolio refers to the predicted or estimated average return that investors anticipate from a portfolio comprising all risky assets in the market (i.e., the market portfolio) over a future period, as used in financial theories such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). It serves as a key benchmark for measuring the overall average return level of the market.

The market portfolio risk premium refers to the additional return or compensation that investors require for bearing the systematic risk of the market portfolio (typically represented by a broad market index such as the CSI 300 Index), exceeding the risk-free rate of return (such as government bond yields). It is a key metric for measuring the overall level of risk compensation in the market.

The expected market portfolio return refers to investors' expectation of the average rate of return for the entire market (typically including all tradable assets) over a future period. It represents the average return level of the overall market, serves as a crucial benchmark for measuring market risk and return, and is commonly used in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) to calculate the required rate of return for individual assets or investment portfolios.

The market portfolio return refers to the expected or actual average rate of return on a theoretical portfolio that includes all risky assets in the market (such as stocks, bonds, etc.). It represents the average profitability level of the entire market and serves as a key benchmark for measuring overall market performance and calculating risk premiums for other assets (e.g., individual stocks).

The market discount rate refers to the interest rate used to discount future cash flows to their present value. It reflects the time value of money and investment risk, serving as a key parameter in financial markets for evaluating asset prices and investment project feasibility.

The Price-to-Sales Ratio is a financial ratio used to evaluate stock valuation levels, reflecting the relationship between a stock's market value and the company's revenue. This metric is commonly used to value companies that are not yet profitable or have unstable earnings.

The Paasche Price Index is a price index calculated using the quantities of the reporting period (current period) as weights, used to measure the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services from the base period to the reporting period. It reflects the impact of price changes on total cost or total expenditure under the current consumption or production structure.

Interest-bearing notes payable refer to commercial bills issued by an enterprise in activities such as commodity purchases and sales or acceptance of services, due to deferred payment, which unconditionally promise to pay a specified amount to the payee or holder on a designated future date, and on which interest must be calculated at the stated rate during the holding period. It is a type of current liability for an enterprise.

Constant e is an important mathematical constant, approximately equal to 2.71828, and is an infinite non-repeating decimal (transcendental number). It serves as the base of the natural logarithm function and is widely applied in various fields including mathematics, physics, engineering, and economics.

A closing fee is a service charge paid by investors to a trading platform or broker when closing (selling or buying to offset) an existing position in a financial transaction. It is a significant component of the total transaction cost.

Average population refers to the mean number of people in a specific region or group over a defined period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the typical population size during that period and serves as the base data for calculating per capita indicators (e.g., per capita consumption).

The average rate of profit, also known as the general rate of profit, refers to the ratio between the total surplus value produced by the entire society or the capitalist class over a given period (usually one year) and the total advanced capital of the whole society. It reflects the result of the equalization of surplus value distribution among different capitals and serves as a key indicator for measuring the overall profitability of social capital.

Average Historical Return refers to an indicator that reflects the average profitability level of an asset or investment portfolio over historical periods, calculated by computing the returns over multiple past periods (such as years or quarters) and taking their arithmetic mean. It is commonly used to evaluate past performance.

Average Construction in Progress refers to the average book value of fixed assets that are under construction or installation and have not yet reached their intended usable state during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is commonly used in financial analysis to more accurately reflect the level of capital actually employed by the enterprise for long-term asset construction during the reporting period.

Average accounts receivable balance refers to the average level of a company's accounts receivable over a specific period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the average scale of funds that the company is entitled to collect from customers for goods sold or services rendered but not yet received during this period, serving as an important indicator for evaluating the efficiency of accounts receivable management and the extent of capital occupation.

Average Total Cost refers to the total cost incurred by a company to produce each unit of product, calculated by dividing the total production cost by the total output. It reflects the average cost level per unit of product.

Average equity refers to the average level of a company's equity over a specific period (typically an accounting period, such as a year). It reflects the average share of the company's net assets attributable to owners during that period and is commonly used in calculating financial metrics such as return on equity.

The Average Rate of Return refers to the average annual investment return generated by an investment project over its entire life cycle. It is used to measure the average profitability of a project investment and is one of the common indicators for evaluating the merits of investment proposals.

Average Collection Period refers to the average length of time required for a company to collect payment from sales, typically expressed in days. It is an important financial metric for measuring the turnover speed of accounts receivable and the efficiency of fund recovery.
The average is the sum of all values in a dataset divided by the number of data points, used to represent the central tendency or general level of the dataset.
