In accounting and finance, it is commonly used to calculate aggregate amounts for items such as revenue, costs, assets, and liabilities, serving as a fundamental operation for financial analysis and statement preparation.

Fair value of equity refers to the price that would be received to sell the owners' equity (i.e., the residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities) in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, or the price paid to transfer a liability. It reflects the true market value of equity, rather than its historical cost or book value.

The Growth Rate of Owners' Equity is a financial metric that measures the growth rate of owners' equity (i.e., net assets) over a specific period (typically one year or an accounting period). It reflects the company's ability to create value for shareholders and the enhancement of its financial strength through retained earnings from operations and shareholder contributions.

Beginning balance of owner's equity refers to the total amount of owner's equity at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1), reflecting the net asset position of the enterprise at the beginning of the year.

Year-end Owners' Equity refers to the book value of the residual interest attributable to the owners (or shareholders) of an enterprise after deducting total liabilities from total assets at the end of each fiscal year (i.e., December 31). It reflects the net asset position of the enterprise at a specific point in time.

Owner's Equity Translated into Renminbi refers to the process, when an enterprise prepares consolidated financial statements or translates foreign currency financial statements, of converting owner's equity items denominated in foreign currency (such as paid-in capital, capital reserve, surplus reserve, and undistributed profits) into amounts denominated in Renminbi, in accordance with specific accounting standards (such as China's Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises) and exchange rates (such as the spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date, historical exchange rates, etc.). This process is a crucial component of foreign currency financial statement translation, and its results affect the balance of the translated statements and the calculation of translation differences.

term_en.name: Opening RMB Balance of Owner's Equity

chinese: 期初股东权益人民币余额
期初所有者权益人民币金额
english: Opening Balance of Owners' Equity in RMB

definition_en: The Opening RMB Balance of Owner's Equity refers to the total book value in Renminbi (RMB) of the equity interests that the owners (shareholders) hold in the net assets of an enterprise at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the closing balance of owner's equity denominated in RMB at the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the basis for calculating changes in owner's equity during the current period.

A handling fee (or commission fee) refers to a charge levied by a service-providing institution (such as a bank, brokerage firm, or payment platform) on a client for financial transactions or related services. It is typically intended to compensate the institution for costs incurred during transaction processing, account management, or the provision of professional services.
Fee rate refers to the ratio of handling fees to the transaction amount in financial or commercial transactions, used to measure transaction costs.

term_en.name: Total Amount of Deduction Adjustment Items

chinese: 扣除类纳税调整项目合计
english: Total Amount of Deduction Adjustment Items

definition_en: The total amount of deduction adjustment items refers to the aggregate sum of all deduction items requiring upward or downward tax adjustments during the enterprise income tax final settlement, based on tax law provisions regarding various costs, expenses, losses, and other deductible items calculated from the accounting profit. It reflects the total difference between accounting treatment and tax law provisions concerning deductible items.

Deduction amount refers to the sum that can be subtracted from total income or the relevant base when calculating taxable income or taxable revenue, in accordance with tax laws and related regulations. It is used to reduce the tax base, thereby lowering the final tax payable.

Deduction amount refers to the total sum of various costs, expenses, taxes, losses, and other expenditures that are permitted to be subtracted from the total revenue according to tax laws and relevant regulations when calculating taxable income. It is a key component in determining the final taxable profit.

The present value of the exercise price refers to the current value, discounted at the risk-free rate, of the exercise price that must be paid (for a call option) or received (for a put option) upon future exercise in option pricing. It is one of the key components in calculating the theoretical value of an option (e.g., in the Black-Scholes model).

The expansion coefficient is an indicator that measures the multiple by which a specific economic or financial variable (such as money supply, deposits, credit, etc.) can expand or amplify under the influence of a particular mechanism or policy. It is commonly used to analyze the money creation capacity of the financial system or the leverage effect in corporate finance.

Wholesale price refers to the price applied when goods or services are sold by producers or large wholesalers to retailers, other wholesalers, or corporate clients during the wholesale stage. It is typically lower than the retail price due to large purchase volumes and the absence of direct sales to end consumers.

The insurance markup rate is a concept in international trade insurance, referring to an additional percentage added to the cost of goods, insurance premium, and freight (CIF value) when calculating the insured amount. This markup primarily serves to protect the insured's expected profits and potential related expenses, ensuring the insured amount exceeds the base value of the goods. In international trade practice, the common insurance markup rate is 10%.

The input-output ratio is a financial metric that measures the relationship between the total cost invested and the total output or value added generated in investment projects or business operations, used to assess project economic viability and investment efficiency.

Invested Value is a financial analysis metric, typically referring to the value derived by deducting necessary capital investments from the cash flow generated by a company's current operating activities, used to measure the company's true value creation capability. It reflects the net cash return that operating activities can provide to investors after meeting reinvestment needs.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR) refers to the discount rate at which the present value of all cash inflows equals the present value of all cash outflows over the entire life cycle of an investment project. In simple terms, it is the actual expected rate of return on a project investment and serves as a key metric for evaluating the profitability of investment projects.

Investment impairment loss refers to the accounting loss recognized when the recoverable amount of various investment assets held by an enterprise (such as long-term equity investments, debt investments, etc.) falls below their carrying value due to reasons such as sustained market price declines or deterioration in the operating conditions of the investee.

Pre-money valuation refers to the total equity or overall value of a company before it receives external investment or financing. This valuation is calculated prior to the injection of new capital into the company's balance sheet and is used to determine the equity stake that investors receive in exchange for their capital contribution.

Capital investment in fixed assets refers to the total monetary funds actually invested by an enterprise within a specific period for constructing, purchasing, installing, or renewing fixed assets. It constitutes a significant component of the initial cash outflow and reflects the scale of the enterprise's capital investment in long-term assets.

Funds invested in current assets, commonly referred to as working capital or liquid funds, denote the portion of capital allocated by an enterprise to current assets to sustain daily operations. It reflects the short-term financial health of the enterprise and is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities. These funds support the occupation of current assets such as accounts receivable, inventory, and cash, representing essential short-term investments for normal business functioning.

Gain on disposal of investments refers to the net profit portion obtained when a company sells, transfers, or exchanges its long-term equity investments, financial assets, and other investment assets, where the disposal proceeds exceed the carrying amount of the asset and related disposal costs.

Investment days refer to the actual number of days elapsed from the initial capital investment until the capital is recovered or the investment concludes. It serves as a crucial temporal basis for calculating investment interest, returns, or assessing investment efficiency.

Total investment expenditure refers to the aggregate sum of cash or cash equivalents paid by an enterprise or individual to acquire, construct, or upgrade long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, technology, etc.) and to undertake other investment projects (such as purchasing stocks, funds). It typically includes all directly related outlays such as purchase costs, associated transaction fees, taxes, and reflects the total initial capital invested to initiate or sustain an investment activity.

Total investment income refers to the aggregate sum of all cash and non-cash returns an investor receives from various investment assets held over a specific period. It typically includes interest, dividends, distributions, and realized or unrealized capital gains, serving as a key metric for measuring the overall return level of investment activities.

Investment loss refers to the outflow of economic benefits incurred by an enterprise or individual from external investment activities, resulting from factors such as operating losses of the investee, asset impairment, decline in market value, or disposal proceeds lower than the cost, which lead to a reduction in the carrying value of the investment or actual recovery amount being lower than the initial investment cost.

term_en.name: Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets of Subsidiary at Acquisition Date

chinese: 购买日子公司可辨认净资产公允价值
投资日子公司可辨认净资产公允价值
合并日子公司可辨认净资产公允价值
english: Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets of Subsidiary at Acquisition Date
Fair Value of Acquiree's Identifiable Net Assets at Investment Date

definition_en: Refers to the amount of net assets of a subsidiary, measured at market value (fair value) for each identifiable asset and liability, at the date when the parent company obtains control over the subsidiary (typically the acquisition date or merger date). It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating goodwill or bargain purchase gain in a business combination.

Net investment income refers to the net profit earned by an enterprise through investment activities (such as trading stocks, bonds, funds, long-term equity investments, etc.). It typically equals investment gains minus investment losses. This portion of income is unrelated to core business operations and falls under non-operating gains and losses, used to measure the profitability of a company's investment activities.

term_en.name: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities

definition_en: Net cash flow from investing activities refers to the difference between cash inflows and outflows generated by a company's investing activities (such as acquisition or disposal of long-term assets, obtaining or recovering equity investments, debt investments, etc.) during a specific accounting period. It reflects the net cash result of the company's capital investment activities undertaken for future operations.

Present Value of Investment refers to the current value of the cash flows an investment is expected to generate at a future point in time, discounted back to the present using a specific discount rate (or interest rate). It reflects the current worth of future funds and is one of the core metrics for evaluating the feasibility of an investment project.

Investment cash flow refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company during a specific accounting period from purchasing or selling long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, securities investments, etc.) and other non-current investment projects. It reflects the company's cash activities in expanding or contracting its long-term asset scale.

Investment-related expenses refer to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise during investment activities (such as purchasing fixed assets, investment projects, etc.) for acquiring, constructing, or improving long-term assets, including direct investment cash outlays as well as related transaction fees, taxes, consulting fees, etc.

Total Portfolio Investment refers to the aggregate sum of capital invested by an investor to construct a portfolio comprising various assets (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.). It reflects the investor's initial capital commitment at the portfolio level and serves as the basis for calculating investment proportions, returns, and risk.

Portfolio weight refers to the proportion of the market value of each asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) within a portfolio relative to the total market value of the entire portfolio. It measures the importance and influence of each asset in the portfolio and serves as key foundational data for asset allocation, risk management, and performance evaluation.

Portfolio current net value refers to the net amount obtained by subtracting all related liabilities (such as borrowings, accrued expenses, etc.) from the total current market value of all assets (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) in an investment portfolio at a specific valuation point in time. It reflects the actual value of the portfolio at the present moment and is a key metric for measuring investment performance and risk exposure.

Investor contribution refers to the total amount of funds actually invested by investors (such as shareholders) into a company in exchange for equity or shares, typically including share capital and any premium over par value, serving as a crucial source of corporate capital.

term_en.name: Average Annual Net Income of Investment Project

english: Average Annual Net Income of Investment Project

definition_en: Average Annual Net Income of an Investment Project refers to the average amount of net income generated annually over the entire life cycle of an investment project. It is commonly used to evaluate the profitability and investment recovery of a project, serving as the basis for calculating metrics such as the average rate of return.

Expected investment return refers to the estimated average rate of return or profit amount that an investor anticipates from an investment in the future, based on known information or historical data prior to making the investment. It reflects the average return level of the investment under normal market conditions, excluding unforeseen events.

Discounts and allowances refer to price reductions granted by a company to buyers from the original selling price, aimed at promoting sales, accelerating cash collection, or addressing product defects when selling goods or providing services. They primarily include cash discounts offered to encourage timely customer payments, as well as trade discounts or sales allowances provided to maintain long-term business relationships or address product issues.

Discounted current price refers to the actual amount the buyer needs to pay after applying a given discount rate or discount amount to the original price of a product or service. It is a common pricing calculation method in commercial transactions.

Discount rate refers to the percentage reduction from the original price granted by the seller to the buyer as a concession. It is commonly used for trade discounts (to maintain long-term cooperation) and cash discounts (to encourage early payment), serving as an important indicator for measuring price concessions. In the financial field, 'Discount Rate' also refers to the interest rate used to calculate the present value of future cash flows or the rate at which commercial banks borrow from the central bank.

Discount amount refers to the price reduction granted by the seller to the buyer on the original price of goods or services in a transaction. It is the difference between the original price and the actual discounted payment price, representing a direct concession made by the seller to promote sales or maintain customer relationships.

A depreciation fund is a special-purpose fund that an enterprise accumulates by pre-withdrawing depreciation amounts from costs or expenses for the purpose of replacing or renewing fixed assets. It originates from fixed asset depreciation, is used for future fixed asset renewal and technical renovation, and serves as an important source of funding for maintaining the enterprise's simple reproduction.

The reporting period GDP deflator is a macroeconomic indicator that measures the change in the price level of all final goods and services in a country or region during a specific period (the reporting period) relative to a base period. It is calculated by dividing nominal GDP by real GDP and multiplying by 100, reflecting the degree of inflation or deflation in the overall economy.

term_en.name: Final Product Output in the Reporting Period

english: Final Product Output in the Reporting Period
Output of Final Goods in the Current Period

definition_en: Final product output in the reporting period refers to the total physical quantity of all products completed and available for final consumption or use by an industrial enterprise within a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a year). These products require no further processing and can be directly sold or used internally.

term_en.name: Nominal GDP for the Reporting Period

definition_en: Nominal GDP for the reporting period refers to the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country or region during a specific period (typically a quarter or a year), calculated at current market prices. It does not exclude the effects of price changes (inflation or deflation) and directly reflects the scale of total economic output measured at current prices.

Reporting period end refers to the cut-off date of the accounting period covered by a financial report (such as a balance sheet or income statement), which is the specific point in time reflecting the company's financial position and operating results.

Reporting period level refers to the indicator value of a specific period in time series analysis that serves as the research object or requires calculation of its changes. It is the basis for comparison with the base period level to calculate dynamic analysis indicators such as growth amount and development rate.

term_en.name: Current Period Prices of Goods and Services

definition_en: Current period prices of goods and services refer to the actual transaction prices of various commodities and services in the market during a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a year). They reflect the nominal price level during that period, unadjusted for inflation or time factors.

term_en.name: Quantity of Goods and Services in the Reporting Period

english: Report Period Quantity of Goods and Services

definition_en: The quantity of goods and services in the reporting period refers to the total physical volume or quantitative measure of all final goods and services produced, traded, or consumed within a specific reporting period (such as a quarter or a year) in a country or region. It is typically used to eliminate the effects of price changes and measure the scale of real economic activity.
Total return refers to the total amount of earnings or returns generated by all investments or assets of an enterprise over a specific period (such as a fiscal year).

Settlement cash refers to the cash that creditors agree to accept as consideration for full or partial debt repayment during corporate debt restructuring. This cash payment is used to offset or reduce the carrying value of the restructured debt and represents the cash outflow component to be considered when determining the fair value or market value of the restructured debt.

term_en.name: Fair Value of Non-cash Assets Transferred in Settlement

chinese: 清偿债务的非现金资产公允价值
非现金偿债资产公允价值
english: Fair Value of Non-Cash Assets Transferred in Debt Settlement
Fair Value of Assets Transferred to Settle Debt

definition_en: The fair value of non-cash assets transferred in settlement refers to the market fair value, as of the transaction date, of non-cash assets (such as inventory, fixed assets, intangible assets, equity investments, etc.) that a debtor uses to settle debts during a debt restructuring process. This value serves as a key basis for determining gains or losses from debt restructuring and is used for comparison with the carrying amount of the restructured debt.

The foreign tax credit limit refers to the maximum amount of foreign income tax paid that a company is allowed to deduct from its domestic tax payable when calculating its income tax liability. Its purpose is to avoid international double taxation while preventing companies from excessively reducing their domestic tax burden through foreign losses or taxes paid in low-tax jurisdictions.

The deduction rate refers to the percentage or ratio used to determine the portion that can be deducted from the tax base or the amount of tax payable when calculating the tax payable or deductible amount. It is widely applied in various tax-related scenarios such as Value-Added Tax (VAT) input tax credit, pre-tax expense deductions for Corporate Income Tax, and calculations for specific tax incentives.

The loan-to-value ratio is the ratio between the principal or total principal and interest of a mortgage loan and the appraised value of the collateral, used to measure loan risk and determine the value of collateral a borrower must provide to secure loan repayment.

Collateral value refers to the market value or appraised value of an asset (such as real estate, securities, equipment, etc.) pledged to secure a debt or obligation in financial or guarantee business at a specific point in time. It serves as a critical basis for assessing the adequacy of collateral and calculating related risk exposures (e.g., haircut rates).

The Laspeyres Price Index is an indicator that measures changes in the price level of a basket of goods and services over time. It uses a fixed base-period quantity as weights to calculate price changes in the reporting period relative to the base period. This method assumes that consumer purchase quantities remain unchanged after the base period, thus primarily reflecting the impact of pure price movements.

term_en.name: Number of Ordinary Shares to be Converted upon Exercise

chinese: 假设转换增加的普通股股数
各稀释性潜在普通股假设转换增加的股数
english: Number of Common Shares Assumed to be Issued upon Exercise

definition_en: Refers to the number of additional ordinary shares that could be issued assuming dilutive potential ordinary shares such as warrants and share options are exercised or converted at the beginning of the period (or issuance date) when calculating diluted earnings per share. It is a key parameter for adjusting the denominator (weighted average number of ordinary shares) in calculating the dilution effect.

Holding period refers to the duration for which an investor or enterprise holds a specific asset (such as a fund, bond, or equipment), typically used for calculating investment returns, asset depreciation, or evaluating investment strategies.

Holding return refers to the total return obtained by an investor during the holding period of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, wealth management products, etc.), typically including asset appreciation (price difference between purchase and sale) and income generated during the holding period (such as dividends, interest, etc.).

Holding period refers to the length of time or number of cycles an investor holds a financial asset (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.) from purchase to sale. It serves as a crucial basis for calculating investment returns, evaluating investment performance, and determining relevant taxes.

Holding period risk-free return refers to the rate of return an investor earns by investing in risk-free assets (such as government bonds) over a specific holding period. It represents the certain return an investor can obtain during that time frame without any default risk, and is commonly used as a benchmark or baseline for measuring the performance of other risky investments.

Interest during the holding period refers to the interest income that an investor accrues or actually earns over a specific timeframe while holding a financial asset (such as bonds or deposits), based on the agreed-upon interest rate or market interest rate.

Useful life (months) refers to the length of time over which an intangible asset is expected to generate economic benefits for the enterprise, typically measured in months. It is a key parameter for calculating the monthly amortization amount of an intangible asset, determining the speed and amount of cost allocation over accounting periods.

Duration refers to the number of years an event, condition, or investment has persisted or is expected to persist. In finance, it is commonly used to measure investment holding periods, debt maturities, or the calculation cycle for specific financial metrics (such as persistency rates).

Shareholding ratio refers to the proportion of a shareholder's (or investor's) capital contribution to the total registered capital of a company, used to measure the size of their equity stake in the company.

In the field of finance and accounting, loss refers to the reduction in economic value or increase in costs due to various reasons (such as poor management, asset impairment, accidents, investment failures, etc.). It reflects the negative financial outcome suffered by an enterprise or individual during a specific period or in specific activities.

Loss severity refers to the degree of economic loss or the monetary amount caused by a single risk event or accident within a specific period. It is used to measure the actual financial impact scale following an accident or risk event, serving as a crucial indicator in risk assessment and management.

Quantity of lost products refers to the number of products that cannot be sold or used as qualified goods due to quality defects, damage, or scrapping during the production process. It is commonly used to calculate production losses, labor hour losses, and quality costs.

Loss frequency refers to the number of times or probability of losses occurring within a specific time period for a given number of risk units. It is a key metric for measuring risk characteristics in risk management, commonly used to assess the likelihood of risk occurrence.

Profit or loss value refers to the final numerical figure of profit or loss generated by a company's operating activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It reflects the difference between revenue and costs/expenses and is a core indicator for measuring a company's financial performance.

Break-even sales volume refers to the quantity of product sales that a company must achieve to cover all fixed and variable costs, thereby reaching a state of neither profit nor loss (i.e., zero profit).

Wastage refers to the quantity of raw materials, products, or goods that is reduced due to unavoidable scrap, defects, evaporation, breakage, or other causes during production, storage, or transportation. It is typically calculated as the original total quantity minus the final usable or remaining quantity.

Measures and methods cost refers to the expenses incurred for non-entity project items before and during the construction process of a building project, which are necessary to complete the project construction. These costs typically arise from essential measures taken to ensure project quality, safety, environmental protection, and civilized construction.

Lead time days refer to the number of calendar days required in advance from placing an order or initiating production to receiving goods or completing product output. It is an important time-quantity standard used for planning and controlling production or procurement activities.

Appropriation of discretionary surplus reserve refers to the appropriation of a specific portion of after-tax net profit, for designated purposes, into retained earnings after the appropriation of the statutory surplus reserve, based on the company's articles of association or resolutions of the shareholders' meeting or board of directors. The appropriation ratio and usage are determined by the company itself, primarily for purposes such as covering losses, expanding production and operations, or converting into capital.

In the field of finance and accounting, the extraction ratio refers to the percentage or rate used to withdraw, accrue, or allocate funds from a specific base (such as profits, revenue, costs, etc.). It is commonly used to calculate the specific amounts for items such as public welfare funds, surplus reserves, employee commissions, or bonuses.

Statutory surplus reserve appropriation refers to the mandatory allocation of a specified proportion (typically 10%) from net profit after tax, as stipulated by the Company Law, to be set aside as accumulated funds for specific purposes during the distribution of annual after-tax profits. Its purpose is to enhance the company's risk resilience and supplement capital.

term_en.name: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Appropriation

chinese: 职工奖励及福利基金提取
english: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Provision

definition_en: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Appropriation refers to a special fund that an enterprise pre-appropriates from costs or profits according to a specified percentage (e.g., 14% or 11%) of the total employee payroll, based on national regulations or internal bylaws, to cover various employee rewards and welfare expenses such as bonuses, medical expenses, hardship allowances, and collective welfare facilities.

The amortization period refers to the number of years over which a company allocates the cost of intangible assets, deferred assets, and other long-term operating assets across the periods during which they are expected to generate economic benefits. It determines the amortization amount to be expensed annually or per period.

Amortization expense refers to the amount by which the cost of long-term assets such as intangible assets and long-term prepaid expenses is systematically allocated and recognized as an expense in a specific accounting period, based on their estimated useful lives or benefit periods. It reflects the consumption of asset value due to usage or the passage of time.

term_en.name: Cash Paid for Other Operating Activities

chinese: 支付的与经营活动有关的其他现金
其他经营活动现金流出
english: Other Cash Payments Related to Operating Activities

definition_en: Cash paid for other operating activities refers to cash outflows related to business operations, excluding major items such as purchasing goods, receiving services, paying employee compensation, and paying taxes. These expenditures typically do not constitute the core part of main business costs but are necessary expenses for maintaining normal business operations.

Payment probability refers to the likelihood or expected rate at which a debt or obligation (such as pension liabilities) will be actually paid in the future under specific conditions. It is commonly used to assess the expected present value of liabilities, particularly when considering time value and uncertainty.

term_en.name: Other Cash Payments Related to Financing Activities

chinese: 筹资活动其他现金支付
筹资相关其他现金支出
english: Other Payments Relating to Financing Activities
Cash Paid for Other Financing Activities

definition_en: Refers to cash payments related to financing activities, as reported in the cash flow statement, other than principal repayments of debt, dividend or profit distributions, and interest payments. These expenditures typically do not constitute the main part of financing activities but are nevertheless related to raising funds or changes in capital structure.

Expenditure Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the degree of change in an organization's (such as an administrative unit or enterprise) expenditure amount during a specific period relative to a base period (e.g., the same period in the previous year), used to reflect the growth status and trend of expenditures.

chinese: 最终使用法国内生产总值

definition_en: Expenditure Approach GDP measures the total final output of all resident units' production activities within a country or region during a specific period (usually one year) from the perspective of final goods and services being purchased and used. It is calculated by summing up total expenditures on final consumption, capital formation, and net exports.

Expenditure Item 1 is a classification unit in budgets or financial statements used to aggregate and account for specific types of expenditures, typically referring to a specific cost or expense outlay.

Expenditure Item 2 typically refers to a specific category of expenses incurred for particular activities, tasks, or objectives in budgeting or financial reporting, serving as a detailed component under total expenditures.

Expenditure Item n refers to an individual expense category or detailed item used to specifically subdivide and classify total expenditures in financial accounting or budget preparation, serving to record and manage the use of funds in detail.

Revenue Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the growth of a company's operating revenue over a specific period (typically two consecutive fiscal years), reflecting the expansion speed of the company's business scale.

term_en.name: Total Amount of Income Adjustment Items

chinese: 收入类纳税调整项目合计
收入调整项目汇总金额
english: Total Amount of Income Adjustment Items

definition_en: Total Amount of Income Adjustment Items refers to the aggregate amount of all income-related adjustment items after reconciling the differences between accounting income recognized under accounting standards and income deductible before tax as permitted by tax laws, during an enterprise's annual corporate income tax filing. It is typically reflected in the 'Detailed Schedule of Tax Adjustment Items' (A105000) and represents the total net increase or decrease in taxable income from income adjustments when calculating taxable income.

Recovered working capital refers to the working capital funds that were advanced into various current assets (such as cash, accounts receivable, inventory, etc.) during the initial or operational phases of an investment project and are recovered by the enterprise at the end of the project's calculation period. These funds are no longer required to maintain operations upon project termination and are therefore recovered as a cash inflow.

Recoverable amount typically refers to the recoverable amount of an asset, which is the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use (present value of estimated future cash flows). It is used to assess whether an asset is impaired.

term_en.name: Cash Received from Recovery of Long-term Debt Investment Principal

chinese: 收回长期债券投资本金
长期债权投资本金收回
english: Cash Received from Recovery of Long-term Debt Investment Principal
Principal Recovery of Long-term Debt Investments

definition_en: Cash received from recovery of long-term debt investment principal refers to the cash inflow actually received by an enterprise from the sale, transfer, or maturity recovery of its held long-term debt investments (such as long-term bonds), representing the portion of the original invested principal. This cash amount excludes interest received during the investment period.

Rate of return is an indicator measuring the ratio of returns obtained from an investment relative to its principal, typically expressed as an annual percentage, used to evaluate the profitability or efficiency of an investment.

Return covariance is a statistical measure of the degree of association between the return movements of two assets (e.g., a security and the market portfolio). A positive value indicates a tendency for the two to move in the same direction, a negative value indicates a tendency to move in opposite directions, and a zero value indicates no linear relationship in their movements. It is a key input parameter for calculating portfolio risk and asset beta.

Return variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or dispersion of returns for an asset or investment portfolio. It measures the uncertainty or risk of returns by calculating the weighted average of the squared deviations of various possible return outcomes from their expected value (mean return). A higher variance indicates greater fluctuation of returns around their mean, typically implying higher risk.

The return correlation coefficient is a statistical measure that quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between the returns of two assets (e.g., stocks, bonds). Its value ranges from -1 to 1, where 1 indicates perfect positive correlation (moving in the same direction), -1 indicates perfect negative correlation (moving in opposite directions), and 0 indicates no linear correlation.

chinese: 应收账款管理成本增加

definition_en: Increase in collection expenses refers to the rise in costs associated with receivables collection resulting from additional measures taken by an enterprise to accelerate the recovery of accounts receivable and reduce bad debt losses, such as hiring more collection personnel or engaging professional agencies.

Improvement priority refers to the key issues or core areas identified during the continuous improvement process that require prioritized resource allocation for resolution. It typically points to aspects with significant impact on quality, efficiency, cost, or safety that demand immediate or focused attention.

Government consumption expenditure refers to the expenditure on goods and services incurred by government departments to provide public services (such as national defense, education, public health, etc.) for the whole society and for their own daily operations. It is an important component of final consumption expenditure in Gross Domestic Product (GDP), reflecting the scale of government spending in non-investment areas.

The Policy Sensitivity Coefficient is a quantitative measure that gauges the sensitivity of key performance indicators (such as profit, revenue, valuation, etc.) of a specific industry or company to changes in particular policy factors (such as interest rates, tax rates, industry regulations, etc.). It indicates the percentage change in the performance indicator resulting from a one percent change in the policy factor.

Education Surcharge is an additional tax levied by the state to fund local education development. It is calculated based on the actual amount of turnover taxes such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by taxpayers, collected by tax authorities, and its revenue is specifically allocated for educational expenditures.

Education Surcharge Payable refers to the additional fee amount, calculated and paid based on the actual amount of Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by entities and individuals according to national regulations, at a specified levy rate, and specifically used for the development of local education.

The Education Surcharge Rate refers to the statutory percentage applied when calculating the education surcharge. It is typically calculated based on the actual amount of turnover taxes such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer, with the surcharge amount determined by applying this rate.

The Education Surcharge Rate is the applicable levy percentage imposed by the state on entities and individuals paying Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax to raise funds for local education expenditures.

Numerical integration is a method that approximates the value of a definite integral by calculating the weighted sum of function values at a finite number of discrete points. It provides an effective computational approach when the antiderivative of certain functions is difficult to express using elementary functions, or when the integration interval is complex.

Quantity discount is a price reduction strategy offered by a business to encourage customers to purchase its products in large volumes. When the quantity purchased by a customer reaches or exceeds a certain threshold set by the seller, the seller provides a specific price concession.

Full Truckload (FTL) freight rate refers to the unit transportation price applicable for the one-time shipment of a full batch of goods (typically reaching the loading capacity of a full truck or railcar) in road or rail transport. It is usually calculated per ton-kilometer (CNY/(t·km)) or per ton (CNY/t) and constitutes the core pricing component of the total freight cost for a full truckload shipment.

New price refers to the transaction price reset for goods, services, or assets after changes in market conditions, cost structures, competitive strategies, or policies. It is typically used to reflect the latest market conditions or corporate decisions and serves as the basis for calculating price change percentages.

New debt borrowings refer to the debt formed by funds newly raised or borrowed by an enterprise or entity within a specific period through channels such as banks, financial institutions, or the bond market. It is part of corporate financing activities, used to supplement working capital, undertake capital investments, or repay existing debt.

Newly borrowed interest-bearing debt refers to debt that is newly incurred during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) and requires interest payments. This includes newly obtained bank loans, newly issued bonds, newly generated finance lease liabilities, etc., but excludes interest-bearing debt that existed and carried over from prior periods. It is an important component when calculating metrics such as 'Net Repayment of Interest-bearing Debt'.

Additional Net Working Capital Investment refers to the amount of net working capital that a company needs to invest additionally during a specific period (such as the initial phase or during a project) to support the operation of a project or business. It typically manifests as the difference between the increase in current assets (such as inventory, accounts receivable) and the increase in current liabilities (such as accounts payable), and is a key component in calculating the initial cash outflow or periodic cash flows of a project.

Incremental fixed cost refers to the additional portion of cost that does not vary with output, incurred due to specific decisions or business expansion such as increasing production volume, introducing new product lines, or expanding operational scale. Examples include rent for newly leased facilities to expand production and fixed salaries for newly hired management personnel.

New fixed capital investment refers to the additional cash outflow incurred by an enterprise within a specific period (such as a project or a fiscal year) to acquire, construct, or upgrade long-term tangible assets (e.g., plants, equipment, land). It typically constitutes a significant component of the initial project investment or capital budgeting decisions, aimed at expanding production capacity, replacing obsolete equipment, or implementing technological upgrades.

New accounts receivable amount refers to the total amount of newly added accounts receivable during a specific accounting period, arising from business activities such as sales of goods or provision of services for which customers have not yet made payment. It reflects the growth of credit sales during that period.

Incremental asset cost refers to the total cash outflow required by a company in the initial stage for acquiring new assets or undertaking project investments. It typically includes capital expenditures such as the purchase cost and installation fees of the assets, and must account for changes in working capital, as well as the impact of proceeds from the sale of old assets and related tax liabilities (or tax credits).

The Average Collection Period is a financial metric that measures the average number of days required for a company to collect cash from the sale of goods or provision of services, reflecting the efficiency of accounts receivable management and the speed of cash recovery.

term_en.name: Unit Variable Cost of New Proposal

english: Unit Variable Cost of New Plan

definition_en: Unit variable cost of a new proposal refers to the cost per unit of production or sales that is expected to vary directly in proportion to the level of activity under a new business proposal being considered or implemented (such as launching a new product, adopting a new process, or entering a new market). It is a key parameter for evaluating the profitability of the new proposal and making related decisions (e.g., whether to increase fixed cost investments).

term_en.name: Total Variable Costs of New Plan

english: Total Variable Costs of New Plan
Aggregate Variable Costs for New Scheme

definition_en: Total Variable Costs of New Plan refers to the sum of all cost items that are expected to vary proportionally with business volume (such as production or sales volume) under a new operational, production, or investment scheme being considered or implemented by an enterprise. These costs typically include direct materials, direct labor, variable manufacturing overhead, variable selling expenses, etc.

term_en.name: Total Fixed Costs of New Plan

english: Total Fixed Cost of New Plan

definition_en: Total fixed costs of the new plan refer to the aggregate costs that are expected to remain unchanged within a specific period and a defined range of business activity volume when a company implements a new operational plan or investment project, regardless of fluctuations in business volume. It represents the additional or adjusted portion of fixed costs attributable to adopting the new plan, relative to the original plan or baseline scenario.

Total Cost of New Project refers to the sum of all costs expected or actually incurred by an enterprise during a specific period (usually one year) for implementing a new technical solution, investment project, or operational plan. It includes all fixed and variable costs directly related to the project, serving as a key financial indicator for evaluating the economic feasibility of new projects and making investment decisions.

english: Maximum Business Volume under New Scheme
Peak Activity Level of New Plan

definition_en: New Program Peak Activity Level refers to the highest level of business activity expected or actually achieved after implementing a new business program or plan. In financial management, particularly in cost behavior analysis (such as the high-low method) or program comparison, this metric is often used as a key data point to calculate or evaluate costs, revenues, or profitability under the new program.

term_en.name: New Scheme Highest Activity Level Cost

definition_en: New Scheme Highest Activity Level Cost refers to the total cost corresponding to the highest activity level under the new scheme when using the high-low method for cost behavior analysis. It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating the unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

New store daily sales typically refer to the daily sales revenue generated by a company's newly opened branches, stores, or business units during their initial operating period (especially on the opening day or within the first month). It is often used as a key performance indicator for evaluating the launch effectiveness and initial operational performance of new ventures.

New Shareholder Capital Contribution refers to the total amount of funds actually invested by a new investor into the company in exchange for equity ownership, typically through methods such as capital increase and share expansion. These funds are usually used to increase the company's registered capital or capital reserve in return for a corresponding shareholding percentage.

New sales revenue refers to the revenue newly generated from operating activities such as selling goods or providing services within a specific accounting period, which has not been recognized in prior periods. It is commonly used to analyze business growth and serves as an important basis for calculating items such as the increase in funds occupied by accounts receivable and the increase in earnings.

New sales volume typically refers to the quantity or value of sales that are newly added or exceed the base period level within a specific period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), used to measure the direct results of business growth and market expansion.

Variance Contribution Rate is an indicator in statistics and data analysis, primarily used in Principal Component Analysis or Factor Analysis. It measures the proportion of the total variance in the original data that can be explained by a specific principal component or common factor. A higher value indicates that the principal component or factor contains more original information and has stronger comprehensive capability.

term_en.name: Net Residual Value of Intangible Assets

english: Net Residual Value of Intangible Assets

definition_en: The net residual value of an intangible asset refers to the amount, net of estimated disposal costs, that an entity expects to obtain from the disposal of the asset at the end of its estimated useful life. According to accounting standards, the net residual value of an intangible asset with a finite useful life is generally assumed to be zero, unless there is a commitment by a third party to purchase the asset at the end of its life, or unless there is an active market from which the residual value can be determined based on market information.

chinese: 无形资产减值损失准备
english: Provision for Impairment of Intangible Assets

definition_en: Impairment provision for intangible assets is an asset contra-account pre-accrued by an enterprise to address situations where the recoverable amount of its intangible assets (such as patent rights, trademark rights, copyrights, etc.) falls below their carrying value due to changes in market conditions, technological obsolescence, or other reasons. It reflects potential losses in the value of intangible assets.

The original value of intangible assets refers to the initial cost or historical cost recognized and recorded on the books according to accounting standards when an enterprise acquires or forms an intangible asset. It serves as the basis for calculating subsequent amortization, impairment, and determining the net book value of intangible assets.

Intangible assets and deferred assets are categories of assets in a company's balance sheet that lack physical form or require long-term amortization. Intangible assets refer to identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance that are owned or controlled by the enterprise, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights, and land use rights. Deferred assets refer to various expenses that cannot be fully recognized in the current period's profit or loss and should be amortized over subsequent fiscal years, such as organization costs and improvement expenditures on leased fixed assets.

Intangible asset investment refers to the act of a company allocating funds or resources to non-monetary assets that lack physical form but can generate long-term economic benefits for the enterprise, such as patent rights, trademark rights, land use rights, software, goodwill, etc., in order to obtain future returns or enhance competitiveness.

term_en.name: Intangible Assets Acquisition and Construction Transfer-in Amount for the Period

english: Intangible Assets Acquired or Constructed in Current Period

definition_en: Intangible Assets Acquisition and Construction Transfer-in Amount for the Period refers to the total value of newly added and recognized intangible assets during the current accounting period through external purchases, self-developed (capitalized portion), or investor contributions. It reflects the net investment scale in intangible assets made by the enterprise within the period.

Intangible asset residual value refers to the estimated recoverable residual value of an intangible asset at the end of its expected useful life. In accounting practice, due to the lack of physical form and uncertainty of future economic benefits of intangible assets, their residual value is generally assumed to be zero.

Intangible assets book value refers to the value of intangible assets presented on the balance sheet, which equals the original cost of intangible assets minus accumulated amortization and impairment provisions, reflecting the actual carrying amount of intangible assets at a specific point in time.

Invalid hours refer to time periods that are excluded from the calculation of total working hours or time efficiency according to specific rules, such as rest periods, non-business hours, or invalid recorded intervals.

An infinite series refers to an expression formed by the sum of infinitely many numbers (or function terms) arranged in a specific order. It is a fundamental concept in mathematical analysis used to study the limiting behavior of sequence sums, with wide applications in fields such as finance, physics, and engineering, for example in calculating continuous compound interest or approximating complex functions.

chinese: 无负债企业权益资本成本
english: Cost of Equity for Unlevered Firm

definition_en: The cost of equity without debt refers to the minimum rate of return required by shareholders when a company has no debt and is financed entirely through equity. It reflects the pure business risk of the company's operations, unaffected by financial leverage (i.e., debt).

The risk-free discount rate refers to the interest rate used to discount future cash flows to their present value under the assumption of no default risk and no reinvestment risk. It is typically regarded as the minimum benchmark for investment returns and is used to evaluate and compare the attractiveness of other risky investments.

The risk-free rate of return refers to the expected return that can be obtained by investing in assets that theoretically carry no default risk. It is typically regarded as the benchmark for all investment returns and serves as a key parameter in financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model.

Daily interest refers to the interest amount calculated based on the principal and the daily interest rate over a one-day accrual period. It is commonly used in short-term lending, deposits, or the yield calculation of certain financial products, serving as a fundamental unit for measuring the daily cost or return of funds.

Daily working hours refer to the length of time an employee actually spends completing work tasks within a calendar day, as stipulated by legal regulations or employment contracts, typically measured in hours.

Daily demand variance is a statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of daily demand. It reflects the degree to which actual daily demand deviates from its average level; a higher variance value indicates more unstable and volatile daily demand.

Daily Demand Standard Deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or dispersion of daily demand. It reflects the extent to which actual daily demand deviates from the average daily demand. A larger standard deviation indicates greater instability and higher volatility in daily demand. In inventory management and supply chain planning, this metric is commonly used to calculate safety stock levels to address demand uncertainty.

Old price typically refers to the price of a commodity, service, or asset at an earlier point in time or before a transaction, serving as the comparative benchmark when calculating the percentage change in price. It is the starting value for measuring the magnitude of price change.

term_en.name: Net Working Capital in Old State

chinese: 旧设备相关净营运资金

definition_en: In capital budgeting or project investment decisions, this specifically refers to the net working capital that a company needs to invest in or occupy in order to maintain the existing (old) operating state before the project begins or before equipment replacement decisions. It is typically used to calculate the net occupancy of current assets and current liabilities when continuing to use old equipment or maintain the old business model, and is an important component in calculating relevant cash flows.

Old cash discounted price refers to the price that the buyer actually needed to pay or had paid for a good or service in past transactions, after applying the cash discount agreed upon at that time to the original price. It reflects the actual transaction price in historical dealings.

english: Current Market Value of Old Equipment

definition_en: Salvage value of old equipment refers to the estimated net cash inflow expected to be obtained from selling or disposing of existing old equipment in the secondary market during equipment replacement decisions. It represents the current market value of the old equipment and is a key parameter used to measure the opportunity cost of the old equipment or the offsetting item for initial cash outflows when calculating the net present value of new equipment investment or related cash flows.

english: Net Book Value of Old Equipment

definition_en: Book value of old equipment refers to the value of an old piece of equipment recorded in a company's accounting books at a specific point in time. It typically equals the equipment's original acquisition cost (historical cost) minus the accumulated depreciation up to that point. This value reflects the equipment's remaining accounting value, which may differ from its current market disposal value.

english: Net Book Value of Old Asset

definition_en: Book value of an old asset refers to its current recorded value in the accounting books, typically equal to the original acquisition cost of the asset minus the accumulated depreciation (or amortization) up to the current date and any accumulated impairment losses. It reflects the net value of the asset on the financial statements and serves as an important basis for calculating gains or losses on asset disposal, cash flows, etc.
Duration refers to the length of time elapsed from one point in time (start time) to another (end time), and is a fundamental concept for measuring time intervals.

The time adjustment factor is a multiplier used in asset valuation to adjust the transaction price or value of a comparable reference asset, reflecting differences arising from changes in market conditions, price levels, or the time value of money between its transaction date and the valuation base date.

The Time-Weighted Rate of Return is a method for measuring portfolio performance. It divides the entire investment period into several sub-periods, calculates the return for each sub-period separately, and then geometrically averages these sub-period returns to obtain a compound return that is unaffected by cash inflows and outflows during the period. This method more purely reflects the investment management skill of the fund manager or the investment strategy itself.

Time quota refers to the working time required for a worker group or individual of a specific trade or technical grade to complete one qualified product under given production technology and organizational conditions. It is typically measured in 'man-days' and serves as a crucial foundation for production planning and cost accounting.

term_en.name: Current Market Price per Share of Common Stock

definition_en: The current market price per share of common stock refers to the immediate trading price at which one share of common stock is bought or sold on the public securities exchange at a specific point in time. It reflects the market investors' immediate assessment of the company's value, future earnings prospects, and risks.

Common stock price per share refers to the immediate price paid or received for one share of a company's common stock at a specific point in time, as agreed upon by buyers and sellers in the securities trading market. It reflects the market's collective expectations regarding the company's future profitability and risk, and serves as the basis for calculating key financial metrics such as total market capitalization and price-to-earnings ratio.

Common stock dividend refers to the cash return distributed by a listed company to its common shareholders from its after-tax profits, after deducting preferred stock dividends. It is a primary form of return that shareholders receive from the company's earnings.

term_en.name: Annual Growth Rate of Common Stock Dividends

definition_en: The annual growth rate of common stock dividends refers to the expected or historical average growth rate of cash dividends paid by a company to its common shareholders over a one-year period. It is a key parameter for assessing a company's future profitability and the intrinsic value of its stock, commonly used in the dividend growth model to calculate the cost of equity capital.

Replacement Cost New refers to the total cost required to rebuild or purchase a brand new asset with the same functionality as the asset being appraised, using modern materials, current technology, design, and standards under prevailing market conditions. It reflects the impact of technological progress and price changes.

Substitute price refers to the price of other goods or services in the market that can satisfy similar consumer needs or functions. It is one of the important factors affecting the demand for a specific product.

The lowest price refers to the minimum transaction price reached by a stock, fund, or other financial asset within a specific time period (such as a trading day, week, month, or since listing). It reflects the lower price limit of the asset in the market and serves as an important indicator for measuring its price volatility and risk.

term_en.name: Present Value of Minimum Lease Receipts

english: Present Value of Minimum Lease Receipts

definition_en: The present value of minimum lease receipts refers to the value, as of the lease commencement date, of the minimum lease receipts that the lessor is certain to receive in future periods, discounted at the lease's implicit interest rate (or the contractually stipulated rate, incremental borrowing rate, etc.). It serves as the basis for the lessor's lease accounting, recognition of long-term receivables, and unearned finance income.

Initial investment refers to the total amount of capital required at the beginning of an investment project (typically at period 0 or project initiation), including all cash outflows such as asset purchases and related expenses. It serves as the foundation for evaluating future project cash flows and calculating metrics such as Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return.

Maximum velocity refers to the highest instantaneous or average speed that an object can achieve under specific conditions (such as over a specific distance or time period). In physics and kinematics, it typically denotes the peak speed of an object during its motion.

Future Value refers to the total amount accumulated at a specific future date when a sum of money is invested or deposited at the present time, growing at a given interest rate (e.g., compound interest). It embodies the time value of money, meaning money available today is worth more than the same amount in the future.

High price refers to the highest level reached by the transaction price of a security (such as a stock) during a specific trading period (e.g., one trading day). It reflects the market's highest valuation of the security or the strongest buyer willingness during that period.

Beginning inventory quantity refers to the actual quantity of all inventory held by an enterprise on the first day of each accounting month (i.e., the beginning of the month) that is available for sale or production. It reflects the inventory balance carried forward from the end of the previous month and serves as the baseline data for calculating inventory changes and costs during the current month.

chinese: 月初结存存货实际成本

definition_en: Actual cost of beginning inventory refers to the total value of all inventory held by an enterprise on the first day of each accounting month (i.e., month beginning), calculated based on its actual incurred procurement or production costs (rather than selling price). It serves as the foundational data for calculating the cost of goods issued during the month and the ending inventory cost.

Monthly income refers to the total sum of all cash or cash equivalents received by an individual or household from various sources within a calendar month. It typically includes wages, bonuses, allowances, benefits, investment returns, rental income, etc., and is a core indicator for measuring the short-term financial inflow status of an individual or household.

Monthly depreciation expense refers to the amount of depreciation cost allocated evenly to each month over the estimated useful life of a fixed asset, based on its cost (net of estimated residual value) in accordance with accounting standards. It is a significant item in calculating a company's monthly costs and profits.

Monthly return refers to the ratio of the profit earned by an investment asset or portfolio within one month to the initial investment principal, commonly used to measure the short-term profitability of an asset.

End-of-month work-in-process quantity refers to the physical count of all products on the production line that have not completed the entire production process and cannot be sold as finished goods (i.e., work-in-process) at the end of an accounting period (typically a month).

Marketable securities interest rate refers to the rate set at the issuance of marketable securities (such as bonds, notes, etc.) for calculating their periodic interest payments, typically expressed as an annualized percentage. It is a key metric for measuring the fixed income level obtainable from holding such securities and is commonly used in financial analysis to assess the opportunity cost of holding cash.

Marketable securities yield refers to the interest return rate that investors can obtain by holding securities such as bonds and notes, usually expressed as a percentage, and is a key indicator for measuring investment returns and opportunity costs of securities.

term_en.name: Annual Interest Rate on Marketable Securities

english: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities

definition_en: The annual interest rate on marketable securities refers to the percentage of interest income, expected or actually earned within one year, relative to the security's principal (face value or purchase cost) when an investor holds securities such as bonds or notes. It is a key metric for measuring the fixed-income level of a security.

Total interest-bearing liabilities refer to the sum of all debts on which a company must pay interest, typically including short-term borrowings, long-term liabilities due within one year, long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables. These liabilities constitute a significant component of a company's financing costs.

Beginning debt book value refers to the recorded value on the books, in accordance with accounting standards, of the debt obligations (such as short-term borrowings, long-term borrowings, bonds payable, etc.) undertaken by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or a quarter). It typically includes the face value of the debt, any premium or discount arising from issuance, and related issuance costs, and serves as the basis for calculating current period interest expense and debt amortization.

Beginning net assets refer to the net amount of a company's total assets minus total liabilities at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), which is the total owner's equity at the beginning of that accounting period.

Total beginning net assets refers to the total economic interests of owners (or shareholders) in the enterprise's assets at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). Its amount equals total beginning assets minus total beginning liabilities, reflecting the enterprise's financial net worth at the beginning of the period.

The opening spot exchange rate refers to the exchange rate at which two currencies are traded and settled immediately in the spot market at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically used for the initial recognition and translation of foreign currency transactions or foreign currency account balances.

term_en.name: Beginning Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision

english: Opening Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision
Beginning Impairment Allowance for Fixed Assets

definition_en: Beginning Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision refers to the cumulative balance of impairment provisions already accrued for fixed assets at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the portion of the carrying amount of fixed assets that may not be fully recoverable through use or disposal at the beginning of the period, and is an item to be deducted when calculating the beginning carrying value of fixed assets.

term_en.name: Original Cost of Fixed Assets at Beginning of Period

english: Original Cost of Fixed Assets at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Original cost of fixed assets at the beginning of a period refers to the total historical cost incurred during the acquisition, construction, installation, and other processes of all fixed assets at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the scale of the enterprise's original investment in fixed assets at the beginning of the period.

term_en.name: Beginning Net Book Value of Fixed Assets

english: Beginning Net Book Value of Fixed Assets
Initial Net Carrying Amount of Fixed Assets

definition_en: Beginning net book value of fixed assets refers to the remaining book value of an enterprise's fixed assets after deducting accumulated depreciation at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the depreciated value of fixed assets at the beginning of the period and serves as one of the bases for calculating current period depreciation.

term_en.name: Beginning Value of Work-in-Process and Semi-Finished Goods

definition_en: Beginning value of work-in-process and semi-finished goods refers to the book value or cost of unfinished products on the production line and partially processed goods that have not yet become final products at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). This value represents the outcome of production activities from the previous period and has already been included in the previous period's total output value. Upon completion during the current period, its value will be incorporated into the finished goods value of the current period. Therefore, when calculating the total output value for the current period, this beginning value must be deducted from the current period's total output to avoid double counting.

term_en.name: Beginning Work in Process Inventory Cost

definition_en: Beginning work in process inventory cost refers to the book value of the accumulated production costs for products that are not yet completed and remain in the production process (i.e., work in process) at the start of an accounting period (typically a month or a quarter). It represents the balance of work in process costs carried forward from the end of the previous accounting period.

term_en.name: Beginning Work in Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost

english: Beginning Work in Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
Opening WIP and Semi-finished Goods Cost
Initial Cost of Work in Process and Semi-finished Products

definition_en: Beginning work in process and semi-finished goods cost refers to the accumulated production costs of all unfinished goods still in the production process at the start of an accounting period (such as a month or quarter). These costs represent the results of production activities from the previous period, already included in the previous period's output value, but will continue to be processed and ultimately converted into finished goods in the current period. Therefore, when calculating the cost of finished goods for the current period, they must be included as beginning inventory value in the current period's cost calculation process.

Beginning inventory quantity refers to the physical count of unsold goods, finished products, or raw materials in a company's warehouse at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It represents the inventory quantity carried forward from the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the starting point for calculating inventory changes, costs, and production budgets for the current period.

Beginning inventory markup refers to the difference between the total value of inventory goods calculated at selling price and the total value calculated at purchase price (or cost) at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a month or a quarter). It represents the unrealized gross profit portion of the beginning inventory.

Beginning balance of notes receivable refers to the total book value of commercial drafts (including bank acceptance drafts and trade acceptance drafts) that have not yet matured or been collected at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the entity's right to collect payment on drafts from customers or other parties held at the beginning of the period.

Beginning owner's equity refers to the total amount of owner's equity at the start of a specific accounting period (typically a fiscal year or an accounting period). It reflects the residual interest in the assets of the enterprise after deducting liabilities, attributable to the owners at the beginning of the period, and serves as the basis for calculating changes in owner's equity during the current period.

term_en.name: Amortized Cost at Beginning of Period

english: Amortized Cost at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Amortized cost at the beginning of a period refers to the carrying amount of a financial asset or financial liability at the start of an accounting period. It is typically the ending amortized cost from the previous accounting period, reflecting the amount after adjustments for effective interest, principal and interest collected, impairment provisions, and other relevant factors.

Beginning Total Interest-Free Liabilities refers to the aggregate book value of all liabilities that do not require interest payments at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). These liabilities typically include operating liabilities such as accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable.

Beginning retained earnings balance refers to the closing amount in the retained earnings account at the start of a specific accounting period (typically a fiscal year or a quarter). It represents the cumulative net profits from past business activities that have not been distributed to shareholders and serves as the basis for calculating changes in retained earnings during the current period.

Beginning balance of surplus reserve refers to the carryover amount in the surplus reserve account at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the cumulative reserve funds appropriated from after-tax profits retained by the enterprise at the end of the previous accounting period, serving as the basis for calculating changes in the current period's surplus reserve and the ending balance.

english: Accumulated Depreciation at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Beginning accumulated depreciation refers to the total amount of depreciation expenses that have been accrued for all fixed assets of an enterprise since their acquisition or commissioning, calculated according to established depreciation methods, at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the cumulative value impairment of fixed assets at the beginning of the period and is a crucial component in calculating the carrying value of fixed assets.

chinese: 经营流动资产期初余额

definition_en: Beginning operating current assets refer to the value of current assets used for daily business operations at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). They typically include cash, accounts receivable, inventory, etc., but exclude non-operating short-term investments or financial assets.

Beginning operating liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities arising from daily business operations at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), which are due to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle. They typically include short-term liabilities directly related to core business activities, such as accounts payable, unearned revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable, and serve as important baseline data for calculating beginning net operating assets.

Beginning Operating Assets refer to the total assets used for core business operations (such as production, sales of goods, or provision of services) at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or quarter). It typically excludes non-operating assets such as financial investments and serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics like beginning net operating assets.

chinese: 经营长期资产期初净值
长期经营资产期初账面价值
经营性长期资产期初净额
english: Net Book Value of Operating Long-term Assets at Beginning of Period

definition_en: Net beginning operating long-term assets refers to the net book value of long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, land use rights, etc.) used for ongoing business activities at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or quarter), after deducting accumulated depreciation or amortization. It reflects the scale of capital invested in long-term business activities at the beginning of the period.

Beginning capital employed refers to the total amount of capital invested and occupied by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), typically including working capital used for operations and non-current capital occupied by long-term assets.
